title: Death Notice: Darlene A. Jamison
Cornell suspends fraternity parties, gives state police role in investigating campus assault reports
text:
Cornell suspends fraternity parties, gives state police role in investigating campus assault reports
Cornell University is suspending parties and other social events at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year and will give the New York State Police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus, university officials announced Tuesday, amid mounting outrage over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.
Video above: NY AG's office takes over Cornell rape investigation
The measures announced by Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff include a suspension of all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses through the end of the 2026-27 academic year and a new “zero tolerance” policy for violations that would result in the immediate emergency suspension of a chapter.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.
Cornell has more than 20 active fraternities affiliated with its Interfraternity Council. The council did not immediately respond to an email request for comment.
The university president said the school would begin conversations with students and faculty experts about “the development of safe social alternatives” to Greek life party culture and invest money to get those initiatives off the ground.
He also committed to adding a case manager to the school’s Office of Civil Rights to help those who report sexual misconduct on the Cornell campus navigate the process, and to working with the New York State Police to allow its criminal investigators — who are independent of Cornell — to investigate allegations.
Crimes reported on Cornell’s campus are generally investigated by campus police, a department that has full law enforcement powers but is controlled by the university. The campus police force operates independently from municipal police in Ithaca, New York, where the university is located. Its officers investigated the 2024 gang rape allegations and presented their initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to prosecute within weeks of the woman making her first report to police.
In a lawsuit filed in September, the woman alleged that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024. She said she was pressured to use drugs and that other men entered the room while she was incapacitated. She also alleges that messages describing her as sexually available to anyone at the house circulated among fraternity members on Snapchat without her knowledge.
Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students following an internal investigation, but no criminal charges have been filed.
New York’s governor removed the district attorney from the case this month after a public outcry over the lack of charges.
The investigation is now being led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, while Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent review of the university’s response. New York State Police sometimes handle major crime investigations for small municipal police agencies, bringing in expertise that isn’t available locally.
Kotlikoff’s announcement came a day before Cornell’s faculty senate was to take up a proposed resolution expressing no confidence in the administration’s ability to effectively address sexual assault on campus.
Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk.
Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programs, including education aimed at encouraging bystanders to intervene, he said, calling the various actions announced Tuesday “first steps toward systemic change on our campus.”
“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said.

title: Susan Collins still working with operatives tied to straw donation scheme
text:
When the investigative news outlet ProPublica reported on Sen. Susan Collins’ ties to a disgraced convicted fraudster, the outlet wrote about how Scott Reed, a key figure in Collins’ political orbit, may have been aware of a scheme to direct an illegal straw donation to the Republican senator from Maine.
But Reed, who heads the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results Super PAC, wasn’t the only Collins ally who may have known of the plan.
MacKenzie Dolan, who co-founded The Morning Group, worked in 2020 with the 1820 PAC, the main pro-Collins Super PAC.
A federal investigator said both Dolan and Reed received an email sent Dec. 13, 2019, from the fraudster, Navatek CEO Martin Kao, updating them on his plans to create a shell company to make a donation to the PAC.
The investigator said in court documents that Kao sent the email from an address associated with a “navatekllc.com.”
“I just received confirmation from our bank that the new account for the Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers will be up and ready to go by early next week,” Kao wrote. “I’ll be in touch next week re getting 1820 a check by year end.”
The group sent a $150,000 check to the PAC about two weeks later, ProPublica reported.
This cycle, Collins for Senator has paid Dolan’s firm, The Morning Group, at least $300,000 for fundraising services in 2025-26. And the firm has received at least $1.1 million from Pine Tree Results PAC. The Morning Group was also hired by Reed and the 1820 PAC during the 2020 cycle.
Neither Reed, Dolan nor Collins has been accused of or charged with wrongdoing by authorities during their investigation into Kao, who is currently in prison for money laundering and bank fraud. Kao pleaded guilty to charges relating to the illegal contribution in 2022.
But Collins’ ongoing relationship with Reed and Dolan may give critics more fodder in their attempts to cast Collins as corrupt in the closing weeks of Maine’s closely watched and tight U.S. Senate race against Democrat Troy Jackson.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a written statement that Reed and Dolan were “thoroughly investigated” and “cleared by the FBI in 2021.”
“Martin Kao was the guilty party and he was sentenced to seven years in federal prison,” Kernen said. “Martin Kao tried to get his sentence reduced by blaming Senator Collins, her staff, Scott Reed and MacKenzie Dolan for his criminal conduct. The FBI, the Biden Department of Justice, and the Federal Election Commission didn’t believe him and the judge did not offer him any leniency.”
A spokesperson for The Morning Group declined to speak with a reporter on Monday.
Democrats are working to keep the ProPublica story in the headlines. The Senate Majority PAC, which is tied to Democratic Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., issued a Sept. 29 memo outlining its plan to tie political corruption to increased living costs in an effort to sway a small number of undecided voters. And they’ve put millions behind an ad campaign here highlighting the ProPublica story.
Local Democrats held a press conference outside of Collins’ office in response to the report. And a Democratic attorney has filed a formal ethics complaint against Collins.
Collins has also leveled corruption allegations against her opponent, former Senate President Troy Jackson, accusing him of using his influence to help his son, who was an Augusta lobbyist while Jackson was in power. Jackson has denied that his son had any influence over his legislative agenda.
But much of the focus has been on Collins’ orbit, with the candidate getting questions about Kao at each of last week’s two Senate debates.
Numerous outlets have reported that Reed, who was the leader of the 1820 PAC that secured Kao’s illegal donation, is leading Pine Tree Results.
Reed is also a close friend of Collin’s husband, Tom Daffron, who was paid for consulting work last year by Reed’s firm, Chesapeake Enterprises.
FEC records show that the Collins Victory Committee has joint fundraising agreements with Pine Tree Results and with other Collins committees — her principal campaign committee (Collins for Senator) and her leadership committee (Dirigo PAC.)
But the ties between the 2020 donation and Dolan have received less scrutiny.
A federal search warrant from April 7, 2021, said that Reed and Dolan were “associated with the 1820 PAC,” and that they received the email from Kao about the bogus Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers group.
As a federal contractor, Kao was prohibited from making political contributions.
ProPublica’s investigation cited emails showing that Kao had told Reed he was working with his attorney to create the Young Women Scientists group to obscure the donation.
“Very smart,” Reed replied, according an email reviewed by ProPublica.
Collins campaign manager Steve Abbott dismissed that exchange when speaking to reporters last month, though he said he did not have any firsthand knowledge of the conversation between Kao and Reed.
“I might also say the same thing if I were trying to do something and had consulted with my attorney,” Abbott said. “I would also say that that is very smart, but I have no idea what any of their conversations were or what was said.”
ProPublica reported that a staffer for the 1820 PAC requested contact information for Kao on Collins’ behalf so she could thank him. Abbott said Collins’ office has no record that Collins made such a call.
Collins’ campaign has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and accused ProPublica of trusting a convicted felon‘s word. The investigation was based in part on what Kao told federal investigators in an effort to earn a lighter sentence.
But the outlet has pushed back, saying that federal investigators corroborated some of Kao’s claims and wanted to launch a wider probe — a move that was thwarted when Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

title: 10 Terrifying Ghost Stories That Are Uniquely Maine
text:
10 Terrifying Ghost Stories That Are Uniquely Maine
Since we are right in the middle of Spooky Season, it only makes sense that we should highlight some of the most common Maine ghost stories.
Considering the state has been inhabited by European settlers for about 400 years, and by Native Americans for thousands of years longer than that, it should not be a surprise that there are a few ghostly hotspots throughout the Pine Tree State.
We've put together a list of some of the wildest, most Maine, ghost stories. These stories take place in a variety of locations including a lighthouse (shocker!), a hotel, a college dorm, and even in an old movie theater.
Check Out These 10 Stories Of Haunted Maine
What other stories need to be added to our list? Let us know by sending a message using our app.
As you saw from the list, Maine has several spooky legends involving tragic deaths, unexplained disappearances, and spirits that supposedly still haunt the places where these events occurred. One tale involves a lighthouse on a 35-acre island about a mile offshore, where a young man reportedly shot and killed his landlord during a confrontation involving a rifle. Overcome with grief and remorse, the young man took his own life later that night, and legend says his spirit still haunts the lighthouse. In Randolph, near Gardiner, the Old Narrow Gauge trail is rumored to be haunted by a man who disappeared while riding his bicycle. Neither his body nor his bike was ever found, and visitors reportedly experience strange orbs, see spirits, and hear frightening screams telling them to leave. Another famous legend comes from Bucksport, where town founder Colonel Jonathan Buck allegedly had a woman burned as a witch after refusing to provide financial support for their son. Before her death, the woman's son reportedly retrieved one of her legs and buried it as a memorial. After Buck died, a stain resembling a leg supposedly appeared on his tombstone and remained even after the stone was replaced. Each story blends Maine history with tragedy, mystery, and supernatural folklore, keeping these eerie legends alive for locals and paranormal enthusiasts.

title: Mt. Ararat moves up in Varsity Maine field hockey poll after big win
text:
The top four teams in the Varsity Maine field hockey poll have been the same and in the same order since the first poll of the season. That changes this week. Mt. Ararat, fourth last week, earned a huge 4-1 victory over Skowhegan on Monday. Now the Eagles are No. 2, while the River Hawks are No. 4.
Further changes to the top four could come next week because No. 1 Cheverus plays at No. 3 Biddeford on Wednesday (the game was postponed due to Tuesday’s rain). The Stags also have a game against No. 10 Sanford/Kennebunk (currently the third-ranked team in Class A South) on their remaining schedule. The Tigers face Falmouth, whose four losses have come to the top four teams in A South and teams either ranked or receiving votes in the Varsity Maine poll.
No. 7 Camden Hills has the opportunity to make an argument for inclusion in the top five with games against both Mt. Ararat and Skowhegan. Meanwhile, fifth-ranked Yarmouth has to face Greely, which is tied for eighth, and Freeport.
Nokomis, tied for eighth, rejoins the poll. The Warriors were ranked ninth in the second week.
The Varsity Maine field hockey poll is based on games played before Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. The top 10 teams are voted on by the Varsity Maine staff, with first-place votes in parentheses, followed by total points.

title: WAGM, WABI to air two election debates this week
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - WAGM, in partnership with WABI, will air two debates this week featuring candidates for U.S. Senate and Maine’s Second Congressional District.
The first debate is tonight at the WABI studio in Bangor. U.S. Senate candidates Republican Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, both Aroostook County natives, will meet in their third debate of the election season.

title: UMaine Extension offers virtual backyard bird learning series for kids
text:
University of Maine Cooperative Extension will offer “Introduction to Project Feeder Watch,” a 10-session online series for Maine youth ages 10-14, from 3:30 to 4:30 p.m. on select Mondays from Nov. 2, 2026, through April 12, 2027. Sessions will be held via Zoom.
Participants will learn to identify common backyard birds while exploring bird beaks, diets and habitats, and developing observation and documentation skills through regular feeder observations. No previous bird identification experience is required. The series will be led by Carolyn Reece, leader of the Pollinator Protectors 4-H club, and Erin McDonald, a 4-H Youth Development Professional in York County. The sessions are modeled after the national Project Feeder Watch program. Families have the option to participate in that program for an additional fee, however it’s not required.
Participation is free; registration is required by 11 p.m. on Oct. 19. Enrollment is limited to 10 participants, with a wait list available after capacity is reached. For event information and registration, visit the program webpage.
If reasonable accommodation is needed, please contact Sarah Sparks at 207.581.8206 or sarah.sparks@maine.edu by October 19, 2026.
Support for 4-H Virtual Learning programs is provided by the Maine 4-H Foundation.

title: Matthew A. Cough | Obituaries
text:
Matthew A. Cough, 68, died October 10, 2026 at Maine Coast Hospital in Ellsworth, Maine. He was born October 8, 1958 in Bar Harbor, the son of L. Vincent and Marjorie L. (Walls) Cough. He was the 11th of 13 children.
Matt attended Mount Desert Island High School and Eastern Maine Technical College before serving several years in the U.S. Air Force. He later worked as a marine electrician, spending a number of years at Hinckley Yachts.

title: Overwhelmed Cat Rescue Asks Community for Help
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - A local cat rescue is overwhelmed and it needs your help. Fixing Their Futures has been pulling sick, flea-infested kittens from colonies across Aroostook County for weeks. Now, the group is asking the community to step up.
Norma Milton, founder of Fixing Their Futures, says they’ve rescued cats from colonies in Caribou, Fort Fairfield, and Van Buren. Some with ear mite infections so severe, they’ll need an emergency vet. “We’re working very hard right now on rescues. We’re working on 3 different large colonies with 15 to 20 nursing babies in there. They’re coming in loaded with fleas and ticks. We’re still cleaning them up and it’s quite a handful. It’s a two-person deal. You look at the babies and say, “Look how big and fat he is.” He’s fat because he’s full of worms. So, those worms and those fleas and those ticks are making those babies anemic. I’ve seen some really bad cases.”
“I found one cat that somebody had said it was abandoned. So, we rescued him/her. Not sure what it is yet, but it was in pretty bad shape. So, we’re trying to help these cats, and rescue what we can, and get them healthy, and find homes for them,” said volunteer Kim Jalbert.
Milton says the rescue is in urgent need of donations and fosters to keep up with the influx. She says they need vaccines known as distemper shots, Nemex (Knee-Mex) for deworming, Capstar for flea treatment, and Revolution Plus for parasite prevention. Donations can be dropped off at 10 Pioneer Avenue in Caribou. For more information or to foster a cat email Kim Jalbert at Kkim2003@hotmail.com.

title: Spruce Mountain CDL program draws more than 75 applicants
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — Demand for Spruce Mountain Adult Education’s new commercial driver’s license training program continues to grow, with more than 75 prospective students on its waiting list or recently applying as the first class prepares for road tests in November.
Robyn Raymond, director of Spruce Mountain Adult & Community Education, told the Regional School Unit 73 board of directors Oct. 8 that 28 new applications arrived in the week following the program’s Sept. 29 ribbon-cutting ceremony, adding to a waiting list of more than 50 people.
The program, developed through partnerships with workforce development organizations and local funders, is intended to expand job training opportunities in a region affected by mill closures.
“Our first cohort, they’ve completed their permit testing,” Raymond said. “All students have their permit and they also all passed their final written exam.”
The inaugural class of 12 students is concentrating on behind-the-wheel training and road experience, with road tests expected during the first week of November.
Raymond said interest in the program remains strong, but class sizes are limited by the amount of individual driving instruction required.
“We did 12 this time and we’re thinking 14 would be the absolute max,” she said.
Interviews for the next class are expected to begin during the final week of October, with training anticipated to start in December. Raymond said scheduling adjustments are being considered as daylight hours shorten.
The Sept. 29 ribbon cutting drew more than 60 attendees, including students, prospective students, local employers, board members and workforce development partners.
Raymond credited collaboration among several organizations, including the Maine Department of Labor, Maine Development Foundation and Skowhegan Savings Bank, with helping establish the program.
She also said she had been asked to submit a proposal for the Maine Talent Summit in Augusta in November, explaining how multiple funding sources were combined to launch the training.
With demand far exceeding the number of available seats, Spruce Mountain Adult Education is continuing to coordinate future training schedules as it prepares to welcome its next group of students in December.

title: Aging Untold: Feeling “off” could be a vitamin deficiency
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we look at how nutrient absorption changes as we age, what warning signs to watch for and the key vitamins to keep on your radar.
We also explore the mental health benefits of spending time solo and how embracing “me time” can boost your confidence and mood.
Then, we examine a concerning rise in cancer among younger adults and what early detection means for families.
When someone does not feel quite like themselves, a handful of nutrient deficiencies could be behind it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Two common deficiencies are vitamin B12 and vitamin D, she said.
Rogers said a check of your blood levels is a good first step, but it has limits.
Spending some time alone can be empowering.
For some, it’s a choice. Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said she needs and wants more solo time as she gets older.
For others, being alone is an adjustment after the loss of a loved one.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommends turning to a friend for support and taking small steps by combining something you enjoy with doing it alone, like a walk.
Brittany Auclair’s baby boy was just 8 months old when she first noticed an issue while breastfeeding.
“He decided that he favored one side over the other,” she said. Then, while pumping milk, she noticed a lump.
Auclair was 29 when she was diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer.
Cancer is increasing in people under 65, and women are now more likely than men to develop it, according to the American Cancer Society.

title: Proposed Norridgewock 1,000-yard shooting range draws questions
text:
NORRIDGEWOCK — A proposed firearms store with shooting ranges of up to 1,000 yards would give the region a facility that does not exist anywhere near central Maine, its owner says.
But some neighbors of the proposed site at 255 Skowhegan Road say they are concerned the ranges would create unbearable noise, harm wildlife like bald eagles and potentially contaminate the water in their area, along the Kennebec River.
“I just really want to make sure that things are done properly,” Rebecca Corcoran, who lives across the street, said at a planning board meeting Thursday. “And I’m very worried about the environment, animals and all of us who are living literally downstream from it.”
The Norridgewock Planning Board began its review of the application from Nicholas Carrier at a well-attended meeting Thursday.
Its five elected members signed off on some site plan review criteria but tabled votes on other items. The board, which heard some comments from the public, also scheduled a formal public hearing at its next regular meeting, Nov. 12 at Mill Stream Elementary School, 26 Mercer Road.
Among the additional information the board requested from Carrier was a more detailed stormwater management plan, to address potential contaminants, like lead.
The board also wants noise study conducted by a qualified professional. The board requested the same of a burnout pit off Ward Hill Road — already constructed and shut down by the town in August for lack of a permit — earlier in Thursday’s meeting.
While both controversial project applications remain pending, town officials have separately proposed a 180-day moratorium on certain noise-intensive nonresidential developments. The pause is aimed at giving town officials time to develop proposed noise regulations before the annual town meeting in March.
Residents are set to vote on the moratorium at a special town meeting Oct. 21.
Carrier, who owns NE Firearms, told the board the Skowhegan Road site would be an expansion of his business, currently run out of his home at 116 Goodwin Lane.
Plans submitted to the town call for a firearms store with a 25-yard test range in its rear. They also include 100-yard, 200-yard, 450-yard and 1,000-yard ranges to the south of the structure. The project is estimated to cost $190,000, records show.
The next closest range of such a long distance open to the public is in New Hampshire, Carrier said. Law enforcement agencies, for example, may be interested in using such a facility in Norridgewock, he said.
Without a range, most people looking to fire guns at such long distances resort to power lines and clear cuts, which poses a safety risk, according to Carrier.
“We don’t have something like this around here,” Carrier said.
Proposed safety measures include designated shooting lanes backstops to catch errantly fired bullets. As for noise, Carrier said plans include some natural sound buffers. And, he said, nearly all of his customers use suppressors on their firearms that soften the noise.
“Yes, there’s going to be some firearms that don’t have suppressors on them, but with the sound buffers and the banks and the designated shooting areas, I don’t see it to be an issue,” Carrier said. “But I’m open to discussion on what we can do to make sure the neighbors are satisfied and stay satisfied.”
His ideas, discussed at Thursday’s meeting, included limiting hours to 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and putting in caliber restrictions.
Lauren Brousseau, who lives on Skowhegan Road and has three young children, was one of eight residents in the area who urged the planning board to consider the negative impacts of the proposal.
Brousseau said she was most concerned about the impacts of constant gunshot noise. She said she found research that shows such exposure can lead to cognitive disabilities in children and adults and affect human’s cardiovascular systems.
“I’ve done tons of research of this,” she said. “… It’s more than just the decibels, it’s the frequency of the sound of the gunshots.”
Lynn Farrin, also of Skowhegan Road, said she was concerned about the effects on her grandchildren who live in the area and on the local bald eagle population. She, like others, was also concerned about runoff from the site.
Farrin told the board members they should not take applicants at their word when it comes to mitigating the impacts of a new development.
“Where are the experts?” she asked.
Robert Crosby, of Burrill Hill Road, on the back side of the proposed ranges, was more optimistic, as were a handful of others who spoke Thursday. He said the Skowhegan Sportsman’s Club has a firing range along the Kennebec River, and its environmental impacts have been mitigated.
“Any good shooting range can be done correctly,” Crosby said.

title: Maine’s September housing market broke the usual mold
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Each month, when Maine Listings and the Maine Association of Realtors release their reports on the state of the housing market, there are a few facts that can almost always be relied on: Cumberland County will be the most expensive county in Maine, and York County will be the second. A critical shortage of inventory will continue to squeeze buyers. Competition will be fierce, and houses will be snapped up quickly.
Last month, none of that was true.
Here are three takeaways from Maine’s September market.
1. High prices in unexpected places
Statewide, the median sale price was $415,000 last month, a 2.6% increase from September 2025, but a roughly 2% decrease from August’s median of $424,050, according to data from Maine Listings.
The modest year-over-year change belies massive price increases in several coastal counties.
In Lincoln and Knox counties, the median sale price skyrocketed more than $100,000 in just a year. In Hancock County, it might as well have, jumping $99,000.
Sagadahoc County also increased substantially, jumping from $490,000 to $577,500.
Those increases also shook up the longstanding rankings of Maine’s priciest counties.
Lincoln County was the most expensive in the state, with a median sale price of $606,500. It was followed by Cumberland County, with a median of $599,900.
Sagadahoc, Hancock and York counties rounded out the top five.
Six of the 16 counties had a median price of over half a million dollars.
Maine’s housing market is small, and in counties with fewer homes changing hands, it only takes a few high-ticket sales to skew the numbers.
For example, in Cumberland County, where year-over-year prices increased a little over 3%, there were 307 sales. In Knox County, where prices shot up 31%, there were 50.
In Islesboro, the lone September home sale clocked in at $3 million, making it the state’s most expensive municipality.
2. Late summer slowdown
Sales fell for the third consecutive month, despite buyers having more options than they’ve had since late 2019.
Real estate agents bought and sold 1,532 homes last month, a 1.4% decrease from the month before, according to Maine Listings.
Meanwhile, there were 6,505 homes on the market in September, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
Sales were also down year-over-year, with 4.5% fewer homes changing hands than in September 2025. And that’s with more than 1,000 more homes to choose from.
“Aside from the traditional slowdown from the summer months, increasing inflationary pressure and higher mortgage rates without a comparable downward adjustment in pricing have sidelined some buyers, especially first-time buyers with no equity from previous home purchases,” Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors, said in a news release.
Houses are also taking longer to sell, sitting on the market for an average of 21 days last month, compared to just 10 days in June, according to Maine Listings.
According to Lawrence Yun, chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, on a seasonally adjusted basis, August and September marked the two slowest months of the year for home sales nationwide.
Nationally, sales fell just shy of 2% year over year, while prices rose just over 1% to a median of $422,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Regionally, sales in the Northeast dropped 4% while the median sale price increased nearly 5% to $523,600.
3. Hard-to-swallow interest rates
In theory, more inventory and a slower pace of sales should mean more time and less competition for buyers, leaving more room for negotiations, said Oberg, who is also an associate broker at Oberg Insurance and Real Estate Agency in Bridgton.
But there’s one snag: Interest rates are the highest they’ve been in three years.
Interest rates were already elevated (6.71%) at the start of September. Then, two weeks later, the Federal Reserve increased its rate by a quarter of a point to curb inflation, and mortgage rates responded.
Last week, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage was 7.40%, according to mortgage buyer Freddie Mac. Rates haven’t been that high since November 2023.
A year ago, the average mortgage rate was 6.3%.
If someone bought a $415,000 home, put 20% down and secured that 6.3% rate, they could expect a monthly payment of about $2,833, not including any HOA fees, according to Fannie Mae, another mortgage buyer.
With the current interest rate of 7.4%, that monthly payment would increase to $3,076. That’s another $244 a month, or almost $3,000 a year.
“Increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home,” said Yun, at the national association.
The Federal Reserve is anticipating another rate hike at the end of the year.

title: Two people killed in high-speed wrong-way crash in construction zone on Maine highway
text:
Two people killed in high-speed wrong-way crash in construction zone on Maine highway
Two people are dead after a crash in a construction zone involving a wrong-way driver in a stolen car and a police chase.
Maine State Police say someone called 911 at 9:21 p.m. on Monday to report someone driving south in the northbound lanes on Interstate 95 in the town of Island Falls.
Police immediately responded to the area and at 9:38 p.m., an officer from the East Millinocket Police Department encountered the car near mile marker 248 as the vehicle was still going south in the northbound lanes. Police say the car was going more than 100 miles per hour at the time.
The officer turned around and tried to stop the wrong-way driver but police say the driver sped away.
The officer used a crossover at mile 244 to get to the correct side of the highway as the wrong-way vehicle continued in the opposing lane.
State Police say the wrong-way vehicle entered a construction zone on a bridge in Medway, just south of Exit 244, where southbound traffic was diverted onto the northbound bridge because of the construction.
Police say the wrong-way vehicle then hit another vehicle head-on.
Both drivers were killed in the crash and both were the only people in their vehicles.
Police said the wrong-way driver was Luis Mendoza, 20, of Indian Township. The driver of the other vehicle was Sandra Lacombe, 67, of Medway.
Police say Mendoza was driving a 2011 Toyota Camry that had been reported stolen from the Hannaford in Houlton.
The death of Mendoza comes just days after a murder in Indian Township where one resident is accused of killing a Penobscot Nation citizen.
The population of Indian Township as of the 2020 census was 760.

title: Hunter facing charges after stray bullet hits, kills pet donkey, officials say
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - South Carolina authorities say a hunter has been charged after a donkey was shot and killed over the weekend.
According to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, officers were called to a property in Anderson County after a report of a shooting involving a pet donkey named Angelique.
Officials said the hunter fired a gun at a deer but missed, and the stray bullet hit the donkey.
Joann Kelly, founder of Hasty’s Haven where Angelique lived, said the donkey’s death feels like a nightmare and that her entire rescue team has been left traumatized.
“Angelique came to us several years ago, along with her other three herd members,” the rescue shared. “They were previously therapy donkeys for special needs children and we have used them for education in the community. They were always the first to greet anyone and gentle in nature.”
Neighbors were seen on Monday adjusting a hunting stand near where officials said the bullet came from.
South Carolina officials said the hunter involved in the shooting was charged with negligent use of a firearm and hunting within 300 yards of a residence.
“This unfortunate incident serves as an important safety reminder,” the Department of Natural Resources said. “Hunters must always positively identify their target, be aware of what lies beyond it, and ensure they are shooting in a safe direction.”
The rescue said they hope other hunters learn from what occurred.
“I just hope this doesn’t happen to anyone else. I hope that other hunters take note and be respectful,” Kelly said.

title: Facebook pages circulate post falsely implying 2 Westbrook student-athletes are trans
text:
The Westbrook community is rallying behind the Westbrook High School girls soccer team after a Facebook post that circulated last week falsely implied two of the players are transgender.
The Parents’ Rights In Education Maine’s Facebook page posted a photo of the team and singled out two of the players with the words “it’s not fair” displayed on top. The Westbrook Beat’s Facebook page shared the post, which was taken down later the same day.
Parents’ Rights in Education is a national parents’ rights group, and its Maine chapter has been advocating for a citizens’ initiative to restrict transgender athletes from participating in girls sports or using school facilities.
“The recent social media posts targeting our student-athletes are unacceptable. Singling out children and using their photographs to advance a political agenda is wrong, and our community should be clear in rejecting it,” Westbrook Mayor David Morse said in a statement on Facebook. “These are young people who deserve to learn, build friendships, play sports, and take pride in representing Westbrook. They should not have to worry that adults will turn their team photos into material for a political attack.”
Rep. Sue Salisbury, D-Westbrook, said her phone started blowing up after the posts were shared Friday.
“I was sick to my stomach,” Salisbury said.
Very quickly, community members worked together to report the posts, find out where they came from, and ask the moderators of the Facebook accounts to take them down, Salisbury said. After a few hours, both pages took down the posts.
“The message was loud and clear that in Westbrook, we’re not going to tolerate this hateful behavior,” she said.
Last year, Rep. Laurel Libby, R-Auburn, posted a photo of a student-athlete from Greely High School she identified as transgender on her official Facebook page. The post sparked a debate about transgender athletes, drawing national attention and leading to a showdown between Gov. Janet Mills and President Donald Trump. Libby was censured for posting the photo, and she later filed a federal lawsuit against the speaker of the Maine House of Representatives, arguing the censure violated her constitutional rights.
Earlier this year, the citizens’ initiative to limit transgender students’ rights did not qualify for the November ballot because organizers did not gather enough valid signatures. Supporters of the referendum said they’re now aiming to qualify for the 2027 ballot.
Caught in the center of a charged debate over transgender athletes participating in sports, some children have become the targets of harassment and bullying.
Superintendent Peter Lancia and the Westbrook High School administration shared a message online condemning the posts, asking the community to continue to support the students.
“Personal attacks, harassment and public targeting of student-athletes have no place in our school community,” the statement read. “We do not tolerate language or behavior that demeans or marginalizes others. We stand firmly in support of all of our students.”
The Portland Press Herald reached out to the parents of one of the players — who are minors — and didn’t hear back. One of the players’ parents criticized the post on Facebook, saying every parent should be outraged.
Allen Sarvinas, director of Parents’ Rights in Education Maine, said in an email, “We disagree with the account presented in its entirety.”
He said his group received a “firsthand report from the Westbrook community” that a male athlete was participating in female athletics and that this was corroborated by another “community source.”
The post was removed after a parent reached out to the group, Sarvinas said. He defended the post and discounted the pushback from the community.
“To be clear, the Westbrook community has no influence on PRE Maine in these situations,” Sarvinas wrote. “Their selective outrage has no value on PRE.”
His wife, Annalyse Sarvinas, is running for Maine House District 51, which covers part of Topsham.
The Westbrook Beat describes itself as Westbrook’s “conservative watchdog,” posting about City Council and school board meetings on Facebook and Substack. It is unclear who runs the account, and the moderator did not respond to requests for comment on Facebook.
In comments under the two accounts’ other Facebook posts, people have criticized the posts targeting the two Westbrook students, saying they put children at risk and demanding accountability.

title: Katie Zacharia, Trump’s new White House press secretary, faces reporters for the first time
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, faced reporters for the first time on Tuesday for a very brief turn at the lectern, taking a handful of questions before abruptly wrapping it up.
Zacharia, a conservative commentator who most recently worked for President Donald Trump’s social media company, was named to the job on Friday, succeeding Karoline Leavitt, who left in August and is taking a job with Fox News Channel.
Zacharia told reporters her goal is to “amplify” what Trump is doing and that the president is “his own best spokesperson.”
She quickly proved that Tuesday, appearing for only 14 minutes and taking questions from just three outlets before telling reporters they could ask the president their questions on the South Lawn when he departs on a campaign trip.
“In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there,” she said.
As the Republican president left the White House for his trip, more than an hour after the briefing’s abrupt end, he praised Zacharia’s performance to reporters.
“I thought she did excellent. She did very good,” he said, as Zacharia stood behind him.
Before taking the questions, Zacharia read slowly from an opening statement that began with a focus on Trump’s recent campaign rallies and his policies on energy, tariffs, immigration and more since he returned to office.
In naming Zacharia, who has a law degree from Pepperdine University, Trump described her as “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.” She briefly worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year and has been a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax.
She told reporters she viewed her role as press secretary to be no different than the way she advocated for Trump while outside the government.
She also thanked Trump and said, “I have wanted to work for him for a very long time.”
She took her first question from Breitbart News, the right-wing outlet that has become more influential in the Trump era, and committed to keeping the “new media” rotation created under her predecessor to bring additional media outlets into news briefings and the White House press pool.
But Zacharia did make some big news: she said Trump had asked for the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
“She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” Zacharia said.
___

title: SK Tours brings King’s Bangor to life (If you dare!)
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - During spooky season, there might not be a more popular stop in Bangor than Stephen King’s house on West Broadway. Did you know traces of King and his work can be found throughout the Queen City?
One local business sees a jump-scare in attendance around Halloween as it showcases uneasy Easter eggs from the king of horror himself.
Like Pennywise coaxing little Georgie into the sewers, bringing folks deeper into the storied streets is SK Tours of Maine.
“It’s a 2 1/2 hour driving, narrated tour about Stephen’s life, his writing, his books, some of the philanthropy from the Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation, and a bit of Bangor history as well,” explains James Tinker, owner of SK Tours.
Started by Tinker’s father 15 years ago, he says carrying on the business after his father’s retirement was an easy choice because of his longtime love of King.
“The first [King] book I ever read was ‘The Eyes of the Dragon,’” Tinker recalls. “I was hooked on King, and then I just started reading everything I could get my hands on.”
Offering public and private tours, an upwards of 4,000 bone-chilling bookworms and frightening film fanatics load into its Pennywise van every year to dissect local landmarks that inspired King.
“We’ve had people come from as far as Siberia, New Zealand, all over the world to take the tour and kind of immerse themselves into the King experience. They’re thrilled to be able to see the landmarks, like the Paul Bunyan statue or the standpipe,” Tinker describes. “Since the Thomas Hill standpipe is the only one of its kind, a lot of people, when they read the book It, they don’t know what it is, so they don’t know what it looks like.”
Beyond the horrors King has imagined happening here, Tinker adds it is important to them to highlight the scare and care King has brought to Bangor.
“The Kings have been so good to my family from way back when my father owned Betts Bookstore in downtown Bangor all the way to starting the tour business. He’s been so good to us that we need to give that back,” says Tinker. “We need to share the stories of how good he is to us and our city and our whole state and share those with people who otherwise wouldn’t know about the foundation or their charitable works.”
That includes showcasing spots like Hayford Park, where Stephen and Tabitha King have supported the stadium, aquatic center and playground.
SK Tours say it’s booked through Halloween.
With their new SK Tours app, a $5 yearly membership unlocks all King-related landmarks to visit independently - if you dare!

title: Stolen Vehicle Chase Ends In Head-on Collision On I-95 Near Medway
text:
Two Killed In Medway After Driver, Trying To Evade Police In Allegedly Stolen Car, Enters Construction Zone The Wrong Way
There was a massive police presence in Medway Monday evening authorities tried to piece together how two people ended up dead following a police chase.
How Authorities Say It All Started
According to the Maine State Police, the incident began in the how of Houlton, when a 2011 Toyota Camry was stolen from the Hannaford parking lot there.
The man driving the stolen Camry, 20-year-old Luis Mendoza of Indian Township, headed south upon allegedly stealing the car. Reports of a wrong-way driver started to come into dispatchers around 9:21 PM. Callers reached out to the Bangor Regional Communications Center stating a car was driving south bound in the north bound lanes in the area of Island Falls.
Read More: Bangor Broadway Bridge Project Final Phases Start October 16
State and local law enforcement agents began to head in that direction. They did not yet know the car was stolen from Houlton, just that it was driving the wrong way.
What Happened Next
According to authorities, Mendoza kept travelling south to the Millinocket, where it was reported that he was driving southbound on the interstate at speeds upwards of 100 miles an hour. A member of the East Millinocket Police Department came across the vehicle at around mile marker 248 at 9:48 PM.
When the officer, who at this point had turned around and caught up with the speeding Camry, attempted to stop the vehicle, the situation went from dangerous to deadly.
"The officer continued south and began entering the crossover at mile marker 244 to enter the correct flow of traffic. The wrong-way vehicle continued south in the northbound lanes and entered a construction zone on a bridge in Medway just south of Exit 244. Due to construction, southbound traffic is diverted onto the northbound bridge, with concrete barriers separating one lane of northbound traffic from one lane of southbound traffic. The wrong-way vehicle entered the construction zone traveling south in the northbound lane and struck another vehicle head on."
The end result of the crash
Mendoza was killed. The collision also killed the driver and sole occupant of the other car involved, 67-year-old Sandra Lacombe of Medway.
Read More: Maine Man Shot And Killed In Indian Township, Suspect Arrested
Authorities had the area shut down for several hours trying to figure out what happened. Later it was determined that the car had been stolen in Houlton. The investigation is still ongoing.

title: Victim releases video of co-worker convicted of poisoning her
text:
BERKELEY, Calif. — A Berkeley engineer is speaking out after a judge expunged a felony conviction against the co-worker who poisoned her on the job nearly a decade ago.
Rong Yuan said she could not believe what she saw when she discovered her co-worker pouring something into her water bottle. The substance was later identified as a toxic chemical.
“Shocked. I don’t know why,” Yuan said when asked what she thought when she saw it.
Symptoms began in 2017
In 2017, Yuan started experiencing symptoms including vomiting and hair loss. For more than two years, she visited doctors seeking answers.
Her mother then noticed her water bottle smelled strange. After a deep cleaning failed to resolve the issue, Yuan set up a small camera at her work desk.
“I never expected that I could capture anybody,” Yuan said.
A sample of the water found 3.5 million times the federal level for cadmium. Yuan and her parents tested positive for cadmium poisoning.
Co-worker pleaded guilty
Yuan’s co-worker, David Xu, was charged with premeditated attempted murder. In a plea deal, he pleaded guilty to poisoning and received two years of probation.
“I don’t think he deserves a second chance. A second chance for a lot,” Yuan said.
Despite an objection from the district attorney’s office, the court agreed to expunge Xu’s felony conviction.
“They couldn’t find out this criminal record,” Yuan said.
Yuan said she still does not know exactly why Xu poisoned her, but she recalled that he had not let her work in the lab and had referred her to other jobs.
“He’s a nobody. He’s a coward,” Yuan said.
Father died last year
Yuan said her father’s health declined after he cooked using her water bottle. He died last year from heart failure. Yuan said she is speaking out in his honor.
“To come out of my comfort zone, to be interviewed about you, to tell the public what kind of effect it had on my family, and how broken the system is,” Yuan said.
Yuan said she continues to experience effects from the poisoning and is only able to work part-time. She requested $500,000 in restitution but has received $7,000.

title: InvestigateTV+: Know the danger before you dig

title: Can Auburn residents put light yard waste in their new household trash carts?
text:
Yes.
Auburn residents can put bagged leaves and other small, light yard waste in their new wheeled trash carts, city spokesperson Liz Allen confirmed.
Branches and brush, however, are prohibited.
Under the city’s collection rules, waste must fit inside the cart with its lid securely closed. Overflow bags left beside carts will not be collected.
The new system uses separate, 64-gallon trash and recycling carts. Yard waste cannot go in recycling carts.
The city also announced free curbside pickup of bagged leaves, twigs and small yard debris Oct. 29-30, Nov. 5-6 and Nov. 12-13. Bags must be placed at the curb at least 3 feet from the carts by 7 a.m. Ordinary plastic trash bags are permitted.
Lewiston’s rules appear somewhat more restrictive. The city’s published guidance permits bagged leaves in regular weekly trash pickups but does not extend that permission to other yard debris.

title: Police confiscate robot that groped 16-year-old girl, probe whether young men were at the controls
text:
COLOGNE, Germany (AP) — German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said.
Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot’s suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault.
They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online.
Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot’s movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time.
Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said.
“We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was ”new territory for us.”
Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men’s mobile phones were confiscated.
North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground.
The robot, said to be 120 cm (about 3 ft 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache.
Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street.
One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area.
On the police’s Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticized inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim.

title: Obituary: Capt. John M. Kaiser Sr.
text:
WINTHROP – Capt. John M. Kaiser Sr. “Jack” of Winthrop, passed away on Oct. 5, 2026. He was born on July 21, 1940, and was originally from Ramsey, New Jersey.
Jack proudly served his country in the United States Navy for many years as a pilot and Captain. His military career took him and his family to many places around the world, providing a lifetime of adventure and experiences. He retired from the Navy in 1989 and moved to Maine permanently, where he continued to work and was an active member of his community.
Jack was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Caro Jane Kaiser, who passed away just three weeks before him. Their family finds comfort in knowing that they are together again.
He was also predeceased by his parents, George and Edith Kaiser.
Jack is survived by his son, John M. Kaiser Jr. and his wife, Rhonda; his daughter, Jane C. Grant and her husband, Steve; his grandchildren, Kayla Kaiser (Keenan) and Lauren Souza (Kameron); his great-grandchildren, Laina and Kaleb; and his brother, Walter Kaiser.
Jack will be remembered for his years of service to his country, the life he built with his beloved wife, and the family he leaves behind.
A service will be held on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, at 2 p.m., at the Maine Veterans’ Memorial Cemetery located at 143 Blue Star Avenue (off of Civic Center Drive) in Augusta. Arrangements and guidance are under the direction of Roberts Funeral Home, 62 Bowdoin Street, Winthrop.

title: Susan Collins still working with operatives tied to straw donation scheme
text:
When the investigative news outlet ProPublica reported on Sen. Susan Collins’ ties to a disgraced convicted fraudster, the outlet wrote about how Scott Reed, a key figure in Collins’ political orbit, may have been aware of a scheme to direct an illegal straw donation to the Republican senator from Maine.
But Reed, who heads the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results Super PAC, wasn’t the only Collins ally who may have known of the plan.
MacKenzie Dolan, who co-founded The Morning Group, worked in 2020 with the 1820 PAC, the main pro-Collins Super PAC.
A federal investigator said both Dolan and Reed received an email sent Dec. 13, 2019, from the fraudster, Navatek CEO Martin Kao, updating them on his plans to create a shell company to make a donation to the PAC.
The investigator said in court documents that Kao sent the email from an address associated with a “navatekllc.com.”
“I just received confirmation from our bank that the new account for the Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers will be up and ready to go by early next week,” Kao wrote. “I’ll be in touch next week re getting 1820 a check by year end.”
The group sent a $150,000 check to the PAC about two weeks later, ProPublica reported.
This cycle, Collins for Senator has paid Dolan’s firm, The Morning Group, at least $300,000 for fundraising services in 2025-26. And the firm has received at least $1.1 million from Pine Tree Results PAC. The Morning Group was also hired by Reed and the 1820 PAC during the 2020 cycle.
Neither Reed, Dolan nor Collins has been accused of or charged with wrongdoing by authorities during their investigation into Kao, who is currently in prison for money laundering and bank fraud. Kao pleaded guilty to charges relating to the illegal contribution in 2022.
But Collins’ ongoing relationship with Reed and Dolan may give critics more fodder in their attempts to cast Collins as corrupt in the closing weeks of Maine’s closely watched and tight U.S. Senate race against Democrat Troy Jackson.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a written statement that Reed and Dolan were “thoroughly investigated” and “cleared by the FBI in 2021.”
“Martin Kao was the guilty party and he was sentenced to seven years in federal prison,” Kernen said. “Martin Kao tried to get his sentence reduced by blaming Senator Collins, her staff, Scott Reed and MacKenzie Dolan for his criminal conduct. The FBI, the Biden Department of Justice, and the Federal Election Commission didn’t believe him and the judge did not offer him any leniency.”
A spokesperson for The Morning Group declined to speak with a reporter on Monday.
Democrats are working to keep the ProPublica story in the headlines. The Senate Majority PAC, which is tied to Democratic Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., issued a Sept. 29 memo outlining its plan to tie political corruption to increased living costs in an effort to sway a small number of undecided voters. And they’ve put millions behind an ad campaign here highlighting the ProPublica story.
Local Democrats held a press conference outside of Collins’ office in response to the report. And a Democratic attorney has filed a formal ethics complaint against Collins.
Collins has also leveled corruption allegations against her opponent, former Senate President Troy Jackson, accusing him of using his influence to help his son, who was an Augusta lobbyist while Jackson was in power. Jackson has denied that his son had any influence over his legislative agenda.
But much of the focus has been on Collins’ orbit, with the candidate getting questions about Kao at each of last week’s two Senate debates.
Numerous outlets have reported that Reed, who was the leader of the 1820 PAC that secured Kao’s illegal donation, is leading Pine Tree Results.
Reed is also a close friend of Collin’s husband, Tom Daffron, who was paid for consulting work last year by Reed’s firm, Chesapeake Enterprises.
FEC records show that the Collins Victory Committee has joint fundraising agreements with Pine Tree Results and with other Collins committees — her principal campaign committee (Collins for Senator) and her leadership committee (Dirigo PAC.)
But the ties between the 2020 donation and Dolan have received less scrutiny.
A federal search warrant from April 7, 2021, said that Reed and Dolan were “associated with the 1820 PAC,” and that they received the email from Kao about the bogus Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers group.
As a federal contractor, Kao was prohibited from making political contributions.
ProPublica’s investigation cited emails showing that Kao had told Reed he was working with his attorney to create the Young Women Scientists group to obscure the donation.
“Very smart,” Reed replied, according an email reviewed by ProPublica.
Collins campaign manager Steve Abbott dismissed that exchange when speaking to reporters last month, though he said he did not have any firsthand knowledge of the conversation between Kao and Reed.
“I might also say the same thing if I were trying to do something and had consulted with my attorney,” Abbott said. “I would also say that that is very smart, but I have no idea what any of their conversations were or what was said.”
ProPublica reported that a staffer for the 1820 PAC requested contact information for Kao on Collins’ behalf so she could thank him. Abbott said Collins’ office has no record that Collins made such a call.
Collins’ campaign has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and accused ProPublica of trusting a convicted felon‘s word. The investigation was based in part on what Kao told federal investigators in an effort to earn a lighter sentence.
But the outlet has pushed back, saying that federal investigators corroborated some of Kao’s claims and wanted to launch a wider probe — a move that was thwarted when Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

title: What’s on the ballot in the Berwicks?
text:
Residents in South Berwick will cast their votes for a handful of local candidates on Nov. 3, while North Berwick will decide on a couple referendum questions. Berwick voters have a light election cycle, with just state and federal races to consider.
In-person voting in each town will take place from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., with an absentee ballot request deadline of Oct. 29. Absentee and early voters have until the end of Election Day to hand in their ballots at their respective town clerk offices.
South Berwick residents can vote in-person at Marshwood High School, North Berwick residents at North Berwick Elementary School and Berwick residents at town hall.
Here’s what’s on the ballot in each town.
NORTH BERWICK
Voters in North Berwick don’t have any local candidates to consider, but will decide on two referendum questions.
The first — a potential change to the comprehensive plan — would expand the town’s growth area parameters in an effort to match state legislation. If it’s approved by voters, the amendment would encourage future development in areas already served by public water and sewer infrastructure, rather than in rural areas.
A “no” vote would mean the comprehensive plan stays the same until officials re-draft the ordinance amendment.
The second question will give North Berwick voters an opportunity to weigh in on a nationwide debate over data center developments.
In June, the Select Board decided to skip a moratorium — a step that several other Maine towns have taken — and pursue voter approval to enact a ban. The proposed ordinance would apply to facilities with an aggregate data center area of 25,000 square feet or larger.
Officials say they haven’t received any data center development proposals, but want to be proactive about preventing future ones by implementing the ordinance.
SOUTH BERWICK
Voters in South Berwick have no local referendums, but will decide on new school board members and town councilors.
MSAD 35 — which also serves Eliot — has two seats to fill, although one is a single-year term and the other is a three-year term.
Both races are uncontested, with first time candidate Perrin Chick running for the partial term and returning member Heather Holland, who was elected to the board in 2020, looking to fill another full term.
Chick said in a response to the Press Herald Voter Guide that she’ll prioritize honoring educators and residents’ concerns, and developing a “robust educational experience possible while being mindful of budget.”
Two new town councilors will replace Chair John James, and Vice Chair Mallory Cook in a nonpartisan race. Voters will consider four candidates vying for the seats, including Jane Brekke, Dorothy Maguire, Ronald Fousek and Anthony Palazzetti.
Brekke and Palazzetti said in voter guide responses that they’d prioritize transparency, affordability and budget issues if elected. Maguire echoed affordability issues and added that she’d focus on making downtown South Berwick more accessible. Fousek didn’t provide responses to the voter guide.
STATE RACES
Voters in House District 148 — covering the western part of town and Berwick — will choose a new representative between Republican incumbent Thomas Lavigne and Democrat Marissa Tasker, who is also an MSAD 60 board member.
Residents in House District 149 — covering eastern North Berwick and part of South Berwick — will choose between Democrat Mallory Cook, who is finishing her term as South Berwick Town Council vice chair, and Republican Timothy Towne, who is the Berwick Police chief and was recently appointed as Berwick’s interim town manager.
South Berwick voters will also choose a District 35 state senator. Democratic incumbent Rep. Michele Meyer is facing Republican Julie Rakic.
Some South Berwick residents, along with Eliot and part of Kittery, will choose a House District 150 representative from a group of two. Democrat Alexandros Orestis is taking on Republican Mark Zimmer.
COUNTY RACES
All three towns will join all York County voters in electing a county sheriff, choosing between Democratic incumbent William King and Republican challenger David Corbett.
A third candidate, independent Brian Pellerin, dropped out of the race in September and took a position as Wells’ police chief. His name will still appear on the ballot because of the timing of his departure from the race.
Voters will also weigh in on whether the county should abolish an elected treasurer position, or to keep it and let county officials appoint someone internally to fill the seat.
The sole candidate for the position, Bobby Mills, is seeking a nonconsecutive term and thinks keeping the position could save voters some money, because a similar but more expensive role on the Budget Committee could be eliminated instead.

title: Newport restaurant hosts fundraiser for Partners for Peace in honor of late coworker
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEWPORT, Maine (WABI) - A Newport restaurant is turning a night out into a way to support domestic violence survivors.
In honor of Domestic Violence Awareness Month, Angler’s Seafood will donate 10 percent of its sales Tuesday, between 4 and 8 p.m., to Partners for Peace.
For Angler’s, it’s personal.
Staff are honoring their late coworker, Amy Nickerson, who was killed in a domestic homicide in Searsmont in 2023.
“They were a big part of when Amy had passed away. They were a big support when we had done a candlelight vigil here. They were always there. They reached out with extra materials and have given us things to support other people. It feels very good. It’s a very sentimental thing. It’s something that really struck a lot of the employees here, so it’s just a way to kind of give back and just remember,” said Connor Grindal, general manager of Angler’s Newport.
Partners for Peace has spent more than 50 years supporting survivors in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties.
Staff expect a busy evening and encourage customers to make a reservation.

title: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis faces life in prison for orchestrating murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — Duane “Keffe D” Davis is set to be sentenced Tuesday for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur, who was gunned down off the Las Vegas Strip over 30 years ago.
Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. He is the only person ever charged in the death of Shakur, whose popularity was peaking at age 25. Davis faces life in prison without the possibility of parole.
On the night of Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was in the passenger seat of a black BMW with music mogul Marion “Suge” Knight when a white Cadillac pulled up at a red light, and shots erupted. Shakur was shot multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived.
Shakur is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time and had a burgeoning film career as an actor at the time of his death. His legend has only grown since. His songs still resonate among fans with themes of hardship, love and Black struggles.
The killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir. He explained how Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis’ nephew hours before the shooting in Las Vegas. He said he sought retaliation, and that he was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to the backseat, where shots were fired. Davis had spoken to detectives years before but avoided prosecution because of an agreement he made with law enforcement.
During the weekslong trial, prosecutors relied on Davis’ own statements he made to law enforcement and documentarians. They argued Davis orchestrated the shooting and provided the gun used in Shakur’s death, which was the result of a rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru. Davis’ defense attorney pointed to a lack of physical evidence that connected his client to the 30-year-old crime, and he portrayed Davis as a liar who was trying to make money.
After nine days of hearing testimony in August, the jury deliberated for three hours before turning over the guilty verdict. Davis said in court that he plans to appeal.
Shakur was an icon, a brother
Shakur’s family is expected to speak at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur.
Following the verdict, prosecutor Binu Palal said that to many people, Shakur was an icon or an idea, “but to the family, Tupac Shakur was a brother, a son, a cousin, a loved person ripped from them 30 years ago.”
Palal said the family had to sit through years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved.”
“They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr. Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said.
Prosecutors say they have insufficient evidence to charge anyone else
Davis is the only person to be charged and convicted in the killing of Shakur. The three other people who allegedly were in the Cadillac — including Davis’ nephew Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson who Davis said was the one who pulled the trigger — have died.
Sean “Diddy” Combs and his alleged role were brought up often throughout the trial. Witnesses testified Combs used members of the South Side Compton Crips for security for Bad Boy Records. In his book and public statements, Davis alleged Combs offered him money to kill Shakur and Knight. Combs, who is serving a four-year prison sentence after being convicted of prostitution-related offenses, has repeatedly denied any involvement in the death of Shakur.
Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson has said his office doesn’t believe it has sufficient evidence to charge anyone else.
“But like any other case, if we come into more information, more evidence, we can always consider filing additional charges,” he said following the guilty verdict. “But today, we don’t believe that’s the appropriate move to make.”

title: Dorene Kimball Mitchell
text:
Dorene Kimball Mitchell, 88, passed away peacefully on Oct. 4, 2026, at Woodlands Senior Living Center in Brewer, Maine.
Born in Bangor on March 23, 1938, she was the daughter of Fred Emanuel Kimball and Katheryn Virginia (Dodge) Kimball.
Dorene worked for more than 20 years as a Certified Nursing Assistant at Summit House in Bar Harbor. Earlier in life, she worked as a waitress in several local restaurants.
Prior to moving to Woodlands Senior Living Center, Dorene was a beloved and active member of the Malvern Belmont Apartments community in Bar Harbor.
She is survived by her three sons: Michael Wayne Mitchell and his wife, Janice, of Buxton; Scott Edward Mitchell of Bar Harbor; and Thomas Charles Mitchell of Sarasota, Fla. She also leaves her granddaughter, Lindsay, and her children, Aubrey, Taryn, and Callen, of Pennsylvania; and granddaughter Holly and her three children of Sarasota, Florida. Dorene was predeceased by her former husband, Charles Edward Mitchell III.
A memorial service will be held in the spring of 2027, with details to be announced.
