title: This Portland program proves gardening is good therapy
text:
Like most people, I feel better when I am gardening. It’s therapeutic.
If I am out picking vegetables, cutting flowers, removing weeds, pruning or doing some other gardening task, it means I am healthy enough to be outside, move around and focus. That isn’t possible for many people.
I’m also getting exercise, keeping my mind active and enjoying whatever conditions the sun and earth conspire to create for that moment.
In the world of medicine, social work and garden professionals, therapeutic gardening goes beyond such simple personal pleasures. It helps people suffering from physical and/or mental problems cope with a wide range of problems.
During this year’s growing season, people being treated at Recuperative Care Program at 934 Congress St. in Portland turned part of an abandoned parking area into a garden that provided flowers, food and a bit of fun.
Carolyn Schnell, a licensed clinical social worker at RCP, said she reached out to Cultivating Well-Being, a program that facilitates horticultural therapy, because many of her clients needed to create something positive after being treated for a variety of problems including physical injuries, disease, blood infections, substance abuse and mental illness.
“A lot of patients have ongoing medical needs coming from hospitalization at Maine Health, treatment at Preble Street and or other places,” Schnell said when I visited with her and Laura Simonds-Rumpf of Cultivating Well-Being at the RCP site.
Schnell said the idea of reaching out to garden therapists came during an art class she was teaching.
“A lot of people would talk about memories of gardening they had throughout their lives, and said they haven’t had opportunities to work in a garden in recent years because of housing issues, disability and illness,” she said. “I felt like it would be a healing process for a lot of patients.”
She said two women bonded during the planting, and went out together to water in between the formal classes. During the classes, the clients would sometimes disagree about what to plant and how the tasks should be done, and working that out was helpful in their treatments.
Schnell said the program started in June this year, but she plans to start it earlier next year, so they can help the clients for a longer period but also to be successful and possibly improve the gardens’ production.
Simonds-Rumpf said scientific studies have shown the benefits of gardening. “When people are gardening they have less cortisol in their system,” she said, explaining that cortisol is the substance that promotes “fight or flight” reaction. “Also contact with plants has been known to lower the heart rate and is just calming.”
Simonds-Rumpf said Cultivating Well-Being often offers programs in public libraries around the state, as well as working with people in their own homes.
Things to do
Although the gardens are still beautiful, fall-cleanup mode has begun. We harvested our onions, garlic, shallots and potatoes over the past couple of weeks. If you haven’t already done that, you should start now.
The gladiolus bulbs have stopped blooming, and the “rules” say they should be dug up 4-6 weeks after, or after the first light frost, which we haven’t had yet. After digging, cut the foliage an inch or so above the corms, store in a warm, dry ventilated area for a few weeks and then store them in a cool place where it won’t freeze.
The dahlias are still blooming. Erica Berman, co-owner of Veggies To Table in Newcastle, says, “Ideally after the first frost you cut the dahlias down and you wait one to two weeks to dig them up. That way, the eyes develop and they’re easier to see when you divide them. If you’re not dividing right away, it doesn’t matter as much when you dig them up, but best practice if you’re going to divide is to wait. It’s also good to know if you’re waiting, it’s best if you see lots of rain to cover them with a tarp because they are hollow and you wouldn’t want them to rot. It’s unlikely but it could happen.”
The grow-to-donate farm currently has 800 plants in the ground and is expecting 4,000 tubers.
For perennial flowers, you should cut them back after the first frost or when they go dormant. Some people recommend not cutting them back until spring because the spent foliage will trap leaves, but we don’t like looking at the piles of leaves in our too frequent snowless winters.
Now is the time to plant garlic and shallots so they get a good head start over the winter. Ours have arrived by USPS but we are waiting a bit to actually plant them.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay has several fall programs scheduled, including a three-day course on ecological plant design on Oct. 23 and 31, and Nov. 1.
Snug Harbor Farm is offering a “Bonsai 101” workshop on Oct. 24.
From The Garden is published in partnership with Eat Drink Lucky and sponsored by Skillins Greenhouses.

title: When world-class chefs need seafood, they give this Maine company a call
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Colin Wyatt’s ordered seafood from Browne Trading Company at every restaurant he’s worked at. That’s not usual for chefs at fine-dining establishments around the country.
Wyatt, the culinary director at Portland restaurants Douro and Twelve, has been in the restaurant business for over 20 years, at places like 555, 11 Madison Park and Daniel, Daniel Boulud’s restaurant in New York City.
It’s the customer service and the quality that keeps him going back to Browne.
Rod Browne Mitchell founded Browne Trading Company in 1991. The high-end seafood and caviar seller has high recognition in the fine-dining world, with customers including Eric Ripert’s Le Bernardin and Thomas Keller’s Per Se, both Michelin-starred restaurants. It sources seafood not only from the Portland Fish Exchange right by its brick building on Portland’s waterfront, but from fisheries and farms around the world, including from Spain, Portugal and Japan.
But it’s Browne’s relationships with chefs that make the company different. In the ’80s, Mitchell partnered with the French chef Jean-Louis Palladin to pioneer the idea of the “diver scallop,” a scallop that’s dove for, not dredged for. Mitchell became close to many fine-dining chefs, including Boulud and Ripert.
“I remember cooking on the roast station at Daniel,” Wyatt said, “and having Rod Mitchell standing next to me at the pass, talking to Daniel Boulud about caviar and fish.”
Dan Boccuzzi, COO of Browne, said the company was founded on the idea that people should care about what they’re eating and where it comes from. Since its founding, he believes the quality has stayed consistently great.
“I think the landscape of seafood companies has changed,” Boccuzzi said, “but for a company that’s been around for 30 years, there’s laurels, a legacy, a story, a background.”
Boccuzzi, 35, was a chef at Per Se before joining the ranks at Browne. He met Mitchell while working at the three-Michelin-starred restaurant — part of his job was ordering seafood. In 2020, he and his girlfriend, now wife, made their way to New England. He called up the only person he knew.
Now instead of cooking, he oversees managers, handles administrative tasks and works with the CEO to identify and hit targets. Browne’s new CEO, David Yourd, took the mantle in May. Mitchell still serves on Browne’s board and is a part owner of the company.
“To me, that job and this job is all about execution and organization, with the underlying necessity for absolute quality,” Buccozzi said. “It’s the same thing. You’re serving guests, you’re serving a clientele. You’re putting food on a plate, you’re wrapping food and putting food in a box.”
Packaging seafood is a major part of Browne’s business, ensuring that seafood and caviar reaches its customers while maintaining quality and freshness. Local orders, which includes Portland to Boston, are delivered the same day they’re packed, while others are shipped UPS to all 50 states. Charles Eames, the chef at Lucky Cheetah in Portland, said he sometimes picks up orders in person.
Josh Finger, co-owner of Claudine Restaurant in Providence, Rhode Island, has ordered seafood from Browne since he worked at Per Se, where Buccozzi taught him how to order seafood.
Recently, Claudine served grilled lubina, a Spanish sea bass, with a buttery Maine Jonah crab ragu, garnished with a brown butter sauce and roasted cauliflower. It was the highlight of their nine-course, $185 seafood-focused tasting menu, which changes weekly.
Browne isn’t his only seafood supplier, but Finger often finds himself building his menu around Browne’s best offerings each week, changing with the seasons.
“In my restaurant, we always rely on the highest quality possible that is available to us, so it’s often the case where Browne Trading will have the highest quality item,” Finger said.
Jake Lee, a chef at 501 Prime in Hot Springs, Arkansas, has been a frequent Browne customer since he joined the team over seven years ago. The restaurant’s owner already had a relationship with the company. Like Finger, his menu is heavily influenced by the seafood Browne offers at any point in time, but Lee’s menu changes daily.
Lee’s currently serving fishes like sablefish, swordfish and Maine bluefin tuna at his landlocked restaurant. And, of course, at least three varieties of caviar.
“Our customers … are constantly commenting, ‘I can’t believe we’re getting this quality of seafood in the middle of Arkansas,’” Lee said.
It all comes down to Browne’s worldwide sourcing. Rachel Lapp, Browne’s director of marketing and e-commerce, believes there are few companies that offer the same products.
December is their busiest time of the year, but types of seafood vary seasonally — scallops in the winter and swordfish in the summer. They get caviar from almost 10 different countries, frozen red prawns from Sicily and lobsters from Casco Bay.
They estimate they sell between 2,000 to 3,000 pounds of caviar each year.
Part of their presence on Commercial Street is a market where they sell wine, cheese, tinned fish and the same catches that end up at fine restaurants. It’s open year-round.
“Yes, we’re on the wharf,” Lapp said, “but we’re so much more than that. We’re sourcing so much more than that and we’re delivering so much more than that.”
Corey Fiske is a freelance writer who lives in Arundel. He can be reached on Instagram @coreyfiskeupdates and on X @coreyfiske7.

title: When Maine soldiers needed someone to listen, Susan Collins did
text:
Richard H. Schmidt III of Patten is a veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom II.
In the summer of 2004, I was in Iraq with the Maine Army National Guard’s 1st Battalion, 152nd Field Artillery (Forward), out of Waterville. Our unit was assigned to a military police mission at Abu Ghraib prison, where incoming mortar and rocket fire was a frequent event. Decisions about our safety were anything but abstract.
We lived in hardened concrete cells within the 250-acre prison compound. At one point, we learned that our unit and others at the prison might be moved into metal trailers elsewhere on the grounds so detainees could occupy the more protected facilities. With incoming fire a daily reality, the prospect of leaving our hardened quarters was deeply concerning.
We relayed our concerns to family members back home, who contacted Sen. Susan Collins’s office. We hoped someone in Washington would listen.
I do not claim to know every conversation that followed or what influenced the eventual decision, but we remained in the hardened quarters. I remember many of those trailers sitting unoccupied for the remainder of our deployment. I have long believed that our families’ outreach and Sen. Collins’ help played a role.
I also remember a civilian contractor whom we frequently escorted outside the prison walls. He lived in one of those trailers. As I recall, he believed someone was knocking at his door, opened it, and was shot in the chest. His death remains a sobering reminder of the dangers we faced. I cannot know what would have happened had our unit been relocated, but I believe the decision to remain in hardened quarters saved Maine soldiers’ lives.
Since returning home, I have had opportunities to meet Collins personally and thank her for whatever role she played in helping our unit. I remain grateful to her for helping protect us when our safety was at stake.
My respect for Collins does not mean I agree with every position she takes or every vote she casts. I do not. No elected official will represent all my views, and we should always hold our representatives accountable.
What I respect is her willingness to explain how she sees an issue and why she makes the decisions she makes. I value listening, engaging with differing viewpoints, and working through disagreements rather than dismissing those who think differently.
Washington needs more of that approach. Public service should be about finding common ground where possible, not simply scoring political points or satisfying one side of the aisle. I believe we need more leaders like Collins, who are committed to working together for the common good rather than putting political or individual interests first.
My experience at Abu Ghraib taught me that decisions made far from the battlefield can have profound consequences for those serving on it. It also taught me the importance of having representation that is willing to listen when concerns are raised.
I believe Collins was effective for our unit at a critical time. I will always be grateful to the families who spoke up for us and that their voices reached someone who could help.
We do not have to agree on every issue to respect a willingness to listen, explain, and work together. As a veteran who remembers what was at stake in Iraq, I believe that spirit of service deserves recognition, support, and the opportunity to continue serving our great state.
Thank you to Sen. Collins. I have not forgotten!

title: Did You Know Maine’s Patrick Dempsey Was a Competitive Juggler?
text:
Did You Know Maine’s Patrick Dempsey Was a Competitive Juggler?
Before he was McDreamy on “Grey’s Anatomy,” did you know the Lewiston native had an interesting talent?
👇 KEEP READING: Maine's Patrick Dempsey: Through the Years 👇
According to his profile on D23, the official Disney fan club, Patrick Dempsey got his start performing as a juggler, placing second in the junior division at the 1981 International Jugglers’ Association Championship.
He later landed a role in a touring production of Harvey Fierstein’s “Torch Song Trilogy,” helping launch his acting career.
His early performances also included unicycling, magic, and slapstick comedy.
Dempsey has said his interest in juggling grew out of his childhood love of skiing, after a ski instructor who performed in a vaudeville troupe introduced him to it.
He went on to build an acting career with roles in “Can’t Buy Me Love,” “Sweet Home Alabama,” and “Enchanted,” and became widely known as Dr. Derek “McDreamy” Shepherd on “Grey’s Anatomy.”
He was honored as a Disney Legend in 2022 and named People magazine’s Sexiest Man Alive in 2023.
And there you have it! Long before McDreamy and Sexiest Man Alive, Dempsey’s path to Hollywood started with juggling clubs and vaudeville-style performance.

title: Spruce Mountain CDL program draws more than 75 applicants
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — Demand for Spruce Mountain Adult Education’s new commercial driver’s license training program continues to grow, with more than 75 prospective students on its waiting list or recently applying as the first class prepares for road tests in November.
Robyn Raymond, director of Spruce Mountain Adult & Community Education, told the Regional School Unit 73 board of directors Oct. 8 that 28 new applications arrived in the week following the program’s Sept. 29 ribbon-cutting ceremony, adding to a waiting list of more than 50 people.
The program, developed through partnerships with workforce development organizations and local funders, is intended to expand job training opportunities in a region affected by mill closures.
“Our first cohort, they’ve completed their permit testing,” Raymond said. “All students have their permit and they also all passed their final written exam.”
The inaugural class of 12 students is concentrating on behind-the-wheel training and road experience, with road tests expected during the first week of November.
Raymond said interest in the program remains strong, but class sizes are limited by the amount of individual driving instruction required.
“We did 12 this time and we’re thinking 14 would be the absolute max,” she said.
Interviews for the next class are expected to begin during the final week of October, with training anticipated to start in December. Raymond said scheduling adjustments are being considered as daylight hours shorten.
The Sept. 29 ribbon cutting drew more than 60 attendees, including students, prospective students, local employers, board members and workforce development partners.
Raymond credited collaboration among several organizations, including the Maine Department of Labor, Maine Development Foundation and Skowhegan Savings Bank, with helping establish the program.
She also said she had been asked to submit a proposal for the Maine Talent Summit in Augusta in November, explaining how multiple funding sources were combined to launch the training.
With demand far exceeding the number of available seats, Spruce Mountain Adult Education is continuing to coordinate future training schedules as it prepares to welcome its next group of students in December.

title: BRHS girls win at Lisbon, boys take third
text:
Pauline “Polly” Nadeau finished first among 35 runners and the Boothbay Region High School girls cross country team took first place in a race at Lisbon Oct. 9.
“Polly out-sprinted a competitor from Monmouth to claim her second individual victory this season,” Coach Nick Scott reported.
The girls team, with 31 points, defeated Winthrop (44), Forest Hills (65) and Lisbon (77).
Two other BRHS runners finished in the top 10 with Audrey Robinson coming in third overall and Maggie McCarthy finishing sixth. Olivia Rittall finished 14th and Emma Scott finished 19th. Robinson improved her time on the course by 2 minutes and 43 seconds and McCarthy improved her time on the course by 2 minutes and 29 seconds.
For the BRHS boys, who finished third, AJ Crocker finished fifth overall among the 58 runners. Jackson Zehm (42 seconds faster than last year’s course run) was the second Seahawk runner to cross the finish line, coming in 11th. John Cooper cut 41 seconds off his time from last season on the course and finished 16th. Alex Ross finished 19th and Miles Hyson came in 22nd.
The strong Winthrop team won the meet with 21 points, followed by Madison (57), Boothbay (62) and Lisbon (88).
The teams will next compete in the Mountain Valley Conference meet on Saturday, Oct. 17 at the University of Maine at Augusta.

title: New non-profit aims for $1M to buy, preserve local newspapers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine (WABI) - An Ellsworth non-profit has started its mission to help preserve journalism in Hancock County.
The Acadia Newspaper Trust is looking to raise one million dollars by next summer to buy the Ellsworth American, the Bangor Historian, and The Mount Desert Islander from current owner, Reade Brower.
The non-profit was formed back in June and achieved 501(c)(3) status last month.
Ellsworth American Publisher Chris Crockett says a transition to non-profit will help them retain local ownership.
He says the trust is an effort to ensure that local communities do not face the difficulties that come when a paper closes.
“There’s been many studies. Tax mill rates go up, and voter participation goes down when newspapers leave a community. We want to be proactive and really secure the next 175 years for these newspapers,” said Crockett.
Crockett says there has been a lot of community support since their fundraising announcement earlier this month. He also says Brower has been very supportive of the ownership change.
The public is also invited to meet those behind the trust during a community kickoff celebration on October 29th at 5pm at Fogtown Brewing Company in Ellsworth.
To learn more about the Acadia Newspaper Trust, you can visit their website here.

title: Down East man charged with murder makes 1st appearance
text:
A man accused of a fatal shooting made his first appearance in court Tuesday.
Jeremy Stevens, 46, of Indian Township is charged with intentional or knowing murder in Washington County. He’s accused of fatally shooting Cory Fields, 41, on Saturday on Peter Dana Point Road on the Passamaquoddy reservation.

title: ‘Sophisticated recording device’ found in OpenAI conference room, FBI and the company say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.
The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.
The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.
“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.
The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.
“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.
Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.
The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.
Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.
The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.
The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

title: Obituary: Charlotte N. Tebbenhoff
text:
PHOENIX, Ariz. – Charlotte N. Tebbenhoff passed away peacefully Oct. 6, 2026, at 94, in Phoenix, Ariz. A lifelong resident of Biddeford, Maine, Charlotte moved to Phoenix October 2025 to live with her daughter, Claire Haines and her children Kyle, Carter and Maria who provided love, safety and the warmth of winter in Arizona, with amazing views of one of her favorite activities, Moon-Gazing.
Born April 10, 1932, one of nine children, Charlotte graduated salutatorian at St. Joseph high school in 1950 then spent five years working for Biddeford Savings Bank. Charlotte applied for and received an appointment to the U. S. State Department in December 1957. After four months in Washington, D. C. she was assigned to the US Embassy in Brussels, Belgium, while there she was assigned to the position of secretary to the assistant coordinator of the American projects for the Brussels World Fair in 1958. It was there that she met and married Godefridus Tebbenhoff on June 13, 1959, who immigrated to the U.S. with Charlotte and together had five children, Peter, Lucy, Eric, Claire and Hans before later divorcing.
Charlotte spent years working for the Biddeford Schools Superintendents office before transitioning to a position where her exceptional skills were welcomed by the Portland Law firm Norman, Hanson and Detroy working as secretary for the founding member, Robert (Bob) Hanson until retirement.
Charlotte had many interests and a competitive spirit. She enjoyed scrabble, traveling, bowling, crossword puzzles, and gardening to name a few. She was an avid non-fiction reader fulfilling curiosity about history as well as every local newspaper available to her including the New York Times, Portland Press Herald, Biddeford Journal Tribune and the weekly distribution of free newspapers distributed in York County and most recently Arizona Republic. Her greatest love was playing the piano which she continued into her 94th year until just before she passed.
Charlotte is survived by “George”, her last living sibling (who has won their bet!); her five children; 11 grandchildren; and four great-grandchildren.
A private service will be held in Phoenix for the many lives she touched in her short time there. A family service will be held in the summer of 2027.

title: Federal agents raid Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. home
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Federal agents carried out a pre-dawn raid Monday at the Washington home of Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar.
The exact location is not being disclosed out of respect for her privacy.
It is not immediately clear what homeland security agents were looking for, but the Department of Justice says the raid is part of a federal criminal investigation.
Background on targeting
Omar, who is Somali-born, has frequently been a target of the Trump administration.
Last January, President Trump criticized her hours before an assailant attacked her with a syringe that ended up containing vinegar.
Last week, Vice President JD Vance accused her of immigration fraud, a claim that has not been substantiated.
Omar responds
Omar responded to the raid in a post on X.
“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar said. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
Timing questions raised
Questions about the timing of the raid are being raised.
A memorandum issued in 2024 under Attorney General Merrick Garland established that public raids and investigations could not be carried out with the purpose of hurting or discrediting a candidate close to an election.
The raid comes 22 days before the midterm elections. Omar is on the ballot.

title: Inside Robert’s Western World: Nashville’s classic honky tonk
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — Lower Broadway is known for high-rise honky tonks and rooftop bars that draw crowds late into the night. Under a large red boot sign sits Robert’s Western World, a bar that plays only traditional country music.
Robert’s Western World has operated for more than 30 years. The bar sells cans of beer starting at $2.50.
“We’ve left it alone. It’s not broke. Don’t fix it,” owner Emily Jones said.
A time capsule on Broadway
Jones and her husband, JesseLee, own Robert’s Western World and are working to keep its legacy going.
“A time capsule when people walk in here,” Emily Jones said. “We are in a society where people are longing for something tangible. They want to know the history.”
JesseLee Jones moved to Nashville from Brazil and worked at Robert’s Western World before getting the chance to buy it.
“Do what’s in your heart, because if you do what’s in your heart, you don’t work a day in your life,” he said.
No distractions
JesseLee Jones said the bar does not have a television inside.
“You come in here and it’s like stepping back into the 50s, and the 60s, and the 70s, the heydays of country music,” he said.
“They just want to tuck in the crowd, have a beer and just be human and take in the vibe,” Emily Jones said.
The bar was named one of USA Today’s best bars in the country.
Expansion plans
Emily and JesseLee Jones have bought the building next door and plan to expand Robert’s Western World.
“But it will still be Nashville. It will still be real,” JesseLee Jones said. “And that is what’s missing nowadays. Believability.”

title: Israel returns over a dozen artifacts as Greece pushes to bring antiques home
text:
Israel returns over a dozen artifacts as Greece pushes to bring antiques home
Israel on Tuesday returned 22 ancient artifacts that had been illegally removed from Greece, as Athens steps up an international repatriation campaign ultimately aimed at securing the return of sculptures taken from the Acropolis.
Related video: Four-legged wedding photographer steals the show
Culture Minister Lina Mendoni received the objects from the Israel Antiquities Authority and Amir Ganor, director of its theft prevention division, at a ceremony held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.
“It is the first time that Israel has returned antiquities to Greece, marking the starting point of closer cooperation between the two countries for the protection of cultural heritage,” Mendoni said. “Every return of a cultural object to its place of origin has a broader symbolic and moral dimension.”
The collection includes a small bronze statuette of a woman and pottery comprising slender oil flasks, two-handled amphorae and drinking cups decorated with mythological scenes and geometric motifs. The objects are provisionally dated to between about 700 B.C. and 320 B.C.
Athens is broadening bilateral cultural ties as part of its campaign to secure the return of the Parthenon Marbles. The 2,500-year-old sculptures were removed from the Acropolis and are now displayed at the British Museum in London.
Greece, under its current conservative government, and Israel have strengthened energy and defense ties in recent years. In August, Israel signed a 3 billion euro (about $3.5 billion) deal to build an air defense system in Greece, dubbed Achilles Shield, in what was described as the largest defense deal between the two countries.
Greek and Israeli officials on Tuesday did not disclose how the artifacts were discovered in Israel or the circumstances of their illegal removal from Greece. In previous cases, antiquities returned from private collections abroad have often been traced to illicit excavations.
Pninat Yanay, the Israeli ambassador to Greece, said the items were recovered during an “investigation by the Israeli authorities into the illegal antiquities trade.”
She added: “In both Greece and Israel, archaeology has a special place in national life. It helps us understand where we came from and who we are.”

title: Hancock County sheriff candidates agree on policing priorities but spar over qualifications
text:
The race for Hancock County’s top law enforcement officer has intensified in recent weeks following four Democratic state legislators’ extraordinary endorsement of the Republican candidate.
Republican Corey Bagley, Ellsworth Police Department detective and former Hancock County chief deputy, and Democrat Dakota Dupuis, current sheriff’s lieutenant, shared similar visions for the future of the sheriff’s office in early October interviews with the Bangor Daily News.
Both favor community policing and mental health services, but they differ on their interpretation of their opponent’s qualifications and ability to manage Hancock County’s chief law enforcement role.
The race has seen four Democratic state legislators cross party lines — an increasingly unique move in today’s hyperpartisan political climate — to endorse Bagley, 57, who left the sheriff’s office in 2023 after 31 years of service.
Current Sheriff Scott Kane, who has endorsed Dupuis, is not seeking re-election. Dupuis, 31, has repeatedly tried to distance himself from his current boss.
“We’re two different people,” Dupuis said. “I don’t agree with every decision he’s done. I don’t want to be painted with a brush for a decision he made in 2021. How did I have any control? I disagreed with it.”
A scathing letter penned by three of the legislators — the fourth’s endorsement came later — criticized Dupuis for his affiliation with Kane, a controversial Republican accused of leading a politically motivated investigation into Rep. Nina Milliken, D-Blue Hill, one of the Democratic lawmakers now endorsing Bagley.
Dupuis adamantly disagreed with some of Kane’s decisions, including when the sheriff in 2021 temporarily barred a provider from giving addiction services to inmates at the county jail over its support of the Black Lives Matter movement. He also refuted what he described as inaccuracies in the legislators’ letter.
The letter stated the sheriff’s office budget had been mismanaged since Dupuis became lieutenant in 2024, during which time he has largely led the department’s daily operations after Kane took a step back from managerial duties.
Contrary to the lawmakers’ letter, which was published in the Ellsworth American and alleged the sheriff’s budget jumped by more than $700,000 in 2025, under Dupuis’ tenure, the budget actually increased by $430,000 between 2024 and 2025, according to documents reviewed by the BDN.
Both candidates favor community policing, saying they would encourage officers to be visible in the towns they serve by visiting schools, libraries and municipal offices.
Each candidate has also promised to add some sort of mental health liaison to their squad.
Bagley wants to replicate a version of Bar Harbor’s Good Morning program, a free initiative that offers daily wellness checks on senior residents and adults with disabilities.
Since his promotion to lieutenant, Dupuis said he’s worked to reestablish the sheriff office’s participation in the county’s drug treatment court.
“Corey and I, we’ve said a lot of the same sentiments — mental health, community programs, community engagement,” Dupuis said. “The difference is there’s one of us that is saying it and has done it, and there’s another that’s saying it because it sounds good in a campaign.”
The two candidates questioned their opponent’s viability as a county sheriff. Bagley, who has been in law enforcement for longer than Dupuis has been alive, said his opponent lacked the experience to lead Hancock County’s law enforcement division.
The sheriff’s office has seen significant turnover since his departure, Bagley said, noting roughly 14 officers have left since 2023.
“I really believe that comes down to leadership,” Bagley said. “I want to hire and retain good quality deputies, officers [and] employees, and I want to enhance our training with mental health, both for the officers and corrections staff.”
The candidates accused each other of repeating contradictory claims.
Dupuis has said leadership roles have changed dramatically since Bagley’s departure, and that the current detective’s time as lieutenant and chief deputy was more akin to a road supervisor role than an administrative manager.
“It’s a double edged sword,” Bagley said. “In one breath he’s saying I didn’t have any of those administration type roles, but in his other breath he’s blaming me for the 2022-23 budget, which I had nothing to do with.”
Although he hasn’t personally prepared a county budget, he’s been involved in budget proposals for other volunteer organizations, he said.
“[During] my time as chief deputy, I was always looking at the budget numbers,” Bagley said. “I also know how to ask people for help or guidance on that if needed— so that is not a concern.”
Outside policing, Bagley spent more than 30 years coaching youth sports and has been involved in several local charities and nonprofits, including the YMCA and veterans groups, he said.
Bagley wants to prioritize fixing what he described as fraught partnerships with various local law enforcement and first responder agencies.
“We used to have a really good relationship with all the other departments in the county, as well as fire, EMS and other organizations,” Bagley said. “I feel that that has gone downhill or diminished a lot over the last few years. I want to build that back up.”
Dupuis has been criticized for only recently joining the Democratic Party, whose local chapter has supported him despite the recent endorsements. He registered as a Democrat in 2024 after his family had difficult experiences with the country’s healthcare system, Dupuis said.
“I agree with the sentiments and beliefs of the Democratic Party — universal healthcare and things such as that,” Dupuis said. “Beyond that, look at what I did professionally. I have more of a community policing approach, which I would say aligns with a lot of Democratic views and beliefs.”
Dupuis and Bagley shared similar views on the county’s role in coordinating with federal immigration officers.
Dupuis said state law does not allow the county to cooperate with federal authorities, adding that the department was not responsible for inquiring about immigration status.
“My personal opinion, when it comes to immigration, is if someone wants to come here to better their lives or for more opportunities, have at it,” Dupuis said. “If you’re going to come and commit crimes that take away from our communities, I do believe in immigration enforcement in that sense.”
Bagley said the county’s partnership with state and federal agencies is important, but agreed that the sheriff’s office had no role in immigration enforcement.

title: CVS to pay $315M over opioid prescriptions in major DOJ settlement
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday.
The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of providing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.”
It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis.
“Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement.
CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.”
The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing.
The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids.
The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden’s administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills,” or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose.
It alleged that poor staffing levels coupled with performance metrics and incentive compensation policies implemented by the company led to pharmacists racing to fill prescriptions without confirming they were legitimate. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says.
Under the settlement, CVS must also “implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement.
Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently.
Most of the settlements -- and dollars -- have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart.
___

title: While helping Maine, Susan Collins failed the nation
text:
John P. Dionne of Bangor formerly worked in construction and spent the last 20 years prior to retirement as the facility manager for a residential vocational training program.
I’ve lived most of my life in Maine, raised on a potato farm in the St. John River Valley in northern Maine. I spent four years in Connecticut going to college, which opened a huge
window of awareness of the world and its complex demographics, some beautiful, others
heartbreaking. 
The year I spent in Iowa as a VISTA volunteer exposed me to dichotomies and similarities of different regions in the United States. While there, I worked with a community action agency, helping the less fortunate and many aged folks to winterize their homes, building and installing passive hot air solar panels to provide them with relief from high energy costs. That was in 1980 and 1981.
Now, 45 years later, we find ourselves facing the same challenges and tribulations we faced when I was a mere 23-year-old spirit looking forward to a good life.
I did vote for Sen. Susan Collins more than once, believing she would uphold these values and advocate for the people of Maine and the United States. Over the last 10 years, however, my respect for her service to this country, its people and international security and prosperity has dwindled.
Whenever I return to northern Maine, where both Sen. Collins and I grew up, I am saddened by the desolation, depression and lack of vitality. Such a crisis exists in many rural areas in this country.
The United State Senate provides equal representation for states regardless of size or demographics. U.S. senators’ primary objective and mission should be to create policies that support the well-being, health, safety and prosperity of the entire nation. Sen. Collins might have thrown a few perks our way, but she and many others have failed the nation.
Sen. Collins has failed to protect the social and civic institutions legally established to benefit the advancement and well-being of Americans. The scaling back of equal opportunity for women is abusive. There are many good public institutions endorsed by altruistic leaders over the past century that are being gutted and attacked.
Sen. Collins has failed to erect guardrails against big business pilfering earthly resources, big- money brokers that celebrate greed over humanitarian values, campaign contributions that soil elections and politics that purposely stoke division instead of embracing national and world harmony.
Sen. Collins and many others have failed to acknowledge the disastrous impact of world climate change and to begin implementing measures to not only mitigate the pain we will suffer but also address how societies can work together to change the momentum and prepare.
Climate change is as much a threat as the risk of nuclear arsenals. It scales worse because eradication of people and communities will happen over time, we will watch, and we will be helpless. What just happened in Nepal is proof, more than 1,400 killed, more than 5,000 people still missing, drowned or buried under a wall of mud. Who’s next?
Sen. Collins has failed to smother the culture of war that persists in this country and across the world. It is still evident in the games our children and even their parents play, glamorized in theaters, marketed by the military-industrial complex as good for the economy, propped up by people of power in the interest of national security to feed fear and retain their influence.
And to our neighbors, friends and family, north, south, east and west, Sen. Collins has compromised American goodwill and common purpose across the world.We can thank Sen. Collins for the early days of her service to the state of Maine.
Obviously, her influence and voice toward righteousness for the nation has been diminished to a whisper. We will need immense corrective action over the next decade and it’s time for better leadership to replace her and many others from both parties.

title: The power of ‘me time’ — why solo time is a gift
text:
(Aging Untold) — A little “me time” isn’t selfish — it can be empowering.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing why solo time gets easier — and more necessary — as we get older, and how to turn alone time into one of life’s most confident experiences.
Why alone time matters more as we age
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck shared a simple benefit of solitude.
“The biggest benefit is you don’t offend anybody else. The biggest benefit is nobody’s going to get mad at you while you’re alone,” Cradduck said.
She emphasized that being alone and feeling lonely are not the same experience.
“You have to understand that being alone and feeling lonely are totally opposite. They’re not the same thing,” Cradduck said.
Even as a self-described extrovert, Cradduck said solo time has become something to look forward to.
“I’m a huge extrovert. I love to be around people, but I actually like being alone. And I embrace the time when I can. And I’m finding the older I get, the more alone time I actually need and want,” she said.
Adjusting to life alone after loss
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke pointed to the example of a long-married couple facing life alone after the death of a spouse.
The transition can come with real anxiety, she said, offering a starting point for anyone adjusting to being on their own.
“I think, what would I tell someone that was in that position — and I’ve had people in that position — is just to ask a friend to help you adjust to life on your own and take really small steps with combining something you enjoy and doing it alone, like if it’s a walk or something,” O’Rourke said.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added that stepping outside a routine built around another person can feel intimidating at first, but that solo time can also offer a kind of relief from the pull of daily obligations.
“Sometimes being able to be alone is really refreshing, you know? Because sometimes I feel like I’m being pulled in all these different areas, so to just be able to have some me time, reflect, it’s really a cool thing,” Rogers said.
A childhood lesson in self-reliance
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose shared a personal story about learning to be comfortable alone at age 10, after walking to a restaurant by herself near a new school.
“I would give myself a pep talk that throughout all my life I would have myself and that I would always be OK alone. Like, promise me you’ll be OK alone and still have fun and still enjoy your life,” Ambrose said.
She said that early habit shaped how she thinks about relationships and independence later in life.
“No matter who’s in the room when you’re born and who’s in the room where you die, you have yourself on the journey. So you may have a spouse, but you really have yourself, and you need to be your own best friend,” Ambrose said.
She also encouraged getting out and trying new things alone as a way to meet people, not avoid them.
“If you go out and you just go out and discover things and do things, you never know when you might meet your next best friend outside yourself. So you’ve got to get out there and mix it up,” Ambrose said.
During a trip by herself to San Francisco, Ambrose started to feel alone, but remembered how she coached herself as a child.
“But my 10-year-old self came through, and I’m like, you’re going to get out there and walk the streets of San Francisco and have a great time. And I did, I made the most out of it,” Ambrose said.
O’Rourke said enjoying alone time isn’t about avoiding people — it’s about self-confidence.
Key takeaways
- Alone and lonely aren’t the same thing. Enjoying solo time doesn’t mean you’re isolated or sad.
- The need for alone time can grow with age. Even committed extroverts may find they want more solo time as they get older.
- Start small when adjusting to life alone. Pairing an enjoyable activity, like a walk, with solo time — and leaning on a friend for support — can ease the transition after a major life change such as losing a spouse.
- Confidence, not avoidance, is the goal. Comfort with solitude is about self-assurance, not about withdrawing from people or relationships.
- Being your own best friend is a lifelong asset. You’re with yourself for the entire journey, even when a spouse or loved ones are present.
- Trying new things alone can open doors. Going out and exploring on your own can lead to unexpected new friendships.

title: AI doomsday fears overshadow current threats, expert says
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Some of the loudest voices in artificial intelligence have warned the technology could someday threaten humanity. A global AI security leader told us those catastrophic headlines are drowning out threats that are already here.
Adam Ely, general manager of AI security at Check Point, a cybersecurity company, said researchers raising alarms about AI are right to call for attention but said the technology does not signal the end of humanity.
“The researchers today are really saying, ‘Hey, let’s be deliberate and pay attention.’ But no, I don’t think this is the end of humanity by any means,” Ely said.
Ely compared the reaction to AI to early fears about automobiles.
“It’s like the people that when cars were first invented said, ‘Wow, this is scary. All humans are going to die.’ And we found safety along the way. Brakes, airbags, crash testing. Technology is very similar,” Ely said.
He said the comparison to cars does not mean AI should go unchecked.
As the technology continues to evolve and becomes a part of daily life, whether directly or indirectly, Ely said we have to think “about what is appropriate and not appropriate.”
His concern is not a far-off doomsday scenario but how AI is already being used.
“We’re seeing more sophisticated groups, and some of this will be military around the world. Some of this will be the most sophisticated cyber crime actors using AI to breach companies and to steal data, to steal money, or even to potentially take down critical infrastructure. Those are real today,” Ely said.
Asked whether an industry pause on AI development is realistic or whether bad actors will keep moving ahead regardless, Ely said we need to find a way to “match pace with safety.”
“Put the right safe guards in place so that they don’t go rogue,” Ely said.
He encouraged people to learn how AI tools work and use them wisely.

title: Op-ed: Maine brewers can make hemp drinks the right way, but Congress is about to stop us
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sebago Brewing Co. was founded in 1998, and today we operate four brewpubs and a production brewery. We have a robust distribution business and our pubs service over 12,000 guests a week. We employ 225 Mainers with a payroll of nearly $5 million a year.
Sebago Brewing is a trusted Maine company that gives back to our communities and has done so for nearly three decades. Our business is built on our core values of quality and value.
A couple of years ago, a guest asked me over the bar when we were going to make a THC [tetrahydrocannabinol] drink.
Around the same time, our sales team started seeing hemp beverages pop up in retail coolers across the state. Several cannabis companies began calling to ask if we could produce drinks for them.
We had just installed a new high-speed canning line and had a team of brewers who understood ingredients, recipes, and quality control, so we listened to our customers and launched Mystic Cove in February 2025.
I grew up on Sebago Lake, where there’s a special place called Mystic Cove. The name has always meant lake life to me, and it felt like the right fit for a drink meant to be enjoyed slowly with friends. We launched with four 5-miligram flavors, including a blueberry lemon that could only come from Maine.
We believe in responsible service and worked with our service staff to implement a THC service policy where a guest who is drinking alcohol could have one Mystic Cove, and two for a guest who is not. Every batch is full-spectrum lab tested, and each packaging run is tested for potency during the run, and nothing ships until the results are in. We track every ingredient from the moment it arrives, so what the label says is exactly what is in the can. We train our distributors and educate our customers because a new product only works when people understand it.
The people who chose these drinks surprised me. The first guest to order one at our brewpub was almost 70 years old. One of our servers, who no longer drinks, told me it was the first time in years she felt like she was having an experience at a bar instead of just ordering an iced tea. These are adults looking for another option alongside beer, wine, and spirits, and they deserve that choice.
Hemp beverages are not the largest part of our business, but they matter a great deal. For an industry facing flat beer sales, two new products gave our distributors and customers something to get excited about. The work also taught us contract production, which has since brought in new brewing contracts. That is real value for a company that has 225 families depending on it.
Imminent ban
Under current federal law, THC drinks will be banned on Dec. 11. The new limit of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container is a ban in all but name, and most of our customers have no idea it is coming. Many of them believe this issue was settled months ago.
When the shelves go empty, Maine retailers and distributors will lose sales, customers will take their business elsewhere and the state will lose tax revenue it could be collecting.
There is a better path forward, and it starts with treating hemp beverages like beer. That means requiring age verification, labeling products clearly, taxing them fairly and selling them through the same distributors and retailers that already handle alcohol responsibly.
The Hemp Beverage Alliance, the national trade group I am a proud member of, is urging Congress toward exactly this kind of framework. Moving these drinks into the cannabis dispensary system would shut out the brewers who have the equipment and experience to make them safely.
Craft beer has been one of this state’s great economic success stories, and hemp beverages can be its next chapter.
Maine brewers are ready to make these products the right way, and I urge lawmakers to regulate this category instead of banning it.

title: Three months after Johan Sebastián’s death, we’re still fighting for the truth
text:
Sean P. Murphy is a former Bronx County and federal prosecutor who fought organized crime and helped lead the Justice Department’s investigation into the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Raised in Vermont and now an attorney at Gideon Asen in Maine, he represents the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
Nearly three months ago, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero left his home in the early morning hours of July 13, 2026. He was thinking, as he did every morning, of the minute he would return to hug his wife, Karolina, and his little girl.
The night before had been like any other. Karolina folded laundry. Johan said he was going to bed. They shared a kiss, and neither had any idea it would be their last.
I never had the privilege of knowing Johan while he was alive. It is an odd and beautiful thing to know a man only through those he left behind.
I came to know him through his parents, Omar and Dora, who traveled from Colombia to collect their son’s body. At the funeral home in Portland, I stepped out of the room, but a mother’s cries over the body of her murdered son pierced the walls. It was a lamentation I never wanted to hear and never want to forget.
I came to know him through his sister, Daniela, who was the first of the family to come to America. Like any older sibling, she carries guilt. Daniela, this is not your fault. We know who is responsible.
And I came to know him through Karolina and his daughter. Karolina’s resilience amazes me. This country has taken so much from her, and I am sorry. To spend two minutes with their little girl is to know that her father’s fire lives on.
Since July, my partner Ben Gideon and I have fought for Johan. Recently, we met with representatives of the Maine Attorney General’s Office, which is the first and only governmental agency to confirm it is investigating the deadly use of force by a federal agent.
At that meeting, we received property found to have no evidentiary value. One item was not returned: his daughter’s car seat. Karolina asked why. She was told that a bullet fired by a federal agent had pierced it, just as bullets fired by a federal agent killed her husband.
Early reports said his daughter was in the car with him. She was not, thank God. But the recklessness is plain, and the horror of what could have been is unthinkable. One tragedy was already too many.
The only justification offered for his death was public safety. You know what actually keeps the public safe? Not shooting innocent, law-abiding fathers whose only dream is to build a better life for their families.
Let’s be clear about what happened here. This administration made a nefarious decision to take a life, and it has met the consequences with silence. A president who wants to be king has decided that the rest of us may be sacrificed for his agenda. He must immediately stop violating our right to life.
Johan was not a citizen, but he was an American in the purest sense of the word. He worked, he loved his family and he dreamed. Anyone who would defend his killing is not a true patriot.
He is not alone. Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo belong to the same club, one whose dues no one would ever choose to pay. Their families are owed answers, not excuses.
But anger rings hollow without hope. Anyone who has lived through a Maine winter knows that even the harshest cold must eventually yield to spring. With the midterm elections approaching, I hope and pray our nation begins charting its path toward that spring. This is not who we are as Americans. We have to do better.
Three months on, Johan’s family is still waiting for truth, justice and accountability. We will not stop fighting until they get it.

title: State says infection control issues at CMMC in Lewiston could jeopardize Medicare agreement
text:
In an investigation of sterile processing contamination issues at Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston in late August, state and federal officials found ongoing infection control deficiencies and said the hospital could be terminated from the Medicare program if they are not resolved by early January.
On Aug. 21, during an investigation of several complaints at the hospital, the state declared that CMMC’s failure to address contamination issues posed an immediate risk to patients. Officials had observed an unknown orange and yellow substance inside four sterile surgical instrument trays marked “ready for use.” All instrument trays that go through the sterile processing department were stained with the same substance, staff confirmed.
This “had been a known issue since 2023,” the department’s staff told state officials.
The Lewiston hospital sent some surgical patients to other hospitals after the state’s finding. The immediate jeopardy situation, “in which a recipient of care has suffered or is likely to suffer serious injury, harm, impairment or death,” was resolved by the afternoon of Aug. 24, but officials from the Maine Department of Health and Human Services and the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) continued investigating the facility and interviewing staff and management about observed issues.
In a written notice to CMMC CEO Allen Stefanek on Oct. 8 detailing the results of that investigation, a CMS enforcement official said “substantial noncompliance remains” with three conditions that allow hospitals to participate in the federal Medicare program, including deficiencies with CMMC’s infection control stewardship, physical environment and governing body.
If the hospital does not comply with the conditions by Jan. 6, 2027, CMS may terminate its Medicare agreement. A CMMC spokesperson said Tuesday the hospital has implemented a plan of correction that includes updated policies, quality audits and ongoing monitoring.
Even so, they said, “we have no evidence that any instrument used in patient care at CMMC was non-sterile or contaminated. CMMC routinely monitors its sterilization processes and equipment, and its surgical site infection rate has consistently remained below the national average.”
According to the investigation report, hospital leadership failed to implement an infection prevention and control program, maintain a clean and sanitary environment, and address infection control findings.
Specifically, officials said, CMMC failed to ensure that supplies used during surgical procedures were sterile, that operating room tables “were free of rust and chipped paint” and that expired supplies were removed from patient care areas, including operating room tubing, tube clamps and airway devices that expired in 2024.
Sanitary issues impacted six out of seven operating rooms, two cardiac operating rooms, the cardiac catheterization lab, the emergency department, common areas and four hospital units, including a rehabilitation ward, the report said.
Staff in the sterile processing department told state investigators they had observed staining in the sterile surgical instrument trays since 2023. When asked how many trays had been returned from the operating room to be reprocessed due to contamination, the department’s manager said: “None, no one turns the trays away. We would have to close the doors due to the prevalence of the issue.”
These issues, and the hospital’s failure to correct them, are of “such character as to substantially limit the hospital’s capacity to furnish adequate care and/or as to adversely affect the health and safety of patients,” the CMS notice said.
The Central Maine Healthcare system includes CMMC, hospitals in Bridgton and Rumford, and several physician practices.
The health system’s infection prevention plan for fiscal year 2025 flagged contamination issues as “high risk” for CMMC’s sterile processing department, also called perioperative services, according to the investigation report.
The health system flagged the same issue in its fiscal year 2026 infection plan.
In 13 CMMC board of directors meetings from fiscal year 2026, there was no discussion of infection control concerns, according to the state’s review of meeting minutes. The most recent meeting was in July. The chair of the board had been absent for three out of five meetings, the state found.
“Regarding concerns in the perioperative and sterile processing department of this magnitude,” the chair told the state in an Aug. 26 interview, “I learned about it during this survey. It came to my knowledge last week.”
Central Maine Healthcare was acquired by California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation in February. In a statement on Sep. 9, a spokesperson said the nonprofit had committed more than $50 million toward replacing Central Maine Healthcare’s electronic medical records system, rebuilding the workforce and improving infrastructure and recruitment.
The spokesperson at the time did not note any investments in the sterile processing department, but said Tuesday that “CMMC continues to invest” in the department and provide oversight as part of an ongoing commitment to quality and safety.
The hospital’s operating rooms are no longer on diversion and have returned to normal operations, the spokesperson said.
The state also identified standard-level deficiencies at Central Maine Healthcare’s outpatient practices, including at Central Maine Obstetrics-Gynecology, where front office staff said they were instructed to turn pregnant patients away due to short staffing and other issues. The state said this was a failure by Central Maine Healthcare to communicate waitlist expectations and provide care to patients in need, as mandated by hospital bylaws.
It’s not uncommon for the state to investigate complaints at Maine’s hospitals. Over the last two years, the state has investigated CMMC 14 other times and identified a handful of standard-level deficiencies, as opposed to the condition-level deficiencies found in August. A complaint investigation from late 2025 even concluded that CMMC was in substantial compliance with infection prevention and control standards.
MaineHealth Maine Medical Center was investigated by the state for complaints 25 times in the same two-year timeframe. St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston was investigated nine times and on one visit the state identified noncompliance with Medicare conditions related to the hospital’s medical staff bylaws.
Noncompliant hospitals have the opportunity to correct deficiencies, but in the meantime, the federal government considers the hospital to be unaccredited and grants full jurisdiction to the state agency to oversee all accreditation complaints and monitoring visits.
This “standard CMS process” is happening at CMMC, said Lindsay Hammes, Maine DHHS spokesperson.
“We are committed to maintaining rigorous sterilization standards, addressing identified opportunities for improvement and ensuring patients receive care in an environment focused on quality and safety,” a CMMC spokesperson said.

title: Judge to decide if Maine serial sex offender is competent for trial
text:
A judge will decide whether a 78-year-old Warren man with a more than 40-year history of sexual assaults is competent to stand trial.
Judge John Martin heard testimony Friday, Oct. 9 in the case of Glenn Reed. Reed is charged with failing to comply with the state’s sex offender registry law for not returning required forms and for moving without notifying law enforcement. He was charged in 2023 but the case has been delayed until a decision was made on his competence to stand trial.
Defense attorney Kayla Alves called one person to testify, Robert Riley of the State Forensic Service which oversees and conducts mental health evaluations of defendants.
Riley said when he interviewed Reed, the man claimed that he has been in regular contact with Sandra Bullock and wanted to get the case cleared up so he could move out of state to be with her.
Assistant District Attorney Christopher Fernald asked the forensics expert on whether Reed could be claiming he believed he had a relationship with Bullock in order to be found incompetent or whether someone could be corresponding with Reed and scamming him.
Riley said he believes that Reed had mild cognitive impairments but did not have dementia. He also said that Reed understands the charge and the court system.
Judge Martin took the matter under advisement.
Reed was last convicted in April 2018 in Waldo County of two counts of unlawful sexual touching in 2016 and was sentenced to 364 days in jail.
Earlier, he had been sentenced to six years and 10 months for sexually assaulting an 11-year-old girl in 2011. He was out on probation when he committed the 2016 assault.
Reed’s history of sexual assault dates back more than 40 years. On multiple occasions he has had convictions delayed or scuttled by mistrials or overturned on appeal. When the convictions have been upheld, suspended sentences and good behavior credits dramatically shortened his time behind bars.
In 1982 he was convicted of raping a 16-year-old girl he picked up in his car in Lincolnville. In that case, Reed offered the girl a ride, then refused to let her out of the car, brought her to his house and sexually assaulted her.
The conviction was overturned by Maine Judicial Supreme Court on grounds that the trial judge should have allowed testimony from Reed that the girl was a voluntary social companion. A second trial ended with a deadlocked jury. After a third trial and failed appeal in 1984, he was convicted and served almost three years in prison.
In 1987, soon after he got out, he was charged with three counts of gross sexual misconduct. One of the allegations was that Reed sexually assaulted a 13-year-old girl whom he was driving to Penobscot Medical Center in Rockport to have casts removed from both arms.
Reed, a lifetime registrant on the Maine Sex Offender Registry, was released on bail after serving 10 months of a 12-year sentence. In 1989, the Maine Supreme Court overturned his conviction on grounds that observations from an expert witness that the victim showed signs of having been abused could not be proven by empirical evidence. The case was eventually dismissed.
In 2013, Reed was sentenced to six months in prison and a year of probation for groping a sales clerk in Belfast. The victim said Reed claimed he was having a bad day and wanted a hug. When she obliged, he groped her and made sexual comments, according to previously published reports.
His 2011 rape of an 11-year-old girl came to light in 2014 when the girl, then 14, wrote about it in a school essay that was turned over to police. Reed was charged, but a mistrial kept him out of jail until 2016 when he negotiated a plea deal for eight years with all but one year suspended.
Reed’s 2016 prison term was stayed for a month so he could have a medical procedure for gallstones.
Reed never had the procedure, and halfway through the month, his stay was revoked after a prescription for 224 oxycodone pills that he filled on the day he was sentenced came up 114 pills short in a random probation check. Reed variously claimed that a dog had knocked them into the toilet and that he himself had knocked them into the toilet after someone walked in on him while he was naked in the bathroom.
A probation officer in 2017 wrote that Reed “does not seem willing or able to stop victimizing people; furthermore, he is not even willing to admit the fact that he is a danger.”
“Based on his performance while on probation,” he wrote, “it seems the only way to manage Mr. Reed and prevent him from victimizing more people will be a full revocation of this probation and long-term incarceration.”

title: Voter registration deadline arrives as new citizens register
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The deadline to register to vote in the midterms ends Tuesday for Kansas, Maine, West Virginia, Oregon and the District of Columbia.
Ninety-eight people born in 50 different countries became American citizens Tuesday morning at the federal courthouse in downtown Washington. The newest citizens navigated interviews, green cards, tests and paperwork to finish the citizenship process - swearing an oath to the U.S. Constitution and flag.
Once out of the courtroom, many completed their first civic duty as Americans and registered to vote. Groups including the League of Women Voters were set up to make the process easy.
Tuesday marks the last day to register in D.C.
According to census data, there are about 174 million registered voters in the U.S. In the last election, 154 million Americans cast ballots.
Some states also allow voters to register at the polls when they go to vote. More information about state registration status is available at vote.org.
