title: Trump administration plans to livestream execution. What parents can do to protect children
text:
(AP) - This is not an article about politics, capital punishment or whether the Fort Hood shooter deserves to be executed in public for his crimes.
Instead, it’s focused on the unprecedented parental challenge of handling the near-certain prospect that children will hear of or see footage of the Dec. 3 U.S. execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan if the Trump administration follows through with plans to livestream the event.
The danger stretches beyond the broadcast itself, because history shows graphic video from the event could be clipped, copied and pushed into children’s social feeds even if the original stream is restricted.
Experts suggest that grownups who care about children start by setting aside matters of politics and public policy — like the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections and the debate over capital punishment. Focus instead on how witnessing someone’s death by firing squad might land with young viewers — and how best to reassure and protect them.
Here are some guidelines that might help.
Keep empathy for kids in mind — and facts at hand
Mis- and disinformation reach children, too. It’s important for parents to have credibility with them, especially because their real, unspoken question might be: Are we safe? Have in hand some basic facts about the case and state them gently.
“It will be easier to have a position, share your family’s values, and discuss things with a potentially overwhelmed child once you’ve taken the time to gather accurate, up-to-date info and assess your child’s needs,” according to Common Sense Media, which advises parents on entertainment and technology.
Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. A few days later, the Pentagon announced the event would be livestreamed.
“People need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people there in 2009 when he walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961.
The last widely recognized public execution took place on Aug. 14, 1936. Kentucky, the last state to permit them, outlawed the practice in 1938.
Stay updated on the plans
Also, experts suggest, parents should stay updated on how a livestreamed execution would unfold. Many questions remained unanswered, such as whether the moment of death and its aftermath will be shown, whether any age restrictions will apply, and whether there will be a broadcast delay or a threshold for stopping the feed.
Be informed about the technology involved. While the government often uses YouTube to carry its livestreams, including those embedded within government websites, YouTube prohibits content that is “violent or gory” and “intended to shock or disgust viewers,” and doesn’t allow livestreams that show someone holding, handling or transporting a firearm.
YouTube does make exceptions in select cases for content it deems to be in an educational, documentary, scientific or artistic context or that it determines to be in the public’s interest. In such cases, the content may be age-restricted. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding how its policies relate to the execution.
But the danger to kids spills beyond the live broadcast to unexpected exposure on social media in the form of memes, for example.
It’s unclear whether the Trump administration is considering children in its decision-making. Emails over two days asking White House spokespeople for thoughts from the president and first lady Melania Trump on the prospect of children seeing the execution went unanswered. Trump said that he’ll soon make a decision on the plan to livestream the event.
Assume kids will at least hear about the execution, if not see it
From the old-fashioned grapevine to social media, grisly news has a way of reaching school-aged children, experts agree. Consider their need for calm and age-appropriate guidance, they suggest.
“With young kids, parents should keep it short and focus on reassurance over explaining the events,” said Jill Murphy, chief content officer at Common Sense Media. “Reassure them that they are safe. With teens, ask honestly what they have heard first, then ask whether they need to watch it.”
Remember you are your child’s parent, not their friend — and don’t overexplain, advises Dr. David Rosenberg, chair of psychiatry and behavioral neurosciences at Wayne State University School of Medicine in Michigan. Answer the questions children ask, and don’t be afraid to assert parental authority by, for example, restricting or banning a child’s access to the footage.
“It’s okay to say, ‘I don’t have all the answers. But here’s what we know, you’re safe, you’re secure, this is what we believe,’” Rosenberg said.
“Where parents get into trouble is when they talk too much, and they usually do that because they’re anxious and insecure,” he added. ”What makes a child feel safest, or an adolescent, is can I count on my parents to be calm in challenging situations and give me the information I need?”
Choosing to watch the footage, one physician said, doesn’t necessarily indicate a child is psychologically ready to do so.
Timothy Lesaca, a Pittsburgh-area psychiatrist, cited a series of studies showing that repeatedly watching footage of events like the Boston Marathon bombings, at least part of an ISIS beheading video and the Oklahoma City bombing can be linked to post-traumatic stress, if not PTSD, in adults and children. He argues that making Hasan’s execution public is a medical and public health issue.
“Ongoing anxiety, trouble sleeping or problems with daily life should be taken seriously,” Lesaca wrote in KevinMD.com, an online publication by physicians.
Watch how this event interacts with existing conditions
The people most at risk of negative long-term effects are those who already have clinical depression or anxiety, or who have already been exposed to other traumatic situations, Rosenberg said. That’s because repeat exposure to trauma can cause cumulative damage.
The part of the brain that handles executive decision-making, emotional regulation, impulsivity and empathy doesn’t finish developing until around age 24, and so parents should consider having proactive conversations even with their older children who may be away at college or living on their own, Rosenberg said.
“We have to at least offer help in these circumstances to be the leaders, to be the decision-makers, to at least help them make informed decisions.”
___
Associated Press journalist Kaitlyn Huamani contributed.

title: Selma Blair Charged With Assault Following Incident on Plane
text:
Selma Blair Charged With Assault Following Plane Incident
Legally Blonde and Hellboy star Selma Blair has been charged with assault following an incident earlier this week on a Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York.
According to TMZ, Blair was arrested and charged after allegedly “punching one flight attendant and biting another in the middle of the flight” headed to John F. Kennedy Airport.
They claim that following the flight’s arrival in New York, “2 flight attendants reported injuries and one was taken to the hospital.” Blair herself was taken to the hospital, and then subsequently arrested. Per TMZ again, “when Blair was in the ambulance en route to the hospital, she repeatedly kicked a Port Authority police officer in the head.”
READ MORE: The Best Movies of 2026 So Far
Blair’s biggest roles include performances in the films Cruel Intentions, The Sweetest Thing, A Dirty Shame, and Storytelling, and she’s appeared in TV series like Anger Management, Kath & Kim, Lost in Space, Heathers, and The People vs. O.J. Simpson. She had a prior incident on a plane in 2016, an outburst which she later attributed to a “total psychotic blackout.”
“It was horrible and frightening and I had empathy for myself actually afterwards because it was actually so out of character for me, especially because I’m a mother,” Blair said in an interview in 2016, several months after the incident.
Blair’s representative told TMZ “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.” According to Variety, Blair has already been released on $20,000 bail.

title: Daffodils, garlic, and tulips — oh my! A guide to fall bulbs
text:
I like to plant hardy bulbs in October. They’re low-maintenance, can come back year after year, and their spring foliage and flowers feel uniquely special — like a gift you planted for yourself the fall before.
According to Michigan State University Extension, a true bulb is an underground storage organ that helps a plant survive unfavorable growing conditions, by storing carbohydrates for future growth when conditions improve. Daffodils, tulips, and garlic are all examples of plants that grow from true bulbs. Many hardy bulbs need a period of winter cold to grow and flower properly in spring.

title: Officers save 2-year-old girl’s birthday after scam leaves her father broke
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - Two Phoenix police officers responded to reports of a scam that left a father penniless days before his 2-year-old daughter’s birthday – then used their own money to buy her presents, moving him to tears.
Officers Alessandro Figuccio and Tanner Schnieder, partners at the Phoenix Police Department’s Cactus Park Precinct, have worked together for about a year. Their paths to policing were different: Figuccio said becoming an officer was a childhood dream, while Schnieder was a truck driver before he decided to change careers.
About two months ago, the officers reviewed their call log and saw a call that stood out. A man who said he worked for DoorDash got a call that appeared to come from the company, Figuccio said. The caller told him his account had been deactivated and directed him to enter a code at a kiosk to reactivate it.
Soon after, the man’s last paycheck was gone.
Officers step in to help
Figuccio and Schnieder went to the man’s house to take his report on the scam, and after hearing his story, they decided to do something more for him. The interaction was caught on their body-worn cameras.
The man told the officers he had just paid his rent and car payment and had nothing left, Figuccio said. His 2-year-old daughter’s birthday was the next day.
“He had his daughter sitting there in a high chair, eating, and he’s just starting to break down to us,” Schneider said. “I look in, see his daughter, and then, it hits me.”
The officers drove to a store, where they filled a cart with clothes and toys for the toddler. They also picked out a small pink bicycle with tassels for her to ride when she gets older.
“We just started throwing stuff in the cart,” Schnieder said. “We’re like, dude, if I was his daughter, I’d be happy as heck.”
The officers paid for the items themselves and brought them back to the family’s home. Schnieder said the father began to cry when he saw the bicycle. He then gave the officers a hug.
“It’s rewarding, especially since I knew he had no money left,” Figuccio said.
For Schnieder, the gesture was personal. He said his family had been in a difficult position before, and he wanted to help someone who needed it.
The officers’ response was a small act of kindness in a difficult moment and another way to serve their community together.

title: Here’s who’s on the ballot for Saco school board
text:
Voting in the Nov. 3 election has begun in Maine, and in Saco, residents will be filling three school board seats in addition to other local, state and federal races.
Two newcomers are vying for seats on the school board, saying there isn’t enough teacher representation on the current board.
(Click here to read about the municipal races in Saco.)
Here’s who’s on the ballot in each ward.
WARD 2
In Ward 2, voters will choose between incumbent Jennifer Preble and newcomer Arianna Parks. Ward 2 covers the area closest to Scarborough, including Saco Heath Preserve.
Preble, a licensed social worker whose father taught at Thornton Academy, is seeking her third consecutive term on the board. She serves as vice chair and previously served as chair.
In her response to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Preble said her priorities are making sure that Saco has educational programming that fits students’ needs and equity for all students, especially students living in poverty.
Preble also highlighted adequate and balanced funding as a priority, noting that Saco families are “feeling the cost of everything” these days.
Parks, a special education professional, said she is running for office because she believes special education students and staff deserve a stronger voice in Saco.
Parks listed her priorities as addressing the high turnover rate among ed techs and examining the subcontracting of special education professionals and how it affects students, staff and consistency of care.
WARD 4
Voters in Ward 4 only have one candidate on the November ballot: Donald Pilon, a real estate broker who served as Saco’s mayor from 2013 to 2015 and served four terms as a Democrat representing the area in House District 131.
In his response to the voter guide, Pilon said his priorities are ensuring staffing levels are sufficient to keep educators’ workloads manageable, making responsible financial decisions and providing professional development opportunities for school board members.
Pilon said he is running for the school board because the education of Saco students is “the most important charge” of city government, and he believes his experience in state and local government will help support to the board’s mission.
Current Ward 4 school board member Kevin Roche is not seeking reelection. Ward 4 covers the oceanfront section of Saco.
WARD 6
In Ward 6, voters will choose between incumbent Sarah Truman and newcomer Maureen “Moe” Cahill. Ward 6 covers part of downtown.
Truman, a photographer whose mother was an educator, has served on the board since 2020. She was elected board chair in 2025.
In her response to the voter guide, Truman said her top priorities are seeing construction of the new elementary school through to completion, keeping the budget balanced, and ensuring equity for all students. Truman added that she hopes to champion meaningful raises for staff while maintaining a balanced budget for taxpayers.
Cahill, an occupational therapist who has worked in Cape Elizabeth schools for 24 years, said she has heard a strong desire for thoughtful leadership and a willingness to see positive change in Saco schools.

On Election Day, Buxton residents can vote in person from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the Buxton Town Office, 185 Portland Road.

Buxton voters approved a referendum question in June to establish a charter commission to revise Buxton’s municipal charter. In November, voters will elect members to that commission.
Eleven candidates are vying for the commission’s six seats. The candidates are Debra Bickford, Meegan Diconzo, Clifford Emery, Julie Gamelson, William Hall, Mary Macleod, Michael Pettis, Henry Sheedy, Emily Weyrauch, Beverly Young and Kevin Young.
MAINE SENATE & HOUSE
Buxton voters will decide between three-term incumbent Democrat Donna Bailey and Republican Scott Benedetto Eccleston for State Senate District 31.
In Maine House District 137, which covers most of Buxton and Hollis, incumbent Republican Nathan Carlow is seeking a third term, facing Democrat Charles Tilburg. The northern area of Buxton falls under Maine House District 138, where Republican former Maine State House District 22 Rep. Jonathan Lee Kinney is running against Democrat Oliver McAvoy.
YORK COUNTY RACES
Democrat Bobby Mills is running unopposed for York County treasurer, incumbent Wendy Caiazzo is the sole candidate for York County register of deeds, and the race for county commissioner forYork District 3 is also uncontested, with Justin Chenette up for a second term.
Incumbent and Democrat William King and Republican David Corbett are running for York County sheriff. Chief Deputy of the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office Brian Pellerin will also appear on the ballot, but he ended his campaign in September.

title: Death Notice: William H. Harmon
Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House
text:
A federal judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking the Trump administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the news organizations as the extraordinary case pitting the president against the media that cover him makes its way through the legal system.
In a victory for media organizations at a time when tension between the White House and journalists is high, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in their constitutional free speech and due process claims.
“Still,” he added in his late-night order, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
Kelly agreed with the plaintiffs that the national security arguments came after the fact and were unsupported by the administration. But the judge wrote that without a preliminary injunction the outlets “are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor.”
An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case on behalf of the administration, was not immediately returned.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge’s ruling.
“When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.”
Judge says no warning given before banishment
Kelly said that, “to put it mildly,” the White House didn’t give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before President Donald Trump’s Sept. 18 social media post about their bans.
“The revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes matters a lot as to how, whether, and to what extent they can do their jobs,” he wrote. “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before,”
Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations.
Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard pass” press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo while the case is pending.
Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary
Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized their reporting as “fake news.” Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C.
Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump’s move as “unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional” under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it’s illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn’t like the content of their reporting.
“The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” plaintiffs’ lawyers wrote.
Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege — not a right — and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation.
“The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President,” Justice Department attorneys wrote. “Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration.”

title: Longtime Portland boys basketball coach Joe Russo retires
text:
Joe Russo has retired as Portland High’s boys basketball coach.
Russo, 69, had been weighing the decision to retire for months — his friends and fellow coaches would say years. On Tuesday he made it public.
“I handed in my resignation. I sat and had a good conversation with Spencer (Allen, the Portland athletic director),” Russo said Tuesday evening. “Something is telling me this is the right time.
“The truth is, I still enjoy it. I wish I could do it forever. But I knew I would have to give it up sometime. When do I pass the torch? And I just said, ‘maybe this is the time.'”
A Portland native, Russo coached the Bulldogs for 36 seasons and won his sixth state championship with the program in February, guiding a gritty, defense-oriented team that lost six regular-season games while dealing with injuries, sickness, and players staying away from practice during a large-scale immigration enforcement operation.
“There’s not many leaders out there who could have navigated all of that and keep teenagers focused,” said South Portland boys basketball coach Kevin Millington.
Millington said he used to joke that “this was the 15th straight year (Russo) had said he was done but I always felt this year was different. Not because they had won (the championship) but because of the way he said it.”
Russo said that his final game being a state championship win had little to do with his decision.
“I never really coached for championships. I always coached to be competitive, for the players to be the best they can, and give a good effort,” Russo said. “When I do look back, it won’t be the last year I won. It will be that I’ve been very fortunate to have 36 great years,” at Portland.
Russo’s boys basketball teams won 517 games, including 11 over his first three seasons at Bonny Eagle. At Portland, he also helped start and coach the Portland girls volleyball program.
In 2018, the same year Russo was inducted into the Maine Basketball Hall of Fame, he overcame non-Hodgkin Large B Cell Lymphoma cancer. Russo was back coaching both volleyball and boys basketball in the 2018-19 school year.
Russo said he is healthy and that was not a factor in his decision to retire.
Russo won his 500th game in a AA North quarterfinal in 2025. That made him the 10th coach in Maine high school basketball history to reach the mark. He is now sixth on the all-time wins list.
After the Bulldogs defeated Camden Hills to win the 2026 Class A title, Russo indicated to friends, peers, and other acquaintances that he had probably just coached his last game.
He had made similar statements for at least a decade, usually in the muted light of a Cross Insurance Arena hallway after Portland had been eliminated. Russo would look tired and worn down. Then he would take a couple of weeks to think about it and by the next season would be back on Portland’s sideline.
Last season felt different. The Bulldogs won a state title and Russo was beaming. In mid-summer, Russo was still waiting to make his retirement final but also saying he was 98% sure he was done. He was letting his assistant coaches run the summer program.
As late as mid-September, Allen, the Portland AD, said he figured each day that passed increased the odds that Russo would return as Portland’s coach. Allen joked that on the days Russo was at the high school as a part-time physical education teacher he would try to avoid crossing paths with Russo.
“If he doesn’t see me he can’t give me his resignation,” Allen said.
As recently as last week, Russo said he was tempted to keep coaching, “because our freshmen are dynamite.”
The first day of practice for the 2026-27 season is Nov. 16, less than five weeks away.
Possible in-program successors as head coach would be top assistant Dan LeGage, a former head coach at Westbrook, and long-time assistant Joe Johnson. Russo’s longest tenured assistant Joe Giordano has indicated previously that he planned to step aside whenever Russo retired.
Russo said there are a “lot of qualified people,” who could succeed him, including several in “our own building.” He added that because he’ll likely know so many of the candidates he doesn’t want to be involved in the hiring process.
Russo was born on Dec. 7, 1956, the same day as Boston Celtics legend Larry Bird. Russo and his family moved from a different Portland neighborhood to Munjoy Hill when he was in third grade. The new house had a basketball hoop.
“So I started playing it. I played all the way through college and rec leagues. I studied the game,” Russo said. A point guard known for his defense, Russo said he was often referred to as “peppery,” by Portland sportscaster Frank Fixaris.
After graduating from Portland High in 1975, Russo earned a degree and played basketball at UMaine Presque Isle. He started his teaching and coaching career at Bonny Eagle, a job he enjoyed, but he and his wife Donna, who met in junior high and began dating as high school juniors, both wanted to stay in Portland. The Russos have been married 46 years. They have three grown children and nine grandchildren.
After his 500th win, Russo talked about what it meant to him to teach and coach at Portland High.
“When this job (at Portland) came, it was the dream job, pretty much,” Russo said. “Mainly because being from Portland and going to Portland High, you’re happy for the players. I was just like them growing up. So it means a lot when you’re doing it for the school you grew up in. I’m happy for the city and the school and the kids.”
Russo’s Portland teams won state championships in 1999, 2004, 2014, 2016, 2017, and 2026, and finished as state runner-up in 2007, 2015, and 2023.
The 2016, 2017, and 2023 state finals were against South Portland.
“From a basketball perspective, Joe’s teams were always an elite defensive team,” Millington said. “The other thing he’s really elite at is, he’s very patient. Maybe that comes with age. He wasn’t trying to win the state championship in the first game or the fifth game and they were always much better at the end of the year than they were in the beginning.”

title: Mainers are in for a harsh winter— thanks to Republicans
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rep. Chellie Pingree is the U.S. congresswoman for Maine’s 1st District.
Between the mountains of snow, the waves of bitter cold and the occasional Nor’easter, we
Mainers are no strangers to harsh winters.
This winter could be one of the hardest in recent memory. And not because of the weather. The statewide average price of heating oil just hit a record $6.02 a gallon. As of Sept. 28, it was still averaging $5.96 — up nearly 79% from the same week last year. At today’s price, a 250-gallon fill-up costs about $1,490 — an expense many Maine families will face more than once this winter.
Meanwhile, gas prices are hovering around $4.40 per gallon as of Sept. 25, according to
Maine Public.
As if all this wasn’t awful enough, the number of Mainers receiving assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has fallen by 13% — 13,000 people in all, including 7,000 children. Another 31,000 Mainers are projected to lose MaineCare coverage over the next year.
Add it all up and this winter is going to put an enormous strain on Maine families — especially those who can least afford it.
This looming crisis is the result of choices President Trump and congressional Republicans made. Choices they continue to defend.
Let’s back up to July 4, 2025, when the president signed his hallmark legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, into law.
The “Big Ugly Bill” is a more accurate name. It slashed Medicaid by $1.2 trillion and SNAP by $211 billion over the next decade, all while handing hundreds of billions of dollars in tax breaks to the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations.
Far from offsetting those devastating cuts, the Big Ugly Bill’s ludicrous tax breaks are projected to increase federal deficits by $4.6 trillion, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also handed $175 billion to the Department of Homeland Security, helping turbocharge the Trump administration’s cruel immigration enforcement agenda and bringing chaos and violence to communities across the country. That includes Maine, where an ICE agent shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13.
The young father was not the target of ICE’s operation that morning. He had no criminal history, and we don’t have body camera footage of the shooting. His family has still not been contacted by the federal government and is still waiting for a full accounting of what happened.
This bill will go down as one of the most irresponsible, destructive, and costly pieces of legislation in American history. Not just in terms of its fiscal recklessness, but its human toll as well: nearly 13 million fewer people enrolled in Medicaid by 2034 and roughly 2.4 million fewer people receiving SNAP in an average month, according to CBO estimates. Its consequences will reach every community in America, in shuttered rural hospitals, overwhelmed food banks and increased costs for state and local governments.
The Big Ugly Bill alone would have been devastating enough for Maine. Then Trump’s reckless, unauthorized war of choice in Iran has kicked every one of these crises into overdrive. In the nearly eight months since the war began — a conflict Trump insisted wouldn’t last more than a few weeks — the global economy has been thrown into turmoil.
The on-again, off-again closure of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, has sent energy prices skyrocketing — and disrupted the flow of goods around the world. When the world’s energy supply gets squeezed, everyone pays more. In a state like Maine, where a colder-than-average winter can mean the difference between keeping the heat on and putting on extra layers just to stay warm, the potential consequences are catastrophic.
None of this had to happen. These crises have been created or made worse by Trump’s policies — and by congressional Republicans’ refusal to push back on the president and stand up for their constituents.
And now, with Americans staring down record energy costs, Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home early for a seven-week campaign recess. Rather than staying to work on the many challenges facing our nation, Republicans tucked tail and left.
Republicans could’ve chosen to help you. They chose to help the already-rich get even richer — and to give an army of masked, heavily armed and utterly unaccountable ICE agents virtually unlimited resources to terrorize our communities.
My Democratic colleagues and I have been fighting them every step of the way. We’ve voted against these devastating cuts. We’ve introduced legislation to protect healthcare and food assistance. We’ve demanded accountability for an administration that continues to put its deeply unpopular agenda ahead of the people it’s supposed to serve.
And we are demanding action on the heating crisis: end the war in Iran, protect the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, reverse changes to the Home Owner Managing Energy Savings Rebates and High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate programs and reinstate the energy efficiency tax credits Republicans eliminated. Speaker Johnson should call the House back to Washington so Congress can get to work.
We will keep fighting — at every turn, and for as long as it takes. Because Mainers deserve better. They deserve a government that makes their lives more affordable — not one that cuts their healthcare and food assistance, sends energy prices through the roof and hands massive tax breaks to the people who need them least.
Mainers have survived plenty of hard winters. But the hardships coming this winter are the result of decisions made by Republicans in Washington, who would rather leave town than fix the problems they created.

title: Springvale BMV location to close for up to 6 months
text:
The Springvale Bureau of Motor Vehicles location will temporarily close its doors beginning on Nov. 20.
Jana Spaulding, a spokesperson for the Secretary of State’s Office, which oversees the BMV, said the closure is to complete “much-needed renovations” to the facility for customers and employees.
Spaulding said the closure is expected to last up to six months. That would tentatively place a reopening around mid-May.
In the meantime, customers can utilize the BMV online portal for a number of services, including title replacements, accessing driving records and purchasing duplicate vehicle registrations.
For services not offered online, residents are encouraged to visit the nearest BMV locations in Kennebunk and Scarborough and to make appointments online to save time. Spaulding also said some AAA locations may be able to provide services, like certain driver’s license and identification renewals.
The Secretary of State’s Office information will release more information about reopening once the renovation nears its completion.

title: Come for Heather Cox Richardson, stay for Troy Jackson
text:
I went to Portland to see Heather Cox Richardson in conversation with Troy Jackson. Really, I was there to see Richardson. Troy was the price I had to pay to see her.
I planned to vote for Troy because he is not Susan Collins. Knowing little about Aroostook County, I had not felt a strong allegiance to him. He warmed quickly and found firm ground.
What I gleaned about Troy: He’s not shiny or sparkly. Good. I don’t like the shiny and sparkly politicians. Instead, Troy is a piece of beautiful hardwood with a warm patina. Once he loosened up, I found genuine Maine charm that comes from being a part of the community of Maine, a straight talker who speaks directly to issues of great concern to me: Medicaid and Medicare for all; affordable, quality childcare with childcare workers who earn a living wage, an education system that pays teachers and teaches students and an end to the war in Iran.
I came away from Portland forgetting that HCR had been there. I am now excited to vote Jackson for senator.

title: Three months after Johan Sebastián’s death, we’re still fighting for the truth
text:
Sean P. Murphy is a former Bronx County and federal prosecutor who fought organized crime and helped lead the Justice Department’s investigation into the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Raised in Vermont and now an attorney at Gideon Asen in Maine, he represents the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
Nearly three months ago, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero left his home in the early morning hours of July 13, 2026. He was thinking, as he did every morning, of the minute he would return to hug his wife, Karolina, and his little girl.
The night before had been like any other. Karolina folded laundry. Johan said he was going to bed. They shared a kiss, and neither had any idea it would be their last.
I never had the privilege of knowing Johan while he was alive. It is an odd and beautiful thing to know a man only through those he left behind.
I came to know him through his parents, Omar and Dora, who traveled from Colombia to collect their son’s body. At the funeral home in Portland, I stepped out of the room, but a mother’s cries over the body of her murdered son pierced the walls. It was a lamentation I never wanted to hear and never want to forget.
I came to know him through his sister, Daniela, who was the first of the family to come to America. Like any older sibling, she carries guilt. Daniela, this is not your fault. We know who is responsible.
And I came to know him through Karolina and his daughter. Karolina’s resilience amazes me. This country has taken so much from her, and I am sorry. To spend two minutes with their little girl is to know that her father’s fire lives on.
Since July, my partner Ben Gideon and I have fought for Johan. Recently, we met with representatives of the Maine Attorney General’s Office, which is the first and only governmental agency to confirm it is investigating the deadly use of force by a federal agent.
At that meeting, we received property found to have no evidentiary value. One item was not returned: his daughter’s car seat. Karolina asked why. She was told that a bullet fired by a federal agent had pierced it, just as bullets fired by a federal agent killed her husband.
Early reports said his daughter was in the car with him. She was not, thank God. But the recklessness is plain, and the horror of what could have been is unthinkable. One tragedy was already too many.
The only justification offered for his death was public safety. You know what actually keeps the public safe? Not shooting innocent, law-abiding fathers whose only dream is to build a better life for their families.
Let’s be clear about what happened here. This administration made a nefarious decision to take a life, and it has met the consequences with silence. A president who wants to be king has decided that the rest of us may be sacrificed for his agenda. He must immediately stop violating our right to life.
Johan was not a citizen, but he was an American in the purest sense of the word. He worked, he loved his family and he dreamed. Anyone who would defend his killing is not a true patriot.
He is not alone. Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo belong to the same club, one whose dues no one would ever choose to pay. Their families are owed answers, not excuses.
But anger rings hollow without hope. Anyone who has lived through a Maine winter knows that even the harshest cold must eventually yield to spring. With the midterm elections approaching, I hope and pray our nation begins charting its path toward that spring. This is not who we are as Americans. We have to do better.
Three months on, Johan’s family is still waiting for truth, justice and accountability. We will not stop fighting until they get it.

title: Hannaford app, website offline as parent company addresses security issue
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford’s website and mobile app have been temporarily shut down as the supermarket chain’s parent company addresses a cybersecurity issue.
Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch company that owns the Scarborough-based grocer, said in a brief news release Monday that it was experiencing an internal network issue and had taken some systems offline to protect them.
That includes the Hannaford app and website, both of which carried messages Tuesday morning that they were unavailable.
Stores remain open as usual, and any unfulfilled online orders will be refunded.
The company said Tuesday that the measures were precautionary and that, although the investigation is ongoing, there is no evidence to suggest that customer or employee data was compromised.
A November 2024 breach of Ahold Delhaize’s systems affected more than 95,000 Mainers — most of them current or former employees, Hannaford said — and over 2 million people worldwide.
Ahold Delhaize did not provide a timeline for when online service was expected to be restored but said teams are “working with urgency” and were starting controlled relaunches of some systems. A Hannaford spokesperson reiterated that the company is working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.
“We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate our customers’ patience and understanding,” Hannaford spokesperson Caitlin Cortelyou said in a written statement Tuesday.
Ahold Delhaize says it has contacted outside cybersecurity experts to help with its response and is “engaging with the appropriate authorities” as necessary.
“As the investigation is ongoing, we are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts,” the company added.
If the cybersecurity issue is deemed to have been a data breach, then Maine law requires it to be reported to the Office of the Maine Attorney General. The office did not immediately respond to an email Tuesday asking whether it had received any reports about this issue.
Ahold Delhaize is one of the world’s largest food retailers and operates more than 2,000 U.S. stores under several brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant Food.
This is a developing story.

title: Student hit after sedan passes stopped school bus, sheriff’s office says
text:
BATTLE GROUND, Wash. (KPTV/Gray News) — A child sustained minor injuries Monday morning when a sedan passed a stopped school bus and hit the student while crossing the road, according to authorities in Washington.
Clark County Sheriff’s Office deputies responded around 8:51 a.m. to NE Allworth Road for the crash.
Investigators said a school bus stopped to pick up an elementary school student. As the child began crossing, a sedan traveling in the opposite direction slowed but did not stop. The sedan’s front passenger-side corner hit the child, who fell to the ground.
The driver stopped immediately and cooperated with investigators. The driver was ticketed for passing a stopped school bus.
The sheriff’s office reminds drivers to stop for school buses when required by law. Failing to stop can result in a fine of more than $400.

title: Father of 5 killed in home by bullet believed fired by hunter, deputies say
text:
SWEET HOME, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A 54-year-old man was killed Saturday when a bullet passed through his home, according to authorities in Oregon.
The Linn County Sheriff’s Office believes the shot came from a nearby hunter.
Deputies found a partially dressed deer near where the shots were fired, Sheriff Michelle Duncan said.
The hunter left the scene. It is unclear whether the hunter knew Robert Church had been hit.
Church leaves behind five children. His daughter, Shy, said her father “was one of a kind” and “loved his children more than anything in the world.”
Neighbors said the area is popular for hunting and that the shooting happened on private property. They urged hunters to follow the rules and be aware of where they are shooting.
Duncan said investigators do not believe the shooting was intentional and urged the hunter to come forward so Church’s family can get answers and closure.
Church’s family started an online fundraiser to help with funeral expenses. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Linn County Sheriff’s Office.

title: 3 takeaways from the 3rd Maine Senate debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The third U.S. Senate debate between Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican incumbent Susan Collins didn’t break much new ground, though the candidates did sharpen their responses to questions about affordability, the Iran war and tariffs.
But Tuesday’s debate did provide a few striking moments, and some new substance. Both Collins and Jackson further elucidated their stances on data centers, saying they supported some form of regulation on where the centers could be located, and on how much water and electricity they use.
Polls show a tight race between the 73-year-old Collins and 58-year-old Jackson in Maine’s pivotal Senate race.
Here are three moments that stood out from their third meeting in a week. They will meet again Thursday for their final debate.
1. They got under each other’s skin
Collins provoked a strong reaction from Jackson about halfway through the debate. The Republican said “once again, Troy is confusing the Medicaid program with the Medicare program.” She proceeded to lecture him about the difference: Medicare largely goes to the elderly; Medicaid largely goes to the poor and sick.
Jackson grew visibly agitated in his response, saying that he understood the issue well because he had visited four birthing centers that have closed recently.
“Don’t act like I don’t know what I’m talking about, because I do,” Jackson said.
At another point, Jackson returned the favor. After Collins raised the issue of Medicaid fraud, the Democrat brought up recent ProPublica reporting about the FBI investigating whether Collins’ orbit was steering federal funding to a defense contractor and donor.
“I’m shocked that you’re talking about fraud, because there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the FBI,” he said. (The ProPublica story said that the FBI had been gearing to investigate Collins, but the bureau has never accused her of fraud.)
Collins didn’t respond at the time, but brought it back up later after Jackson said she does the bidding of billionaires.
“Troy has repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long,” she said. “He lied when he said that I was under investigation and found to have committed fraud by the FBI. And I just cannot continue to ignore these attacks on my integrity.”
At yet another point, Collins noted that Jackson has not yet filed a campaign finance report, which would show who his donors are. (Jackson entered the race after the last quarterly reporting period ended on June 30.)
The next round of reports are due by midnight on Thursday, but Jackson offered to release his early.
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning. How about that? Is that enough?” Jackson said. “Because we see yours and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me … I’ll give you the report tomorrow and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday.”
2. Collins finds differences in agreement
At several points, Collins deployed a new strategy to highlight her experience — and it came when the candidates seemed to agree on an issue.
Jackson has repeatedly hit Collins for advancing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which extended tax cuts for the wealthy and slashed $1 trillion in public health funding. Many of the cuts will take effect after the midterms.
But Collins noted that she voted against enacting the bill, which became law in 2025 after Vice President JD Vance broke a tie in the Senate. Despite her vote, she touted her ability to ensure that a $50 billion fund was included to help rural hospitals.
“Troy would have never been able to get that into the bill,” Collins said.
Jackson noted that the funding Maine would receive because of Collins’ amendment pales in comparison to the cuts.
Collins deployed the same tactic later when it came to Canadian tariffs, which both candidates oppose.
“The bottom line is that Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs,” she said. “But here’s the key difference: I’ve been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list. Troy would have gotten nothing.”
Jackson protested, noting that he’s been in contact with the Canadian ambassador and the consulate in Boston. But Collins made it clear she was referring to the Trump administration.
“Well, it wasn’t the Canadians that started this problem — it was the Trump administration,” she said.
3. Jackson leans into ICE shooting in Biddeford
Jackson came into the debate planning to make an issue of Collins’ votes to fund U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Tuesday was the three-month anniversary of federal agents fatally shooting Johan Sebastián Guerrero in Biddeford.
But he had to wait for the end of the debate to do it.
Jackson criticized Collins for supporting $70 billion in new funding for ICE and other agencies. He called ICE a “rogue agency” that needs to be abolished, with immigration enforcement being shifted to U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the FBI.
Collins, however, noted that she was able to include several reforms in the funding bill, including $20 million for body-worn cameras and de-escalation training.
“But more needs to be done,” she said.
Jackson pounced on Collins’ contention that some ICE agents are properly vetted and trained.
“I don’t know how you could stand up here and argue that it’s a good thing to let them out onto our population, out onto the American public, when we’ve seen consistently that they will murder people if you don’t comply explicitly with them,” Jackson said.

title: Car rolls, woman seriously injured in chase with deputies Monday in Auburn
text:
A woman was seriously injured late Monday after the vehicle she was in went off Minot Avenue in Auburn during a chase with police, went into a ditch and rolled over onto its roof, according to authorities.
Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office and Auburn Police Department are investigating the crash that started when a deputy attempted to stop the vehicle for an alleged traffic violation, according to William Gagne, chief deputy for Androscoggin County.
The driver of the vehicle failed to stop in Poland near the Minot line about 10:45 p.m., Gagne said, and kept going into Auburn. Along the 1600 block of Minot Avenue near the John Deere dealership, it appeared the driver lost control of the vehicle, which went off the road and rolled over.
A female in the vehicle was taken to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston by Auburn Fire Rescue Department personnel and later taken to Maine Medical Center in Portland with serious, possibly life-threatening injuries, Gagne said.
Authorities released no additional information as of early Tuesday evening.
County deputies and Auburn police continue to investigate the incident, Gagne said.

title: While helping Maine, Susan Collins failed the nation
text:
John P. Dionne of Bangor formerly worked in construction and spent the last 20 years prior to retirement as the facility manager for a residential vocational training program.
I’ve lived most of my life in Maine, raised on a potato farm in the St. John River Valley in northern Maine. I spent four years in Connecticut going to college, which opened a huge
window of awareness of the world and its complex demographics, some beautiful, others
heartbreaking. 
The year I spent in Iowa as a VISTA volunteer exposed me to dichotomies and similarities of different regions in the United States. While there, I worked with a community action agency, helping the less fortunate and many aged folks to winterize their homes, building and installing passive hot air solar panels to provide them with relief from high energy costs. That was in 1980 and 1981.
Now, 45 years later, we find ourselves facing the same challenges and tribulations we faced when I was a mere 23-year-old spirit looking forward to a good life.
I did vote for Sen. Susan Collins more than once, believing she would uphold these values and advocate for the people of Maine and the United States. Over the last 10 years, however, my respect for her service to this country, its people and international security and prosperity has dwindled.
Whenever I return to northern Maine, where both Sen. Collins and I grew up, I am saddened by the desolation, depression and lack of vitality. Such a crisis exists in many rural areas in this country.
The United State Senate provides equal representation for states regardless of size or demographics. U.S. senators’ primary objective and mission should be to create policies that support the well-being, health, safety and prosperity of the entire nation. Sen. Collins might have thrown a few perks our way, but she and many others have failed the nation.
Sen. Collins has failed to protect the social and civic institutions legally established to benefit the advancement and well-being of Americans. The scaling back of equal opportunity for women is abusive. There are many good public institutions endorsed by altruistic leaders over the past century that are being gutted and attacked.
Sen. Collins has failed to erect guardrails against big business pilfering earthly resources, big- money brokers that celebrate greed over humanitarian values, campaign contributions that soil elections and politics that purposely stoke division instead of embracing national and world harmony.
Sen. Collins and many others have failed to acknowledge the disastrous impact of world climate change and to begin implementing measures to not only mitigate the pain we will suffer but also address how societies can work together to change the momentum and prepare.
Climate change is as much a threat as the risk of nuclear arsenals. It scales worse because eradication of people and communities will happen over time, we will watch, and we will be helpless. What just happened in Nepal is proof, more than 1,400 killed, more than 5,000 people still missing, drowned or buried under a wall of mud. Who’s next?
Sen. Collins has failed to smother the culture of war that persists in this country and across the world. It is still evident in the games our children and even their parents play, glamorized in theaters, marketed by the military-industrial complex as good for the economy, propped up by people of power in the interest of national security to feed fear and retain their influence.
And to our neighbors, friends and family, north, south, east and west, Sen. Collins has compromised American goodwill and common purpose across the world.We can thank Sen. Collins for the early days of her service to the state of Maine.
Obviously, her influence and voice toward righteousness for the nation has been diminished to a whisper. We will need immense corrective action over the next decade and it’s time for better leadership to replace her and many others from both parties.

title: Woodfords Club revives its underground bowling league
text:
PORTLAND — Ethan Hipple says he spends about as much time in the machine room behind the lanes as he does bowling, dealing with pins that get stuck, belts that come off their tracks, blown fuses.
It’s not a job he chose. When Hipple, the city’s parks and recreation director by day, and his wife, Sarah, a real estate agent, started using the candlepin alley in the basement of the Woodfords Club after joining three years ago, the president asked if he’d be in charge of the pinsetters — no one else was going down there much.
There was once an active bowling league at the social club, founded in 1913 on Woodford Street. Old booklets in a basement closet list the rules, each season’s schedule and the names of the players, in 16 teams of four some years. Their trophies sit on shelves, right by a wall-mounted rack for resting lit cigars.
Learning about the league, Sarah Hipple thought, why not start it up again?
“I feel like there’s such a need for gathering in places that don’t cost a ton and aren’t drinking-focused,” she said.
Two years ago, she put out the call to club members and people she knew. About 10 players signed up.
After a summer hiatus, the league is back for the fall, and the 16 players participating in this eight-week session (for $65 per person) are the most they’ve had.
A NEW SESSION BEGINS
On the last Tuesday in September, teams of two sat on wood-slat benches looking onto the five lanes as the Hipples went over the quirks of the league and the alley.
Each player needs to complete three strings during the night, but there are no set lanes. Find an open one, roll a few frames, write down your scores, then take a break. Drink a beer, if you brought one.
Keep in mind that lane 5 tilts, so you’ll have to adjust accordingly. In fact, lane 4 does a little, too. Don’t be alarmed when your hands turn black from the balls rolling through the old equipment. You might not want to hug anyone with them, either.
If you get a spare or strike (which is much harder to come by than in tenpin bowling), ring the bell that hangs from the ceiling. If you score over 100 in a single game — again, no small feat — add your name to the dozen on the chalkboard.
Be as competitive as you want to be or just play for fun, but know that the team that has won every session so far is sitting this one out.
“It’s a wide-open field right now,” Ethan Hipple said.
MEET THE PLAYERS
Ellie Osborn and her teammate, DeAnna Massey, always seem to come in third. They both signed up for the league solo last year, were paired by Sarah Hipple and have played together ever since. Now, they have bowling shirts from Etsy with their team name, Splits & Giggles, and their picture is on the front of the club’s brochure.
“It’s just something fun to do, especially in winter,” said Osborn, a recent empty nester who went to high school with Hipple in Massachusetts.
Georgea and Kosta Johnson call themselves Pin & Tonic. The couple, who moved a year ago from Philadelphia to Portland, just up the street from the club, heard about the league from Massey, their neighbor. This is their third session, and they have team shirts, too.
“We ended up joining the club so we can practice because we’re competitive,” Georgea Johnson said.
Among the new players this session are Ross Little and his daughter’s partner, Angela Mavrich.
Little grew up candlepin bowling in Nova Scotia. He heard about the league from a friend who played last session and, knowing Mavrich was a tenpin bowler back in her home state of Ohio, asked if she’d be his teammate.
Hearing the thunder of the balls rolling down the lanes, the clanging equipment and the crack of the pins that first week was bringing back memories of her own father’s bowling league.
“It’s a nice, nostalgic, warm sound to me,” she said.
SOMEWHERE TO GATHER
For bridge players upstairs, it’s a different story. The alley is closed during their games because it’s so loud.
That’s not an issue, however, for the Tuesday night swing dancers, whose steps can be heard heaving the floor above the lanes whenever there’s a break in bowling. One couple comes down to join the league after the class gets out.
Tuesday is the busiest weeknight at the club, though there are public activities scheduled most days: meetings of the Portland Camera Club, a drop-in improv group, mahjong.
The desire to gather is clearly still there, even though a decline in league participation is among the reasons candlepin alleys continue to close.
West-Port Bowling Lanes in Westbrook cited the age of its equipment and the difficulty of replacing parts when it shut its doors last month.
The Woodfords Club pinsetters are different and easier to fix, so that’s not as much of a concern, Sarah Hipple said.
Neither is keeping the lights on at the club or, thanks to her husband, paying someone to maintain the equipment.
It might have been hard to get a league like this back up and running somewhere else, but in this place, with these people, it’s working.

title: 'What is your favorite bird?'
text:
I started birding at ten years old. One of the first questions asked of me about birding was, “What is your favorite bird?” It is not only one of the questions most frequently asked, it is also one far more complicated than you might think. I have had different favorite birds at different points in my life. And often there are multiple favorites, each with a specific feature, trait, behavior, or cultural rationale for ranking on my list.
My first favorite was American Goldfinch, a species I learned as Wild Canary. Common around the hillside adjacent to my Niagara River home, it was the first bird I learned to identify. The males were a splash of brilliant yellow in the breeding season landscape, a hue that in direct sunlight was almost too bright to gaze upon. Their glossy black cap was a beautiful contrast. Depending on the season, they fed on the White Birch catkins or the Bull Thistle seeds. Their undulating flight intrigued me: flap, flap, glide, wings tucked in, a lemon bullet speeding through the air. Repeat. Flapping on the upstroke, they call, “Perchickory, perchickory,” a moniker I would bestow upon a friend’s eight-year-old daughter years later when she helped me band birds.

title: What’s on the ballot in Kittery?
text:
Kittery residents will see a short local ballot on Nov. 3, when they cast their votes in two races, on top of state and county decisions.
In-person voters can stop by the Kittery Community Center from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. to fill out their ballots. Absentee and early voting is already underway, with a deadline of Oct. 29 to request ballots, and an Election Day deadline to bring them to the town clerk’s office.
Here’s what will be on the ballot.
TOWN COUNCIL RACE
Town Council members H. Scott Mason, who is also a member of the Housing Committee, and Megan Greenwood’s terms are set to expire on Election Day.
Voters will elect two members to join the seven member council in a three-way race. Both Mason and Greenwood are seeking their second terms, though Greenwood’s first term was only partial as she filled in to finish former councilor Cameron Hamm’s post in 2025 when he stepped down.
They’ll take on another Housing Committee member, William Peirce who ran unsuccessfully for the council in 2025.
SCHOOL BOARD RACE
There two seats open for three-year terms on the Kittery School Committee in an uncontested race.
Edie Davis Quinn and Carol James, both first-time candidates, are running to fill two seats, one vacant and another replacing member Eric Lemont, whose term expires in November.
STATE RACES
Residents in House District 150 will join Eliot and some South Berwick voters in electing a new representative. Democrat Alexandros Orestis, who serves on the Eliot Select Board, will take on Republican Mark Zimmer, who ran unsuccessfully in the same race in 2024.
Republican Suzanne Johnson and Democrat Kristi Matheison are vying to fill a House District 151 seat, which covers the eastern side of town. Johnson ran unsuccessfully in 2025, while Matheison is running for a fourth term as a representative.
Voters will join Eliot, Ogunquit, South Berwick and York in electing a District 35 senator. Democratic incumbent Rep. Michele Meyer is facing Republican Julie Rakic.
COUNTY RACES
Voters will weigh in on the York County sheriff race between Democratic incumbent William King and Republican David Corbett.
Brian Pellerin dropped out of the race in September and took on a position as the police chief of Wells. His name will still appear on the ballot because ballots had already been printed by the time he dropped out.
Another ballot item will ask voters countywide whether they support eliminating an elected treasurer position, which some officials say is purely a ceremonial role.
The sole candidate for the position, Bobby Mills, is seeking a nonconsecutive term and believes keeping the position could save voters some money. He said he’ll try to get rid of a similar but more expensive role on the Budget Committee if he’s elected.
If county residents decide to eliminate the elected treasurer position, the role would become one that is appointed internally by county officials.

title: Houlton council candidate wants to ease property tax burden
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rising fuel costs, school budgets and county obligations add up quickly, making any local tax increase incredibly difficult for household budgets, a Houlton Town Council candidate said Monday.
“Our most immediate challenge is easing the property tax burden on residents,” said sitting Councilor John “J.J.” Schools, who is seeking a three-year council term in November.
Schools, 55, was appointed to a Town Council seat last October, following the resignation of several councilors in the wake of the former town manager’s arrest.
Since that time, Schools, a retired U.S. Navy senior chief petty officer, and other town leaders have focused on righting the ship following a challenging time for this Aroostook County town of 6,000.
“I am running for a three-year term to keep our positive momentum going and protect the town we love,” he said. “I am confident that with the right leadership at the helm, we can revitalize Houlton.”
In recent years it has been a challenge to fill town leadership roles, but the upcoming November election has drawn seven candidates for five open seats.
In addition to Schools, also on the ballot for one of three open three-year terms is Councilor Sue Tortello, who picked up a one-year seat with 1,035 votes in last year’s special general election. Declared write-in candidates Matt Carr and former Council Chairman Chris Robinson are also vying for a three-year seat.
Councilor Fred Grant and declared write-in candidate Daniel Dobbs are running for one open two-year term and Councilor Jeffrey Maquire is running against challenger Darrell Scott White for a one-year term.
At this time, the council has a “delicate, beautiful balance to maintain” by preserving a close-knit, small-town vibe while also growing the local business base, Schools said, adding that the council must manage hurdles through strict fiscal discipline and strategic planning.
“My role as a councilor is to serve as a practical steward of your tax dollars,” he said. “This means digging deep into operational budgets to eliminate inefficiencies rather than cutting services.”
The retired Navy officer advocates for patience when filling municipal vacancies.
The town can rebuild community trust by executing a disciplined, quality-first hiring strategy to fill vital vacant town positions with the right leadership instead of rushing to fill employment vacancies with quick fixes, he said.
His top three priorities include: Taxpayer relief by vetting municipal expenses aggressively to keep local property taxes stable; infrastructure investment by prioritizing the long-overdue repair and replacement of the town’s streets that are in “desperate need of replacement”; and balanced growth by expanding the downtown commercial base while attracting outside investment that fits the community’s character.
“My priority is, and always will be, the long-term good of Houlton and its residents,” Schools said. “By prioritizing road rehabilitation and supporting our new town manager, the council can systematically fix our infrastructure while maintaining absolute transparency.”
Schools lives in Houlton with his wife, Alysia. They have three children and four grandchildren.

title: Obituary: Lisa E. Christian
text:
PORTLAND – On Sept. 23, 2026 at 8:35 a.m., Lisa E. Christian passed away after a battle with cancer.
Born and raised in Maine, Lisa will be remembered as a warm and nurturing home daycare provider of 45 years. She offered a place of welcome and comfort to all of her children’s friends and daycare parents.
Lisa is survived by her parents Donna and Robert Sanborn; her four children, Alyson, Cameron, Kenton, and Claire; as well as three grandchildren, Evangeline, Colson, and Caeden.
Lisa will be remembered for her delicious baked goods, and her love of dancing in the kitchen after baking. She wanted to be known for her sharpei ass (her words) and her fiery Aries attitude, which she passed down to her grandchildren.
We will remember Lisa in a celebration of life on Nov. 7 2026.

title: Another top swap in Varsity Maine boys soccer poll
text:
What is a voter to do? On Sept. 29, Brunswick eked past Lewiston 3-2 and last week became the unanimous No. 1 in the Varsity Maine boys soccer poll, a week after the Dragons took over the top spot by one point over the Blue Devils. Easy enough. But then last Thursday, Lewiston turned the tables with a 1-0 overtime win over Brunswick.
The teams split their two matches. Both teams have scored three goals in those two games. How do you split that difference? Most Varsity Maine voters appear to have gone with the “latest is the greatest” approach, giving the top spot back to the Blue Devils after they were ranked second the previous two weeks following two weeks at No. 1.
Lewiston still has a matchup with rival and ninth-ranked Edward Little on its schedule. Brunswick, which earned its second five-goal victory over the Red Eddies on Saturday (winning 7-2), has three games against Class A North playoff contenders: Mt. Blue, Messalonskee and Mt. Ararat.
Behind the Blue Devils and the Dragons in the poll are four Class A South squads, who are also the top four teams in their region, in the same order: Thornton Academy, Deering, Gorham and Scarborough. Those four teams don’t play each other in the final week of the regular season, but Portland, the fifth-place team in A South, has a chance to play spoiler with games against Thornton and Scarborough.
Fryeburg is back in the rankings at No. 10, the same spot they held in the Sept. 22 poll.

title: A list of US roller coaster fatalities dating back to 2003
text:
(AP) - A man who fell to his death from a roller coaster at an Atlanta-area amusement park was not the first to die on such a ride in recent years.
Authorities have not released information about how 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was thrown from Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Several people also were injured.
Here’s a look at other fatalities and injuries on U.S. roller coasters:
Six Flags Magic Mountain
The park in Southern California announced last month that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious brain injuries. The park settled one wrongful-death lawsuit with the family of a 22-year-old rider who was rushed to a hospital with severe brain bleeding in 2022. He died a day later. The medical examiner’s office determined he died from “blunt head trauma.” Six Flags Entertainment Corp. said the ride had consistently passed safety tests.
Epic Universe
A medical examiner concluded last year that a man who was unresponsive after riding a roller coaster at the Universal Orlando Resort park died from blunt impact injuries. Joshua Stephany, the medical examiner for the Orlando area, ruled the death an accident. The man in his 30s was found unresponsive after riding Stardust Racers.
Texas Giant
In 2013, a woman riding a roller coaster in Texas died after she was thrown from her seat, fell 75 feet (23 meters) and struck a metal beam. Witnesses said the woman expressed concern about the Texas Giant roller coaster’s safety bar not completely engaging as the ride was starting.
Darien Lake
A U.S. Army veteran who lost both legs in Iraq was killed in 2011 after he was thrown from a roller coaster at Darien Lake Theme Park & Resort in upstate New York. Investigators said operators did not follow rules posted at the ride’s entrance, which require that riders have both legs.
Dixie Landin’
A 21-year-old rider fell to her death from a roller coaster at the amusement park in Louisiana in 2010. A state investigation could not determine a cause.
Disneyland
In 2003, a locomotive broke loose from a train on the Big Thunder Mountain Railroad roller coaster in California, killing a man and injuring multiple other riders. The car derailed after a guide wheel fell off. State investigators found the wheel was not tightened according to Disney’s standards and a safety wire was not installed.
