title: In Maine’s 1st District, Chellie Pingree and Ron Russell square off again
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The election in Maine’s 1st Congressional District may have fallen to the wayside amid more contentious statewide races, but the names on the ballot are still familiar — it’s the same two candidates who ran for the seat two years ago.
Republican Ron Russell is back again to challenge incumbent Democrat U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree for her seat in Congress. Pingree had a solid win in 2024, beating Russell and independent Ethan Alcorn.
Russell, 72, grew up in Fort Fairfield, and is a retired Army colonel. He served for more than 30 years as an airborne ranger Green Beret, and was in combat in Panama, Somalia, Afghanistan and other crisis response operations.
After retiring, he founded the North Carolina-based defense contractor Far Ridgeline Engagements, and returned to Maine in 2021. Russell knows he’s a repeat candidate for voters but hopes it works in his favor.
“There’s certainly nothing different in the way I feel about the issues, probably have refined them somewhat,” Russell said. “But I’m the same person I was back then, and I think, unfortunately, the issues facing the nation and Maine are the same.”
Pingree has represented the district since 2009, and is currently the ranking Democratic member on the Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies under the Committee on Appropriations.
“I never take any campaign for granted,” Pingree said. “The voters deserve to both see us and hear from us, and know that you’re taking it seriously.”
She also served in the Maine Senate from 1992-2000, and was majority leader in her final four years in the state Legislature.
“We all know this is an extremely critical election,” Pingree said. “This has been one of the most challenging two years in our country, and it doesn’t matter which side of the aisle that you’re on.”
The two will meet for one debate, on Oct. 29 in Portland, jointly hosted by Maine Public, NewsCenter Maine and the Portland Press Herald.
President Trump
Like most federal races across Maine and the country, even if President Donald Trump’s name is not on the ballot, he is very much still a central factor in the race, and the 1st District is no exception.
Pingree said in her latest term in office, she has spent a lot of time pushing back against Trump’s actions.
“Especially in the last two years, unfortunately, much of our focus has just been on fighting back from an out-of-control administration,” Pingree said. “I mean, the amount of things they have done that are illegal or unconstitutional or just extremely damaging to Maine is greater than anything I’ve ever seen before.”
But she said constituents have been incredibly engaged in the issues, and want to see Maine’s congressional delegation protect their interests — and Pingree hopes to do more of that if Democrats can regain a majority in the U.S. House of Representatives.
“So I think this year people want to know that we’re fighting for them, that our goal is if I’m reelected to do everything we can to undo the damage that they’ve done, particularly if we’re in the majority and we have more power to do that,” Pingree said.
Russell has a very different approach, and while he hopes to bring an independent mindset to Congress, he doesn’t disagree with Trump’s priorities.
“I said before I’m not going to be a rubber stamp for President Trump, but I really kind of agree with the things that we are doing and in getting our nation back on board,” Russell said.
But Russell said he doesn’t agree with the way the president goes about enacting his agenda.
“Sometimes how he does what he does, I’m not a big fan of,” Russell said.
Russell added that he thinks Congress can do more to assert its authority to be on par with the president.
“We have three equal branches of government, and I think, to a degree, he does things the way he does because a couple of the branches of government have abdicated their responsibilities,” Russell said.
That point is one Pingree agreed with, and said many Republicans have relinquished a lot of Congress’s constitutional responsibilities.
“As much as I have good friends on the other side of the aisle and I like working with them, uniformly the Republicans have stopped using the power of Congress,” Pingree said. “They forgot we’re a co-equal branch.”
Immigration
Immigration has been a major issue in the 1st District during Trump’s second term, and came to the forefront in July when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero in Biddeford.
“The officer was unqualified,” Pingree said. “They literally shot a person who they weren’t even intending to pick up.”
Pingree has been vocal about her opposition to ICE activity around the country, and participated in two “shadow” hearings on the shooting with fellow Democrats.
The federal government has so far declined to investigate or reveal any information about the fatal shooting of Guerrero, a pattern seen across the country in response to violence and wrongful detentions by ICE.
“It’s not what anybody believed that the president was talking about, and he said he was only going to pick up the worst of the worst, the murderers and rapists, and it’s not how you want your tax dollars spent,” Pingree said.
Russell said he doesn’t know if the results of the federal investigation into the Biddeford shooting would be made public, but he said will push for that information to be released.
“Releasing the results of that investigation would be very, very valuable for obvious reasons,” Russell said. “People want to know, and people should know.”
Russell said he thinks that a lack of coordination between federal, state and local agencies has contributed to the death in Biddeford and other shootings by ICE agents around the country.
“You can’t have it both ways,” Russell said. “You can’t insist upon cooperation during the investigation when you’re not coordinating and cooperating before the investigation. And if you did, the investigation would be necessary, from my perspective.”
More broadly, Russell said he opposes “sanctuary cities” and supports immigration enforcement.
“The fact that the border is closed, our Southern border, I think, is a great accomplishment,” Russell said. “And we are having to deal with the millions of illegal immigrants who came across the border during the last administration, and that is what has been problematic.”
On the other side, Pingree said she strongly opposes the quotas in place for ICE agents, and called the agency’s actions unconstitutional.
“It’s just an outrageous use of the taxpayer dollars,” Pingree said. “It doesn’t make us safer, and it goes against what people think is fundamental in a democracy.”
Pingree said her staff regularly hear from constituents struggling to navigate the immigration system, and are confused about the enforcement actions.
She said her Portland office “has a steady stream of new Mainers who come in there, sometimes just looking for a work permit to be renewed.”
“Sometimes it’s employers saying, ‘Hey, I have a whole carload of roofers and I can’t figure out where they’ve been taken,’” she said. “Family members who say to us, ‘Someone was picked up and now they’ve been moved.’”
Pingree pointed to her efforts to get Olivia Andre, a 19-year-old asylum-seeker and Portland resident, released from detention after six months. Pingree and other Democratic members of Congress traveled to the detention center in Texas where Andre was held.
“But it took a congressperson to visit all the way to Texas to get them moving on that,” Pingree said. “But that happens every single day.”
Heating costs and the Iran war
As temperatures begin to drop, many Mainers are watching the cost of heating oil, which has reached historic levels this fall as the war in Iran drives up prices.
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. According to the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the average statewide price of heating oil was $5.97 per gallon on Oct. 5, up roughly 79% from last year. That is down slightly from Sept. 21, when the average price reached a record high of $6.02.
Pingree called the latest prices “unthinkable,” and said she is particularly concerned about programs like the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, known as LIHEAP, going far enough for Maine residents this year.
“It’s a bad picture to start,” Pingree said. “And if we get a cold winter, even without a cold winter, this will be a strain on a lot of people there.”
According to a press release from U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office on Friday, Maine is set to receive more than $36 million through LIHEAP, one of the earliest releases of funds in the program’s history.
“We need to end the war on Iran to try to bring down that price, but there’s no good reason not to up the amount of money in LIHEAP,” Pingree said.
Pingree has repeatedly voted for war powers resolutions in Congress, and said the war in Iran is a clear example of Trump abusing the limited exception for the president to defend the country from an imminent attack.
Russell agreed that the war is driving up heating oil, gas and diesel prices, but said he still supports the U.S. military action.
“I think that war was necessary, and I support President Trump doing it,” Russell said. “I’m dismayed that it’s taken as long as it has, for obvious reasons. It’s having a significant impact on gas prices around the world, but I think eventually, and fairly soon, actually, those prices will get back into normal parameters. I think prices will drop precipitously once that situation is resolved, and I think that will resolve itself within a month.”
Russell said he thinks another factor in the price spikes is the lack of natural gas refineries in the country.
“Until we get those up and running again, where we are self-sufficient in terms of refining our own heating oil and diesel fuel, then we’re catching up once again,” he said.
Russell said he would support building those refineries in Maine or other parts of the country, to be less reliant on other countries for processing.
“I would not shy away from not doing it in our backyard because it’s going to be beneficial to the United States,” Russell said. “It will be beneficial to Mainers, and it will get us back on track fixing a lot of the problems that are broken right now.”

title: Women’s singles wrestling returns to Aroostook County
text:
FORT FAIRFIELD, Maine (WAGM) - A Crown of Maine Wrestling event featured the first women’s singles match in Aroostook County in decades, preceded by a confrontation outside the ring.
Referees separated wrestlers Tiffani Avatar and Wolf Eye Nashoba Naira after the two got into a fight outside the ring. This took place before the first women’s singles match in the area in decades, according to Crown of Maine Wrestling co-owner Amanda Brown.
“It was really important to us to have them do our first women’s singles match because it’s been since, I believe, 1988 that there’s been a women’s singles match in Aroostook County,” Brown said.
Reactions among the crowd varied.
“(Some people were) Like, hey, this is great. And some people are like, oh my God, is that real? Do they really hate each other that much?,” Brown said.
Brown confirmed the fight was planned, even though some referees were unsure if it was real.
“I mean, I don’t want to ruin anything, but they did decide that would be a great way to bring attention and excitement to the match that they were going to have later on in the night,” Brown said.
About 100 people attended the event at the Fort Fairfield Recreation Center. Brown said the stunt accomplished what it was meant to do: excite fans.
Crown of Maine Wrestling is entering its slower season and plans to return in April. Brown says they have a goal to hold more women’s singles matches next season.
“Especially with like how successful that was and what a great job they did”, Brown said.

title: Real estate agents turn to AI to make listings shine. When is it ‘house fishing?’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tom Landry had been trying to find his clients a home on one of Maine’s unbridged islands for over a year, when the listing popped up.
It was ideal. The rustic, classic cottage with its screened-in porch was charming, but the real showstopper was the backyard. A string of cafe lights hung over a ring of Adirondack chairs and a striking stone fireplace.
But when Landry and his clients made it to the 900-square foot house, listed for $579,000, they did a double take. The porch was less rustic and more dilapidated. The backyard scene built for entertaining didn’t exist at all. The house’s best features had been AI-generated.
“You arrive and it’s literally falling down,” said Landry, owner of Benchmark Real Estate in Portland. “There were parts of the house you couldn’t even walk through. It was laughable.”
It’s a concept known as “house fishing” — the real estate version of “catfishing,” or making something appear better online than it does in reality.
As AI becomes more advanced and accessible, real estate agents are increasingly using the technology to touch up photos, virtually stage a room or write listings.
Landry said agents have an obligation to make things look as good as possible for their clients, but when does it become deceptive or false advertising?
“It is a bit of an ethical quandary here,” Landry said.
AI DISCUSSIONS INCREASING
That sentiment is growing locally and nationally.
“We are definitely looking into AI and the proper ways to be using AI in real estate,” said Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors.
Members at the organization’s recent conference had a three-hour class about AI use in the industry, and AI guidelines will be included as a “core course” that The Maine Real Estate Commission requires licensees to take every two years, she said.
AI was the central topic of the Maine Real Estate and Development Association’s annual Forecast Conference in February, and it will also be a major focus of the National Association of Realtors “NTX” conference next month.
“Everybody is dealing with it,” Oberg said.
Legislators in Wisconsin and California have passed laws requiring that digitally altered photos in listings be clearly labeled and that the unedited photos also be included. Lawmakers in New Jersey and New York are considering similar restrictions.
The National Association of Realtors’ code of ethics recommends that members “refrain from exaggerating, misrepresenting or concealing pertinent facts” and to present a “true picture” in advertising and marketing.
‘OVER AND ABOVE’
Real estate agents have been known to add a little spin to spruce up a listing. A house in disrepair is waiting for “a little TLC,” from “an investor with a vision.” Creative camera angles can make a shoebox-sized living room look spacious.
It’s also commonplace for agents to touch up photos. They might digitally remove a trash can blocking the garage or some clutter the seller didn’t put away. The lights might be brightened to create an inviting atmosphere, or a sunset enhanced. A fire might even be added to the fireplace.
“Some things are up for grabs,” Landry said, “but this has gone over and above.”
A discerning buyer could have spotted that some things in the listing weren’t quite right. One porch photo looked a little shabbier, and was missing the rug, the string lights and the potted plants that brightened up the other. The aerial shots of the backyard didn’t show the fireplace.
But the porch photos weren’t next to one another, making side-by-side comparisons harder, and the listing didn’t disclose that any photos had been edited, nor were the altered shots labeled.
“People were doctoring photos before AI,” but the ease, speed and intensity with which people can change things now is “mind-boggling,” said Steve Weikal, Industry Chair of the Real Estate Transformation Lab at the MIT Center for Real Estate.
“We’ll have to figure out a way to police that,” he said. “How do we trust what we’re seeing and who we’re interacting with? … AI is opening up the Pandora’s box.”
Weikal, however, believes AI can be a powerful tool for the industry, and said it could help solve the problem as more time and money is invested in verification technology.
THE IMPORTANCE OF TRUST
Matt Pouliot, owner of Pouliot Real Estate in Augusta, said labeling will be key moving forward.
“It’s critical that consumers know that the property they’re buying looks as close as possible to what’s online,” he said.
Trust is crucial in the business, he added, and “we need to maintain that by not putting in a swimming pool where there isn’t one.”
Pouliot said his company recently adopted an AI policy based on the National Association of Realtors’ best practices. He sees the technology as a boon, provided there are still human-centered checks and balances.
Writing listings has never been faster, Pouliot said, and AI often comes up with zippy turns of phrase that he wouldn’t have.
It can eliminate a lot of back-and-forth administrative work, help with scheduling, respond to emails or draft social media posts.
“Automate the part that’s drudgery, that prevents you from being out in the field and out meeting with people and out networking and taking people on tours,” said Weikal, at MIT.
‘A FUNDAMENTAL TRUST PROBLEM’
Not all real estate agents have jumped on the bandwagon.
Andy Mooers, owner of Mooers Realty in Houlton, said using AI in listings is not only lazy, but also dangerous.
“Anyway you slice and dice it, AI slop is a fundamental trust problem,” he wrote in a blog post on his website.
Mooers said in an interview that he’d rather his clients see “the good, the bad and the ugly” — that the house is on a busy road, that the living room is small or that there are power lines over the roof.

title: Here’s what’s on the municipal ballot in Saco and Biddeford
text:
Absentee voting is now open for the Nov. 3 municipal and state elections in Biddeford and Saco. Mainers statewide will chime in on state legislative races and high-profile elections for governor and U.S. Senate.
In Saco, residents will decide on various local races, including City Council, school board and mayor. (To learn about the school board races, click here.)
There are no local races on the ballot in Biddeford — voters will only decide on state candidates.
Here’s what’s you need to know:
SACO MUNICIPAL RACES
City Council, Ward 2
Voters in Ward 2 will choose from two candidates for one three-year seat on the City Council: Joshua Parks and Trevor Nason. Ward 2 covers the area closest to Scarborough, including Saco Heath Preserve.
Parks, the incumbent, is serving his first term on the council; he also serves as deputy mayor. He is a lifelong Saco resident and produce associate at Hannaford with an educational background in political science.
In his responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Parks said his priorities include fighting for the best interests of his ward and continuing work on reducing the budget so residents don’t feel priced out of their community.
He also highlighted the increasing threat of data centers and said he supports small, strategic development in the city rather than large-scale projects.
Nason did not respond to the voter guide survey.
City Council, Ward 3
Two candidates are vying for the Ward 3 seat on the City Council: Sandra Guay and John Shannon III. Ward 3 covers much of Route 1.
Guay, an attorney, was appointed to the council in August to fill a vacancy after the previous councilor, William Doyle, stepped down. She has lived in Saco for 30 years and has served on several committees in the city during that time. Her priorities include balancing commercial and residential development, supporting residential opportunities for people of all income levels, and traffic safety.
Shannon, a youth services supervisor at Biddeford’s McArthur Library, is a lifelong resident of the Biddeford-Saco area. This is his first time running for office.
In his responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Shannon said his top priorities if elected are: creating responsible growth that expands housing and economic opportunity, building strong infrastructure, and encouraging an accessible, collaborative local government.
City Council, Ward 7
Incumbent Nathan Johnston is running uncontested for reelection to the Ward 7 seat. Ward 7 covers downtown Saco.
A lifelong Saco resident with several relatives in community roles, Johnston has served on the City Council for 10 years. According to his social media pages, Johnston is a strong supporter of education, economic development and infrastructure.
Mayor
Saco Mayor Jodi MacPhail is running uncontested for a second term. She was first elected in 2023.
In an August news release announcing her candidacy, MacPhail said her achievements as mayor so far include creating a consistent and stable environment for staff, working with the City Council on key initiatives, working closely with the school department and investing in local projects.
“It has been an honor and a privilege to serve the residents of Saco,” she wrote. “We are all finally getting the upgrades we deserve, and I intend to fully see them through.”
STATE AND COUNTY RACES
Voters in Biddeford and Saco are tasked this with choosing their state representatives in two Senate districts and four House districts.
In Senate District 31, which includes Saco, Old Orchard Beach and Buxton, voters will choose between incumbent Democrat Donna Bailey and Republican challenger Scott Eccleston.
In Senate District 32, which includes Biddeford, Lyman, Hollis, Dayton and Arundel, voters will choose between incumbent Democrat Henry Ingwersen and independent Jason Litalien.
In two of the state House races, the Democratic incumbents are running unopposed: Marshall Archer in House District 129, which includes the southwestern portion of Saco, and House Speaker Ryan Fecteau in District 132, covering much of downtown Biddeford.
In House District 130, covering northern and coastal parts of Saco, Democratic incumbent Rep. Lynn Holland Copeland is facing a challenge from independent Todd Davis.
And in House District 133, covering the rest of Biddeford, incumbent Democrat Marc Malon faces independent Marc Lessard, a member of Biddeford City Council.
Voters across York County will also weigh in on a referendum that would abolish a county treasurer position and elect a sheriff. Incumbent Sheriff William King, a Democrat, is seeking a fifth term and is facing Republican challenger David Corbett. Independent Brian Pellerin dropped out of the race after ballots were printed; he was recently hired as Wells’ new police chief.

title: Kroger to lay off 3,000 corporate employees as it leans into AI
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kroger to lay off 3,000 corporate employees as it leans into AI
Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.
“Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.”
Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.”
Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer.
Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO.
Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities.
Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells.
Kroger has also felt pressure from fast-growing discount chains like Aldi and Lidl and online behemoths like Amazon.
Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed.
A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value.
Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee.
Albertsons is facing the same competitive headwinds as Kroger and other grocery chains as customers turn to cheaper alternatives and faster delivery from bigger retailers.
On Tuesday during its second-quarter earnings conference call with investors, CEO Susan Morris alluded to further cost-cutting and streamlining of the company's structure, including layoffs.
“We did some work last year and saw a substantial reduction in headcount, but quite frankly, there’s more to be had," Morris said. "And you’ll see us taking aggressive action there in the next 12 to 18 months as well.”
Kroger shares fell 2.2% in afternoon trading Tuesday, to $61.21. Albertsons rose 2.8%, but its shares are down more than 25% this year.

title: Husband accused of bludgeoning wife to death with flashlight in front of 3 kids
text:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX/Gray News) - A Vermont man is facing charges after police say he bludgeoned his wife to death with a large flashlight.
Burlington Police say they received multiple 911 calls just before 6 a.m. Saturday reporting a fight. They responded to an apartment and found a woman unresponsive in bed with head injuries. She was taken the hospital, where she was pronounced dead Sunday evening.
The victim’s name has not been released.
Investigators identified the suspect as 44-year-old Bal Khadka, the victim’s husband. Police allege he bludgeoned his wife with a large flashlight in front of three children.
Khadka was initially charged with attempted murder, but after his wife’s death, detectives updated the charge against him to second-degree murder.
Khadka is expected in court Tuesday.

title: Real estate agents turn to AI to make listings shine. When is it ‘house fishing?’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tom Landry had been trying to find his clients a home on one of Maine’s unbridged islands for over a year, when the listing popped up.
It was ideal. The rustic, classic cottage with its screened-in porch was charming, but the real showstopper was the backyard. A string of cafe lights hung over a ring of Adirondack chairs and a striking stone fireplace.
But when Landry and his clients made it to the 900-square foot house, listed for $579,000, they did a double take. The porch was less rustic and more dilapidated. The backyard scene built for entertaining didn’t exist at all. The house’s best features had been AI-generated.
“You arrive and it’s literally falling down,” said Landry, owner of Benchmark Real Estate in Portland. “There were parts of the house you couldn’t even walk through. It was laughable.”
It’s a concept known as “house fishing” — the real estate version of “catfishing,” or making something appear better online than it does in reality.
As AI becomes more advanced and accessible, real estate agents are increasingly using the technology to touch up photos, virtually stage a room or write listings.
Landry said agents have an obligation to make things look as good as possible for their clients, but when does it become deceptive or false advertising?
“It is a bit of an ethical quandary here,” Landry said.
AI DISCUSSIONS INCREASING
That sentiment is growing locally and nationally.
“We are definitely looking into AI and the proper ways to be using AI in real estate,” said Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors.
Members at the organization’s recent conference had a three-hour class about AI use in the industry, and AI guidelines will be included as a “core course” that The Maine Real Estate Commission requires licensees to take every two years, she said.
AI was the central topic of the Maine Real Estate and Development Association’s annual Forecast Conference in February, and it will also be a major focus of the National Association of Realtors “NTX” conference next month.
“Everybody is dealing with it,” Oberg said.
Legislators in Wisconsin and California have passed laws requiring that digitally altered photos in listings be clearly labeled and that the unedited photos also be included. Lawmakers in New Jersey and New York are considering similar restrictions.
The National Association of Realtors’ code of ethics recommends that members “refrain from exaggerating, misrepresenting or concealing pertinent facts” and to present a “true picture” in advertising and marketing.
‘OVER AND ABOVE’
Real estate agents have been known to add a little spin to spruce up a listing. A house in disrepair is waiting for “a little TLC,” from “an investor with a vision.” Creative camera angles can make a shoebox-sized living room look spacious.
It’s also commonplace for agents to touch up photos. They might digitally remove a trash can blocking the garage or some clutter the seller didn’t put away. The lights might be brightened to create an inviting atmosphere, or a sunset enhanced. A fire might even be added to the fireplace.
“Some things are up for grabs,” Landry said, “but this has gone over and above.”
A discerning buyer could have spotted that some things in the listing weren’t quite right. One porch photo looked a little shabbier, and was missing the rug, the string lights and the potted plants that brightened up the other. The aerial shots of the backyard didn’t show the fireplace.
But the porch photos weren’t next to one another, making side-by-side comparisons harder, and the listing didn’t disclose that any photos had been edited, nor were the altered shots labeled.
“People were doctoring photos before AI,” but the ease, speed and intensity with which people can change things now is “mind-boggling,” said Steve Weikal, Industry Chair of the Real Estate Transformation Lab at the MIT Center for Real Estate.
“We’ll have to figure out a way to police that,” he said. “How do we trust what we’re seeing and who we’re interacting with? … AI is opening up the Pandora’s box.”
Weikal, however, believes AI can be a powerful tool for the industry, and said it could help solve the problem as more time and money is invested in verification technology.
THE IMPORTANCE OF TRUST
Matt Pouliot, owner of Pouliot Real Estate in Augusta, said labeling will be key moving forward.
“It’s critical that consumers know that the property they’re buying looks as close as possible to what’s online,” he said.
Trust is crucial in the business, he added, and “we need to maintain that by not putting in a swimming pool where there isn’t one.”
Pouliot said his company recently adopted an AI policy based on the National Association of Realtors’ best practices. He sees the technology as a boon, provided there are still human-centered checks and balances.
Writing listings has never been faster, Pouliot said, and AI often comes up with zippy turns of phrase that he wouldn’t have.
It can eliminate a lot of back-and-forth administrative work, help with scheduling, respond to emails or draft social media posts.
“Automate the part that’s drudgery, that prevents you from being out in the field and out meeting with people and out networking and taking people on tours,” said Weikal, at MIT.
‘A FUNDAMENTAL TRUST PROBLEM’
Not all real estate agents have jumped on the bandwagon.
Andy Mooers, owner of Mooers Realty in Houlton, said using AI in listings is not only lazy, but also dangerous.
“Anyway you slice and dice it, AI slop is a fundamental trust problem,” he wrote in a blog post on his website.
Mooers said in an interview that he’d rather his clients see “the good, the bad and the ugly” — that the house is on a busy road, that the living room is small or that there are power lines over the roof.
Choosing to show a property as it really is, rather than what it could be, ultimately saves everyone time and energy, he said.
“AI makes everything perfect … and life isn’t like that,” he said.
AGENTS OBSOLETE?
AI is also helping clients become more informed. They’re doing research ahead of time and asking more and smarter questions.
A 2025 Realtor.com survey found that of 1,000 people in various stages of the market, 82% had used AI for real estate insights.
In some cases, the technology is helping sellers cut out agents altogether.
New platforms like Ridley offer AI software packages to help people sell their homes for a flat fee instead of paying a sellers’ commission.
A New York Times reporter recently wrote about selling his house with the help of an AI chatbot, and reportedly received a higher selling price.
But Weikal doesn’t think agents are going to be out of a job anytime soon.
People thought online listing platforms like Zillow and Redfin would also put agents out of work. The job has just adapted.
“The role is changing to a more advisory role,” Weikal said.
Landry, at Benchmark, said people still want human advice.
“When you’re negotiating over the most consequential life and financial decision you’re going to face … do you really want to chance it?”
The public’s trust in real estate agents is still high, Pouliot said.
“It only stays that way if we stay dedicated to accuracy.”

title: Oxford Hills school board changes its meeting day, effective Oct. 21
text:
Maine School Administrative District 17 is changing up its business meeting routine.
Starting Oct. 21, the board of directors will shift its meeting schedule from Mondays to Wednesdays. Meetings will start at 6 p.m., an hour earlier, at the Central Office on Main Street in Paris.
The move was proposed by then-acting Superintendent Steve Ciembroniewicz in July and required that directors revise policy on board meetings.
The revised policy was presented and approved at SAD 17’s Sept. 8 meeting. Immediately following the change in policy the board voted to change the day from Monday to Wednesday and the time from 7 p.m. to 6 p.m.
District staff had requested the switch, citing challenges with first-day-of-the-week pressing demands. Wednesday, which is also an early student release day, was determined to be more feasible.

title: How this spa offers specialized facials for cancer patients
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (InvestigateTV) - An estimated four million people in the U.S. receive radiation therapy, an effective way to kill cancer.
But this treatment can bring an uncomfortable and sometimes painful side effect: radiation burn. One in five people who receive radiation therapy may develop more serious symptoms, such as blistering or open sores.
For cancer patients dealing with harsh treatments, one Baton Rouge spa is offering specialized care to help them feel their best during treatment.
Finding healing through skin care
Ashley Roberts was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2017, leading to a double mastectomy and 26 weeks of chemotherapy. During treatment, she found that caring for her skin helped her maintain strength and confidence.
“I, as a young girl, was often complimented on my complexion and my eyebrows and things like that. These are things that are taken away during treatment that all the things you’re complimented on, your hair, your eyebrows, you know, your skin,” Roberts said.
Roberts discovered that nourishing her body inside and out, including getting facials, became part of her recovery journey.
“From there, I started my journey of getting the cancer out of my body and becoming a well person again,” she said.
Skin during cancer treatments can be extremely sensitive and require special care. Julie Piedrahita, owner of Simply Facials in Baton Rouge, understood this need after watching her husband battle cancer for two years.
“People don’t realize a lot of time treating the cancer is just the first part of cancer treatment,” Piedrahita said.
Simply Facials offers a service called a Restore Facial designed specifically for cancer patients’ fragile skin. The spa’s aestheticians receive special training to meet both physical and emotional needs of patients and their families.
“For physical needs, they have dry skin. There are things that happen as a result of their radiation and perhaps their chemo treatments that they’re on, but emotionally, sometimes you just want to do something to feel normal,” Piedrahita said.
Jan Vaccaro, an aesthetician at Simply Facials, said the treatment is modified for cancer patients’ specific needs.
“This facial is slowed down. It’s very gentle, relaxing. It’s nourishing for their skin as well as their emotional well-being,” Vaccaro said.
Safe techniques for patients
The spa uses nontoxic products and techniques safe for people who are immunocompromised. Staff members are trained in special massage techniques for patients with lymph node involvement.
“We know that if there is any lymph node involvement in the cancer, we have to do the techniques a special way when we work on the massage,” Piedrahita said.
Vaccaro said the treatments address the uncomfortable side effects of cancer treatment.
“Chemo and radiation basically are poison. It’s what it takes to kill the cancer, and that of course is the first order of business, but the cascade of things that happen to your body from the treatment are so uncomfortable and so unpleasant, and we thought, is there one little thing we can do to help them feel more comfortable?” she said.
Roberts, now seven years past completing her cancer treatment, continues to prioritize skin care as part of feeling her best.
“When you want to live, you’ll do whatever it takes,” Roberts said.
She said maintaining healthy skin remains important for her confidence and overall well-being.
“That’s why it’s important to continue doing facials because having that glow shows that your skin is healthy, and that’s from the inside out, and this is when everybody sees us. They see our face first,” Roberts said.
Simply Facials also recommends that family members and patients get facials together for a more comforting experience for everyone involved.

title: Saco father detained by ICE at jetport on way to visit deaf son
text:
Nguinamau Celestino’s wife dropped him off at the Portland jetport at 3 a.m. to catch an early flight to Washington, D.C. He was on his way to visit Abel, his youngest son, who had just begun his first semester at a high school for the deaf.
Nguinamau never arrived.
Celestino’s daughter, Margarida, 24, said her brother checked their father’s location on his phone after his flight was scheduled to land. He was at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Scarborough.
Margarida, a medical technician based in Auburn, woke at 6 a.m. to two missed calls from her dad, which she returned, but he didn’t pick up. She was on her way to work when her mom called; Margarida told her employer there was a family emergency and headed to Saco, where her parents live, to put the pieces together.
“Usually we see videos of people being taken, but unfortunately, everything with my dad was so silent,” she said. “Nobody said anything.”
The Celestino family — which includes Nguinamau, his wife Sukombo, their eldest Margarida and three sons, Lionel, 21, Nludi, 18, and Abel, 15 — are originally from Angola, later lived in Namibia and came to the U.S. in 2017 as asylum seekers. Their application is still ongoing. Only Margarida has a green card.
Early on Friday, Oct. 9, Margarida said her father walked into the airport and went straight to security. He saw ICE agents around, but didn’t have any reason to think they were there for him. But when he showed his ID to a TSA agent, she said, ICE agents looked at his picture, said they were there for Celestino, and detained him.
Immigration enforcement has been ramping up at airports nationwide, and local advocates said there were several detentions at the jetport in August, including of asylum seeker and registered nurse Debora Kapisha, who has since been released.
Margarida said her father has no criminal history, but agents told him he had overstayed his visa.
An ICE spokesperson confirmed Tuesday that Nguinamau was arrested during “targeted operations” last week, and said that he entered the country legally but violated the terms of his lawful admission and “remained in the U.S. illegally for nearly eight years.”
He was processed at the Scarborough facility, but by the time Margarida’s husband arrived at 9 a.m., Nguinamau had already been transferred out of the state. Margarida’s husband, a U.S. citizen, had come to bring Nguinamau a jacket, because she heard from another detained family member that the facility is chilly, and Nguinamau gets cold easily.
The agency’s online detainee locator showed Tuesday that Celestino is now being held at the Strafford County Corrections facility in Dover, New Hampshire.
Margarida said her father has been in touch every day via phone, and seems to be doing alright. The family organized a GoFundMe, which has raised nearly $30,000, and they’ve transferred some funds to him. He was able to keep his medications, but she said his work authorization card, Social Security card and Angolan ID were all missing from his wallet when they picked up his belongings.
Nguinamau works in plumbing and HVAC for Pine State Services, and got his associate’s degree at Southern Maine Community College. All of the Celestino children attended Portland Public Schools, including King Middle and Casco Bay High.
Their youngest sibling, Abel, received special services at East End Community School and played for the Baxter Seagulls, an ASL basketball team for students with the Maine Educational Center for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing.
The center announced Nguinamau’s detention on Facebook over the weekend, describing him as a beloved member of the Greater Portland and center community.
“Our Deaf and Hard of Hearing community has always been strengthened by the connections we build, the families we support, and our willingness to stand together when someone is in need. This is a time to put those values into action,” center co-directors Steve Connolly and Catherine Lushman wrote in the post.
Connolly and Lushman said they were drafting letters to Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, asking them to intervene on behalf of the Celestino family.
For now, Margarida is worried about the impact Nguinamau’s detention will have on the rest of her family. Her mom has lupus and high blood pressure, and travels to Boston every three weeks for treatment, which she worries could be impacted by her husband’s detention.
Abel, who was awaiting his father’s visit in D.C., had to leave his school for the long weekend, and the family scrambled to find a friend in the city to look after him. The friend stepped up to the challenge, Margarida said, but it wasn’t the same as Abel spending the weekend with his father.

title: A list of US roller coaster fatalities dating back to 2003
text:
A man who fell to his death from a roller coaster at an Atlanta-area amusement park was not the first to die on such a ride in recent years.
Authorities have not released information about how 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was thrown from Goliath at Six Flags over Georgia on Monday. Several people also were injured.
Here’s a look at other fatalities and injuries on U.S. roller coasters:
Six Flags Magic Mountain
The park in Southern California announced last month that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious brain injuries. The park settled one wrongful-death lawsuit with the family of a 22-year-old rider who was rushed to a hospital with severe brain bleeding in 2022. He died a day later. The medical examiner’s office determined he died from “blunt head trauma.” Six Flags Entertainment Corp. said the ride had consistently passed safety tests.
Epic Universe
A medical examiner concluded last year that a man who was unresponsive after riding a roller coaster at the Universal Orlando Resort park died from blunt impact injuries. Joshua Stephany, the medical examiner for the Orlando area, ruled the death an accident. The man in his 30s was found unresponsive after riding Stardust Racers.
Texas Giant
In 2013, a woman riding a roller coaster in Texas died after she was thrown from her seat, fell 75 feet (23 meters) and struck a metal beam. Witnesses said the woman expressed concern about the Texas Giant roller coaster’s safety bar not completely engaging as the ride was starting.
Darien Lake
A U.S. Army veteran who lost both legs in Iraq was killed in 2011 after he was thrown from a roller coaster at Darien Lake Theme Park & Resort in upstate New York. Investigators said operators did not follow rules posted at the ride’s entrance, which require that riders have both legs.
Dixie Landin’
A 21-year-old rider fell to her death from a roller coaster at the amusement park in Louisiana in 2010. A state investigation could not determine a cause.
Disneyland
In 2003, a locomotive broke loose from a train on the Big Thunder Mountain Railroad roller coaster in California, killing a man and injuring multiple other riders. The car derailed after a guide wheel fell off. State investigators found the wheel was not tightened according to Disney’s standards and a safety wire was not installed.

title: Washington County sheriff investigating death near Grand Lake Stream
text:
The Washington County Sheriff’s Office is investigating a death near Grand Lake Stream.
A body was found off Amazon Road late Tuesday morning, according to a sheriff’s dispatcher. Grand Lake Stream, in northeastern Washington County, is a popular fishing destination.
Police are still investigating the death and have not released any information about the victim or circumstances.
Washington County Chief Deputy Mike Crabtree said officials don’t think the death is suspicious and are treating it as an “unattended death.”
A spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety directed inquiries to the Washington County Sheriff’s Office.
The death is the second death investigation to hit Washington County this week after Cory Fields, a 41-year-old Indian Island man, was killed Saturday night in a shooting on the Passamaquoddy reservation, roughly 12 miles from Grand Lake Stream. Jeremy Stevens, 46, of Indian Township was arrested for murder following the shooting.

title: Experts urge parents to prepare kids for possible livestreamed execution
text:
This is not an article about politics, capital punishment or whether the Fort Hood shooter deserves to be executedin public for his crimes.
Instead, it’s focused on the unprecedented parental challenge of handling the near-certain prospect that children will hear of or see footage of the Dec. 3 U.S. execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan if the Trump administration follows through with plans to livestream the event.
The danger stretches beyond the broadcast itself, because historyshowsgraphic video from the event could be clipped, copied and pushed into children’s social feeds even if the original stream is restricted.
Experts suggest that grownups who care about children start by setting aside matters of politics and public policy — like the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections and the debate over capital punishment. Focus instead on how witnessing someone’s death by firing squad might land with young viewers — and how to best to reassure and protect them.
Here are some guidelines that might help.
Keep empathy for kids in mind — and facts at hand
Mis- and disinformation reach children, too. It’s important for parents to have credibility with them, especially because their real, unspoken question might be: Are we safe? Have in hand some basic facts about the case and state them gently.
“It will be easier to have a position, share your family’s values, and discuss things with a potentially overwhelmed child once you’ve taken the time to gather accurate, up-to-date info and assess your child’s needs,” according to Common Sense Media.
Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. A few days later, the Pentagon announced the event would be livestreamed.
“People need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people there in 2009 when he walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961.
The last widely recognized public execution took place on Aug. 14, 1936. Kentucky, the last state to permit them, outlawed the practice in 1938.
Stay updated on the plans
Also, experts suggest, parents should stay updated on how a livestreamed execution would unfold. Many questions remained unanswered, such as whether the moment of death and its aftermath will be shown, whether any age restrictions will apply, and whether there will be a broadcast delay or a threshold for stopping the feed.
Be informed about the technology involved. While the government often uses YouTube to carry its livestreams, including those embedded within government websites, YouTube prohibits content that is “violent or gory” and “intended to shock or disgust viewers,” and doesn’t allow livestreams that show someone holding, handling or transporting a firearm.
YouTube does make exceptions in select cases for content it deems to be in an educational, documentary, scientific or artistic context or that it determines to be in the public’s interest. In such cases, In such cases, the content may be age-restricted. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding how its policies relate to the execution.
But the danger to kids spills beyond the live broadcast to unexpected exposure on social media in the form of memes, for example.
It’s unclear whether the Trump administration is considering children in its decision-making. Emails over two days asking White House spokespeople for thoughts from the president and first lady Melania Trump thoughts on the prospect of children seeing the execution went unanswered. Trump said that he’ll soon make a decision on the plan to livestream the event.
Assume kids will at least hear about the execution, if not see it
From the old-fashioned grapevine to social media, grisly news has a way of reaching school-aged children, experts agree. Consider their need for calm and age-appropriate guidance, they suggest.
“With young kids, parents should keep it short and focus on reassurance over explaining the events,” said Jill Murphy, chief content officer at Common Sense Media, which advises parents on entertainment and technology. “Reassure them that they are safe. With teens, ask honestly what they have heard first, then ask whether they need to watch it.”
Remember you are your child’s parent, not their friend — and don’t overexplain, advises Dr. David Rosenberg, chair of psychiatry and behavioral neurosciences at Wayne State University School of Medicine in Michigan. Answer the questions children ask, and don’t be afraid to assert parental authority by, for example, restricting or banning a child’s access to the footage.
“It’s okay to say, ‘I don’t have all the answers. But here’s what we know, you’re safe, you’re secure, this is what we believe,’” Rosenberg said.
“Where parents get into trouble is when they talk too much, and they usually do that because they’re anxious and insecure,” he added. “What makes a child feel safest, or an adolescent, is can I count on my parents to be calm in challenging situations and give me the information I need?”
Choosing to watch the footage, one physician said, doesn’t necessarily indicate a child is psychologically ready to do so.
Timothy Lesaca, a Pittsburgh-area psychiatrist, cited a series of studies showing that repeatedly watching footage of events like the Boston Marathon bombings, at least part of an ISIS beheading video and the Oklahoma City bombing can be linked to post traumatic stress, if not PTSD, in adults and children. He argues that making Hasan’s execution public is a medical and public health issue.
“Ongoing anxiety, trouble sleeping or problems with daily life should be taken seriously,” Lesaca wrote in KevinMD.com, an online publication by physicians.
Watch how this event interacts with existing conditions
The people most at risk of negative long-term effects are those who already have clinical depression or anxiety, or who have already been exposed to other traumatic situations, Rosenberg said. That’s because repeat exposure to trauma can cause cumulative damage.
The part of the brain that handles executive decision-making, emotional regulation, impulsivity and empathy doesn’t finish developing until around age 24, and so parents should consider having proactive conversations even with their older children who may be away at college or living on their own, Rosenberg said.
“We have to at least offer help in these circumstances to be the leaders, to be the decision-makers, to at least help them make informed decisions.”
___
Associated Press journalist Kaitlyn Huamani contributed.

title: Six Flags closes 9 rides after roller coaster rider reportedly falls to his death in Georgia
text:
(Gray News) - Six Flags has temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks after police say a person was killed and several others were injured in an incident involving a coaster in Georgia.
Witnesses say a man fell to his death late Monday afternoon from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia in Cobb County. Several riders were stuck on the coaster after the deadly incident, WANF reports.
Neither Cobb County Police nor Six Flags officials have said what happened nor identified anyone involved. The park was closed after the incident.
In the aftermath, Six Flags has closed nine other roller coasters across six amusement parks that are similar to the coaster involved in the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks. The safety of our guests and team members remains one of our highest priorities,” Six Flags said.
The rides closed include Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Illinois, Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey and Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California.
Roller coasters were also closed at Ohio’s Kings Island, North Carolina’s Carowinds and Canada’s Wonderland in Ontario. All three parks are owned by Six Flags.

title: InvestigateTV+: Know the danger before you dig
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Construction work can quickly turn to catastrophe when crews break ground before natural gas and power lines are properly marked. InvestigateTV+ uncovers a rise in utility line strikes and what you need to know before you dig.
Plus, we examine the specialized service one spa offers to cancer patients.
Then, we introduce you to a group of seniors who make volunteering fun.
Digging dangers
We rely on natural gas and electricity every day to heat and light our homes. But one mistake underground can turn an energy source into an instant threat.
In 2024, the country saw more than 83,000 reports of damage to gas and electrical lines. One in four of those damage reports were because people failed to call 811.
That number connects you to a free, national service designed to prevent damage to utility lines by marking where they are located. Calling 811 is required by law.
Specialized spa treatment for cancer patients
An estimated four million people in the U.S. receive radiation therapy, an effective way to kill cancer.
But this treatment can bring an uncomfortable and sometimes painful side effect: radiation burn. One in five people who receive radiation therapy may develop more serious symptoms, such as blistering or open sores.
For cancer patients dealing with harsh treatments, one Baton Rouge spa is offering specialized care to help them feel their best during treatment.
A promise to mom, a century-old farm
Two Upstate South Carolina families have placed more than 250 acres under conservation easements through Upstate Forever, permanently restricting development on land that has been in their families for generations.
The announcement is part of a broader milestone for the organization, which now protects more than 40,000 acres across a 10-county area.
Sassy Seniors bring community service
A Las Vegas group called the Sassy Seniors has spent the past year showing up to community events across the valley dressed in pink and carrying pom-poms.
The group was founded by a woman named Kathy Yanke, who wanted to find others her age to do community work alongside. She has since recruited about a dozen women who rotate in and out of events throughout the Las Vegas Valley.

title: 🎃👻 MAINE’S SPOOKIEST LEGEND? The Mysterious Cursed Tomb in Bucksport!

Bucksport, Maine, Is Home to a Spooky Cursed Tomb Legend
This is such an exciting time of year! Fall really is the best, especially here in Maine. Between the beautiful foliage, crisp air, and all the Halloween-themed events happening across the state, there's no shortage of ways to get into the spooky spirit. And when it comes to creepy stories and local legends, it's hard to beat Bucksport!
Honestly, this is the perfect time of year to explore Bucksport. The fall scenery, historic charm, and spooky stories make it a fun destination for anyone looking to get out and enjoy the season.
One of Maine's greatest spooktacular days is almost here! Be sure to mark your calendar for Bucksport's 17th Annual Ghostport, Saturday, October 17th, from 10am-10pm.
Ghostport offers a full day of Halloween and fall-themed fun along the waterfront walkway!
Read More: Bucksport, Maine Transforms Into "Ghostport" For One Spooky Day
Did you know that Bucksport is home to one of Maine's most famous spooky legends: The Cursed Tomb of Colonel Buck. If you've never heard the story, prepare to enjoy a scary treat!
The tomb features a mysterious stain that looks quite a bit like a woman's stocking-clad leg and foot. Some people say it looks more like a boot, but either way, it's certainly not something you would ever expect to see on a memorial!
According to local legend, Colonel Jonathan Buck ordered a woman accused of witchcraft to be burned at the stake. As the story goes, one of her legs rolled out of the fire, and before her death, she placed a curse on the colonel. Then the strange leg-shaped stain later appeared on his tomb as a reminder of that curse.
Of course, it's a legend, but the story has been passed down through generations, making the tomb one of Bucksport's most talked about attractions.
If you're looking for a fun fall adventure in Maine, why not add Bucksport to your list? You can enjoy the autumn scenery, explore the town's historic charm, and check out the legendary tomb, it really is a perfect Halloween season adventure. Just don't forget to look for that mysterious stain!

title: Hannaford app, website offline as parent company addresses security issue
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford’s website and mobile app have been temporarily shut down as the supermarket chain’s parent company addresses a cybersecurity issue.
Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch company that owns the Scarborough-based grocer, said in a brief news release Monday that it was experiencing an internal network issue and had taken some systems offline to protect them.
That includes the Hannaford app and website, both of which carried messages Tuesday morning that they were unavailable.
Stores remain open as usual, and any unfulfilled online orders will be refunded.
The company said Tuesday that the measures were precautionary and that, although the investigation is ongoing, there is no evidence to suggest that customer or employee data was compromised.
A November 2024 breach of Ahold Delhaize’s systems affected more than 95,000 Mainers — most of them current or former employees, Hannaford said — and over 2 million people worldwide.
Ahold Delhaize did not provide a timeline for when online service was expected to be restored but said teams are “working with urgency” and were starting controlled relaunches of some systems. A Hannaford spokesperson reiterated that the company is working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.
“We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate our customers’ patience and understanding,” Hannaford spokesperson Caitlin Cortelyou said in a written statement Tuesday.
Ahold Delhaize says it has contacted outside cybersecurity experts to help with its response and is “engaging with the appropriate authorities” as necessary.
“As the investigation is ongoing, we are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts,” the company added.
If the cybersecurity issue is deemed to have been a data breach, then Maine law requires it to be reported to the Office of the Maine Attorney General. The office did not immediately respond to an email Tuesday asking whether it had received any reports about this issue.
Ahold Delhaize is one of the world’s largest food retailers and operates more than 2,000 U.S. stores under several brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant Food.
This is a developing story.

title: Midterms could set up power struggle between Congress and Trump
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The November midterm elections could dramatically reshape the balance of power in Washington, potentially setting up a confrontation between President Donald Trump and a Democratic-controlled Congress.
With just three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are fighting to maintain their congressional majorities, while Democrats are seeking to regain control. In the House, Democrats need a net gain of just four seats to flip the chamber.
Democratic leaders have already outlined an agenda focused on lowering the cost of living. But they are also promising to use their congressional authority to investigate President Donald Trump and his administration.
“Our promise to the country in the new Congress is that beginning on Day 1 we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in early October.
Even without control of the Senate, a Democratic majority in the House could significantly increase congressional oversight of the Trump administration.
Debbie Mucarsel-Powell, a former Democratic congresswoman who now leads the Graduate School of Political Management at George Washington University, said investigations would likely be among Democrats’ top priorities.
“I think that part of their priority will be to investigate,” Mucarsel-Powell said. “They also want to tackle the affordability issue and look into Medicaid cuts.”
Democratic-led committees could hold hearings, issue subpoenas and investigate the administration’s spending, policies and conduct.
“It’s a very large responsibility of the House and the Senate to ensure the American public understands how their taxpayer dollars have been used under this administration, what kind of actions the president, his family and his friends have taken,” she said.
A Democratic House could also block Republican legislation and use its authority over federal spending to negotiate changes to administration priorities. However, Democrats would still need the Senate’s cooperation to pass legislation.
Control of both the House and Senate would give Democrats greater authority over federal spending, congressional investigations and the legislative agenda.
A Democratic-controlled Senate could also block Trump’s judicial and Cabinet nominees, preventing the president from filling positions that require Senate confirmation.
Democrats would also control both chambers involved in the impeachment process. The House could vote to impeach the president by a simple majority, but removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate.
Still, even with majorities in both chambers, Democrats would face significant obstacles to reversing the president’s policies.
“It would be difficult for Democrats to actually repeal some of those laws or that funding that’s has already been in place. The president also has veto power,” Mucarsel-Powell said.
Congress would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto, making it difficult for Democrats to enact legislation without some Republican support.
Regardless of which party controls Congress, Trump would retain broad executive authority.
The president could continue issuing executive orders, granting federal pardons, conducting diplomacy and directing military operations, subject to constitutional and legal limits.
He could also veto legislation passed by Democrats and continue implementing existing laws through federal agencies.
Congress, meanwhile, could use its oversight and spending powers to challenge the administration, potentially leading to legal disputes over the limits of presidential authority.
The division of power could make it difficult for either party to advance its legislative agenda, raising the possibility of prolonged gridlock.
However, Mucarsel-Powell said the election could also create an opportunity for bipartisanship, particularly as voters express frustration with both parties.
Whether Democrats gain control of one chamber, both chambers or neither will be decided in the Nov. 3 elections, with the next Congress taking office in early January.

title: Blue Hill stops advertising top administrator job but still looking locally
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Blue Hill’s town administrator job, its top municipal management position, has been empty for more than a year and isn’t publicly posted — but the town is still looking for candidates.
After hiring three administrators in four years since it created the job, Blue Hill still needs the role filled but is instead trying to find a lasting candidate locally in a “more low-key way,” according to Select Board Chair Ellen Best.
“We don’t feel like it’s probably going to work well for somebody to move here to take over,” she said Friday, noting housing costs as one challenge.
Towns across Maine have had increasing trouble recruiting and retaining managers to run their daily operations in recent years, often meaning key positions are unfilled for months as municipalities look for applicants and face high turnover. Blue Hill’s approach shows a different way one town is trying to meet that statewide challenge, though it hasn’t yet filled the job.
Maine is already an older state and existing managers are nearing retirement age, experts previously told the BDN. Housing is also expensive, and smaller towns often can’t compete with cities or other states on salaries for the complex, often demanding roles.
The state’s university system no longer offers a pipeline for municipal leaders, either, and increasing public vitriol is often directed at managers, the Maine Monitor reported this summer.
Blue Hill residents voted to create the position in 2019.
The part-time Select Board had directly supervised town employees before, a system that officials said at the time grew antiquated as management became more complex with factors like new technology, increased expectations for government services, town growth and Blue Hill’s position as a service center for the surrounding peninsula.
The first administrator, Shawna Ambrose, was promoted from within the town office that fall and resigned in early 2022 to spend more time with family.
The position was vacant for months until Nicholas Nadeau was hired from Vermont in August 2022. He left a year later, partway through his contract. Julie Atwell, who moved from New Hampshire to take the position after Nadeau in September 2023, left last June to work as a business manager for local School Union 93.
The town didn’t have immediate plans to try to rehire then, Best told the Weekly Packet newspaper at the time.
The job opening still isn’t publicly posted, but the select board “definitely” knows the town needs a person to manage its affairs on an ongoing basis, she said Friday.
Town hall staff and the Select Board are sharing responsibilities as they wait to find someone through local connections to take on the role. Town office hours were reduced last summer amid other staff departures, she said, but are close to full capacity again.
The interim plan has created more work for both groups, according to Best.
Having an administrator would help board members focus more on long-term planning and the bigger-picture issues that may have motivated them to run for office, rather than administrative details, she previously said.

title: Congress pushes breast cancer legislation during awareness month
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Capitol Hill lawmakers have recently been marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month by sharing their stories and pushing for legislation to combat the disease.
“So many women, more than 1 in 10 women are going to get breast cancer eventually. And so you want to get that information out there,” said Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), a breast cancer survivor who has introduced several screening and prevention bills throughout her time in Congress.
Despite the busy midterm election season, House and Senate lawmakers have been speaking out about the deadly disease that impacts millions of American women, including some who work in Congress.
“My mom is a triple negative breast cancer survivor, and I was having issues,” said Rep. Julia Letlow (R-LA), who is currently running for U.S. Senate.
Letlow announced last week she had undergone a preemptive double mastectomy three years ago after being screened and learning that she was at high risk for the disease.
“It was one of the hardest experiences that I’ve ever been through,” she said. “But every day I wake up grateful that I no longer have to have that in the back of my mind, worried that I might have have to deal with breast cancer one day.”
The experience, along with advocacy efforts by breast cancer survivor and actress Olivia Munn, inspired her to introduce her Know Your Risk Act bill last Tuesday. The bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to create a single universal breast cancer risk assessment tool.
“I really want women of every age to know that this exists, because I had no idea that there was there was a tool like that out there,” Letlow said. “And for me, I just want to make sure that it’s available to all women and men, and also that there is one that everybody agrees on.”
On the Senate side, Klobuchar’s breast cancer legislation that reauthorizes Centers for Disease Control and Prevention breast cancer programs for young women, known at the EARLY Act, passed in September. It now awaits House passage.
Klobuchar said awareness and education remain one of the most important parts of the fight against the disease. And she has seen firsthand just how much those efforts can help after announcing her diagnosis in 2021.
“I found out I had breast cancer. And when I put that information out there, I could not believe the number of people that wrote me,” she said. “Women calling, saying I got my appointment and a number of them found out they had cancer.”
Klobuchar, who is running for governor of Minnesota, has also been pushing for legislation that requires health insurance plans to cover screening and diagnostic breast imaging with no out-of-pocket costs.
“It’s been rewarding because, you know, we’ve seen a lot of a lot of success stories with people getting help,” Sen. Klobuchar said.
Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., also said in a statement this week that he will continue to work to combat the disease.
“Breast Cancer Awareness Month is a reminder that early detection saves lives,” Sen. Kelly said. “Women deserve to know about all the cancer screening options available to them. I’ll keep working to make sure women in Arizona and across the country can get the preventive care and treatment they need.”
Despite how difficult it can be to get legislation through Congress, advocates say congressional efforts that put a spotlight on breast cancer can be helpful.
“Having legislation and politicians promote the awareness of this disease, amongst other cancers, is very helpful in just bringing the resources to us as cancer patients,” said Natasha Parker, a registered nurse, clinical educator and breast cancer survivor.
Parker also said Letlow’s bill could be helpful for women who are trying to assess their breast cancer risk.
“Hopefully with a bill such as this, if it were to get passed, that would allow more access to the screening tools,” she said. “Which could then potentially discover cancer in patients much younger, in a much earlier phase of their treatment.”

title: Congress pushes breast cancer legislation during awareness month
