title: Fire destroys Maine variety store
text:
A fire destroyed a New Gloucester store early Sunday morning.
A passerby spotted heavy smoke coming from Link’s Variety Store on Lewiston Road about 2:07 a.m., according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Firefighters quickly tamed the flames, but the store and its contents were extensively damaged and are considered a total loss.
Investigators believe the fire started near the furnace, where boxes had been placed.
No one was injured.

title: Spruce Mountain schools target fourth grade math decline as scores improve
text:
JAY — Math scores are improving among younger students in Regional School Unit 73, but a decline in performance beginning in fourth grade has prompted a closer examination of classroom instruction, curriculum consistency and teacher training.
Chris Hollingsworth, the district’s curriculum and technology coordinator, presented three years of assessment data during the Oct. 8 board of directors meeting, highlighting gains in third grade math performance while identifying challenges as students advance to more complex material.
“We actually have shown growth in math over the last three years,” Hollingsworth said.
Third-grade assessment scores increased from 1495 to 1499 and then to 1501 over the three years, approaching the state benchmark of 1505, according to figures Hollingsworth presented.
He also reported that the percentage of third grade students in a performance category identified as green increased from 42% to 55% between the first two years reviewed, compared with statewide figures of 48% and 49%, respectively.
Despite those gains, Hollingsworth said students struggle to maintain their progress as they move into fourth grade, when instruction introduces more challenging concepts and additional word problems.
“The bad news is things seem to go well until the end of third grade and then we kind of hit a cliff,” he said.
The findings have prompted a review of how teachers use Math in Focus, the district’s mathematics curriculum. Hollingsworth said conversations with elementary school teachers revealed considerable variation in the instructional resources being used across classrooms.
He is working with building principals to align Math in Focus lessons with the district’s established scope and sequence, which outlines the progression of mathematical skills students are expected to master before reaching high school algebra.
The effort is intended to provide more consistent instruction across classrooms while making better use of curriculum materials the district already purchases. Hollingsworth said he plans to review the curriculum and identify lessons that correspond with the instructional sequence.
Principals will work with teachers to ensure classroom lessons follow that progression. The district hopes to use existing professional development periods and other scheduled staff time to complete the alignment work. Providing additional training to help teachers implement the curriculum effectively, however, remains a challenge.
“Unfortunately we’re not a district that has a lot of professional development money,” Hollingsworth said. He explained that funding allocated for teacher stipends associated with committee work reduces the money available for professional development. Training costs have also increased, making it difficult to bring in outside specialists.
RSU 73 participates in a regional educational collaborative that offers professional development opportunities, but Hollingsworth said relatively few neighboring districts use Math in Focus, limiting access to training tailored to the program.
He is contacting the collaborative’s director to explore opportunities for additional support, including training focused on elementary mathematics instruction.
The district’s approach involves two related efforts: aligning existing curriculum materials with instructional expectations and identifying affordable ways to give teachers the training needed to use those materials effectively.
Hollingsworth said much of the curriculum alignment can be completed through planning and collaboration with principals, while additional training will depend on available funding. He expects the work to continue throughout the school year, with principals taking a central role in coordinating instructional changes across buildings.
The district also plans to revisit professional development needs during upcoming budget discussions, when the costs and potential benefits of additional training can be considered. Hollingsworth cautioned that the challenges facing RSU 73 are not unique to Spruce Mountain schools, pointing to broader concerns about math achievement across Maine.
“It’s not a Spruce Mountain issue,” he said. “It’s a whole state issue.”
While the district works to address declining performance in higher grades, Hollingsworth emphasized the importance of making full use of the resources already available. “When we’re paying for Math in Focus, we want to make sure that we’re getting everything out of that as well,” he said.
RSU 73 includes Jay, Livermore and Livermore Falls.

title: Auburn residents want to see changes along Minot Avenue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Auburn residents would like to see the downtown section of Minot Avenue improved, with a focus on redeveloping vacant properties, and using those properties to support new business and enhance the area’s appearance.
That’s the essence of more than 600 responses from the public when asked their thoughts on the corridor as part of the city’s Downtown Minot Avenue Revitalization Plan.
Eric Cousens, Auburn’s director of public service, said the feedback the city received so far comes from an online survey, Facebook, a public input session in August, and interviews done with property owners along Minot Avenue over the summer.
Most of the feedback Auburn officials received focused on addressing vacant properties, whether by redeveloping or removing them. That includes the former large shoe factory building at 67 Minot Ave.
Other feedback focused on improving pedestrian safety, upgrading the appearance and helping current businesses in the area remain successful.
The Downtown Minot Avenue Revitalization Plan targets the area of Minot Avenue from Court Street to Washington Street. Cousens said the plan comes after the city implemented a vacant property ordinance last year in response to a large number of empty buildings along that stretch of the street.
Eight properties along the corridor appear to be vacant — buildings or lots. Some are more notable, such as the former Auburn Police Station at 1 Minot Ave. and the former Lunn & Sweet Shoe Co., which was a major employer for many years starting in 1908.
None of the properties are owned by the city, said Cousens.
“We had a really good response from the public on this matter,” Cousens said. “It really seems to be an important corridor to people that live here in Auburn, whether they live in the corridor or not.”
In total, the city has received 653 responses so far from the community, according to the plan summary. Of those, 445 came from an online survey, 22 on an online map, 151 on Facebook and 35 from interviews with property owners and a public input session.
The online survey showed that of those expressing an opinion, 258 people preferred significant transformation to the corridor, 138 wanted to see moderate change, and 41 favored little or no change.
According to the summary, residents see the area as an “opportunity to bring visible investment and renewed activity to a corridor that participants believe has not reached its potential,” including possible use of vacant space and properties for childcare operations, retail and restaurants, parks and gathering spaces.
The city’s online map allows residents to put markers along the corridor and suggest what they would like to see there. Some responses mentioned unsafe conditions for residents. Others called for the former factory building to become mixed-use development and for expansion of trails in and around the area to better connect the city.
Comments on Facebook also mentioned the former factory, with some calling for its razing and others wanting to preserve it for business use, retail and housing.
Cousens highlighted the importance of the corridor to the city, calling it an important gateway to downtown Auburn.
“Over 20,000 cars a day pass through that corridor,” he said. “What happens in that corridor has a significant impact on Auburn residents and even those that don’t live in that area.”
The next public meeting on the plan is at 6 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, at the Senior Community Center, 48 Pettengill Park. Cousens said the meeting will include a look at public feedback and concept ideas for what the corridor could look like.
The goal, he said, is to have a final action plan for the area complete by December or January 2027.
Auburn residents can continue sharing their thoughts at tinyurl.com/minotavenuefeedback.

title: Susan Collins will not move off script
text:
I expect my representatives to have the courage and courtesy to stand in front of the people they’re supposed to serve. In refusing to take questions from her constituents, Sen. Collins shows neither.
Collins hides behind a veil of smear advertising, paid for by those from away who have no interest in Maine. They’re investing in her allegiance to them, not we the people. The senator will hide behind the theater of scripted “debate” by a media that profits outrageously from that advertising. That media doesn’t have the courage to ask meaningful questions. It’s a charade.
I’ve gone to a “town hall” with Troy Jackson. He took random unscripted questions from a big audience of everyday people. He was asked some hard ones. He answered them forthrightly. He has the courage and character to earn my vote.
Leo Ojala
Kennebunk

title: Fog and scattered showers overnight
text:
Fog and scattered showers overnight
Another round of beneficial rain is likely later this week
Fog and scattered showers overnight
Another round of beneficial rain is likely later this week
Widespread, steady rain becomes more scattered Tuesday evening, with showers expected off and on overnight. Patchy fog continues and will linger into Wednesday morning.
Another half inch of rain is possible overnight, with showers expected to wind down early Wednesday morning. However, mist and drizzle may linger along with clouds and fog, especially during the first half of the day. Milder temperatures are expected in the afternoon, with highs mainly in the 50s and 60s.
A bright but breezy day is expected on Thursday as northwest winds gust to around 20 mph. Temperatures run slightly cool on Thursday afternoon, with highs in the 40s and 50s.
The next storm to impact Maine races across the Great Lakes Thursday night, arriving in Maine on Friday with another widespread, soaking rainfall. A half inch to an inch of rain is possible by Saturday morning.
Gusty winds from the south are likely on Friday as the storm arrives. Winds then shift to the northwest heading into Saturday, a cold day with highs in the 30s and 40s. Winds gust 30 to 45 mph on Saturday, enough to down branches and create wind chills in the 30s throughout the afternoon.
Mountain snow showers are likely on Saturday, and a few flurries may spill further south. Sunday is still cool but less windy with temperatures expected to return to average next week.

title: Tres meses después de la muerte de Johan Sebastián, seguimos luchando por la verdad
text:
Sean P. Murphy fue fiscal en el Bronx y fiscal federal, combatió el crimen organizado y ayudó a dirigir la investigación del Departamento de Justicia sobre el ataque del 6 de enero al Capitolio. Criado en Vermont y hoy abogado de Gideon Asen en Maine, representa a la familia de Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
Hace casi tres meses, en la madrugada del 13 de julio de 2026, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero salió de su casa. Pensaba, como cada mañana, en el momento en que volvería para abrazar a su esposa, Karolina, y a su pequeña hija.
La noche anterior había sido como cualquier otra. Karolina dobló la ropa. Johan dijo que se iba a acostar. Se dieron un beso. Ninguno de los dos imaginó que sería el último.
Nunca tuve la fortuna de conocer a Johan en vida. Hay algo extraño y hermoso en llegar a conocer a alguien solo a través de quienes lo amaron y hoy tienen que vivir sin él.
Lo conocí a través de sus padres, Omar y Dora, quienes viajaron desde Colombia para reclamar el cuerpo de su hijo. En la funeraria de Portland, salí de la sala, pero los gritos de dolor de una madre ante el cuerpo de su hijo asesinado atravesaron las paredes. Fue un lamento que nunca hubiera querido escuchar y que jamás quiero olvidar.
Lo conocí a través de Daniela, su hermana, quien fue la primera de la familia en llegar a Estados Unidos. Como le pasaría a cualquier hermana mayor, carga con una culpa que no le corresponde. Daniela, nada de esto fue culpa tuya. Sabemos quién es responsable.
Y lo conocí a través de Karolina y de la hija que tuvieron juntos. Me asombra la fortaleza de Karolina. Este país les ha arrebatado demasiado. Lo siento de corazón. Basta pasar dos minutos con esa niña para saber que la llama de su papá sigue viva en ella.
Desde julio, mi socio Ben Gideon y yo hemos luchado por Johan. Hace poco nos reunimos con representantes de la oficina del fiscal general del estado de Maine, la primera y única entidad gubernamental que ha confirmado que investiga el uso de fuerza letal por parte de un agente federal.
En esa reunión nos devolvieron varios objetos que habían sido considerados sin valor probatorio. Pero faltaba uno: la silla de seguridad de su hija para el carro. Karolina preguntó por qué. Le dijeron que una bala disparada por un agente federal la había atravesado, así como otras balas disparadas por un agente federal habían matado a su esposo.
Las primeras versiones decían que su hija iba con él en el carro. Gracias a Dios, no era así. Pero la temeridad salta a la vista, y cuesta siquiera imaginar el horror de lo que pudo haber ocurrido. Una sola tragedia ya era demasiado.
La única justificación que han dado para la muerte de Johan ha sido la «seguridad pública». ¿Saben qué protege de verdad a la gente? No dispararles a padres de familia inocentes, que cumplen la ley y cuyo único sueño es darles una vida mejor a los suyos.
Hablemos claro sobre lo que pasó aquí. Este gobierno tomó la infame decisión de quitarle la vida a Johan y, ante las consecuencias, ha guardado silencio. Un presidente que quiere ser rey ha decidido que cualquiera de nosotros puede ser sacrificado con tal de imponer su agenda. Tiene que dejar de violar nuestro derecho a la vida, y tiene que hacerlo ya.
Johan no tenía la ciudadanía estadounidense, pero encarnaba lo mejor de lo que significa ser estadounidense. Trabajaba, amaba a su familia y soñaba. Quien justifique que lo hayan matado no puede llamarse patriota.
Y Johan no es el único. Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good, Alex Pretti y Lorenzo Salgado Araujo forman parte del mismo club, uno al que nadie querría pertenecer y cuya cuota se paga con la vida. A sus familias les deben respuestas, no excusas.
Pero de poco sirve la indignación si perdemos la esperanza. Quien haya vivido un invierno en Maine sabe que incluso el frío más crudo termina por cederle el paso a la primavera. Ahora que se acercan las elecciones de mitad de período en Estados Unidos, espero y le pido a Dios que nuestro país empiece a abrirse camino hacia esa primavera.
Esto no es lo que somos los estadounidenses. Tenemos que ser mejores.
Tres meses después, la familia de Johan sigue esperando verdad, justicia y que los responsables rindan cuentas. No dejaremos de luchar hasta que eso ocurra.

title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis gets 40 years to life in prison in Tupac Shakur’s murder case
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — Duane “Keffe D” Davis has been sentenced in the 1996 shooting death murder case of Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas.
On Tuesday, Judge Carli Kierny sentenced Davis to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of Shakur.
A jury found Davis guilty on Aug. 31 after less than three hours of deliberations on charges that included first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.
Davis had already been in police custody since his arrest in September 2023.
Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars.
Shakur’s killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir.
According to DiGiacomo, Davis was trying to profit off a killing that he committed, and for that he does not deserve the minimum sentence.
“In my mind he deserves the maximum possible sentence,” DiGiacomo added.
Davis’ lawyer, Michael Sanft, said he plans to appeal the verdict.

title: 3 arrested after abandoned infant found alive in trash can
text:
SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A newborn baby was found alive in a trash can near the Quality Inn on Abercorn Street early Saturday morning, according to Savannah police.
Three people are now facing charges.
What happened
Chatham EMS Director Chuck Kearns said crews initially responded to a call for a patient experiencing hemorrhaging. At the hospital, the EMS crew realized the patient had given birth. They alerted police, who searched the hotel and found the baby alive.
SPD responded around 2:45 a.m. Oct. 10 to a report of child abandonment on Abercorn Street.
After an initial investigation, Sgt. Howard Crosby and Ofc. Richard Taylor with the Southside Precinct discovered the infant in a nearby trash can.
The child was given immediate medical attention. The baby is now in the care of the Department of Human Services’ Division of Family and Children Services, known as DFCS.
SPD thanked Memorial Health medical staff, Chatham EMS and Savannah Fire for their assistance in locating the child quickly and safely.
Charges filed
Dominique Welcome, 29, Chiquita Roche, 39, and Jamal West, 44, were arrested and face charges in connection with the case.
Welcome is charged with cruelty to children. Roche is charged with party to a crime and willful obstruction of law enforcement officers by use of threats or violence. West is charged with cruelty to children.
Chatham County jail records show Roche was arrested at the hotel, West was arrested on scene at the hotel and Welcome was arrested at Memorial Hospital.
Safe haven law
SPD reminded the public that under Georgia’s Safe Place for Newborns Act, state law gives criminal immunity to a mother who leaves her baby, if the baby is no more than 30 days old, with a staff member or volunteer at an authorized medical facility, fire station or police station.
Examples include the Memorial Health Dwaine & Cynthia Willett Children’s Hospital of Savannah and the Savannah Fire Department. Designated “Safe Place” facilities are marked with signage.
Michael Bossak, vice president of Children’s Hospital of Savannah, said the hospital serves as a safe space for children of all ages, including newborns.
“I think as a pediatrician and as a vice president of the Children’s Hospital, I think it’s important. We are the safe space for children of all ages that includes the youngest ones, so being able to place where mothers can come guilt-free to be able to drop off a child and say, ‘Look, I’m not able to do this, but I want this baby to survive and have the best life possible,’ is an important part of what we do here at Children’s Hospital,” Bossak said.

title: Oxford fire chief lauded for saving lives in fire
text:
Oxford Fire Chief Ashley Wax-Armstrong was recognized Oct. 1 with a Lifesaving Award for her actions during a structure fire last year.
Wax-Armstrong was presented with the award during the Select Board meeting in which representatives of the Office of State Fire Marshal, Deputy Chief Joel Davis, Sgt. Ken MacMaster, Sgt. Jeremy Damren and Senior Investigator Andrew Whitney attended.
She was enroute to an emergency call on Nov. 28, 2025, when she, MacMaster and Davis saw a house on fire in Paris and stopped to investigate. Occupants were trapped on the second floor.
According to a statement posted by the fire marshal’s office on its Facebook page, the three located a ladder and used it to access occupants.
Wax-Armstrong saved an infant from the building and assisted in rescuing an elderly person.
“We are incredibly proud to have Chief Wax-Armstrong serving our community and are grateful for her courage, quick thinking, and dedication to helping others,” the town of Oxford posted on social media.
MacMaster and Whitney separately received Lifesaving Awards during a state fire marshal’s office meeting in August.
“We are incredibly proud of Chief Wax-Armstrong, Sgt. MacMaster, and Senior Investigator Whitney,” the marshal’s office wrote on its Facebook page. “Their actions are a powerful reminder that sometimes the most important part of the job isn’t investigating how a fire started, but making sure everyone gets out safely.”

The president mocked the protester from the stage and said people who disrupt his rallies are “scum.” Messages seeking more information were left with the Youngstown police and Mahoning County sheriff’s office.
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia to hold first briefing
Zacharia officially started the job on Monday and watched from the sidelines as Trump answered questions from reporters as he departed the White House for a campaign trip to Ohio.
Her first press briefing was scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Tuesday.
Zacharia is a conservative commentator and had been a communications adviser to the media company that Trump owns and operates his social media site.
Trump announced her appointment last week. Zacharia succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August following the birth of her second child.
FACT FOCUS: Posts falsely claim Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico was at a mental facility
Republican officials and conservative social media users spread unfounded rumors in recent days that state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in a competitive Texas Senate race, had suffered a mental health crisis.
Questions about Talarico’s whereabouts began spreading after the candidate was not seen in public for nine days. But he and his campaign have repeatedly attributed his absence to the flu.
Here’s a closer look at the facts:
CLAIM: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico was being treated in an Ohio mental health facility last week.
THE FACTS: This is false. The facility where he was said to have been treated has denied he was ever a patient there. Both he and his campaign have said he was recovering from the flu. Talarico has type 1 diabetes, which means he has a higher risk of developing complications from the flu. Regardless, Talarico’s schedule doesn’t align with what was presented as evidence of his stay at the mental health facility and images reviewed by The Associated Press showed Talarico at home over several days last week.
Federal judge orders Trump administration to halt work for a day on historic DC golf course
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Monday ordered a 24-hour halt to tree-cutting at the East Potomac Golf Course, a historic D.C. course that has been part of President Donald Trump’s plans to remake the city.
Reyes issued the order following a tense three-hour hearing in which she harshly criticized the government for having deceived her with its actions over the holiday weekend.
Reyes said the 24-hour temporary order could be extended to 14 days if necessary. It was limited to one day while the government tries to find a key Trump administration official to discuss why a massive tree-cutting at the park needed to occur over the holiday weekend, with little notification to plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to halt renovation plans or the judge.
It’s the latest example of the erosion of trust between the government and the independent judiciary, as the Trump administration tries to steamroll scrutiny of its actions, from the White House ballroom to immigration enforcement.
Trump is heading all the way to Alaska in a sign of just how close its Senate race may be
It’s a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn’t backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years.
Yet Trump on Tuesday will devote a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head all the way to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.
Trump is headlining a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles (72 kilometers) north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state.
Trump’s stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday.
“Dan Sullivan’s a great senator,” Trump said last week, adding, “You look at the things he’s done. He would call me all the time because I think — I definitely know — nobody has helped Alaska like Donald Trump.”
Trump’s diesel deal with Putin draws criticism from a frustrated Congress
House Speaker Nancy Pelosi stood before Donald Trump during his first term at the White House and pointed a finger, declaring that with this president, “All roads lead to Putin.”
The stark assessment years ago from Pelosi echoed anew after Trump’s surprise announcement last week that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. as a way to ease sky-high prices at the pumps for Americans ahead of the midterm elections.
Trump’s diesel deal with Putin has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats as fueling Russia’s war against Ukraine, violating existing U.S. laws and drawing the U.S. closer to Russia. It joins a growing list of instances where the president has sided with Putin, often at the expense of Ukraine — and America’s own standing.
“The harm to the Ukrainians is real,” said William Taylor, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, now a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, in an interview Monday.
“And the cost to us, the United States, is high.”

title: Westbrook woman charged in connection with school bus crash
text:
A Westbrook woman was charged following a Friday crash with a school bus that had 19 children on board in addition to staff members.
Annemarie Napolitano, 40, of Westbrook, has been charged with operating under the influence, aggravated criminal mischief and violation of conditions of release, the Westbrook Police Department said in a news release Tuesday.
The department said first responders were dispatched to the area of 93 County Road for the crash at about 9:35 a.m. Friday.
Investigators determined that an SUV operated by Napolitano had crossed the center line and crashed into the front driver’s side corner of the Bonny Eagle bus. The SUV then continued traveling and struck the side of the bus and nearly hit another vehicle “before ending up on the side of the road,” the department said.
The 19 children on the bus were between the ages of 4 and 12, and another five staff members were also on board, according to police.
“A few children on the bus complained of pain, and were evaluated by the Westbrook Fire Department, but no children or staff members required transportation to the hospital,” the department stated.

title: Glowing 'space jellyfish' effect lights up sky after rocket launch
text:
Glowing 'space jellyfish' effect lights up sky after rocket launch
SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket launch Tuesday morning created a glowing, jellyfish-like effect in the sky.
See video in the player above.
The rocket lifted off at 6:33 a.m. from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Cape Canaveral, Florida, carrying the company’s 35th commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station.
What is a 'space jellyfish'?
The unusual visual effect, often called a “space jellyfish,” can occur when a rocket launches around sunrise or sunset.
Sunlight illuminates the rocket’s exhaust plume at high altitudes, while the ground below remains dark, creating a glowing, spreading shape in the sky.
After an approximately 52-hour flight, the Dragon spacecraft is expected to autonomously dock at the space station on Thursday at about 11 a.m.
Following stage separation, the Falcon 9’s first-stage booster was set to attempt a landing at Landing Zone 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.

title: Come for Heather Cox Richardson, stay for Troy Jackson
text:
I went to Portland to see Heather Cox Richardson in conversation with Troy Jackson. Really, I was there to see Richardson. Troy was the price I had to pay to see her.
I planned to vote for Troy because he is not Susan Collins. Knowing little about Aroostook County, I had not felt a strong allegiance to him. At first, Troy seemed slightly starstruck and stumbled a bit in the presence of Richardson. Who wouldn’t be starstruck? Thankfully, she is generous with whomever she shares the stage or microphone. He warmed quickly and found firm ground.
What I gleaned about Troy: He’s not shiny or sparkly. Good. I don’t like the shiny and sparkly politicians. Instead, Troy is a piece of beautiful hardwood with a warm patina. Once he loosened up, I found genuine Maine charm that comes from being a part of the community of Maine, a straight talker who speaks directly to issues of great concern to me: Medicaid and Medicare for all; affordable, quality childcare with childcare workers who earn a living wage, an education system that pays teachers and teaches students and an end to the war in Iran.
I came away from Portland forgetting that HCR had been there. I am now excited to vote Jackson for senator.
Lisa Eaton
Kennebunk

title: Kaydenz Kitchen requests donations of everyday items
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DEAR SUN SPOTS: At Kaydenz Kitchen (550 Center St. in Auburn) we have everyday needs and appreciate community members’ donations so much. Right now we are requesting coffee, creamer, sugar, paper plates, all-purpose cleaner, disinfectant wipes and hand soap.
At the Warming Center at 70 Horton St. in Lewiston, needed items include hand warmers, warm socks, gloves, hats, and new underwear. — No name, no town
ANSWER: Items can be dropped off at Kaydenz Kitchen on Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m.
The Warming Center is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, except for 10:30-11:30 a.m. for staff cleaning.
I urge Sun Spotters to choose an area nonprofit this winter that assists the unhoused and focus on one thing you can do to help, either with a financial donation, needed items, or by volunteering a few hours of your time. Let’s band together and spread some sunshine.
DEAR SUN SPOTS: A huge thank you to Women Giving Back for their generous donation of paper plates to the Drop-In Center!
We’re so grateful for the continued support of our community and organizations like Women Giving Back. Thank you for supporting the Drop-in Center and the people we serve.— No name, Auburn
ANSWER: Here’s another tidbit about this hardworking organization. Guests can be connected with a case manager on Wednesdays.
DEAR SUN SPOTS: We rake up leaves on our property that fill on average, over 100 bags or more per year. In the past, we put them out with trash collection. Now with the new collection schedule, we have been informed that leaves will only be collected one week in November in Lewiston.
We certainly cannot pile up that many bags curbside for November. In the meantime, we’re told we can take them to the transfer station or put a bag in with the trash bin, if they fit.
We are seniors and do not have a truck to transport bags of leaves every week so if anyone would like leaves for mulching or to use the bags as insulation around your house foundation, you may contact me at 784-5953, and we will gladly have the leaves bagged and ready for curbside pickup. — Denise, Lewiston

I think Denise is smart to ask Sun Spotters if they want to use these bags of leaves for their gardens and for insulation. The leaves are also great for those large Halloween bags that can be stuffed with leaves and look like jack o’lanterns.
I do hope some Sun Spotters will volunteer to help move these bags of leaves to be used or taken to the transfer station as a favor to this fellow reader.

title: Inside the Maine unit investigating online child exploitation
text:
VASSALBORO, Maine (WABI) - A specialized unit in the Maine State Police investigates online child exploitation and works to educate the public about it.
Unit changed name last year
The unit shifted last year from the Computer Crimes Unit to the Major Crimes Unit–Special Victims. Investigators say the name is more appropriate for the type of investigations they conduct.
“We’re partnered up with agencies from all the way to Madawaska and Fort Kent all the way down to Kittery,” said Lt. Taylor Bagley, of the Special Victims Unit, Maine State Police.
The unit works in cooperation with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which facilitates cybertips. Those tips have increased in recent years.
“With 4,000 cyber tips coming in over the course of a year, we have to find creative ways because we can’t staff our way out of that particular issue,” Bagley said.
The unit also manages the Northern New England Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, known as ICAC. Its mission is to identify, arrest and prosecute anyone who uses the internet to produce or share child sexual abuse material, including anyone who uses the internet to lure minors into illicit relationships.
“We’re still working with child pornography on the ICAC side but the increase in just the chat cases that we’re seeing and sextortion related offenses throughout the state has grown substantially. That has taken a toll on our resources in the lab,” Bagley said.
“We have nine analysts with two supervisors, and they will usually go out with every search warrant to help assist with examining devices,” said Sgt. Joshua Lander, of the Special Victims Unit, Maine State Police.
A forensic investigator with the unit described the process. “We work off our forensic images, so we’ll make a forensic copy of the evidence which we then process and look for artifacts relevant to the case.”
Dog trained to detect electronic devices
In addition to technology, the unit is also utilizing a dog. Marley is Maine’s first electronic storage detection K-9.
“There have been multiple cases over the last two years that detectives have not found devices. I bring Marley in. Marley finds the device. In multiple cases, that was the only device that Marley found had the CSAM (child sexual assault material) on the device. Had it not been for Marley finding that device, the suspect would not have been charged,” said Sgt. Christopher Crawford, of the Special Victims Unit, Maine State Police.
Crawford said Marley has also been an asset in other investigations. “He has found cell phones that were thrown out that were critical for a homicide investigation.”
Investigators urge parents to talk with children
Investigators say the single most important thing parents can do is talk to their kids about their online activity.
“Anytime a person online is starting to ask those personal questions about like how old they are, where they go to school – those are the red flags that you really want the kids to know about,” Lander said.
The Major Crimes Unit–Special Victims is headquartered in Vassalboro, with satellite offices in Bangor and Gray.

title: Sanford leaders weigh future of Woolen Mill amid health, safety concerns
text:
Sanford officials say they are working to address health and safety issues at the old Woolen Mill that prompted an emergency closure of Heritage Crossing last week.
The Sanford City Council voted Tuesday night to extend that emergency closure until public safety officials advise it’s safe to lift it and the council votes to do so.
The city announced Thursday that it was temporarily closing the road near the mill complex to both vehicles and pedestrians because the area has been continually accumulating trash and other waste, establishing an “attractive nuisance and extraordinary public safety hazard.”
Officials say it has been frequented by homeless residents, and that’s caused nearby residents and business owners to raise concerns about safety, particularly syringe waste and fire hazards. The City Council voted in July to declare the mill officially abandoned, which city officials say allows them to take further action.
Multiple council members, city staff and the police chief stressed at Tuesday’s meeting that they have been working for months to address issues at the former mill. Some specifically refuted claims that they had only taken action due to recent media reports.
“I don’t police on media reports,” Police Chief Eric Small said at Tuesday’s meeting. “I police on facts and to keep the public safe. … To do an operation like we did today is complicated.”
In a social media statement earlier Tuesday, Small said officers swept the area that morning and arrested three people for criminal trespass, violating release conditions and outstanding warrants and issued three other summonses for criminal trespass. The chief added that officers also conducted a sweep last week that reduced the number of people allegedly trespassing.
“We recognize that this closure may cause some inconvenience,” Small said in a statement on Facebook last week following the emergency declaration. “However, protecting the public, neighboring businesses, and emergency personnel must remain our priority.”
ENFORCEMENT
Police Maj. Mark Dyer said in an interview Tuesday that the department has been aware of the concerns for a while and has been working to determine how to tackle the issue.
Because the town doesn’t own the mill, enforcement has been difficult, Dyer said. Now, with the property declared abandoned and permission from the mill’s now-defunct owner, police have been granted more leeway to sweep the property.
Dyer said police will continue to pay close attention to the area.
“We’re not gonna just do this operation and be done,” he said. “We have been stepping up our drive-bys, our footbeats, officers just parked in the area — that will continue.”
Small went into detail on the recent sweeps, the lead-up, and potential paths forward at Tuesday night’s meeting when responding to questions from councilors.
Among recent safety concerns raised, the chief said, was someone throwing objects off the roof.
“That’s why it needs to be closed: so someone doesn’t get hit with a cement block off the roof,” Small said.
He stressed that the sweeps and increased presence have already had an effect. However, he noted that large-scale operations likely aren’t sustainable in the long run.
Tuesday morning’s operation required 18 law enforcement officers, including members of the Maine State Police, York County Sheriff’s Office and Old Orchard Beach Police Department, with additional assistance from the fire department. Small said they’d ideally like to have 25 people on scene to conduct a safe sweep.
“Frankly, we couldn’t have done it without those other agencies,” Small said, noting their ability to consistently assist Sanford with such operations “will run out eventually.”
The chief also suggested the city bring on a consultant or other expert to help.
“We’re law enforcement,” he said. “We work with people with homelessness and substance use disorder, but we’re not the ones who are going to solve homelessness and substance use disorder.”
Small also pushed back against comments he said he’s seen on social media, including people asking the city to “get rid” of the homeless population. He noted many of the people officers have encountered at the old mill are longtime residents of the area.
“They live here; they have their whole lives, just like you,” Small said. “They just encountered different circumstances than all of us sitting in this room that made them turn a corner in a different way.
“We’ve got to remember that.”

title: Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House publicly asked for U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct, and she announced within two hours that she was quitting, ending days of talk and speculation about her professional fate. Guilfoyle insisted that she would “vigorously defend” herself.
President Donald Trump’s administration had said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
That revelation came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”
“She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump said just after Guilfoyle’s resignation, which was posted on her X account. He said he had not spoken to her but “she will not be there.”
Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct.
Guilfoyle denies the accusations and cites her ‘decades of public service’
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in her resignation post on X, saying, “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”
“I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”
In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations.”
They did not immediately return calls Tuesday.
The allegations began surfacing weeks ago
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
There was no immediate response to Zacharia’s statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.
Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.
Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa’s “Dance the Night,” from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie “Barbie.”
Greece has taken on an increasingly important and influential role because of its geographic location in Southeastern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly on energy issues as the war with Iran has spiked global oil prices. Besides the vast number of Greek-registered oil tankers that regularly ply the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Greece is well positioned to be a pipeline conduit for liquefied natural gas imports into the Balkans and beyond.
As the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Guilfoyle had put an emphasis on energy issues, although her close association with executives in that sector was part of what got her into trouble.
Democrats call for an investigation
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco’s mayor, before he became California’s governor. She later was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr.
___
AP journalists Derek Gatopoulos in Athens and Darlene Superville at the White House contributed.

title: Young mom’s breast cancer diagnosis highlights rising rates among younger adults
text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (Aging Untold) — Cancer is increasing in people under 65, and women are now more likely than men to develop it, according to the American Cancer Society.
Brittany Auclair, of Tallahassee, was diagnosed with breast cancer at 29, shortly after her son Brayden was born.
A mother notices something while breastfeeding
Brayden was 8 months old when Auclair first noticed an issue while breastfeeding.
“He decided that he favored one side over the other, but I did notice that while I went to work and I was pumping that there was a lump,” Auclair said.
She followed up with her doctor, who is also a breast cancer survivor.
“She said, ‘I’m not waiting to make an appointment. I want you to come in as soon as possible,’” Auclair said.
Thinking she had a clogged milk duct, Auclair underwent scans and tests. A few days after her 29th birthday, she received her diagnosis.
“I remember kind of hitting a brick wall hearing her say, ‘You have cancer’ and how we’re going to move forward. And then I shut down,” Auclair said.
Diagnosis and treatment
Auclair was diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer.
“At one point if I heard one more time, ‘You’re so young to have cancer,’ I thought I was going to scream,” Auclair said.
During months of treatment, including surgery and chemotherapy, daily tasks became difficult.
“Doing normal activities, going to the grocery store, going to make dinner or plan meals became super stressful,” Auclair said.
With support from family, friends and coworkers, Auclair completed treatment in October 2013. She has been cancer-free for more than 12 years.
“When I went through my story, I felt like I was the only one. I’ve now read several stories where there are young mothers that are finding their cancer,” Auclair said.
Doctors report a rising trend in younger patients
Dr. Amit Jain, an oncologist at Tallahassee Memorial HealthCare, specializes in colorectal and lung cancer treatment and has treated patients for more than a decade.
“I have definitely seen men and women as young as 29, 30, with colorectal cancer, with no family history, no predisposition, no risk factors,” Jain said. “How they present, you’re never thinking cancer.”
A study by the American Cancer Society found that young adults identified as Gen Xers and millennials may be at higher risk of being diagnosed with cancer. Researchers found that 17 of 34 types of cancer are increasing among these two groups compared with older generations, including breast, pancreatic and kidney cancer
Jain said studies are ongoing, but more research and awareness are needed for this age group.
“Never ignore any symptom,” Jain said.
Calls for awareness and earlier detection
Auclair said she believes experts should consider lowering age guidelines to help with early detection and prevention.
“They need to be aware. I don’t think it’s something that they need to stress about every day, but I think young people need to understand that it is occurring,” Auclair said.
Asked what may be driving the trend, Aging Untold expert Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, pointed to several potential factors.
“Well, I think we have an obesity epidemic. We are living in the middle of toxic soup everywhere we go. And all these different things play a role on it, along with the genetics,” Rogers said. “You know, we’re used to looking at people’s genetics when they were getting these cancers at a young age.”
Rogers said she believes the medical community needs to move away from associating cancer primarily with older people.
“But now we understand with no family history and anything like that, we have to pay attention. We have to get out of that mindset that cancer is a disease for older people and start really being proactive and educate people about the symptoms and the signs and how things present and not the age,” Rogers said.

title: 2 killed in wrong-way collision on I-95 in Medway
text:
Two people were killed in a wrong-way collision on Interstate 95 in Medway on Monday night.
Luis Mendoza, 20, of Indian Township was allegedly driving a stolen 2011 Toyota Camry south on the northbound side of I-95 about 9:21 p.m. in Island Falls, according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
East Millinocket police spotted Mendoza about 9:38 p.m. still driving the wrong way on I-95, going at speeds over 100 mph, Moss said Tuesday morning.
Police gave chase, but Mendoza continued speeding down the highway into a construction zone, near mile marker 244, where southbound traffic was being diverted onto the northbound side of the highway on a bridge.
On the bridge, north- and southbound traffic were separated by concrete barriers.
Mendoza continued south on the northbound side of the bridge, where he collided with another vehicle driven by 67-year-old Sandra Lacombe of Medway, killing both of them, Moss said.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: 3 takeaways from the 3rd Maine Senate debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The third U.S. Senate debate between Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican incumbent Susan Collins didn’t break much new ground, though the candidates did sharpen their responses to questions about affordability, the Iran war and tariffs.
But Tuesday’s debate did provide a few striking moments, and some new substance. Both Collins and Jackson further elucidated their stances on data centers, saying they supported some form of regulation on where the centers could be located, and on how much water and electricity they use.
Polls show a tight race between the 73-year-old Collins and 58-year-old Jackson in Maine’s pivotal Senate race.
Here are three moments that stood out from their third meeting in a week. They will meet again Thursday for their final debate.
1. They got under each other’s skin
Collins provoked a strong reaction from Jackson about halfway through the debate. The Republican said “once again, Troy is confusing the Medicaid program with the Medicare program.” She proceeded to lecture him about the difference: Medicare largely goes to the elderly; Medicaid largely goes to the poor and sick.
Jackson grew visibly agitated in his response, saying that he understood the issue well because he had visited four birthing centers that have closed recently.
“Don’t act like I don’t know what I’m talking about, because I do,” Jackson said.
At another point, Jackson returned the favor. After Collins raised the issue of Medicaid fraud, the Democrat brought up recent ProPublica reporting about the FBI investigating whether Collins’ orbit was steering federal funding to a defense contractor and donor.
“I’m shocked that you’re talking about fraud, because there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the FBI,” he said. (The ProPublica story said that the FBI had been gearing to investigate Collins, but the bureau has never accused her of fraud.)
Collins didn’t respond at the time, but brought it back up later after Jackson said she does the bidding of billionaires.
“Troy has repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long,” she said. “He lied when he said that I was under investigation and found to have committed fraud by the FBI. And I just cannot continue to ignore these attacks on my integrity.”
At yet another point, Collins noted that Jackson has not yet filed a campaign finance report, which would show who his donors are. (Jackson entered the race after the last quarterly reporting period ended on June 30.)
The next round of reports are due by midnight on Thursday, but Jackson offered to release his early.
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning. How about that? Is that enough?” Jackson said. “Because we see yours and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me … I’ll give you the report tomorrow and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday.”
2. Collins finds differences in agreement
At several points, Collins deployed a new strategy to highlight her experience — and it came when the candidates seemed to agree on an issue.
Jackson has repeatedly hit Collins for advancing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which extended tax cuts for the wealthy and slashed $1 trillion in public health funding. Many of the cuts will take effect after the midterms.
But Collins noted that she voted against enacting the bill, which became law in 2025 after Vice President JD Vance broke a tie in the Senate. Despite her vote, she touted her ability to ensure that a $50 billion fund was included to help rural hospitals.
“Troy would have never been able to get that into the bill,” Collins said.
Jackson noted that the funding Maine would receive because of Collins’ amendment pales in comparison to the cuts.
Collins deployed the same tactic later when it came to Canadian tariffs, which both candidates oppose.
“The bottom line is that Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs,” she said. “But here’s the key difference: I’ve been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list. Troy would have gotten nothing.”
Jackson protested, noting that he’s been in contact with the Canadian ambassador and the consulate in Boston. But Collins made it clear she was referring to the Trump administration.
“Well, it wasn’t the Canadians that started this problem — it was the Trump administration,” she said.
3. Jackson leans into ICE shooting in Biddeford
Jackson came into the debate planning to make an issue of Collins’ votes to fund U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Tuesday was the three-month anniversary of federal agents fatally shooting Johan Sebastián Guerrero in Biddeford.
But he had to wait for the end of the debate to do it.
Jackson criticized Collins for supporting $70 billion in new funding for ICE and other agencies. He called ICE a “rogue agency” that needs to be abolished, with immigration enforcement being shifted to U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the FBI.
Collins, however, noted that she was able to include several reforms in the funding bill, including $20 million for body-worn cameras and de-escalation training.
“But more needs to be done,” she said.
Jackson pounced on Collins’ contention that some ICE agents are properly vetted and trained.
“I don’t know how you could stand up here and argue that it’s a good thing to let them out onto our population, out onto the American public, when we’ve seen consistently that they will murder people if you don’t comply explicitly with them,” Jackson said.

title: 'RuPaul's Drag Race' music producer Lucian Piane dead at 46
text:
'RuPaul's Drag Race' music producer Lucian Piane dead at 46
"RuPaul's Drag Race" personality and composer Lucian Piane has died. He was 46.
Related video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
Piane was hit by a car in Los Angeles on Monday night and died in the street after the incident, according to TMZ.
Fans of Piane had been concerned for his safety recently. Piane had shared several concerning videos on his Instagram of him loitering outside of businesses and interacting with police in the past week. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner's Office listed the location of his death as in the street and also said a post-mortem exam is scheduled.
According to People Magazine, EMS workers attended to an injured person at the location of the crash who later died at the scene, and police confirmed a pedestrian identified as Piane was struck by a car at the intersection. Piane died from blunt trauma, and his death was ruled accidental by the medical examiner. The case into his death remains open.
Piane was a composer and internet celebrity known for his work with RuPaul and for his memetic remixes. His YouTube channel, revolucian, gained notoriety in 2009 for a remix he made from audio of an on-set outburst by Christian Bale during the filming of "Terminator Salvation," which itself went viral. Bale later apologized for the rant.
Piane was a guest judge on "RuPaul's Drag Race" and was also nominated for a Grammy Award for his work on the soundtrack to the 2007 film adaptation of the musical "Hairspray."

title: How to find real deals at outlet malls, according to an expert
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Outlet malls can still offer real savings, but only for shoppers who know certain tricks, according to Kyle James, a writer for ConsumerAffairs.
James said outlet malls are skilled at creating the appearance of a great deal.
“You see these huge signs everywhere, 60% off, close-out sale — well, the thing is, you show up next week or a month from now, the signs are still there collecting dust,” James said. “So it’s important to be aware of that, and a lot of the products you’re going to find at these outlet malls are stuff that’s made specifically for the outlet mall, and so a lot of times the quality isn’t as good.”
James said if a store has every size and color of an item in stock, that item was likely manufactured specifically for the outlet rather than being overstock from a regular retail location. Items that are harder to find in every size are more likely to be genuine overstock from the main store.
James recommends skipping the merchandise displayed at the front of an outlet store.
“When you first walk into one of these outlet stores, the stuff in the front that’s going to be all close to full price — the stuff they’re trying to make the most money on,” James said. “So I like to give the tip of shopping the store backwards. Go to the back of the store or the backside of the store, that’s where the clearance items are.”
James said shoppers can save even more by checking an outlet mall’s website and customer service desk for coupon books or hidden coupon pages. An extra 10% to 15% off can make a meaningful difference on larger purchases.

title: A list of US roller coaster fatalities dating back to 2003
text:
(AP) - A man who fell to his death from a roller coaster at an Atlanta-area amusement park was not the first to die on such a ride in recent years.
Authorities have not released information about how 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was thrown from Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Several people also were injured.
Here’s a look at other fatalities and injuries on U.S. roller coasters:
Six Flags Magic Mountain
The park in Southern California announced last month that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious brain injuries. The park settled one wrongful-death lawsuit with the family of a 22-year-old rider who was rushed to a hospital with severe brain bleeding in 2022. He died a day later. The medical examiner’s office determined he died from “blunt head trauma.” Six Flags Entertainment Corp. said the ride had consistently passed safety tests.
Epic Universe
A medical examiner concluded last year that a man who was unresponsive after riding a roller coaster at the Universal Orlando Resort park died from blunt impact injuries. Joshua Stephany, the medical examiner for the Orlando area, ruled the death an accident. The man in his 30s was found unresponsive after riding Stardust Racers.
Texas Giant
In 2013, a woman riding a roller coaster in Texas died after she was thrown from her seat, fell 75 feet (23 meters) and struck a metal beam. Witnesses said the woman expressed concern about the Texas Giant roller coaster’s safety bar not completely engaging as the ride was starting.
Darien Lake
A U.S. Army veteran who lost both legs in Iraq was killed in 2011 after he was thrown from a roller coaster at Darien Lake Theme Park & Resort in upstate New York. Investigators said operators did not follow rules posted at the ride’s entrance, which require that riders have both legs.
Dixie Landin’
A 21-year-old rider fell to her death from a roller coaster at the amusement park in Louisiana in 2010. A state investigation could not determine a cause.
Disneyland
In 2003, a locomotive broke loose from a train on the Big Thunder Mountain Railroad roller coaster in California, killing a man and injuring multiple other riders. The car derailed after a guide wheel fell off. State investigators found the wheel was not tightened according to Disney’s standards and a safety wire was not installed.

title: Tres meses después de la muerte de Johan Sebastián, seguimos luchando por la verdad
text:
Sean P. Murphy fue fiscal en el Bronx y fiscal federal, combatió el crimen organizado y ayudó a dirigir la investigación del Departamento de Justicia sobre el ataque del 6 de enero al Capitolio. Criado en Vermont y hoy abogado de Gideon Asen en Maine, representa a la familia de Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
Hace casi tres meses, en la madrugada del 13 de julio de 2026, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero salió de su casa. Pensaba, como cada mañana, en el momento en que volvería para abrazar a su esposa, Karolina, y a su pequeña hija.
La noche anterior había sido como cualquier otra. Karolina dobló la ropa. Johan dijo que se iba a acostar. Se dieron un beso. Ninguno de los dos imaginó que sería el último.
Nunca tuve la fortuna de conocer a Johan en vida. Hay algo extraño y hermoso en llegar a conocer a alguien solo a través de quienes lo amaron y hoy tienen que vivir sin él.
Lo conocí a través de sus padres, Omar y Dora, quienes viajaron desde Colombia para reclamar el cuerpo de su hijo. En la funeraria de Portland, salí de la sala, pero los gritos de dolor de una madre ante el cuerpo de su hijo asesinado atravesaron las paredes. Fue un lamento que nunca hubiera querido escuchar y que jamás quiero olvidar.
Lo conocí a través de Daniela, su hermana, quien fue la primera de la familia en llegar a Estados Unidos. Como le pasaría a cualquier hermana mayor, carga con una culpa que no le corresponde. Daniela, nada de esto fue culpa tuya. Sabemos quién es responsable.
Y lo conocí a través de Karolina y de la hija que tuvieron juntos. Me asombra la fortaleza de Karolina. Este país les ha arrebatado demasiado. Lo siento de corazón. Basta pasar dos minutos con esa niña para saber que la llama de su papá sigue viva en ella.
Desde julio, mi socio Ben Gideon y yo hemos luchado por Johan. Hace poco nos reunimos con representantes de la oficina del fiscal general del estado de Maine, la primera y única entidad gubernamental que ha confirmado que investiga el uso de fuerza letal por parte de un agente federal.
En esa reunión nos devolvieron varios objetos que habían sido considerados sin valor probatorio. Pero faltaba uno: la silla de seguridad de su hija para el carro. Karolina preguntó por qué. Le dijeron que una bala disparada por un agente federal la había atravesado, así como otras balas disparadas por un agente federal habían matado a su esposo.
Las primeras versiones decían que su hija iba con él en el carro. Gracias a Dios, no era así. Pero la temeridad salta a la vista, y cuesta siquiera imaginar el horror de lo que pudo haber ocurrido. Una sola tragedia ya era demasiado.
La única justificación que han dado para la muerte de Johan ha sido la «seguridad pública». ¿Saben qué protege de verdad a la gente? No dispararles a padres de familia inocentes, que cumplen la ley y cuyo único sueño es darles una vida mejor a los suyos.
Hablemos claro sobre lo que pasó aquí. Este gobierno tomó la infame decisión de quitarle la vida a Johan y, ante las consecuencias, ha guardado silencio. Un presidente que quiere ser rey ha decidido que cualquiera de nosotros puede ser sacrificado con tal de imponer su agenda. Tiene que dejar de violar nuestro derecho a la vida, y tiene que hacerlo ya.
Johan no tenía la ciudadanía estadounidense, pero encarnaba lo mejor de lo que significa ser estadounidense. Trabajaba, amaba a su familia y soñaba. Quien justifique que lo hayan matado no puede llamarse patriota.
Y Johan no es el único. Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good, Alex Pretti y Lorenzo Salgado Araujo forman parte del mismo club, uno al que nadie querría pertenecer y cuya cuota se paga con la vida. A sus familias les deben respuestas, no excusas.
Pero de poco sirve la indignación si perdemos la esperanza. Quien haya vivido un invierno en Maine sabe que incluso el frío más crudo termina por cederle el paso a la primavera. Ahora que se acercan las elecciones de mitad de período en Estados Unidos, espero y le pido a Dios que nuestro país empiece a abrirse camino hacia esa primavera.
Esto no es lo que somos los estadounidenses. Tenemos que ser mejores.
Tres meses después, la familia de Johan sigue esperando verdad, justicia y que los responsables rindan cuentas. No dejaremos de luchar hasta que eso ocurra.

title: Cornell bans fraternity parties in wake of gang rape allegation
text:
(AP) — Cornell University suspended parties at fraternity houses until next year and is giving state police a role in investigating reports of sexual assault on campus in the school’s latest response to outrage over its handling of a gang rape allegation.
The measures announced Tuesday by Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff include a suspension of all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses through the end of the 2026-27 academic year and a new “zero tolerance” policy that would immediately suspend chapters for violations.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.
Cornell has more than 20 active Interfraternity Council fraternities. The council did not immediately respond to an email request for comment. It’s unclear whether the restrictions extend to off-campus parties.
It’s not the first time Cornell has cracked down on fraternity parties. The university temporarily suspended them in 2022 after reports of a sexual assault and students being drugged at fraternity-affiliated housing.
Cornell also tightened fraternity safety rules in 2019 after freshman Antonio Tsialas was found dead in a gorge following an alleged hazing incident. A year earlier, a fraternity was placed on probation over a contest in which members competed to have sex with women they considered overweight.
Cornell plans alternatives to fraternity parties
Cornell said it will solicit input about “the development of safe social alternatives” to Greek life party culture and direct university resources toward those alternatives.
Kotlikoff also committed to adding a case manager to the school’s Office of Civil Rights to help those who report sexual misconduct on the Cornell campus navigate the process, and to working with New York State Police to allow its criminal investigators — who are independent of Cornell — to investigate allegations.
Crimes reported on Cornell’s campus are generally investigated by campus police, a department that has full law enforcement powers but is controlled by the university.
The campus police force operates independently from municipal police in Ithaca, New York, where the university is located. Its officers investigated the 2024 gang rape allegations and presented their initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to prosecute within weeks of the woman making her first report to police.
New York’s governor removed the district attorney from the case this month after a public outcry over the lack of charges.
The investigation is now being led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, while Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent review of the university’s response.
A state police spokesperson declined to comment.
A gang rape allegation sparks scrutiny of Cornell’s response
In a lawsuit filed in September, the woman alleged that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024.
She said she was pressured to use drugs and that other men entered the room while she was incapacitated. She also alleges that Snapchat messages describing her as sexually available to anyone at the house circulated among fraternity members without her knowledge.
Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students following an internal investigation, but no criminal charges have been filed. The seven men accused in the woman’s lawsuit have all denied her allegations, either saying that the sexual activity was consensual or that they weren’t involved.
Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for one of the men accused in the woman’s lawsuit, criticized the restrictions announced Tuesday as a sweeping response to problems that extend beyond fraternities, arguing that universities promote Greek social life but distance themselves from it when controversies arise.
“Greek life has become the convenient target,” he said in an emailed statement. He warned that parties could simply move off campus, where there would be less oversight. “Changing the address doesn’t change the behavior.”
Cornell faces broader pressure for reform
Kotlikoff’s announcement came a day before Cornell’s Faculty Senate was to take up a proposed resolution expressing no confidence in the administration’s ability to effectively address sexual assault on campus.
Paul Ortiz, a Cornell labor history professor who is the lead sponsor of the resolution, said Tuesday that he welcomed the new measures but regretted that it took student protests, media coverage and the suffering of people like the woman suing the university over an alleged gang rape to prompt action.
“That the administration is only acting the day before they might be held accountable in the faculty senate is deeply troubling,” Ortiz said in an email to The Associated Press, adding that he believes the no-confidence resolution is “more important than ever.”
“The key point to understand is that scores of students, staff, faculty and alumni have approached the sponsors of the resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but the tip of the iceberg,” he continued. “Students and alumni have shared experiences of being raped at Cornell.”
“These women testify that they were frightened to report assaults because they felt that Cornell has at times treated rape as more of a ‘PR problem’ than a heinous crime,” Ortiz said.
In his Tuesday letter, Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk.
Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programs, he said, calling the actions “first steps toward systemic change on our campus.”
“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said.
