title: Who’s running for City Council, School Board in South Portland
text:
South Portland residents will be voting for new city councilors and school board members as well as weighing in on big elections like governor and Senate.
Residents may vote absentee in person at the city clerk’s office in city hall during regular business hours (7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday) and from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Tuesday. Oct. 29 is the last day to vote absentee at city hall, or request or pick up your absentee ballot.
CITY COUNCIL
District 1
Carter Scott is unopposed in her reelection for her seat in the city that’s been her home for 20 years. She recognizes that the city is growing, and she values sustainability, both environmental and economic. In addition to serving on the council, she’s also served on the South Portland Land Trust board and elementary school PTA.
District 2
Ellen Clancy is unopposed, and it’s her first time running for office. She’s campaigning on minimizing tax increases, making the budget as efficient as possible and finding new sources of revenue, with the goal of keeping South Portland affordable.
District 5
Elyse Tipton, the current mayor, is up for reelection, and is campaigning on keeping South Portland affordable, expanding city services and protecting public health and safety.
Prior to serving on the council, beginning in 2023, she served four terms on the school board, and she wants to strengthen the partnership between the school department and the city.
John Holman III, a production supervisor who has lived in the city for more than a decade, is running for office for the first time because he wants the city to pursue more affordable housing, revenue generation and youth outreach.
He views affordability as a major problem in the city, and he’s also interested in changing the city’s prohibition on selling flavored tobacco products.
SCHOOL BOARD
At- Large
South Portland residents can vote for two at-large school board members.
Eleni Richardson, an incumbent elected last November, is running for reelection. She thinks the board’s agenda should focus on financial stability, equitable elementary school reconfiguration and evaluating technology in the classroom.
Wheeler Boyd-Boffa is a data and analytics consultant and the parent of two elementary school students, and it’s his first time running for office. His priorities are to stabilize the budget, prioritize educational equity and staff morale, and to create clear rules for technology use in the classroom.
Stephanie Edwards is a special education teacher in the district and a South Portland parent, and her three priorities are promoting fiscal responsibility, supporting educators, staff and students, and transparently communicating board decisions and processes.
Ishmeel Davis is also running for an at-large seat.
District Five
Carlton “Carl” Parsons, a renter, parent and community organizer, is running for school board and wants to prioritize support for working class families and children, elevate marginalized groups in the city and create long-term financial stability.

title: Much-Needed Rain Arrives Today With Snow Possible Across The North
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Low pressure approaching from the Great Lakes Region will bring some much needed rain to the area. Rain will continue to spread eastward across the state this afternoon. Temperatures will be borderline... but may be just cold enough for some wet snow or rain/snow mix over northern and western locales... especially in the higher terrain with a coating to 1” not out of the question... otherwise it looks like a mainly rain event. The combination of clouds... rain... a colder air mass... and an easterly breeze will make for a cool day with highs only reaching the mid-30s to low 40s north and 40s to near 50° elsewhere.
Rain will continue through tonight and could be moderate to heavy at times. Overnight lows will hold steady in the mid-30s to low 40s north and 40s elsewhere. It’ll be breezy tonight too with easterly winds gusting to 25-30 MPH at times.
Lingering showers will wind down Wednesday morning with most of the wet weather done... and over with... by noontime followed by mostly cloudy and drier conditions for the afternoon. Rainfall totals from this morning through noontime Wednesday will range from .5” to 1.5” with some locally higher amounts closer to 2” in the foothills and mountains.
Temperatures will be a bit better on Wednesday with highs climbing to the upper 40s to low 50s north and 50s to near 60° elsewhere. As the system exits Wednesday... it will be strengthening as it moves up into the Maritimes Thursday. This will cause the pressure gradient to tighten up... leading to a breezy day Thursday with a gusty northwest wind up to 25-35 MPH at times. Thursday overall looks like the nicest day of the week with a good deal of sunshine and highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s. Clouds will move back in Thursday night with another storm system bringing more beneficial rain for Friday and Friday night with another .5” to 1” or so of rain possible. There are some indications too that we could see some wintry precipitation... possibly some accumulating snow... mainly over Northern Aroostook County so stay tuned for updates as we get closer. It looks like we’ll see drier, breezy and chilly weather for the upcoming weekend.
Rest of Today: Mostly cloudy with rain likely. Some wet snow or rain/snow mix possible north. Cooler with highs in the upper 30s to low 40s north and 40s to near 50° elsewhere. East wind 5-15 MPH.
Tonight: Rain. Rain will taper to showers from west to east late. Lows in the mid-30s to mid-40s from north to south. East wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Wednesday: Morning showers possible then mostly cloudy and drier for the afternoon. Highs mainly in the 50s. Northwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Thursday: Partly to mostly sunny. Breezy. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.
Friday: Rain likely. Some rain/snow mix possible across the north. Highs in the 40s to near 50°.
Saturday: Morning showers possible then brightening skies and breezy. Highs mainly in the 40s.

title: How this spa offers specialized facials for cancer patients
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (InvestigateTV) - An estimated four million people in the U.S. receive radiation therapy, an effective way to kill cancer.
Finding healing through skin care
Ashley Roberts was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2017, leading to a double mastectomy and 26 weeks of chemotherapy. During treatment, she found that caring for her skin helped her maintain strength and confidence.
“I, as a young girl, was often complimented on my complexion and my eyebrows and things like that. These are things that are taken away during treatment that all the things you’re complimented on, your hair, your eyebrows, you know, your skin,” Roberts said.
Roberts discovered that nourishing her body inside and out, including getting facials, became part of her recovery journey.
“From there, I started my journey of getting the cancer out of my body and becoming a well person again,” she said.
Skin during cancer treatments can be extremely sensitive and require special care. Julie Piedrahita, owner of Simply Facials in Baton Rouge, understood this need after watching her husband battle cancer for two years.
“People don’t realize a lot of time treating the cancer is just the first part of cancer treatment,” Piedrahita said.
Simply Facials offers a service called a Restore Facial designed specifically for cancer patients’ fragile skin. The spa’s aestheticians receive special training to meet both physical and emotional needs of patients and their families.
“For physical needs, they have dry skin. There are things that happen as a result of their radiation and perhaps their chemo treatments that they’re on, but emotionally, sometimes you just want to do something to feel normal,” Piedrahita said.
Jan Vaccaro, an aesthetician at Simply Facials, said the treatment is modified for cancer patients’ specific needs.
“This facial is slowed down. It’s very gentle, relaxing. It’s nourishing for their skin as well as their emotional well-being,” Vaccaro said.
Safe techniques for patients
The spa uses nontoxic products and techniques safe for people who are immunocompromised. Staff members are trained in special massage techniques for patients with lymph node involvement.
“We know that if there is any lymph node involvement in the cancer, we have to do the techniques a special way when we work on the massage,” Piedrahita said.
Vaccaro said the treatments address the uncomfortable side effects of cancer treatment.
“Chemo and radiation basically are poison. It’s what it takes to kill the cancer, and that of course is the first order of business, but the cascade of things that happen to your body from the treatment are so uncomfortable and so unpleasant, and we thought, is there one little thing we can do to help them feel more comfortable?” she said.
Roberts, now seven years past completing her cancer treatment, continues to prioritize skin care as part of feeling her best.
“When you want to live, you’ll do whatever it takes,” Roberts said.
She said maintaining healthy skin remains important for her confidence and overall well-being.
“That’s why it’s important to continue doing facials because having that glow shows that your skin is healthy, and that’s from the inside out, and this is when everybody sees us. They see our face first,” Roberts said.
Simply Facials also recommends that family members and patients get facials together for a more comforting experience for everyone involved.

title: Man struck by vehicle in Palermo; state police investigating
text:
Man struck by vehicle on Route 3 in Palermo; Maine State Police investigating
Maine State Police officials said the department is investigating a pedestrian crash in Palermo that left a man seriously injured.
The crash happened at about 5:35 a.m. Tuesday on Route 3, near the Level Hill Road intersection.
Investigators determined that a driver had pulled over to the side of Route 3 and exited his vehicle. According to state police, the man intentionally entered the roadway and was struck by an oncoming vehicle.
The man sustained life-threatening injuries and was transported to Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor by Liberty Ambulance.
The driver of the vehicle that struck the pedestrian was not injured, police said.
State police said the crash remains under investigation, and that troopers were assisted at the scene by members of the Waldo County Sheriff's Office and several fire and emergency medical services departments.

title: Home prices increased in September, total sales decreased
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Home prices were up last month; but sales were down.
According to the Maine Association of Realtors, more than 1,500 existing homes changed hands in September, a 4% decrease from last year.
The homes that did sell had a median sales price of $415,000, which is 2% higher than September of 2025.

title: Katie Zacharia, Trump’s new White House press secretary, faces reporters for the first time
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, faced reporters for the first time on Tuesday for a very brief turn at the lectern, taking a handful of questions before abruptly wrapping it up.
Zacharia, a conservative commentator who most recently worked for President Donald Trump’s social media company, was named to the job on Friday, succeeding Karoline Leavitt, who left in August and is taking a job with Fox News Channel.
Zacharia told reporters her goal is to “amplify” what Trump is doing and that the president is “his own best spokesperson.”
She quickly proved that Tuesday, appearing for only 14 minutes and taking questions from just three outlets before telling reporters they could ask the president their questions on the South Lawn when he departs on a campaign trip.
“In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there,” she said.
As the Republican president left the White House for his trip, more than an hour after the briefing’s abrupt end, he praised Zacharia’s performance to reporters.
“I thought she did excellent. She did very good,” he said, as Zacharia stood behind him.
Before taking the questions, Zacharia read slowly from an opening statement that began with a focus on Trump’s recent campaign rallies and his policies on energy, tariffs, immigration and more since he returned to office.
In naming Zacharia, who has a law degree from Pepperdine University, Trump described her as “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.” She briefly worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year and has been a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax.
She told reporters she viewed her role as press secretary to be no different than the way she advocated for Trump while outside the government.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” she said.
She also thanked Trump and said, “I have wanted to work for him for a very long time.”
She took her first question from Breitbart News, the right-wing outlet that has become more influential in the Trump era, and committed to keeping the “new media” rotation created under her predecessor to bring additional media outlets into news briefings and the White House press pool.
But Zacharia did make some big news: she said Trump had asked for the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
“She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” Zacharia said.
___

title: Maine’s September housing market broke the usual mold
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Each month, when Maine Listings and the Maine Association of Realtors release their reports on the state of the housing market, there are a few facts that can almost always be relied on: Cumberland County will be the most expensive county in Maine, and York County will be the second. A critical shortage of inventory will continue to squeeze buyers. Competition will be fierce, and houses will be snapped up quickly.
Last month, none of that was true.
Here are three takeaways from Maine’s September market.
1. High prices in unexpected places
Statewide, the median sale price was $415,000 last month, a 2.6% increase from September 2025, but a roughly 2% decrease from August’s median of $424,050, according to data from Maine Listings.
The modest year-over-year change belies massive price increases in several coastal counties.
In Lincoln and Knox counties, the median sale price skyrocketed more than $100,000 in just a year. In Hancock County, it might as well have, jumping $99,000.
Sagadahoc County also increased substantially, jumping from $490,000 to $577,500.
Those increases also shook up the longstanding rankings of Maine’s priciest counties.
Lincoln County was the most expensive in the state, with a median sale price of $606,500. It was followed by Cumberland County, with a median of $599,900.
Sagadahoc, Hancock and York counties rounded out the top five.
Six of the 16 counties had a median price of over half a million dollars.
Maine’s housing market is small, and in counties with fewer homes changing hands, it only takes a few high-ticket sales to skew the numbers.
For example, in Cumberland County, where year-over-year prices increased a little over 3%, there were 307 sales. In Knox County, where prices shot up 31%, there were 50.
In Islesboro, the lone September home sale clocked in at $3 million, making it the state’s most expensive municipality.
2. Late summer slowdown
Sales fell for the third consecutive month, despite buyers having more options than they’ve had since late 2019.
Real estate agents bought and sold 1,532 homes last month, a 1.4% decrease from the month before, according to Maine Listings.
Meanwhile, there were 6,505 homes on the market in September, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
Sales were also down year-over-year, with 4.5% fewer homes changing hands than in September 2025. And that’s with more than 1,000 more homes to choose from.
“Aside from the traditional slowdown from the summer months, increasing inflationary pressure and higher mortgage rates without a comparable downward adjustment in pricing have sidelined some buyers, especially first-time buyers with no equity from previous home purchases,” Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors, said in a news release.
Houses are also taking longer to sell, sitting on the market for an average of 21 days last month, compared to just 10 days in June, according to Maine Listings.
According to Lawrence Yun, chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, on a seasonally adjusted basis, August and September marked the two slowest months of the year for home sales nationwide.
Nationally, sales fell just shy of 2% year over year, while prices rose just over 1% to a median of $422,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Regionally, sales in the Northeast dropped 4% while the median sale price increased nearly 5% to $523,600.
3. Hard-to-swallow interest rates
In theory, more inventory and a slower pace of sales should mean more time and less competition for buyers, leaving more room for negotiations, said Oberg, who is also an associate broker at Oberg Insurance and Real Estate Agency in Bridgton.
But there’s one snag: Interest rates are the highest they’ve been in three years.
Interest rates were already elevated (6.71%) at the start of September. Then, two weeks later, the Federal Reserve increased its rate by a quarter of a point to curb inflation, and mortgage rates responded.
Last week, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage was 7.40%, according to mortgage buyer Freddie Mac. Rates haven’t been that high since November 2023.
A year ago, the average mortgage rate was 6.3%.
If someone bought a $415,000 home, put 20% down and secured that 6.3% rate, they could expect a monthly payment of about $2,833, not including any HOA fees, according to Fannie Mae, another mortgage buyer.
With the current interest rate of 7.4%, that monthly payment would increase to $3,076. That’s another $244 a month, or almost $3,000 a year.
“Increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home,” said Yun, at the national association.
The Federal Reserve is anticipating another rate hike at the end of the year.

title: Caregivers for older Mainers are facing mounting challenges
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Marvella Heard has faced more challenges than most in caring for her aging father.
She spent over a year back in her hometown in New York, after she discovered her father was living in squalor, his health was deteriorating, his meager finances were in jeopardy and his house was in foreclosure, she said.
A Navy veteran and retired federal prison employee, she stepped in and wrangled repeatedly with family members, government officials and social service agencies — even after she became her father’s legal guardian, she said.
“He was living in filth when I got there,” said Heard, 56, of Biddeford. “He had no food, no clean clothes. He didn’t recognize me at first.”
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
Now 79, Samuel Heard has since been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and heart disease, and the retired hospital worker has mobility issues that require him to use a walker, his daughter said.
Despite many setbacks, Heard said she managed to navigate unfamiliar caregiver territory by being resourceful, searching the internet for solutions and being tenacious when she ran into roadblocks. She still struggles to reconcile how hard it was to help her father.
“I was treated awfully — the system didn’t support me at all,” Heard said. “We had confrontations again and again, and I just wanted to take care of my dad.”
Finally, last December, Heard was able to move her father to her home in Biddeford, where they’ve settled into a routine of medical appointments, grocery shopping, barber shop visits and adult daycare programs.
THE ROLE TAKES A TOLL
While Heard’s experience was severe, a growing number of Mainers are facing challenges as caregivers for aging and disabled loved ones. They’re providing assistance with all aspects of daily living, including meals, medications, bathing, dressing, toileting, transportation and advocacy at medical appointments and in long-term care.
Most of that help goes unpaid and can take a significant toll on other areas of their lives, consuming free time and affecting job performance. The role reversal of caring for once-vital adults can be emotionally devastating, and managing their complicated medical needs and finances can be overwhelming. Some caregivers also support their loved ones financially — Heard figures she has spent about $3,000 on her father’s behalf.
She and others in the thick of it have learned the benefits of planning ahead, becoming expert problem solvers and seeking support from other caregivers. They don’t have to look far.
In 2025, an estimated 310,000 Mainers provided the full-time equivalent of 220 million hours of unpaid care for aging or disabled adult family members valued at $5.5 billion, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. That value of that care more than doubled in the past decade, up from $2.2 billion provided by 178,000 Mainers in 2015.
The same is true nationwide, where the value of adult family caregiving also has more than doubled, from $470 billion to $1 trillion in the same period, and the number of caregivers increased 22.5%, from 40 million to 59 million, according to Caregiving in the US 2025, the latest report from AARP and NAC.
The exponential increase has solidified family caregivers as an invaluable contingent in the wider landscape of long-term care, AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said. It doesn’t matter if the help is provided to loved ones at home, in assisted living or at a skilled nursing facility.
“The long-term care system would crumble without those family caregivers,” Bonam said. “Whether what they do is big or small, without caregivers spending hours and personal resources while juggling other responsibilities, the system would collapse.”
CAREGIVING IN THE OLDEST STATE
As the oldest state, Maine is on the leading edge of this trend — nearly one-quarter of 1.4 million residents are age 65 and up. At the same time, it has a shortage of 2,300 workers to care for older Mainers as they age, according to the progressive Maine Center for Economic Policy.
Yet the important role that family caregivers play in filling the gap is critically undervalued, advocates say, especially when at least 60% of caregivers are juggling jobs outside the home and nearly 30% are part of the so-called sandwich generation, caring for both an adult and children.
“The federal and state funding and services available right now don’t cover the tip of the iceberg,” Bonam said.
Some MaineCare recipients may receive funding to pay a family member to provide care, but it comes with significant restrictions. The State Respite Care Program provides funding so family caregivers of dementia patients can hire occasional help, but there’s often a waiting list.
The new Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave program may be providing some relief — 11.6% of 4,720 claims approved in the first three months, April through June, were to care for family members with serious health conditions, according to the Maine Department of Labor.
Some advocates are pushing for a non-refundable federal tax credit up to $5,000 for eligible working family caregivers to cover 30% of qualified expenses. However, this proposal also comes with restrictions and would cover only a small portion of care provided. In Maine, that care is valued at $25 per hour or about $52,000 annually based on a 40-hour work week, according to AARP.
Although family caregiver funding is widely recognized as lacking, advocates say it’s not showing up as a legislative priority despite dire predictions that the need will only intensify.
“There’s been a tremendous increase over the past 10 years and that’s just going to continue,” said Amanda Rector, state economist. “We have more people not only over 65, but also over 75. That’s a larger older population that will need more care from a smaller younger population that’s still working.”
The issue may draw more attention as more families and employers experience the impact of caregiving on daily living, especially in a labor market with a worker shortage, Rector said.
“If (a caregiver is) a really valuable worker, they may not be working at their best,” she said. “You may want to provide support to relieve their mental and financial stress so they don’t leave.”
REACHING OUT FOR HELP
Jim Vollmar started showing signs of vascular dementia nearly a decade ago, when the former build contractor and his wife, Clare Herrmann, were living in Georgia.
“He started not remembering things he should have remembered, like my birthday or what we did last week,” said Herrmann, who, like her husband, is now 78.
Initially, Herrmann cared for him on her own, reluctant to even ask friends for help. But the difficulty mounted as his disease progressed, so she decided to accept her daughter’s invitation to come live with her family in Portland.
As Herrmann prepared to move north, the retired office manager reached out to the Southern Maine Agency on Aging for guidance on what services and programs would be available to them, including peer support groups she still attends.
After the couple moved to Portland in 2024 — into an accessory dwelling unit they had built at her daughter’s house — Herrmann was relieved to have backup assistance from her daughter, son-in-law and grandchild. Still, she was overwhelmed by round-the-clock responsibilities.
Again, she reached out to SMAA, who helped her secure respite care for her husband so she could have a few hours off each week. One of the first things she did was take a meditation course.
“I wanted to learn how to chill,” Herrmann said. “I was so hyperaware of everything, I never really slept because I didn’t want him to fall and I didn’t want him to leave the house. He never did, but I worried about it.”
Herrmann reached out to SMAA again last spring, after her husband broke his left femur in a fall and it became clear he needed to be in a memory care facility. The agency helped her find Fallbrook Woods in Portland, where he lives now.
“They have been so supportive,” Herrmann said of SMAA. “Whenever I call, they always know who to refer me to. I can’t even enumerate all they ways they have helped me.”
REBRANDING WITH CAREGIVERS IN MIND
SMAA this month changed its name to AgeMaine and launched a new website, support network and membership program to better serve family caregivers.
“We want to create one place where family caregivers can find trusted information and training, connect with other caregivers, and get help figuring out what resources and services are available,” CEO Megan Walton said.
AgeMaine.org/Caregiver, a caregiver-focused page that goes live Oct. 16, will start as an online resource hub for information and support, then expand to provide individualized guidance for family caregivers and help employers support workers who are caring for an aging adult. The agency will eventually offer a paid membership option, but the cost and structure have yet to be established, Walton said.
“We want more caregivers sharing their experiences and letting legislators know what they’re going through,” Walton said. “Peer support especially is so important. It can be so valuable to hear that other people are going through the same thing.”
The goal is to help caregivers like Marvella Heard find the support they need. While her father, Samuel, regularly attends adult daycare programs at the Samuel L. Cohen Center in Biddeford, which is an AgeMaine facility, she said she has yet to participate in caregiver support groups and other programs.
She admits that she should.
“I’m burned out because nobody is taking care of me,” Heard said. “Everybody needs a break sometimes, and I need a break, like, yesterday.”

title: First Mainers who received $500 Alfond Grant at birth now putting it toward college
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The first Maine children who received a $500 Alfond Grant at birth are now using it to help pay for college 18 years later.
Colleen Quint with the Harold Alfond Scholarship Foundation said 650 kids received the grant during the program’s first year, and 75 of them have already been used to pay for higher education.
“Our hope and full expectation is that a lot of students will find that grant is going to become available right when they need it most, which might be next semester or might even be next fall,” Quint said.
Quint said many of the children who received grants during the first year were born later in 2008 and therefore have not yet graduated from high school. In total, Quinn said nearly 185,000 children have received Alfond grants, totaling more than $800 million through the foundation’s initial investment, individual family contributions, and accrued interest.
She said the vision of the grants was to inspire families to begin saving early for their child’s higher education.
“Any dollar you have saved is $1 you don’t need to borrow, and so those small dollars really do add up. Invested dollars really do grow over time, at least historically, and it brings it all within reach,” Quint explained.
Quint said that initial $500 investment is now worth roughly $2,400. Many families invested their own contributions, so Quint said, their account totals are much higher.

title: Flight grounded after passengers noticed bed bugs crawling and biting them
text:
PERTH, Australia (CNN) - Passengers on a Qantas flight from Rome, Italy, to Perth, Australia, were delayed over the weekend after bed bugs were found on the aircraft.
A few passengers on the plane’s previous flight on Friday reported seeing bugs and being bitten. One woman said she saw them crawling on her clothes and along the window.
Qantas said the problem was limited to a small area of the aircraft, and crews conducted a deep clean while the plane was grounded.
Bed bugs are known to hitch rides on luggage.
The airline rescheduled all the passengers on other flights.

title: Foxcroft Academy boys soccer contends with 10 international players
text:
DOVER-FOXCROFT, Maine (WABI) - The Foxcroft Academy Ponies have stormed out of the gate to a 9-1-1 record in Class B North boys soccer.
The players explained what’s made this season a fun ride so far with 10 international players.
They’re chasing the program’s first regional and state titles this season.
“The biggest thing is that we put a lot of work in preseason,” said Olivers Luckovskis, Latvian senior center defensive midfielder.
“(There’s) a lot of diversity in our team. It helps us a lot (with) different play styles from all over the world,” said Zaid Abed Elnoor, Jordanian senior striker, right wing.
“We really shout a lot because in Spain we usually shout a lot, so here we motivate (by) shouting,” said Jesus Moreno, Spanish junior right back.
“Our tactic this year is really tailored towards our needs and what we’re good at. As long as we can have the opponent have them play our game, we’re always going to win,” said Alex Schafberg, German senior left wing.
“Every team in the league has talent, but we have connections that a lot of teams don’t have,” said Nick McCorrison, American junior striker.
Foxcroft Academy is riding a five-match winning streak into its home game against Hermon on Wednesday at 4 p.m.
After that, the Ponies finish the regular season with a home-and-home series against John Bapst, another regional contender.

Starting in May, Breeze Airways will offer nonstop flights between the Portland International Jetport and Myrtle Beach, S.C.
The carrier announced on Tuesday that the new route will start on May 27, 2027, with flights operating on Thursdays and Sundays. One-way fares start at $79.

title: Pres. Trump to campaign for Alaska Sen. Sullivan
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump heads West on Tuesday to campaign for Senator Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). The Alaska Republican is in a tough fight for re-election.
Alaska is traditionally a ruby red state. President Trump won Alaska by 13 and a half points in 2024. But the 2026 Midterm cycle is proving to be challenging to Republicans - even in Alaska.
Polls are showing the race between Senator Dan Sullivan (R) and former Congresswoman Mary Peltola (D) is essentially a dead heat. Earlier in August, President Trump confirmed to Gray Media’s White House correspondent Jon Decker that he’ll make the long trip to support Senator Sullivan.
Jon Decker, White House Correspondent, “Do you anticipate actually traveling to Alaska?”
President Donald Trump: “Yeah I do. I’ll go out there to fight for him.”
Sullivan is welcoming the President’s visit - hoping that President Trump can energize the President’s base in Alaska. “Well, look, I always have close races and my 2014 race was very close.”
But Sullivan is confident that he’ll win another six-year-term, “We’ll debate the issues and we’ll work hard to get out the vote. But, you know, my view is races are about your record. And as I talked about there, I have a strong record for Alaska.”
Mary Peltola is hoping that Democrats and Alaska’s independent voters send her back to Washington to serve in the U.S. Senate. She says she thinks that Alaskans, by and large, vote for the person and not their party affiliation.
Peltola says affordability remains the number one issue for Alaska’s voters.
“And if you look at my voting record on things that are important to Alaska, like energy production, like protection of our Second Amendment rights, fighting for Alaskans when it comes to things like the Albertson-Kroger Mega merger, I am just focused on serving the everyday Alaskan.”
It’s rare for a Republican President to fly out to Alaska to campaign during the Midterms. The race in Alaska could determine who controls the Senate for the next two years.

title: 92-year-old father found beaten to death inside his home; son taken into custody, police say
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - Authorities in Louisiana say a man has been taken into custody in connection with the death of his 92-year-old father.
According to the Baton Rouge Police Department, the victim was identified as Larry Salisbury. Police said he was found with injuries consistent with blunt-force trauma Monday night inside a home on Archery Drive during a welfare check.
Baton Rouge Sgt. L’Jean McKneely said officers received a description of a person of interest in the case, Salisbury’s son.
Officers on Tuesday said they took the man’s son into custody after he led officers on a vehicle pursuit in a car that also matched the description of one believed to be connected to the murder scene.
According to McKneely, Salisbury’s son is considered a suspect in his father’s killing. But authorities said he has not been officially named in the case, with any official charges being immediately announced.
Emergency crews said the vehicle the son was driving ended up flipping during the pursuit. No injuries were reported.
Baton Rouge police said the homicide investigation remains ongoing.

title: Coast Guard uses helicopter to rescue Maine lobstermen
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — The Coast Guard rescued two lobstermen Monday night after their vessel took on water about 7 miles offshore from St. George, where it struck some rocks.
The 43-foot vessel had two people aboard at the time of the grounding. They were returning to port to offload their catch. Both mariners made it safely onto the island.
At approximately 7:15 p.m. Monday, Coast Guard Sector Northern New England received a mayday call over VHF radio from the lobster boat Gulf Traveler, reporting that the vessel had run hard aground on the southern portion of Metinic Green Island.
A Coast Guard Station Rockland response boat crew and a Coast Guard helicopter crew were dispatched to assist. The Station Rockland crew arrived on scene but was unable to remove the mariners safely from the island.
A Coast Guard helicopter crew successfully hoisted both mariners from the island and transported them to Knox County Regional Airport in Owls Head, where emergency medical services personnel were waiting to provide further evaluation.
No injuries were reported.
The cause of the grounding remains under investigation by the Coast Guard.
The Coast Guard’s Sikorsky MH-60 Jayhawk medium-range recovery helicopter helicopter was launched from Air Station Cape Cod.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Midterms could set up power struggle between Congress and Trump
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The November midterm elections could dramatically reshape the balance of power in Washington, potentially setting up a confrontation between President Donald Trump and a Democratic-controlled Congress.
With just three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are fighting to maintain their congressional majorities, while Democrats are seeking to regain control. In the House, Democrats need a net gain of just four seats to flip the chamber.
Democratic leaders have already outlined an agenda focused on lowering the cost of living. But they are also promising to use their congressional authority to investigate President Donald Trump and his administration.
“Our promise to the country in the new Congress is that beginning on Day 1 we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in early October.
Even without control of the Senate, a Democratic majority in the House could significantly increase congressional oversight of the Trump administration.
Debbie Mucarsel-Powell, a former Democratic congresswoman who now leads the Graduate School of Political Management at George Washington University, said investigations would likely be among Democrats’ top priorities.
“I think that part of their priority will be to investigate,” Mucarsel-Powell said. “They also want to tackle the affordability issue and look into Medicaid cuts.”
Democratic-led committees could hold hearings, issue subpoenas and investigate the administration’s spending, policies and conduct.
“It’s a very large responsibility of the House and the Senate to ensure the American public understands how their taxpayer dollars have been used under this administration, what kind of actions the president, his family and his friends have taken,” she said.
A Democratic House could also block Republican legislation and use its authority over federal spending to negotiate changes to administration priorities. However, Democrats would still need the Senate’s cooperation to pass legislation.
Control of both the House and Senate would give Democrats greater authority over federal spending, congressional investigations and the legislative agenda.
A Democratic-controlled Senate could also block Trump’s judicial and Cabinet nominees, preventing the president from filling positions that require Senate confirmation.
Democrats would also control both chambers involved in the impeachment process. The House could vote to impeach the president by a simple majority, but removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate.
Still, even with majorities in both chambers, Democrats would face significant obstacles to reversing the president’s policies.
“It would be difficult for Democrats to actually repeal some of those laws or that funding that’s has already been in place. The president also has veto power,” Mucarsel-Powell said.
Congress would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto, making it difficult for Democrats to enact legislation without some Republican support.
Regardless of which party controls Congress, Trump would retain broad executive authority.
The president could continue issuing executive orders, granting federal pardons, conducting diplomacy and directing military operations, subject to constitutional and legal limits.
He could also veto legislation passed by Democrats and continue implementing existing laws through federal agencies.
Congress, meanwhile, could use its oversight and spending powers to challenge the administration, potentially leading to legal disputes over the limits of presidential authority.
The division of power could make it difficult for either party to advance its legislative agenda, raising the possibility of prolonged gridlock.
However, Mucarsel-Powell said the election could also create an opportunity for bipartisanship, particularly as voters express frustration with both parties.
Whether Democrats gain control of one chamber, both chambers or neither will be decided in the Nov. 3 elections, with the next Congress taking office in early January.

title: Greely volleyball battles past Gardiner in cross-class showdown
text:
GARDINER — A first set that couldn’t have possibly had less breathing room Tuesday evening did not go the way of the Greely volleyball team.
The Rangers bounced back in the next two, and when a resilient Gardiner team fought back in the fourth, Class B Greely still found a way to close out a 3-1 (24-26, 25-12, 25-15, 25-23) victory in a high-profile cross-class showdown with the Class C Tigers.
“It was all grit,” said Greely coach Autumn Vargo. “Gardiner is a team we hadn’t seen, so it took us a little bit to figure out their hitters. Once we did, I thought we were really able to settle in and battle.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
The opening set was even as could be. Neither team led by more than two points the entire way, and Gardiner’s four-point run after trailing 11-9 was the longest of the set. After the teams alternated 11 straight points late in the set, the Tigers (10-3) won two in a row to take a one-game lead.
The next two sets, though, went swimmingly for Greely (11-1), the fourth-ranked team in the Varsity Maine poll. Tied 2-2 in the second, the Rangers scored 20 of the next 25 points to tie the match. Then, after Greely sided out trailing 7-4 in the third, freshman Lilah Rosenfeld served 10 straight points and the Rangers notched another double-digit win.
Gardiner, seventh in the Varsity Maine poll, fought back in the fourth set, winning seven of eight points after Greely took a 9-8 lead. Yet the Rangers responded with another run spurred by Avery Enos’ serving to take a 19-17 lead, and after Gardiner battled to pull ahead 23-21, Greely hit back with the final four points to seal the victory.
“We just made sure to not get in our own heads, and we kept supporting each other and cheering each other on,” Rosenfeld. “We’re practicing better together and understanding how we play as a team and the support we need.”
WHAT IT MEANS
• Greely notches its 10th straight victory to snatch back the top spot in Class B from Washington Academy. The Rangers have not lost since falling to Class A Cheverus, the No. 2 team in the Varsity Maine poll, in the second match of the season Sept. 8.
• Gardiner showed mettle against a team from a higher class. Coach Bill Boardman could not have been much happier about his team’s performance, after it delivered the first blow, scored six of seven points late in the third set and forced Greely to claw out of a late deficit in the fourth.
“We made our fair share of mistakes, but to fight and to compete like we did against one of the best teams in the state, that was awesome,” Boardman said. “We talked in the huddle and in-between sets about how they didn’t give up. That’s what this team is all about: They don’t ever, ever give up.”
UNSUNG HERO
Greely’s Maddie Hussey. Enos, Anabelle Talley and Alena Tierney put up the gaudy numbers for Greely, but Rosenfeld also spoke highly of Hussey, whom she called “a big help” in the middle. Vargo also extolled the play of Hussey and the rest of the Rangers’ middle blockers.
NOTABLE QUOTABLE
“We’re coming off playing Cony, who is having a down year, so to go from that to this, back-to-back, is a little rough sometimes. It’s been a rollercoaster of a week in terms of the opponents we’re playing, but I thought they responded well. I’m real happy.” — Bill Boardman
STAT LEADERS
Greely: Anabelle Talley (21 kills, three aces, two blocks, five digs), Avery Enos (three kills, 13 assists, two aces), Alena Tierney (one kill, 14 assists), Maddie Hussey (four kills, two blocks)
UP NEXT
Greely: vs. Lewiston (11-1), 1 p.m. Saturday
Gardiner: at Camden Hills (6-6), 5:30 p.m. Friday

title: Husband charged after pregnant wife’s bloodied, beaten body found in their garage
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KOLD/Gray News) - Court documents have revealed gruesome new details after a man allegedly beat and stabbed his pregnant wife to death in their Arizona home.
Warning: This article contains disturbing details that may be upsetting to readers.
Deputies with the Pima County Sheriff’s Department responded to a home in Vail on Friday after 49-year-old Joseph Clark called saying he killed his wife, 39-year-old Noelle Clark. Upon arriving on the scene, they immediately detained Joseph Clark as he tried to walk out of the home’s front door.
Inside the home, deputies found Noelle Clark’s bloodied and beaten body covered with a blanket in the garage. She was pregnant and appeared to be in her second or third trimester, investigators say.
Two children, ages 2 and 5, were found unharmed on the stairs inside the home.
What the evidence shows
Investigators allege Joseph Clark beat his wife with his hands and a belt before stabbing her in the chest in their children’s bedroom. He later allegedly ran her over with a car after dragging her body through the home and putting her in the garage.
Deputies say Noelle Clark’s body showed signs of blunt force trauma to her head and face, a deep stab wound in the middle of her chest and marks on her back that matched a belt found in the children’s bedroom. A bloody knife, a pool of blood and blood splatter were also found in the bedroom.
Deputies say bloody drag marks led from the bedroom to the garage. There were tire marks on Noelle Clark’s arms and bloody tire marks on the garage floor, indicating her arms were run over by a car, according to investigators.
Based on the evidence at the scene, investigators allege Joseph Clark also had plans to dispose of his wife’s body.
Suspect claims his wife had ‘tortured’ him
Joseph Clark was arrested on two counts of second-degree murder, and his bond was set at $1 million.
He claimed that his wife had been electrically torturing him, and that’s why he killed her. He said he had been “tortured, shocked over a couple of years” and that all his teeth “popped out from being zapped.” Investigators said they found no visible or obvious injuries on his body.
Joseph Clark is scheduled to appear in court again next Tuesday.

title: Obituary: Darlene A. Jamison
text:
FARMINGTON – Darlene A. Jamison, 92, died Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, at Pinewood Terrace in Farmington. She was formerly of Mexico.
Darlene was born in Rumford, on June 7, 1934, the daughter of William and Edna (Simpson) Avery. She was a graduate of Stephens High School class of 1952. She worked as a secretary for her husband Richard at Dick and Sons Garage in Mexico and then at Frosty Delight in Mexico for many years.
Darlene was a member of the Mexico Congregational Church and was formerly a member of the Junior Mother’s Craft Club in Mexico.
She was married to Arthur Drouin in September of 1952, he passed away on June 19, 1953, and was then married in 1955 to Richard Jamison who passed away on Dec. 17, 1991.
Survivors include her sons, Arthur Drouin and wife Yvonne of Mexico and Mark Jamison and wife Shelley of Turner; daughters, Lorraine Durrell and husband Loren “Duke” of New Sharon, Doris Porter and husband Michael of New Sharon, and Jo Hebert and husband Michael of Dixfield; grandchildren, Jamie Drouin, Kristy Hatch, Katie Bailey, Robert Drouin, Richard Jamison, Harley Jamison, Nicholas Durrell, Mark Durrell, David Durrell, Michele Araujo, Kelley Skillein, Alycia Stevens York and many great-grandchildren. She was predeceased by her parents and sisters, Edith Milligan, Natalie Reed, Mary Smith, and Edna Heath.
Friends and family are invited to share memories of Darlene at http://www.meaderandson.com.
Funeral services will be held 11 a.m., Friday Oct. 23, 2026, at the Mexico Congregational Church. Interment will be in the Demeritt Cemetery in Peru.

title: Rain Continues Overnight. Breezy & Warmer Days Ahead
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Cold, raw and rainy weather hangs on through the night, with snow showers possible in far northern Maine. Temperatures will rise a few degrees overnight, changing any rain/snow mix to all rain and helping limit icy conditions. Additional rainfall from 0.10″ to 0.75″.
Wednesday: Rain exits, clouds linger
Rain showers will move out of northern and eastern Maine by midday. Clouds stick around through the afternoon, with a few breaks more likely farther south and west. Those brighter breaks could help temperatures climb: highs in the 40s in the far north, 50s for most and some 60s in southern areas. Northwest winds gust to 25 mph.
Thursday: Brighter, breezy
High pressure brings more sunshine. Highs reach the 40s and 50s, with northwest wind gusts up to 30 mph.
Friday: Rain returns
Rain showers arrive in western Maine during the morning, then spread east through the afternoon. A few flakes could mix in at the far northern tip. Highs will be in the 40s and low 50s.
Saturday: Cold and windy
Rain ends early Saturday morning as the low moves away, pulling colder air in behind it. Expect plenty of sunshine and highs in the 40s, but strong northwest winds gusting to 40 mph will make it feel at or below freezing. Light snow is possible in the mountains and northern Maine, with minor accumulations possible. Bundle up, especially if you’ll be outside.
Sunday: Sunshine, but still chilly
Mostly sunny skies are expected, with highs in the 40s and low 50s. Northwest gusts could still reach 30 mph. Overnight lows Saturday night into Sunday morning will dip into the 20s, and the breeze will make it feel even colder.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast

WEDNESDAY: Showers in the morning across the north and east. Mostly cloudy to overcast with highs in the 40s, 50s, and low 60s. NW winds will gust to 25 mph.
THURSDAY: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 40s and 50s. NW gusts to 30 mph.
FRIDAY: Rain spreads across the region. Highs in the 40s and 50s.
SATURDAY: Mostly sunny skies with snow showers in the mountains. Highs in the 40s and will FEEL colder. NW gusts to 40 mph.

title: Maine firewood banks seeing increased demand as heating oil prices soar
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With outdoor temperatures dipping and heating oil prices soaring nearly 80% higher than last year, Maine’s community-run firewood banks are already seeing increased requests for firewood as residents feel severe anxiety over the coming winter.
Kevin Dunn, founder and president of the Bethel Wood Bank, said people are “bracing for a tough winter.”
“Anecdotally, it seems to be busier earlier than we expected, and the people we’re providing for so far have some higher anxiety and almost desperate behavior around their heat — and other things,” Dunn said in an email. “Rising costs for many of their life essentials is adding to their burden.”
A wood bank in Maine operates like a food pantry, collecting, processing, and distributing free firewood to elderly, disabled, and low-income households facing fuel insecurity. Some wood banks sell firewood to other people in need for a donation or a lower cost than full-market value.
Many wood bank operators say they are currently struggling with high demand. They say they are expecting their supply to deplete early in the season, and are actively seeking equipment, delivery trucks, and grants to keep operating.
“The number of requests from our location in Freeport and surrounding communities is definitely higher than it was last year at this time,” Tony DiMarco, of the Maine Wood Bank Network, wrote in an email. “I can also tell you that we have seen requests coming from all over the state in locations where we do not have wood banks.”
As of Oct. 12, the heating oil average price was $5.97 a gallon, with a high of $6.81 per gallon and a low of $5.45 per gallon, according to Maine Department of Energy Resources. Filling a 275-gallon heating oil tank costs approximately $725 more than it did a year ago, according to the state.
The average price of kerosene in Maine is $6.89 per gallon compared to $6.57 in September 2025.
Wood pellets in Maine averaged $357 a ton in 2025, or roughly $7.14 per 40-pound bag, and has remained steady for the 2026 heating season, according to data from the Maine Department of Energy Resources. Wood pellets are made from sawdust and waste wood.
Dan MacLeod, an operator at the Kennebec Wood Bank, which is in its first year of operation, said visitors to the bank are telling him they’re worried.
“The folks we have given wood to so far are telling me that they are very concerned about their heating costs this year, given oil and electricity costs and the cost of food and general inflation,” MacLeod wrote.
MacLeod noted that Kennebec Wood Bank doesn’t have any history to compare to. “However, I do know that existing wood banks are definitely seeing an uptick in requests this year. There has also been an increase in the number of new wood banks that have formed this year.”
The Webster Wood Bank, operated by the United Methodist Economic Ministry in Salem Township in Franklin County, opened in 2025 as well. “We have been steadily delivering wood this summer. Expecting that when Low-Income Home Energy Assistant Program (LIHEAP) vouchers are available we will start getting busy filling orders for multiple cords,” Jim Webster, the ministry’s property manager and wood bank founder, said in an email.
The ministry’s wood bank program is still working to become self-sustaining. Leaders started a fundraising effort and are exploring grant opportunities.
“We still need a delivery truck and a storage facility as well (as) equipment needed to respond to donations of fire wood,” Webster wrote. “Free wood is not without cost. We also have to purchase next year’s wood.”
The Midcoast Firewood Bank based in Topsham provides emergency firewood to nine nearby towns. The organization also offers two cords of wood to any household that needs it. The volunteer-run operation prepares firewood in Topsham, stockpiling it in the lead-up to the winter months.
Founder Bruce Wildes said he expects high demand this year because of the rising oil prices and people struggling to also pay for food and fuel for their cars.
Operators at the Lake Region Woodbank in Bridgton are already inundated with requests, mostly from people who live on fixed incomes with limited resources, coordinator William Shuttleworth wrote in an email.
“With the price of fuel right now at $6.09 a gallon, we can only anticipate a burgeoning request need for our wood. On our wood site right now, we have somewhere between 50 to 60 cords, and it probably will be depleted by the 1st of December,” he wrote.
“We are also seeing an increase in people requesting help with food support, rent support, and even items at the regional clothing outlet that we provide at one of our churches,” Shuttleworth wrote. “I believe that with the forecast of a tough winter, the need for firewood is going to only increase.”
Mainers using wood stoves should take care to do so safely, Shuttleworth noted.
“I only hope that people who burn wood have safe operating wood stoves and well-inspected chimneys. The last thing that we want would be an unexpected fire due to a faulty wood stove.”

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
It has been said that friendship is one of the great human accomplishments, and if this is so, Robert Douglas, known to many as “Big Bob,” was exceptionally accomplished.
Big Bob, 64, who died on Aug. 27, 2026, made friends in just about every walk of life. He even kept bags of biscuits in his pickup to hand out to every dog he met. He was himself a great bear of a fellow with a deep, rumbling, and much exercised laugh.
Bob was born in Union in 1962. After a short enlistment in the Army (where he achieved an expert rating in M-16 and hand grenades!), he came to Lincoln County to attend The Carpenter’s Boat Shop in Pemaquid. In 1982, he found work as an electrical assembler at Contact Inc. in Nobleboro, owned by Dick and Rick Reid, and then moved to Edgecomb when Dick, with his wife Millie, and Contact’s shop moved there.
In 2018, Bob faced a serious setback when health issues led to the loss of his lower left leg. After a period of adjustment and through various issues regarding his prosthetic and new living arrangements, and with help from the Community Resource Council, Bob gradually worked his way back to nearly his previous levels of activity and helpfulness.
Bob went to work for the Boothbay Railway Village Museum as a ticket-taker and station master in 2019 and was much treasured there by both staff and visitors. In 2024 he moved to Boothbay Harbor.
Bob made friends wherever he went. People were drawn to this gentle giant with a sense of humor that was often its best when it was self-deprecating. Bob was always ready to help others, running errands for the elderly, taking people to appointments, or lending his strong back and his truck.
He enjoyed watching movies and PBS and football, but most of all he liked visiting and phoning his friends. He made friends at work, at poker games (he was good!), the YMCA, the credit union, the post office, the town hall, the barbershop, and the gas station, and he cherished the staff at the doctors’ offices and clinics he came to rely on.
Despite various hardships, he accomplished much.
He is survived by his sister, Lynne White and her husband, Brian, of Union, and a long list of dear friends including Stan and Pam Dalton, of Wiscasset, Peter Albright, of Union, Rick and Judy Reid, of Jefferson, Van Reid and Maggie Hunter, of Edgecomb, Bill and Kathy Lord, of Albion, John and Cathy Orne, of Edgecomb, George and Ethel Brewer, of Boothbay Harbor, and Bonnie, “Cake,” Rachel, Emily, Avery, and many more.
A memorial service will be held to celebrate Bob’s life at the Boothbay Railway Village Museum, in the town hall, on Oct. 24 at 2 p.m. Please come, and bring your stories of Bob Douglas!
In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation to the Boothbay Railway Village Museum or the Community Resource Council in Boothbay Harbor.

title: Bryan Cranston Pays Tribute to RJ Mitte
text:
Bryan Cranston Pays Tribute to ‘Breaking Bad’ Co-Star RJ Mitte
Bryan Cranston posted a tribute on Instagram to the late actor RJ Mitte, who he co-starred with on five seasons of Breaking Bad. Cranston played chemistry teacher turned drug dealer Walter White; Mitte played his son, Walter Jr.
“I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight,” Cranston wrote. “RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died.”
“I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm,” he continued. “Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never - ever - allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination.”
“He was one of the stars of a hit TV show - but still a kid. That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor. He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community.
All that promise and potential now is such a loss.”
READ MORE: The Best New TV Shows on Streaming This Week
Mitte passed away in Texas on Monday. While no official cause of death has been given, TMZ reported that their sources indicated Mitte “died by suicide.”
Cranston called that aspect of the tragic news “especially devastating,” and added “We were texting each other just a few weeks ago - figuring out when we could meet for lunch. I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future ... But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed.”
He closed with the message “I’ll miss you, son” and information for readers about a 24/7 lifeline available for anyone contemplating suicide.

title: Come for Heather Cox Richardson, stay for Troy Jackson
text:
I went to Portland to see Heather Cox Richardson in conversation with Troy Jackson. Really, I was there to see Richardson. Troy was the price I had to pay to see her.
I planned to vote for Troy because he is not Susan Collins. Knowing little about Aroostook County, I had not felt a strong allegiance to him. At first, Troy seemed slightly starstruck and stumbled a bit in the presence of Richardson. Who wouldn’t be starstruck? Thankfully, she is generous with whomever she shares the stage or microphone. He warmed quickly and found firm ground.
What I gleaned about Troy: He’s not shiny or sparkly. Good. I don’t like the shiny and sparkly politicians. Instead, Troy is a piece of beautiful hardwood with a warm patina. Once he loosened up, I found genuine Maine charm that comes from being a part of the community of Maine, a straight talker who speaks directly to issues of great concern to me: Medicaid and Medicare for all; affordable, quality childcare with childcare workers who earn a living wage, an education system that pays teachers and teaches students and an end to the war in Iran.
I came away from Portland forgetting that HCR had been there. I am now excited to vote Jackson for senator.
Lisa Eaton
Kennebunk

title: Katie Zacharia, Trump's new White House press secretary, makes a brief appearance before reporters
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, faced reporters for the first time on Tuesday for a very brief turn at the lectern, taking a handful of questions before abruptly wrapping it up.
Zacharia, a conservative commentator who most recently worked for President Donald Trump’s social media company, was named to the job on Friday, succeeding Karoline Leavitt, who left in August and is taking a job with Fox News Channel.
Zacharia told reporters her goal is to “amplify” what Trump is doing and that the president is “his own best spokesperson.”
She quickly proved that Tuesday, appearing for only 14 minutes and taking questions from just three outlets before telling reporters they could go ask the president their questions on the South Lawn of the White House as he prepared to leave for a campaign trip.
“In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there,” she said.
Before taking the questions, Zacharia read slowly from an opening statement that began with a focus on Trump’s recent campaign rallies ahead of the midterm elections and his policies on energy, tariffs, immigration and more since he returned to office.
In naming Zacharia, who has a law degree from Pepperdine University, Trump described her as “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.” She briefly worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year and has been a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax.
She told reporters that she viewed her role as press secretary to be no different than the way she advocated for Trump while outside the government.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” she said.
She also thanked Trump and said, “I have wanted to work for him for a very long time.”
She took her first question from Breitbart News, the right-wing outlet which has become more influential in the Trump era, and committed to keeping the “new media” rotation created under her predecessor to bring additional media outlets into news briefings and the White House press pool.
But Zacharia did make some big news: she said that Trump had asked for the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
“She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” Zacharia said.

title: Proposed livestreamed execution raises concerns
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The first livestreamed execution in American history has forced the country to ask itself an uncomfortable question: is this who we are?
Nidal Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad December 3 at Fort Hood. Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in a 2009 mass shooting at the Texas Army base. It would be the first military execution since 1945, and the first public execution since 1937.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the unprecedented decision October 7 during an interview with the conservative broadcast outlet Real America’s Voice. President Donald Trump doubled down and backed Hegseth’s decision late last week.
“Exposure to graphic images of that kind of violence is not good for you,” said Alison Holman, a psychology professor at UC Irvine who specializes in collective trauma.
Her research has shown that witnessing graphic violence can cause post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms.
“Our team has had young people reaching out from across the country saying they’ve seen these acts of horrific violence,” Holman said about her research into the long-term impacts of witnessing trauma. “I’m not saying that it will cause PTSD, but… it is definitely associated with PTSD symptoms that are distressing and can increase a person’s sense of worry about the future and can disrupt their ability to function.”
Many Republicans quickly shared concern about what a state-sanctioned live execution would do to America’s collective humanity.
“Seneca warned that Rome’s bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) wrote on X. “The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”
Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.), who is a veteran running for re-election in a swing district, shared similar concerns.
“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X last week. “The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”
Across the world, Pope Leo reiterated his opposition to the death penalty as a whole. Pietro Parolin, the Vatican Secretary of State, said in part, “It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle.”
Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, stopped short of opposing the livestream, but said he wouldn’t watch. Holman urges people not to watch, but knows that is difficult in this technological age.
“You could open up a social media account and a video would start on its own, by itself, auto-start, and you could see something before you really had a chance to turn it off,” Holman explained.
Holman said a public execution goes against current American culture, but is painfully reminiscent of a darker time, when lynchings of mostly Black people took place, particularly in the South.
“[A lynching] was considered something that they should all go and watch,” said Holman. “So I guess in some ways, the live streaming of this really isn’t totally counter to our culture, but it’s bringing back a part of our culture that we had put behind us.”
The Federal Bureau of Prisons bans the recording and broadcasting of executions, but Hasan’s case is through military courts, which have a whole other set of governing rules.
A public or video-distributed execution, by any method, is exceptionally rare in the 21st century. Recent examples include Iran, Somalia and videos of beheadings from the Taliban and ISIS.
Shortly after Hegseth posted on X confirming his decision, Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.) quoted it to add his concern.
“I absolutely support the sentence of death,” Scott started. “But live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Some, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, have shared concerns a video of executions — particularly an ideological extremist like Hasan — would serve as a recruitment tool for America’s adversaries.
Legal proceedings could delay the execution, which is common in death penalty cases. If Hasan faces the firing squad in December, it is unclear what a livestream would logistically look like and if any media outlet or digital platform would be willing to share any part of it.
When asked about the possible livestream as he departed for Alaska, President Trump would only confirm “they’re looking at it.”

title: Husband accused of bludgeoning wife to death with flashlight in front of 3 kids
text:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX/Gray News) - A Vermont man is facing charges after police say he bludgeoned his wife to death with a large flashlight.
Burlington Police say they received multiple 911 calls just before 6 a.m. Saturday reporting a fight. They responded to an apartment and found a woman unresponsive in bed with head injuries. She was taken the hospital, where she was pronounced dead Sunday evening.
The victim’s name has not been released.
Investigators identified the suspect as 44-year-old Bal Khadka, the victim’s husband. Police allege he bludgeoned his wife with a large flashlight in front of three children.
Khadka was initially charged with attempted murder, but after his wife’s death, detectives updated the charge against him to second-degree murder.
Khadka is expected in court Tuesday.

title: Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House publicly asked for U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct, and she announced within two hours that she was quitting, ending days of talk and speculation about her professional fate. Guilfoyle insisted that she would “vigorously defend” herself.
President Donald Trump’s administration had said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
That revelation came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”
“She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump said just after Guilfoyle’s resignation, which was posted on her X account. He said he had not spoken to her but “she will not be there.”
Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct.
Guilfoyle denies the accusations and cites her ‘decades of public service’
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in her resignation post on X, saying, “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”
“I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”
In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations.”
They did not immediately return calls Tuesday.
The allegations began surfacing weeks ago
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
There was no immediate response to Zacharia’s statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.
Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.
Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa’s “Dance the Night,” from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie “Barbie.”
Greece has taken on an increasingly important and influential role because of its geographic location in Southeastern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly on energy issues as the war with Iran has spiked global oil prices. Besides the vast number of Greek-registered oil tankers that regularly ply the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Greece is well positioned to be a pipeline conduit for liquefied natural gas imports into the Balkans and beyond.
As the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Guilfoyle had put an emphasis on energy issues, although her close association with executives in that sector was part of what got her into trouble.
Democrats call for an investigation
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco’s mayor, before he became California’s governor. She later was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr.
___
AP journalists Derek Gatopoulos in Athens and Darlene Superville at the White House contributed.
