title: Obituary: Jeffrey Stuart Ray D.O
text:
FRYEBURG – Jeffrey Stuart Ray, D.O. left this world on Oct. 6, 2026, after a long battle with colon cancer. He was 74 years old, the son of Donald B. Ray of Portland, Maine and Margaret K. Lewis of Perth-Andover, New Brunswick, Canada.
Jeff was born in Portland, Maine and grew up in the Rosemont neighborhood where his childhood was filled with fishing, skiing, hunting, scouting, and adventures with friends. After attending Deering High School he went on to graduate from the University of Maine at Orono in 1975.
Many of Jeff’s lifelong friendships began during those early years, particularly through his college fraternity, Phi Eta Kappa. He was predeceased by his closest fraternity brother, George “Scorpio” Foster, with whom he shared some unforgettable adventures in the 1970s. They travelled cross-country on Harley-Davidsons, camped, hiked, and attended rock concerts. Jeff loved a good adventure, big or small, and that spirit stayed with him throughout his life.
He liked to say that he had “retired” after college, having taken the time to do the things he wanted while he was still young. When he eventually made his way back home, he went to work for the Crosby-Laughlin Company, a marine hardware firm on Fore Street and the Harris Company, a fishing supply business on Commercial Street. There, he began saving money to continue his education.
In 1980, Jeff began his medical journey at the Palmer School of Chiropractic in Davenport, Iowa. The following year, he married Nancy D. Eustis of Portland, Maine. After graduating and welcoming their first child, Jeff and Nancy returned to Maine, where he established his chiropractic practice on Brighton Avenue in Portland. Jeff’s heartfelt compassion for his patients was evident from the very beginning. Dedicated to caring for people regardless of their circumstances, he sometimes bartered his services in exchange for goods such as fresh fish, artwork, and jewelry—a reflection of both his generosity and the close connections he formed with those he served.
After ten years, and three additional children, Jeff decided he wanted to do more for his patients. At age 38, he entered medical school, attending the University of New England in Biddeford and earning his Doctorate of Osteopathic Medicine with the assistance of the Federal Rural Health Care Program.
Jeff was fortunate to remain in Maine, practicing at Sacopee Valley Health Care Center in Porter. What began as a four-year assignment became a 20-year career, including many years as Medical Director. His medical knowledge, curiosity and genuine concern for his patients made him a beloved physician. His friend MaryAgnes Gilman, Executive Director at SVHC during that time, described him as “a brilliant diagnostician” whose clinical knowledge and background benefited countless patients. Jeff was also known for making house calls when patients could not make it to the Health Center, providing care to people and families in the comfort of their own homes.
The Ray family settled in Fryeburg in 1998, where Jeff has thrived. He thoroughly enjoyed the Mount Washington Valley area and raising a family among its natural beauty and recreational opportunities. He gladly gave back to the community by assisting the Fire Department with annual physicals and serving on the town’s Planning Board.
He spent the last five years of his medical career as a primary care physician at the Veterans Administration Clinic in Lewiston. He retired in 2024 and enjoyed having more time for reading, cooking, travelling to Ireland and Florida, gardening, bee keeping, or simply relaxing by the pool with a cigar and looking out at his beautiful view of the mountains and the Saco River. Above all, Jeff treasured time spent with family and friends, often gathering with familiar faces at North Conway’s Original Cigar Bar.
Jeff leaves behind his wife of 45 years, Nancy; son, Dawson, and his partner, Jeanine Clark, of Conway, NH; grandson, Logan, of Rochester, NH; daughter, Justine Bales, her husband Travis, and grandchildren Cora and Max of Crestview, Fla.; daughter, Phoebe Martin and her husband, Michael, of Osprey, Fla.; and son, Ethan and his partner, Daya Hall-Stratton, of Haymarket, Va.
He was predeceased by his parents and older brother, Donald S. Ray of Portland. He is survived by his younger brother, David, and his wife, Linda, of St. Petersburg, Fla., and his sister, Betty Pease, and her husband, Fred, of Andover, Mass.
Visiting hours will take place at Woods’ Funeral Home, 9 Warren St., Fryeburg, Maine, on Friday, Oct. 23, 3 to 5 p.m.. A funeral mass will be held at St. Elizabeth Ann Seton Church, 857 Main St., Fryeburg, Maine on Saturday, Oct. 24, at 9 a.m. followed by a celebration of life from 11 to 2 p.m. at the Fryeburg Fairgrounds Expo Building, 1154 Main St., Fryeburg.

memorial donations may be made in honor of
Dr. Jeffrey Ray to

title: Kroger to lay off 3,000 employees as it leans into artificial intelligence
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) - Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.
“Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.”
Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.”
Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer.
Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO.
Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities.
Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells.
Kroger has also felt pressure from fast-growing discount chains like Aldi and Lidl and online behemoths like Amazon.
Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed.
A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value.
Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee.
Albertsons is facing the same competitive headwinds as Kroger and other grocery chains as customers turn to cheaper alternatives and faster delivery from bigger retailers.
On Tuesday during its second-quarter earnings conference call with investors, CEO Susan Morris alluded to further cost-cutting and streamlining of the company’s structure, including layoffs.
“We did some work last year and saw a substantial reduction in headcount, but quite frankly, there’s more to be had,” Morris said. ”And you’ll see us taking aggressive action there in the next 12 to 18 months as well.”
Kroger shares fell 2.2% in afternoon trading Tuesday, to $61.21. Albertsons rose 2.8% but its shares are down more than 25% this year.

title: Young mom’s breast cancer diagnosis highlights rising rates among younger adults
text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (Aging Untold) — Cancer is increasing in people under 65, and women are now more likely than men to develop it, according to the American Cancer Society.
Brittany Auclair, of Tallahassee, was diagnosed with breast cancer at 29, shortly after her son Brayden was born.
A mother notices something while breastfeeding
Brayden was 8 months old when Auclair first noticed an issue while breastfeeding.
“He decided that he favored one side over the other, but I did notice that while I went to work and I was pumping that there was a lump,” Auclair said.
She followed up with her doctor, who is also a breast cancer survivor.
“She said, ‘I’m not waiting to make an appointment. I want you to come in as soon as possible,’” Auclair said.
Thinking she had a clogged milk duct, Auclair underwent scans and tests. A few days after her 29th birthday, she received her diagnosis.
“I remember kind of hitting a brick wall hearing her say, ‘You have cancer’ and how we’re going to move forward. And then I shut down,” Auclair said.
Diagnosis and treatment
Auclair was diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer.
“At one point if I heard one more time, ‘You’re so young to have cancer,’ I thought I was going to scream,” Auclair said.
During months of treatment, including surgery and chemotherapy, daily tasks became difficult.
“Doing normal activities, going to the grocery store, going to make dinner or plan meals became super stressful,” Auclair said.
With support from family, friends and coworkers, Auclair completed treatment in October 2013. She has been cancer-free for more than 12 years.
“When I went through my story, I felt like I was the only one. I’ve now read several stories where there are young mothers that are finding their cancer,” Auclair said.
Doctors report a rising trend in younger patients
Dr. Amit Jain, an oncologist at Tallahassee Memorial HealthCare, specializes in colorectal and lung cancer treatment and has treated patients for more than a decade.
“I have definitely seen men and women as young as 29, 30, with colorectal cancer, with no family history, no predisposition, no risk factors,” Jain said. “How they present, you’re never thinking cancer.”
A study by the American Cancer Society found that young adults identified as Gen Xers and millennials may be at higher risk of being diagnosed with cancer. Researchers found that 17 of 34 types of cancer are increasing among these two groups compared with older generations, including breast, pancreatic and kidney cancer
Jain said studies are ongoing, but more research and awareness are needed for this age group.
“Never ignore any symptom,” Jain said.
Calls for awareness and earlier detection
Auclair said she believes experts should consider lowering age guidelines to help with early detection and prevention.
“They need to be aware. I don’t think it’s something that they need to stress about every day, but I think young people need to understand that it is occurring,” Auclair said.
Asked what may be driving the trend, Aging Untold expert Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, pointed to several potential factors.
“Well, I think we have an obesity epidemic. We are living in the middle of toxic soup everywhere we go. And all these different things play a role on it, along with the genetics,” Rogers said. “You know, we’re used to looking at people’s genetics when they were getting these cancers at a young age.”
Rogers said she believes the medical community needs to move away from associating cancer primarily with older people.
“But now we understand with no family history and anything like that, we have to pay attention. We have to get out of that mindset that cancer is a disease for older people and start really being proactive and educate people about the symptoms and the signs and how things present and not the age,” Rogers said.

title: Florida to execute a prisoner who killed his cellmate in hopes of getting a death sentence
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A Florida prisoner who claimed he killed his cellmate so he could be moved to death row is set to be executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the fatal attack.
James Robertson, 63, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and waived all appeals in the 2008 strangling of Frank Hart. Robertson is set to receive a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke starting at noon.
Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason for withdrawing Thompson’s death warrant but had temporarily stayed his execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation.
Records show that this is the first time DeSantis has withdrawn a death warrant, which does not technically change Thompson’s sentence. He will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future.
Robertson’s execution comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the U.S. In Tennessee, Christa Pike survived an execution attempt two weeks ago despite receiving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. And last week, the Pentagon announced that the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be livestreamed.
Florida Department of Corrections spokesperson Jordan Kirkland was asked at a press conference early Tuesday how the state planned to make sure what happened to Pike in Tennessee wouldn’t happen in Florida.
“Florida has a sound lethal injection process and protocol,” Kirkland said, noting he can’t speak to Tennessee’s lethal injection procedure. “We are very committed to carrying that out in a humane and dignified manner.”
All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.
Robertson wanted to be executed
According to court records, Robertson was incarcerated at Charlotte Correctional Institution, north of Fort Myers, in December 2008 when he tied several socks together and strangled Hart while the other man slept. Robertson told investigators that the attack was unprovoked and that he killed his cellmate so that he would be sentenced to death, rather than having to live out his days in prison.
Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart was sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction.
Robertson pleaded guilty and waived a penalty phase, where a jury would recommend the death penalty or life in prison. A judge sentenced Robertson to death, and he later waived all post-conviction proceedings. Robertson reiterated his position during a hearing earlier this month, telling a judge that he understood his execution had been scheduled and that he didn’t want to make any final appeals to the Florida Supreme Court or U.S. Supreme Court.
Opponents of the death penalty say Robertson’s case undermines claims that executions deter murder. Maria DeLiberato, the legal and policy director for Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty, said Hart deserved to be safe in prison and argued that “the existence of the death penalty may have caused the very violence it purportedly prevents.
A rare reprieve leaves another Florida prisoner on death row
Meanwhile, DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state’s method of execution at the time. The 74-year-old death row inmate was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester.
Thompson will remain on Florida’s death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future. His attorneys have said he has dementia, and his health is failing. They said he should be relocated to an adequate medical facility to get the care he needs.
Only one other Florida inmate remains alive following a death warrant signed by DeSantis. James Dailey, 80, was scheduled to die in late 2019 for the murder of a 14-year-old girl, but a federal judge halted the execution as attorneys argued against his guilt. The stay was eventually lifted, but DeSantis didn’t sign a new death warrant. The state halted all executions during the COVID-19 pandemic and didn’t restart until 2023.
Florida has the nation’s busiest death chamber
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson would be the state’s 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson.
DeSantis has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions, but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. 5. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.
If Robertson, Reaves and Guardado are all executed as planned, that would match the state’s 2025 total, with eight weeks remaining in 2026.
A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 30 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

title: 7 children removed from ‘filthy and deplorable’ home, 8 adults facing multiple charges, police say
text:

Police said the seven children and eight adults lived in a home where feces and urine were allegedly smeared on the floors, stairs and various other surfaces throughout the home, WDKY reported.

The following people were charged:
Christine Carter, 41 — first-degree criminal abuse/neglect of a child under 13 and first-degree criminal abuse

Sarah Carter, 28 — first-degree criminal abuse/neglect of a child under 13, first-degree criminal abuse, distribution of obscene matter and incest
Mark Brumbaugh, 30 — first-degree criminal abuse/neglect of a child under 13, first-degree criminal abuse and third-degree sexual abuse
Green Schindler, 63 — first-degree criminal abuse/neglect of a child under 13, first-degree criminal abuse, human trafficking, first-degree rape and first-degree sodomy

title: Here’s what North Yarmouth voters will see on the ballot
text:
Absentee voting is underway leading up to Maine’s Nov. 3 election. On Election Day, North Yarmouth residents can vote in person at Wescustogo Hall and North Yarmouth Community Center from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
In addition to federal, gubernatorial and county races, here’s what North Yarmouth voters will see on their ballots. For the complete ballot and dive more into candidate responses, explore the 2026 Maine Voter Guide.
CUMBERLAND COUNTY COMMISSIONER DISTRICT 3
The Board of Cumberland County Commissioners includes five commissioners who are elected for a four-year term. The board oversees the financial operations, approved budgets and manages county property. North Yarmouth residents, as part of Cumberland County’s 3rd district, will choose between two candidates:
Amy Leshure, Democrat
What are your top three priorities?
1) Responsible budgeting and the county’s long-term fiscal stability. 2) Building stronger partnerships with municipalities and the state to share services, reduce duplication and secure sustainable funding. I will aim to have county government delivering essential services efficiently and transparently. 3) Right-sizing the county jail by strengthening behavioral health, substance-use and public safety services.
Why are you running?
I am running because county government has a meaningful impact on our communities. I bring more than 20 years of financial and operational experience and a collaborative leadership style. I will use this experience to strengthen fiscal oversight, increase transparency and help Cumberland County work more effectively with municipalities to solve our regional challenges.
Robert P. Vail, Independent
What are your top three priorities?
The expansion of county services to reduce local taxes. Ensure that training for first responders are standardized across the county. Include school departments with regionalization to offset rising costs.
Why are you running?
The challenges facing us today, whether housing, social issues, job creation, aging, childcare, lack of a workforce in our police, fire, rescue and public works departments need to have different approaches, and I believe I can contribute to that end.
MAINE STATE HOUSE DISTRICT 105
Anne Palmer Graham is unopposed in her reelection bid for the Maine House of Representatives.
MAINE STATE SENATE DISTRICT 25
Teresa S. Pierce is running unopposed for reelection to represent North Yarmouth as part of Maine’s 25th State Senate district.

title: Police arrest 51-year-old man allegedly found in hidden room during underage party bust
text:
YORK COUNTY, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) - Police in Nebraska arrested a 51-year-old man found in a hidden room during an underage party bust.
York County sheriff’s deputies responded to a home in a rural part of the county at 10:42 p.m. following multiple reports of an underage drinking party occurring after a school homecoming event.
Deputies obtained a search warrant for the property, which appeared to be owned by Chad Stuhr.
Deputies and the Nebraska State Patrol executed the search warrant at 1:38 a.m. the next morning and found 28 juveniles, along with numerous alcoholic beverage containers inside the loft of a barn.
According to the sheriff’s office, multiple juveniles reported that Stuhr was the only adult present at the party. Statements allege that he was drinking alcohol at the party and his behavior toward young girls was uncomfortable or inappropriate.
The investigation led deputies to believe that Stuhr allegedly had “inappropriate contact with a juvenile at the party,” the sheriff’s office said.
Authorities found Stuhr hiding inside a concealed room behind a movable wall in the barn loft, where he was taken into custody.
He’s facing several drug and weapon charges along with second-degree sexual assault of a child, child abuse and contributing to the delinquency of a minor.
A search of the property uncovered numerous alcoholic beverages, marijuana, a bayonet and 62.7 grams of suspected psilocybin mushrooms, according to the sheriff’s office.

title: Longtime Portland boys basketball coach Joe Russo retires
text:
Joe Russo has retired as Portland High’s boys basketball coach.
Russo, 69, had been weighing the decision to retire for months — his friends and fellow coaches would say years. On Tuesday he made it public.
“I handed in my resignation. I sat and had a good conversation with Spencer (Allen, the Portland athletic director),” Russo said Tuesday evening. “Something is telling me this is the right time.
“The truth is, I still enjoy it. I wish I could do it forever. But I knew I would have to give it up sometime. When do I pass the torch? And I just said, ‘maybe this is the time.'”
A Portland native, Russo coached the Bulldogs for 36 seasons and won his sixth state championship with the program in February, guiding a gritty, defense-oriented team that lost six regular-season games while dealing with injuries, sickness, and players staying away from practice during a large-scale immigration enforcement operation.
“There’s not many leaders out there who could have navigated all of that and keep teenagers focused,” said South Portland boys basketball coach Kevin Millington.
Millington said he used to joke that “this was the 15th straight year (Russo) had said he was done but I always felt this year was different. Not because they had won (the championship) but because of the way he said it.”
Russo said that his final game being a state championship win had little to do with his decision.
“I never really coached for championships. I always coached to be competitive, for the players to be the best they can, and give a good effort,” Russo said. “When I do look back, it won’t be the last year I won. It will be that I’ve been very fortunate to have 36 great years,” at Portland.
Russo’s boys basketball teams won 517 games, including 11 over his first three seasons at Bonny Eagle. At Portland, he also helped start and coach the Portland girls volleyball program.
In 2018, the same year Russo was inducted into the Maine Basketball Hall of Fame, he overcame non-Hodgkin Large B Cell Lymphoma cancer. Russo was back coaching both volleyball and boys basketball in the 2018-19 school year.
Russo said he is healthy and that was not a factor in his decision to retire.
Russo won his 500th game in a AA North quarterfinal in 2025. That made him the 10th coach in Maine high school basketball history to reach the mark. He is now sixth on the all-time wins list.
After the Bulldogs defeated Camden Hills to win the 2026 Class A title, Russo indicated to friends, peers, and other acquaintances that he had probably just coached his last game.
He had made similar statements for at least a decade, usually in the muted light of a Cross Insurance Arena hallway after Portland had been eliminated. Russo would look tired and worn down. Then he would take a couple of weeks to think about it and by the next season would be back on Portland’s sideline.
Last season felt different. The Bulldogs won a state title and Russo was beaming. In mid-summer, Russo was still waiting to make his retirement final but also saying he was 98% sure he was done. He was letting his assistant coaches run the summer program.
As late as mid-September, Allen, the Portland AD, said he figured each day that passed increased the odds that Russo would return as Portland’s coach. Allen joked that on the days Russo was at the high school as a part-time physical education teacher he would try to avoid crossing paths with Russo.
“If he doesn’t see me he can’t give me his resignation,” Allen said.
As recently as last week, Russo said he was tempted to keep coaching, “because our freshmen are dynamite.”
The first day of practice for the 2026-27 season is Nov. 16, less than five weeks away.
Possible in-program successors as head coach would be top assistant Dan LeGage, a former head coach at Westbrook, and long-time assistant Joe Johnson. Russo’s longest tenured assistant Joe Giordano has indicated previously that he planned to step aside whenever Russo retired.
Russo said there are a “lot of qualified people,” who could succeed him, including several in “our own building.” He added that because he’ll likely know so many of the candidates he doesn’t want to be involved in the hiring process.
Russo was born on Dec. 7, 1956, the same day as Boston Celtics legend Larry Bird. Russo and his family moved from a different Portland neighborhood to Munjoy Hill when he was in third grade. The new house had a basketball hoop.
“So I started playing it. I played all the way through college and rec leagues. I studied the game,” Russo said. A point guard known for his defense, Russo said he was often referred to as “peppery,” by Portland sportscaster Frank Fixaris.
After graduating from Portland High in 1975, Russo earned a degree and played basketball at UMaine Presque Isle. He started his teaching and coaching career at Bonny Eagle, a job he enjoyed, but he and his wife Donna, who met in junior high and began dating as high school juniors, both wanted to stay in Portland. The Russos have been married 46 years. They have three grown children and nine grandchildren.
After his 500th win, Russo talked about what it meant to him to teach and coach at Portland High.
“When this job (at Portland) came, it was the dream job, pretty much,” Russo said. “Mainly because being from Portland and going to Portland High, you’re happy for the players. I was just like them growing up. So it means a lot when you’re doing it for the school you grew up in. I’m happy for the city and the school and the kids.”
Russo’s Portland teams won state championships in 1999, 2004, 2014, 2016, 2017, and 2026, and finished as state runner-up in 2007, 2015, and 2023.
The 2016, 2017, and 2023 state finals were against South Portland.
“From a basketball perspective, Joe’s teams were always an elite defensive team,” Millington said. “The other thing he’s really elite at is, he’s very patient. Maybe that comes with age. He wasn’t trying to win the state championship in the first game or the fifth game and they were always much better at the end of the year than they were in the beginning.”

title: A more balanced Congress requires Democrats

text:
In most midterm elections, voters are looking for candidates that will balance the power in Washington, D.C. This is more critical than ever this year, after two years of domination by President Trump and the Republicans.
More than half of the citizens in our country have no real representation in the U.S. Congress today; Democrats have been silenced and Republicans are not allowed to disagree with the White House.
The high prices and hardships Mainers are facing today are a direct result of the president’s whims and decisions. Nothing will change if we don’t send enough Democrats to Congress in November to balance the decision-making.

Please consider what’s at stake for Maine and our country when we vote in the midterms.
Beverly Wood
North Berwick

title: Three months after Johan Sebastián’s death, we’re still fighting for the truth
text:
Sean P. Murphy is a former Bronx County and federal prosecutor who fought organized crime and helped lead the Justice Department’s investigation into the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Raised in Vermont and now an attorney at Gideon Asen in Maine, he represents the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
Nearly three months ago, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero left his home in the early morning hours of July 13, 2026. He was thinking, as he did every morning, of the minute he would return to hug his wife, Karolina, and his little girl.
The night before had been like any other. Karolina folded laundry. Johan said he was going to bed. They shared a kiss, and neither had any idea it would be their last.
I never had the privilege of knowing Johan while he was alive. It is an odd and beautiful thing to know a man only through those he left behind.
I came to know him through his parents, Omar and Dora, who traveled from Colombia to collect their son’s body. At the funeral home in Portland, I stepped out of the room, but a mother’s cries over the body of her murdered son pierced the walls. It was a lamentation I never wanted to hear and never want to forget.
I came to know him through his sister, Daniela, who was the first of the family to come to America. Like any older sibling, she carries guilt. Daniela, this is not your fault. We know who is responsible.
And I came to know him through Karolina and his daughter. Karolina’s resilience amazes me. This country has taken so much from her, and I am sorry. To spend two minutes with their little girl is to know that her father’s fire lives on.
Since July, my partner Ben Gideon and I have fought for Johan. Recently, we met with representatives of the Maine Attorney General’s Office, which is the first and only governmental agency to confirm it is investigating the deadly use of force by a federal agent.
At that meeting, we received property found to have no evidentiary value. One item was not returned: his daughter’s car seat. Karolina asked why. She was told that a bullet fired by a federal agent had pierced it, just as bullets fired by a federal agent killed her husband.
Early reports said his daughter was in the car with him. She was not, thank God. But the recklessness is plain, and the horror of what could have been is unthinkable. One tragedy was already too many.
The only justification offered for his death was public safety. You know what actually keeps the public safe? Not shooting innocent, law-abiding fathers whose only dream is to build a better life for their families.
Let’s be clear about what happened here. This administration made a nefarious decision to take a life, and it has met the consequences with silence. A president who wants to be king has decided that the rest of us may be sacrificed for his agenda. He must immediately stop violating our right to life.
Johan was not a citizen, but he was an American in the purest sense of the word. He worked, he loved his family and he dreamed. Anyone who would defend his killing is not a true patriot.
He is not alone. Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo belong to the same club, one whose dues no one would ever choose to pay. Their families are owed answers, not excuses.
But anger rings hollow without hope. Anyone who has lived through a Maine winter knows that even the harshest cold must eventually yield to spring. With the midterm elections approaching, I hope and pray our nation begins charting its path toward that spring. This is not who we are as Americans. We have to do better.
Three months on, Johan’s family is still waiting for truth, justice and accountability. We will not stop fighting until they get it.

title: Landmark Aroostook hotel installs massive ‘I ❤️ Presque Isle’ sign as new managers work to rehabilitate image
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The message is a simple one, though it’s 55 feet long and flanked by a tractor and potato barrels.
Perched along Route 1 at the top of the hill that descends into Aroostook County’s most populous city, a giant sign declares “I love Presque Isle,” with “love” represented as a heart.
New managers installed the sign three weeks ago outside the Presque Isle Hotel, where they hope to create a tourist attraction that brings guests through their doors and erodes stigma that has followed the iconic hotel from its previous owner.
Formerly known as the Presque Isle Inn & Convention Center — and, before that, the Swamp Fox and Keddy’s Motor Inn — the 151-room facility is the biggest hotel in northern Maine and has stood as a landmark near the city’s southern edge since it opened in 1973.
But it has faced its share of controversy in recent years. The hotel abruptly closed and was subsequently condemned in early 2023 after its owner said he did not have the money to make payroll. Twenty-five employees and family members who lived in the hotel were forced to leave in the middle of a snow storm as a fleet of police vehicles waited outside.
The building sold at auction a few months later and again in August 2024 to LMA Presque Isle LLC, which has taken on major renovations, hotel management said.
“It’s been through so many upheaves and ‘down heaves,’” hotel manager Leslie Dias said. “We want to get rid of all the bad memories and bring something fresh.”
The front lawn of the Presque Isle Hotel is already a tourist attraction. It’s home to the planet Mercury in the Maine Solar System model.
Hotel General Manager AK Sharma kept seeing people stop to take photos with it, which spawned an idea. Other cities have signs proclaiming their civic pride. Why not Presque Isle?
The concept originated from the “I Love New York” logo, designed in 1977, which is the state’s official tourism slogan and blankets signs and souvenir shops throughout The Empire State.
Today, similar signs exist across the world, from Tashkent, Uzbekistan, to Fargo, North Dakota.
In Presque Isle, the tractor and potato barrels reference the city’s agricultural industry. The hotel also plans to add a sculpture of a hot-air balloon, to reference the Presque Isle’s ballooning history, among other items.
“We wanted to bring all of the iconic things of this area,” Dias said.
Inside the hotel, all of the rooms have been renovated, Dias said. Siding has been replaced and the indoor pool was redone. New landscaping greets visitors as they walk inside. Management is currently in the process of replacing rugs in the hotel’s main corridor.
“It never ends,” Dias said with a laugh. “It’s like having a house multiplied by 100.”
It has not been all smooth sailing. Time Out Sports Bar, a bar and restaurant inside the hotel, was closed for more than a month this summer after its permit to sell alcohol expired.
Presque Isle leadership requested that the City Council deny a new liquor authorization over public safety concerns, but the council approved a license after Dias and Sharma proposed that the bar would eliminate live music and hire experienced bouncers.
The restaurant has reopened, and the hotel is looking forward with a focus on its guests and promoting what’s great about Presque Isle, Dias said. The sign outside says as much.
“We’re not a franchise, we’re a standalone. We work closely with customers,” she said. “We do everything that we possibly can for people.”

title: Pres. Trump to campaign for Alaska Sen. Sullivan
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump heads West on Tuesday to campaign for Senator Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). The Alaska Republican is in a tough fight for re-election.
Alaska is traditionally a ruby red state. President Trump won Alaska by 13 and a half points in 2024. But the 2026 Midterm cycle is proving to be challenging to Republicans - even in Alaska.
Polls are showing the race between Senator Dan Sullivan (R) and former Congresswoman Mary Peltola (D) is essentially a dead heat. Earlier in August, President Trump confirmed to Gray Media’s White House correspondent Jon Decker that he’ll make the long trip to support Senator Sullivan.
Jon Decker, White House Correspondent, “Do you anticipate actually traveling to Alaska?”
President Donald Trump: “Yeah I do. I’ll go out there to fight for him.”
Sullivan is welcoming the President’s visit - hoping that President Trump can energize the President’s base in Alaska. “Well, look, I always have close races and my 2014 race was very close.”
But Sullivan is confident that he’ll win another six-year-term, “We’ll debate the issues and we’ll work hard to get out the vote. But, you know, my view is races are about your record. And as I talked about there, I have a strong record for Alaska.”
Mary Peltola is hoping that Democrats and Alaska’s independent voters send her back to Washington to serve in the U.S. Senate. She says she thinks that Alaskans, by and large, vote for the person and not their party affiliation.
Peltola says affordability remains the number one issue for Alaska’s voters.
“And if you look at my voting record on things that are important to Alaska, like energy production, like protection of our Second Amendment rights, fighting for Alaskans when it comes to things like the Albertson-Kroger Mega merger, I am just focused on serving the everyday Alaskan.”
It’s rare for a Republican President to fly out to Alaska to campaign during the Midterms. The race in Alaska could determine who controls the Senate for the next two years.

title: After surging troops to the border, US Army showcases a quieter Rio Grande
text:
ROMA, Texas (AP) — Standing on a high bank of the Rio Grande, Army Lt. Col. Ray Richards points to a stretch of river that was, until recently, one of the busiest spots for illegal border crossings from Mexico.
But on a recent afternoon, the area is quiet. American soldiers gather at a border monitoring post in Roma, Texas, where an infantry vehicle with camouflage netting sits between houses. A Blackhawk helicopter drops soldiers onto an island in the river, while U.S. Border Patrol agents breeze by on fan-propelled boats.
“At any given time, there would be multiple rafts full of people trying to get to this side,” Richards said of the area before U.S. forces made it a priority last year.
The Army has been inviting reporters to the Rio Grande Valley as it deploys hundreds more soldiers to the region this month by shifting some of the thousands of troops already serving along the 2,000-mile border. U.S. officials said the troop surge follows signs of elevated activity from drug cartels and has been accompanied by increased cooperation from the Mexican military. The U.S. Coast Guard said it recently encountered gunfire from the Mexican side of the river, prompting the Americans to fire back.
In this small patch at the southern edge of the United States, a slow saga is playing out — a curious mix of policing, policy and politics.
Some question a troop surge just weeks before midterm elections
While Republicans face increasing headwinds because of President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, persistently high prices and the fallout from the war in Iran, border security has remained a relative bright spot in Trump’s polling numbers, with about half of Americans saying they approve of his performance there.
But some experts have questioned the need for such a large military presence. They suggest it’s less about effective strategy and more about political theater.
Illegal crossings have plummeted due in large part to asylum restrictions that began before Trump returned to the White House. Meanwhile, a large percentage of the fentanyl, cocaine and heroin seized along the border was being smuggled in cars and trucks passing through checkpoints, not the areas in between.
David Shirk, a University of San Diego political science professor, said the Trump administration wants to remind voters it’s been very aggressive on border security.
“I don’t dispute there’s some benefit to having personnel in areas at risk for people smuggling and drug trafficking,” Shirk said. “But the vast majority of that is now happening at ports of entry.”
Dessa Bergen-Cico, a professor of public health at Syracuse University who studies drug trafficking, said street prices for cocaine and fentanyl are still low, suggesting the drug flow remains unimpeded.
But Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, who commands the military’s southern border task force, said the work has been vital and effective, particularly for targeting human trafficking.
The moral argument for the Army’s mission is “dismantling this marketplace of human trafficking that is bringing people into the border,” Taylor said. “An added benefit of that is there’s an awful lot of drugs moving with that human trafficking.”
Efforts to secure a former epicenter of illegal crossings
Roma, a city of about 10,000 people, lacks a border wall in some places because homes sit close to the steep slopes along the Rio Grande. Directly across the water is Miguel Alemán, a town in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas that’s been plagued by decades of cartel violence. From Roma, it’s a football field’s distance across the river at best and much less in some places.
In 2021, Roma became a center of illegal crossings when thousands of families and unaccompanied children arrived each day to seek asylum. Border crossings fell sharply after President Joe Biden introduced severe asylum restrictions in 2024 and dipped after Trump suspended asylum at the border.
After Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, the Army and Coast Guard expanded operations to back up the Border Patrol, which remains the lead agency for border security. The Army now commands some 8,000 U.S. troops along the entire border, while the U.S. Coast Guard and Texas law enforcement have brought in more personnel.
Army officials said people still try to cross into Roma despite multiple obstacles. A barrier of strung-together buoys, each the size of a hay bale, stretched along the river. Concertina wire lined the U.S. river bank, while a surveillance blimp hung in the sky. A river island was recently cleared of trees that hid people trying to cross.
Army Sgt. Nathaniel Decker said he recently saw people on three rafts set out from the Mexican side at dusk. He reported to Border Patrol that one group had cleared the buoys. They were eventually caught by a house in Roma.
Mexico also has sent more troops
The U.S. has stopped many of the drones used by the cartels to surveil the border and ferry drugs, by electronically jamming or capturing them or shooting them down with a laser.
The U.S. has gotten better at tracking them and coordinating with Mexican officials to locate the drones’ operators. But some still get across.
“We have reduced a lot of the flights,” said Richards, the Army lieutenant colonel, who has deployed with the Massachusetts Army National Guard. “But in the middle of the night, those drones can fly into the U.S. airspace, and that’s a true threat to any soldier on the ground.”
Under pressure from Trump, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has cracked down more heavily on crime than her predecessors. Mexico this month sent 500 National Guard and military officers to Tamaulipas as part of a coordinated effort with the U.S. to prevent drug and human trafficking.
Mexico’s deployment “is based on intelligence gathered regarding the movements of criminal groups,” a federal official in Mexico told The Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to comment on the matter.
As part of the operation, the Mexican Army is using two UH-60 helicopters, drones and anti-drone equipment.
The U.S. Coast Guard has also boosted patrols on the Rio Grande, bringing in more than 300 personnel in October of last year. While stopping a boat on the river last month, the Coast Guard encountered gunfire from the Mexican side of the water near Garceno, Texas, the service said in a statement. The Americans returned fire. None were hurt.
U.S. Coast Guard Cmdr. Jeff Miller wouldn’t give additional details about the exchange of gunfire, except to say the personnel are “working in a very challenging environment” and are authorized to use force to protect themselves.
On a recent patrol, the scene along the river was quiet. A Coast Guard boat armed with machine guns motored along the greenish water. Two men fished from a small boat. A privately funded border wall, made from galvanized steel, lined the American side. In Mexico, there was a park with soccer goal posts, homes and a woman waving.
A Coast Guardsman driving the boat, who declined to give his name, said he’s seen kids on the Mexican side get excited as if a fire truck were passing. Others have offered the Americans cold beer. Some have reacted with offensive gestures.
Joel Garcia, Border Patrol’s acting deputy chief patrol agent for the Rio Grande Valley, said the agency has proof that U.S. operations have been effective based on the amount of drug seizures, the number of people apprehended and decreasing traffic within certain areas.
“Border security, when done right, if we have truly secured the line, should be boring,” he added. “It should look as if no one is crossing and nothing is happening.”
___
Associated Press writers Fabiola Sánchez and Megan Janetsky in Mexico City contributed to this report.

title: Flight grounded after passengers noticed bed bugs crawling and biting them
text:
PERTH, Australia (CNN) - Passengers on a Qantas flight from Rome, Italy, to Perth, Australia, were delayed over the weekend after bed bugs were found on the aircraft.
A few passengers on the plane’s previous flight on Friday reported seeing bugs and being bitten. One woman said she saw them crawling on her clothes and along the window.
Qantas said the problem was limited to a small area of the aircraft, and crews conducted a deep clean while the plane was grounded.
Bed bugs are known to hitch rides on luggage.
The airline rescheduled all the passengers on other flights.

title: A New ‘Narnia’ Begins in the First ‘Magician’s Nephew’ Trailer
text:
Greta Gerwig Travels to Narnia in First ‘Magician’s Nephew’ Trailer
All eyes will be on theaters next February when the new Narnia film debuts — and not just because people like those fantasy novels by C.S. Lewis. The movie will be one of the first from Netflix to get a wide (and IMAX) release in theaters, and it is writer/director Greta Gerwig’s follow-up film to Barbie, one of the biggest movies of the 21st century.
Her Narnia is essentially a reboot with no connection to the earlier film versions, and it’s based on The Magician’s Nephew, the sixth book in the series — but chronologically the one that takes place first, in which the world of Narnia is created.
The new film features Meryl Streep as the lion Aslan and Daniel Craig as the magician of the title — young David McKenna plays his nephew, Digory. You may have seen him recently in the miniseries adaptation of The Lord of the Flies as Piggy. If you want to adapt a great work of children’s literature of the1950s, David McKenna is your guy! (He was also excellent in Lord of the Flies.)
You can see all of them in action in the first Narnia trailer below:
READ MORE: The Best Netflix Movies of the Year
There’s a new poster for the film as well.
Yes, the book does apparently involve the beginning of a universe. But phrasing that as a tagline on a poster — “A Universe Begins” — sure does sound like Netflix plans to make a whole franchise of these movies, does it not?
Here is The Magician’s Nephew’s official synopsis, via Netflix:
Academy Award–nominated filmmaker Greta Gerwig brings C. S. Lewis’ beloved story The Magician’s Nephew to the screen for the first time in a sweeping adventure that invites dreamers of all ages to experience the creation of Narnia.
Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew is scheduled to open in theaters and IMAX on February 12, 2027.

title: Political candidates must value an effective and ethical justice system
text:
Jason Cherry, a Maine attorney with a practice focused on data privacy and criminal law, is a former special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. While at the FBI, he served as an assistant section chief for more than 430 employees and a budget of $150 million as well as a legal instructor.
I am interested in voting for a U.S. Senate candidate who understands the importance of an objective, professional and efficient U.S. Justice Department. Presidents from both political parties have shown overt favoritism to donors and other individuals in exchange for favors or to appease allies.
The Clinton administration was notorious for the 11th-hour pardon of 140 people, to include Marc Rich, a serial fraudster. On the other side, the Trump administration has granted over 1,900 pardons (and counting) across his terms in office.
The extensive list of pardons includes several fraudsters who have stolen hundreds of millions of dollars. These acts of “clemency” raise costs in healthcare, defense and other industries if the perpetrators of the fraud can expect to be freed by their political connections and influence. They fear no repercussions, so their behavior will continue onward.
In addition, these political indulgences send an extremely demoralizing message to everyone working diligently to establish an objective, professional and efficient justice system in their town, county, state and nation. Furthermore, the legitimacy of the entire justice system is at stake as these political indulgences send an alarming message to the public. Why should anyone obey the laws if they can get use their political influence to avoid any repercussions?
It is unclear why the U.S. Congress has not acted to restore legitimacy to the federal system of justice by restricting these apparent pay-to-pardon schemes. Perhaps, like many states, it is time to consider forming bipartisan clemency boards to prevent the executive branch from engaging in political indulgences.
As an FBI special agent, I took an oath to uphold the U.S. Constitution and to protect and serve the public. The acronym and motto of the FBI (Fidelity, Bravery and Integrity) used to mean only one thing — service and protection of my neighbors, my community, state and nation. Given the rampant rise in political indulgences, particularly the enabling of lawlessness in D.C., fidelity to whom? Bravery for whom? Integrity to whom and for what?
In his farewell address of Sept. 19, 1796, President George Washington described the importance of our justice system: “The due administration of justice is the firmest pillar of good government, I have considered the first arrangement of the judicial department as essential to the happiness of the country, and to the stability of its political system.”
The need for federal and state legislators to function as a true check and balance to restore legitimacy to our national justice system is long overdue. Instead, what is happening is a number of blank checks are being written in exchange for pardons galore.
I find it difficult to vote for a political party or politician who does not understand the importance of an objective, professional, efficient and ethical justice system, but merely stands aside or even enables the practice of unethical behaviors like these modern-day political indulgences.

title: 3 arrested after abandoned infant found alive in trash can
text:
SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A newborn baby was found alive in a trash can near the Quality Inn on Abercorn Street early Saturday morning, according to Savannah police.
Three people are now facing charges.
What happened
Chatham EMS Director Chuck Kearns said crews initially responded to a call for a patient experiencing hemorrhaging. At the hospital, the EMS crew realized the patient had given birth. They alerted police, who searched the hotel and found the baby alive.
SPD responded around 2:45 a.m. Oct. 10 to a report of child abandonment on Abercorn Street.
After an initial investigation, Sgt. Howard Crosby and Ofc. Richard Taylor with the Southside Precinct discovered the infant in a nearby trash can.
The child was given immediate medical attention. The baby is now in the care of the Department of Human Services’ Division of Family and Children Services, known as DFCS.
SPD thanked Memorial Health medical staff, Chatham EMS and Savannah Fire for their assistance in locating the child quickly and safely.
Charges filed
Dominique Welcome, 29, Chiquita Roche, 39, and Jamal West, 44, were arrested and face charges in connection with the case.
Welcome is charged with cruelty to children. Roche is charged with party to a crime and willful obstruction of law enforcement officers by use of threats or violence. West is charged with cruelty to children.
Chatham County jail records show Roche was arrested at the hotel, West was arrested on scene at the hotel and Welcome was arrested at Memorial Hospital.
Safe haven law
SPD reminded the public that under Georgia’s Safe Place for Newborns Act, state law gives criminal immunity to a mother who leaves her baby, if the baby is no more than 30 days old, with a staff member or volunteer at an authorized medical facility, fire station or police station.
Examples include the Memorial Health Dwaine & Cynthia Willett Children’s Hospital of Savannah and the Savannah Fire Department. Designated “Safe Place” facilities are marked with signage.
Michael Bossak, vice president of Children’s Hospital of Savannah, said the hospital serves as a safe space for children of all ages, including newborns.
“I think as a pediatrician and as a vice president of the Children’s Hospital, I think it’s important. We are the safe space for children of all ages that includes the youngest ones, so being able to place where mothers can come guilt-free to be able to drop off a child and say, ‘Look, I’m not able to do this, but I want this baby to survive and have the best life possible,’ is an important part of what we do here at Children’s Hospital,” Bossak said.

title: US hits Bank of America with $1.2 billion fine, saying it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
text:
US hits Bank of America with $1.2 billion fine, saying it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
The US Treasury Department on Tuesday announced it was imposing a more than $1.2 billion fine on Bank of America, accusing the bank of violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
The bank, which is the second-largest in the US, failed to mitigate and report “priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border,” the Treasury Department said in its announcement.
“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement.
“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institution(s) are not above the law,” Bessent added.
Bernard Mensah, president of international for Bank of America, told CNN’s Richard Quest at CNN’s Global Perspectives panel in Bangkok on Wednesday that the bank is working hard to get its compliance on track following the fine.
“Financial crimes compliance is very serious and really important. We we take it very, very seriously. We spent a huge amount of resources, trying to get it right, and we think we are getting it right. But these are very high standards, and so we’re working towards that,” Mensah said.
In a statement, Bank of America said it was working with regulators to reach penalty resolutions.
“We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators,” a Bank of America spokesperson said. “We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year.”
The spokesperson also said the Treasury Department’s penalty will impact the company’s quarterly earnings results, which are expected to be released Wednesday.
“Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share. We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base,” the spokesperson said.
The $1.2 billion fine is the third-largest ever imposed by the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), following a record $3.4 billion fine against Binance in 2023 and a $1.3 billion penalty against TD Bank in 2024. Both of those fines were also accompanied by charges from the Justice Department, though there is no accompanying Justice Department action for the Bank of America fine.
The second Trump administration has taken actions against big banks for the practice of “debanking,” including through executive orders. Earlier this year, President Donald Trump also filed a $5 billion personal lawsuit against JPMorgan Chase, alleging that the country’s biggest bank closed his account for political reasons. However, the fine against Bank of America is the largest anti-money-laundering penalty the Trump administration’s Treasury Department has imposed on a major bank.
As part of the total fine, $750 million will go to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) as a civil penalty, making it the largest OCC penalty in history.
As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully failed to have proper safeguards in place and failed to report suspicious activity, the Treasury Department said.
Failure to flag issues
Bank of America failed to respond in a timely and meaningful way to red flags involving suspicious customers, including those with ties to narcotics trafficking, even after compliance personnel escalated concerns, Treasury said. As a result, the bank, which processed more than $9 trillion in transactions last year, failed to report over $5 billion in suspicious activity.
CNN learned that Bank of America’s sanctions-screening filter had a design flaw that prevented it from appropriately prioritizing certain potentially prohibited transactions. Specifically, when a transaction matched an individual’s name and date of birth on the US Treasury Department’s sanctions list, the bank’s system did not flag the transaction as high priority. The Treasury Department maintains a list of thousands of individuals and entities, including terrorists, narcotics traffickers, and companies subject to sanctions, whose assets may be blocked and who are generally prohibited from conducting transactions with US persons or entities.
These breakdowns can cause harm to US sanctions programs, including the country’s Iran and counter-narcotics programs, which was the case with Bank of America, CNN learned.
Dennis Kelleher, the CEO of Better Markets, which advocates for tougher regulations against banks, said in a statement that the $1.2 billion fine was small compared to Bank of America’s revenue.
“Banks don’t break laws; people do, and until those people – including most importantly executives and supervisors – are personally and meaningfully punished by firings, prosecution, fines and being barred from employment in the industry, these crimes are not going to be stopped,” Kelleher said.
Bank of America’s stock (BAC) fell more than 2.5% in after-hours trading after the fine was announced.
“The OCC and FinCen are sending a message to BoA and to all banks — if you don’t fix the problem quickly they’ll be a big fine,” said Aaron Klein, the former deputy assistant secretary for economic policy at the Department of Treasury under President Barack Obama. “The OCC and FinCen have a lot of penalties they could impose beyond money — they can essentially fire people not just from BoA but from the entire business of banking.”
“Everything the OCC is asking BoA to do to have a stronger anti-money laundering compliance program costs money, reducing the banks’ profit,” Klein added.
CNN’s Matt Egan and Kathleen Magramo contributed to reporting.

title: Trump administration plans to livestream execution. What parents can do to protect children
text:
(AP) - This is not an article about politics, capital punishment or whether the Fort Hood shooter deserves to be executed in public for his crimes.
Instead, it’s focused on the unprecedented parental challenge of handling the near-certain prospect that children will hear of or see footage of the Dec. 3 U.S. execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan if the Trump administration follows through with plans to livestream the event.
The danger stretches beyond the broadcast itself, because history shows graphic video from the event could be clipped, copied and pushed into children’s social feeds even if the original stream is restricted.
Experts suggest that grownups who care about children start by setting aside matters of politics and public policy — like the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections and the debate over capital punishment. Focus instead on how witnessing someone’s death by firing squad might land with young viewers — and how best to reassure and protect them.
Here are some guidelines that might help.
Keep empathy for kids in mind — and facts at hand
Mis- and disinformation reach children, too. It’s important for parents to have credibility with them, especially because their real, unspoken question might be: Are we safe? Have in hand some basic facts about the case and state them gently.
“It will be easier to have a position, share your family’s values, and discuss things with a potentially overwhelmed child once you’ve taken the time to gather accurate, up-to-date info and assess your child’s needs,” according to Common Sense Media, which advises parents on entertainment and technology.
Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. A few days later, the Pentagon announced the event would be livestreamed.
“People need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people there in 2009 when he walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961.
The last widely recognized public execution took place on Aug. 14, 1936. Kentucky, the last state to permit them, outlawed the practice in 1938.
Stay updated on the plans
Also, experts suggest, parents should stay updated on how a livestreamed execution would unfold. Many questions remained unanswered, such as whether the moment of death and its aftermath will be shown, whether any age restrictions will apply, and whether there will be a broadcast delay or a threshold for stopping the feed.
Be informed about the technology involved. While the government often uses YouTube to carry its livestreams, including those embedded within government websites, YouTube prohibits content that is “violent or gory” and “intended to shock or disgust viewers,” and doesn’t allow livestreams that show someone holding, handling or transporting a firearm.
YouTube does make exceptions in select cases for content it deems to be in an educational, documentary, scientific or artistic context or that it determines to be in the public’s interest. In such cases, the content may be age-restricted. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding how its policies relate to the execution.
But the danger to kids spills beyond the live broadcast to unexpected exposure on social media in the form of memes, for example.
It’s unclear whether the Trump administration is considering children in its decision-making. Emails over two days asking White House spokespeople for thoughts from the president and first lady Melania Trump on the prospect of children seeing the execution went unanswered. Trump said that he’ll soon make a decision on the plan to livestream the event.
Assume kids will at least hear about the execution, if not see it
From the old-fashioned grapevine to social media, grisly news has a way of reaching school-aged children, experts agree. Consider their need for calm and age-appropriate guidance, they suggest.
“With young kids, parents should keep it short and focus on reassurance over explaining the events,” said Jill Murphy, chief content officer at Common Sense Media. “Reassure them that they are safe. With teens, ask honestly what they have heard first, then ask whether they need to watch it.”
Remember you are your child’s parent, not their friend — and don’t overexplain, advises Dr. David Rosenberg, chair of psychiatry and behavioral neurosciences at Wayne State University School of Medicine in Michigan. Answer the questions children ask, and don’t be afraid to assert parental authority by, for example, restricting or banning a child’s access to the footage.
“It’s okay to say, ‘I don’t have all the answers. But here’s what we know, you’re safe, you’re secure, this is what we believe,’” Rosenberg said.
“Where parents get into trouble is when they talk too much, and they usually do that because they’re anxious and insecure,” he added. ”What makes a child feel safest, or an adolescent, is can I count on my parents to be calm in challenging situations and give me the information I need?”
Choosing to watch the footage, one physician said, doesn’t necessarily indicate a child is psychologically ready to do so.
Timothy Lesaca, a Pittsburgh-area psychiatrist, cited a series of studies showing that repeatedly watching footage of events like the Boston Marathon bombings, at least part of an ISIS beheading video and the Oklahoma City bombing can be linked to post-traumatic stress, if not PTSD, in adults and children. He argues that making Hasan’s execution public is a medical and public health issue.
“Ongoing anxiety, trouble sleeping or problems with daily life should be taken seriously,” Lesaca wrote in KevinMD.com, an online publication by physicians.
Watch how this event interacts with existing conditions
The people most at risk of negative long-term effects are those who already have clinical depression or anxiety, or who have already been exposed to other traumatic situations, Rosenberg said. That’s because repeat exposure to trauma can cause cumulative damage.
The part of the brain that handles executive decision-making, emotional regulation, impulsivity and empathy doesn’t finish developing until around age 24, and so parents should consider having proactive conversations even with their older children who may be away at college or living on their own, Rosenberg said.
“We have to at least offer help in these circumstances to be the leaders, to be the decision-makers, to at least help them make informed decisions.”
___
Associated Press journalist Kaitlyn Huamani contributed.

title: Witnesses detail moment man fell to his death from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia
text:
ATLANTA (AP) - Witnesses watched in horror as a man riding a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia was ejected from his seat, almost seeming to hover above the car before hitting several people and falling to his death.
The nightmarish death prompted Six Flags to temporarily close nine similar coasters across North America.
Police and a state agency that oversees ride inspections are investigating, but many questions remained Tuesday, including how the man fell out and whether there were problems with his restraints.
The man, a school employee from Atlanta, was killed Monday while riding Goliath, the park’s tallest roller coaster with a first hill of 200 feet (61 meters).
“It looked like he was hovering because the car was moving underneath him,” said Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead.
The man fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, then was ejected from the ride on its final turn.
“It felt like slow-motion, but it happened in an instant,” Mendenhall said. “I was just praying in those moments. I was praying: ‘God, please let him stay in that car.’”
Goliath towers above the entrance at Six Flags Over Georgia just outside Atlanta with a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down. There are no seat belts. Instead, riders are restrained with lap bars that pull down over their legs and waist.
In a theme park industry that it is constantly introducing new thrills, it’s far from the world’s tallest, fastest or wildest coaster.
One family watched as the man flew out of the roller coaster
The man who died was 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, according to Cobb County police. Investigators and park employees told investigators that he was thrown from the coaster before striking other patrons.
Officials have not released any other information about the people who were hurt.
Kariem worked as the information technology manager at a public charter school and before that was a technology teacher.
In a statement, the Wesley International Academy said it was devastated, saying Kariem’s “dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did.”
Summer Bates, who was at the park with her husband and three children, saw Kariem fall. “One thing I think that will stick with us is the sound of his body coming down,” she said.
Bates said she and her family rode Goliath earlier in the day.
“My older two children rode on the cart ahead of us,” she said. “I noticed they kept trying to push theirs down tighter. I assured them that they were OK. But once my husband, youngest child and I loaded our cart and headed up the incline, I quickly understood why my older two were messing with theirs. It just didn’t feel secure and tight.”
Amusement ride oversight varies by state
In the U.S., roller coasters and other rides at major amusement parks such as Six Flags are not regulated by the federal government. That responsibility falls to states.
Georgia’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees annual ride inspections, is “conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review,” of what happened, said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson.
In California, the state approves new rides and ones that have been modified and either directly inspects them or relies on an annual inspection by the owner. Florida’s largest theme parks are exempt from state safety inspections, unlike smaller venues and fairs. Instead, the largest theme parks like Walt Disney World and Universal conduct their own inspections and have their own protocols.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to change the federal law that allows U.S. safety officials to regulate mobile rides but exempts major amusement parks.
Opponents of federal oversight say serious injuries and fatalities on amusement park rides are rare and often the result of riders not following rules.
Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the industry has multiple layers of inspection.
Six Flags closes roller coasters elsewhere
Six Flags Entertainment Corp. temporarily shut down roller coasters at six of its theme parks in the U.S. and Canada. The parks were already scheduled for seasonal midweek closures on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Those rides include a second coaster named Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California; Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Illinois; Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey; Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds in North Carolina; and the rides Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada’s Wonderland in Ontario, Canada.
The company did not say why those specific rides were shut down or what would be done before they reopen.
Bolliger & Mabillard, the Swiss company that manufactured the coaster and many others worldwide, said it is actively investigating and won’t comment “until we have a better understanding of what happened.”
“Our thoughts are with the family and those affected,” it said.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia; McCormack from Concord, New Hampshire; and Seewer from Toledo, Ohio. Associated Press writers Sudhin Thanawala in Atlanta; Michael Biesecker in Pittsburgh; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed.
