title: Saco father detained by ICE at jetport on way to visit deaf son
text:
Nguinamau Celestino’s wife dropped him off at the Portland jetport at 3 a.m. to catch an early flight to Washington, D.C. He was on his way to visit Abel, his youngest son, who had just begun his first semester at a high school for the deaf.
Nguinamau never arrived.
Celestino’s daughter, Margarida, 24, said her brother checked their father’s location on his phone after his flight was scheduled to land. He was at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Scarborough.
Margarida, a medical technician based in Auburn, woke at 6 a.m. to two missed calls from her dad, which she returned, but he didn’t pick up. She was on her way to work when her mom called; Margarida told her employer there was a family emergency and headed to Saco, where her parents live, to put the pieces together.
“Usually we see videos of people being taken, but unfortunately, everything with my dad was so silent,” she said. “Nobody said anything.”
The Celestino family — which includes Nguinamau, his wife Sukombo, their eldest Margarida and three sons, Lionel, 21, Nludi, 18, and Abel, 15 — are originally from Angola, later lived in Namibia and came to the U.S. in 2017 as asylum seekers. Their application is still ongoing. Only Margarida has a green card.
Early on Friday, Oct. 9, Margarida said her father walked into the airport and went straight to security. He saw ICE agents around, but didn’t have any reason to think they were there for him. But when he showed his ID to a TSA agent, she said, ICE agents looked at his picture, said they were there for Celestino, and detained him.
Immigration enforcement has been ramping up at airports nationwide, and local advocates said there were several detentions at the jetport in August, including of asylum seeker and registered nurse Debora Kapisha, who has since been released.
Margarida said her father has no criminal history, but agents told him he had overstayed his visa.
An ICE spokesperson confirmed Tuesday that Nguinamau was arrested during “targeted operations” last week, and said that he entered the country legally but violated the terms of his lawful admission and “remained in the U.S. illegally for nearly eight years.”
He was processed at the Scarborough facility, but by the time Margarida’s husband arrived at 9 a.m., Nguinamau had already been transferred out of the state. Margarida’s husband, a U.S. citizen, had come to bring Nguinamau a jacket, because she heard from another detained family member that the facility is chilly, and Nguinamau gets cold easily.
The agency’s online detainee locator showed Tuesday that Celestino is now being held at the Strafford County Corrections facility in Dover, New Hampshire.
Margarida said her father has been in touch every day via phone, and seems to be doing alright. The family organized a GoFundMe, which has raised nearly $30,000, and they’ve transferred some funds to him. He was able to keep his medications, but she said his work authorization card, Social Security card and Angolan ID were all missing from his wallet when they picked up his belongings.
Nguinamau works in plumbing and HVAC for Pine State Services, and got his associate’s degree at Southern Maine Community College. All of the Celestino children attended Portland Public Schools, including King Middle and Casco Bay High.
Their youngest sibling, Abel, received special services at East End Community School and played for the Baxter Seagulls, an ASL basketball team for students with the Maine Educational Center for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing.
The center announced Nguinamau’s detention on Facebook over the weekend, describing him as a beloved member of the Greater Portland and center community.
“Our Deaf and Hard of Hearing community has always been strengthened by the connections we build, the families we support, and our willingness to stand together when someone is in need. This is a time to put those values into action,” center co-directors Steve Connolly and Catherine Lushman wrote in the post.
Connolly and Lushman said they were drafting letters to Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, asking them to intervene on behalf of the Celestino family.
For now, Margarida is worried about the impact Nguinamau’s detention will have on the rest of her family. Her mom has lupus and high blood pressure, and travels to Boston every three weeks for treatment, which she worries could be impacted by her husband’s detention.
Abel, who was awaiting his father’s visit in D.C., had to leave his school for the long weekend, and the family scrambled to find a friend in the city to look after him. The friend stepped up to the challenge, Margarida said, but it wasn’t the same as Abel spending the weekend with his father.

title: Chicago police say DNA ties a former detective to decades-old unsolved killing of 8-year-old girl
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Chicago police say DNA evidence ties one of their former homicide detectives to the decades-old murder of an 8-year-old girl who was abducted as she was walking to church more than 65 years ago.
Gloria Kowalewicz was found shot dead in a ditch in 1960, just hours after she went missing. Chicago police say new technology allowed them to match a fingerprint and DNA from the crime scene to Thomas F. McInerney Jr., then a detective working on violent crimes.
“McInerney should never have worn the CPD star, and it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive,” police said in a statement provided to The Associated Press on Tuesday.
Gloria was walking just a few blocks from her home to a morning Mass on Nov. 12, 1960, but she never made it, according to police. She was found around four hours later, her body dumped in a forest preserve in southwest Chicago.
Authorities formed a task force to investigate. They “knocked on hundreds of doors,” interviewed more than 1,300 people and questioned more than a dozen people under polygraph, according to the statement.
Police collected and preserved a bullet, Gloria’s coat and shoes, and a white communion purse that held her prayer book. Using modern forensic technology and with assistance from the FBI and Illinois State Police, investigators linked DNA found on those items and a “carefully preserved” fingerprint lifted from Gloria’s purse strap to McInerney.
The FBI said in a statement to The AP that it was “pursuing every investigative lead that may bring closure on other potential unsolved crimes that occurred during that time period in our area.”
The technology used to identify McInerney allows federal and local law enforcement agencies to compare evidence with genetic profiles on genealogical websites. It was previously used to identify the Golden State Killer more than four decades after the case was first opened by identifying DNA from a tissue left in a trash can. The technology has prompted privacy concerns.
McInerney joined the Chicago Police Department a year before the murder and retired in 1987, police said. He then worked for the Federal Public Defender’s Office in Reno and Las Vegas until he retired in 2004, according to a Chicago Tribune obituary. He died in 2006.
___
Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Six Flags closes 9 rides after roller coaster rider reportedly falls to his death in Georgia
text:
(Gray News) - Six Flags has temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks after police say a person was killed and several others were injured in an incident involving a coaster in Georgia.
Witnesses say a man fell to his death late Monday afternoon from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia in Cobb County. Several riders were stuck on the coaster after the deadly incident, WANF reports.
Neither Cobb County Police nor Six Flags officials have said what happened nor identified anyone involved. The park was closed after the incident.
In the aftermath, Six Flags has closed nine other roller coasters across six amusement parks that are similar to the coaster involved in the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks. The safety of our guests and team members remains one of our highest priorities,” Six Flags said.
The rides closed include Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Illinois, Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey and Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California.
Roller coasters were also closed at Ohio’s Kings Island, North Carolina’s Carowinds and Canada’s Wonderland in Ontario. All three parks are owned by Six Flags.

title: Caregivers for older Mainers are facing mounting challenges
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Marvella Heard has faced more challenges than most in caring for her aging father.
She spent over a year back in her hometown in New York, after she discovered her father was living in squalor, his health was deteriorating, his meager finances were in jeopardy and his house was in foreclosure, she said.
A Navy veteran and retired federal prison employee, she stepped in and wrangled repeatedly with family members, government officials and social service agencies — even after she became her father’s legal guardian, she said.
“He was living in filth when I got there,” said Heard, 56, of Biddeford. “He had no food, no clean clothes. He didn’t recognize me at first.”
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
Now 79, Samuel Heard has since been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and heart disease, and the retired hospital worker has mobility issues that require him to use a walker, his daughter said.
Despite many setbacks, Heard said she managed to navigate unfamiliar caregiver territory by being resourceful, searching the internet for solutions and being tenacious when she ran into roadblocks. She still struggles to reconcile how hard it was to help her father.
“I was treated awfully — the system didn’t support me at all,” Heard said. “We had confrontations again and again, and I just wanted to take care of my dad.”
Finally, last December, Heard was able to move her father to her home in Biddeford, where they’ve settled into a routine of medical appointments, grocery shopping, barber shop visits and adult daycare programs.
THE ROLE TAKES A TOLL
While Heard’s experience was severe, a growing number of Mainers are facing challenges as caregivers for aging and disabled loved ones. They’re providing assistance with all aspects of daily living, including meals, medications, bathing, dressing, toileting, transportation and advocacy at medical appointments and in long-term care.
Most of that help goes unpaid and can take a significant toll on other areas of their lives, consuming free time and affecting job performance. The role reversal of caring for once-vital adults can be emotionally devastating, and managing their complicated medical needs and finances can be overwhelming. Some caregivers also support their loved ones financially — Heard figures she has spent about $3,000 on her father’s behalf.
She and others in the thick of it have learned the benefits of planning ahead, becoming expert problem solvers and seeking support from other caregivers. They don’t have to look far.
In 2025, an estimated 310,000 Mainers provided the full-time equivalent of 220 million hours of unpaid care for aging or disabled adult family members valued at $5.5 billion, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. That value of that care more than doubled in the past decade, up from $2.2 billion provided by 178,000 Mainers in 2015.
The same is true nationwide, where the value of adult family caregiving also has more than doubled, from $470 billion to $1 trillion in the same period, and the number of caregivers increased 22.5%, from 40 million to 59 million, according to Caregiving in the US 2025, the latest report from AARP and NAC.
The exponential increase has solidified family caregivers as an invaluable contingent in the wider landscape of long-term care, AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said. It doesn’t matter if the help is provided to loved ones at home, in assisted living or at a skilled nursing facility.
“The long-term care system would crumble without those family caregivers,” Bonam said. “Whether what they do is big or small, without caregivers spending hours and personal resources while juggling other responsibilities, the system would collapse.”
CAREGIVING IN THE OLDEST STATE
As the oldest state, Maine is on the leading edge of this trend — nearly one-quarter of 1.4 million residents are age 65 and up. At the same time, it has a shortage of 2,300 workers to care for older Mainers as they age, according to the progressive Maine Center for Economic Policy.
Yet the important role that family caregivers play in filling the gap is critically undervalued, advocates say, especially when at least 60% of caregivers are juggling jobs outside the home and nearly 30% are part of the so-called sandwich generation, caring for both an adult and children.
“The federal and state funding and services available right now don’t cover the tip of the iceberg,” Bonam said.
Some MaineCare recipients may receive funding to pay a family member to provide care, but it comes with significant restrictions. The State Respite Care Program provides funding so family caregivers of dementia patients can hire occasional help, but there’s often a waiting list.
The new Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave program may be providing some relief — 11.6% of 4,720 claims approved in the first three months, April through June, were to care for family members with serious health conditions, according to the Maine Department of Labor.
Some advocates are pushing for a non-refundable federal tax credit up to $5,000 for eligible working family caregivers to cover 30% of qualified expenses. However, this proposal also comes with restrictions and would cover only a small portion of care provided. In Maine, that care is valued at $25 per hour or about $52,000 annually based on a 40-hour work week, according to AARP.
Although family caregiver funding is widely recognized as lacking, advocates say it’s not showing up as a legislative priority despite dire predictions that the need will only intensify.
“There’s been a tremendous increase over the past 10 years and that’s just going to continue,” said Amanda Rector, state economist. “We have more people not only over 65, but also over 75. That’s a larger older population that will need more care from a smaller younger population that’s still working.”
The issue may draw more attention as more families and employers experience the impact of caregiving on daily living, especially in a labor market with a worker shortage, Rector said.
“If (a caregiver is) a really valuable worker, they may not be working at their best,” she said. “You may want to provide support to relieve their mental and financial stress so they don’t leave.”
REACHING OUT FOR HELP
Jim Vollmar started showing signs of vascular dementia nearly a decade ago, when the former build contractor and his wife, Clare Herrmann, were living in Georgia.
“He started not remembering things he should have remembered, like my birthday or what we did last week,” said Herrmann, who, like her husband, is now 78.
Initially, Herrmann cared for him on her own, reluctant to even ask friends for help. But the difficulty mounted as his disease progressed, so she decided to accept her daughter’s invitation to come live with her family in Portland.
As Herrmann prepared to move north, the retired office manager reached out to the Southern Maine Agency on Aging for guidance on what services and programs would be available to them, including peer support groups she still attends.
After the couple moved to Portland in 2024 — into an accessory dwelling unit they had built at her daughter’s house — Herrmann was relieved to have backup assistance from her daughter, son-in-law and grandchild. Still, she was overwhelmed by round-the-clock responsibilities.
Again, she reached out to SMAA, who helped her secure respite care for her husband so she could have a few hours off each week. One of the first things she did was take a meditation course.
“I wanted to learn how to chill,” Herrmann said. “I was so hyperaware of everything, I never really slept because I didn’t want him to fall and I didn’t want him to leave the house. He never did, but I worried about it.”
Herrmann reached out to SMAA again last spring, after her husband broke his left femur in a fall and it became clear he needed to be in a memory care facility. The agency helped her find Fallbrook Woods in Portland, where he lives now.
“They have been so supportive,” Herrmann said of SMAA. “Whenever I call, they always know who to refer me to. I can’t even enumerate all they ways they have helped me.”
REBRANDING WITH CAREGIVERS IN MIND
SMAA this month changed its name to AgeMaine and launched a new website, support network and membership program to better serve family caregivers.
“We want to create one place where family caregivers can find trusted information and training, connect with other caregivers, and get help figuring out what resources and services are available,” CEO Megan Walton said.
AgeMaine.org/Caregiver, a caregiver-focused page that goes live Oct. 16, will start as an online resource hub for information and support, then expand to provide individualized guidance for family caregivers and help employers support workers who are caring for an aging adult. The agency will eventually offer a paid membership option, but the cost and structure have yet to be established, Walton said.
“We want more caregivers sharing their experiences and letting legislators know what they’re going through,” Walton said. “Peer support especially is so important. It can be so valuable to hear that other people are going through the same thing.”
The goal is to help caregivers like Marvella Heard find the support they need. While her father, Samuel, regularly attends adult daycare programs at the Samuel L. Cohen Center in Biddeford, which is an AgeMaine facility, she said she has yet to participate in caregiver support groups and other programs.
She admits that she should.
“I’m burned out because nobody is taking care of me,” Heard said. “Everybody needs a break sometimes, and I need a break, like, yesterday.”

title: Why There Have Been Less Humpty Chips on Store Shelves in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Why There Have Been Less Humpty Chips on Store Shelves in Maine
For just about 80 years, Humpty Dumpty potato chips have been part of Maine snack culture.
Most people who grow up in the state end up falling in love with at least one Humpty Dumpty flavor, from their version of BBQ or salt n' vinegar to more unique flavors like ketchup or all dressed.
But over the past few months, that snack staple has been more difficult to find on store shelves across the state of Maine.
And there's one specific reason why.
A Packaging Shortage is The Problem For Humpty Dumpty Chips in Maine
According to a social media post, one of the biggest reasons you may be seeing less Humpty Dumpty potato chips on store shelves revolves around their distinct bags.
There has been a packaging shortage from the supplier to Humpty Dumpty, leaving the chip company unable to deliver as much product to stores as they typically would.
That packaging shortage has primarily caused problems with the largest-sized Humpty Dumpty chip flavors as well as the smallest-sized snack bags.
Humpty Dumpty Expects to Return in Full to Maine Store Shelves Soon
There have been a lot of rumors swirling as to what the cause of the Humpty Dumpty shortage has been in Maine and whether or not the chip brand was being phased out.
The Humpty Dumpty chip brand is owned by Minnesota-based Old Dutch Foods which manufactures their potato chips in Canada. Some believed that the shortage on store shelves was caused by issues related to tariffs involving the United States and Canada.
That isn't the case. In fact, Humpty Dumpty chips should be returning to store shelves across Maine in near full stock before the end of the year.

title: Hannaford’s parent company taking precautions following ‘cybersecurity incident’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine (WABI) - Hannaford’s parent company, Ahold Delhaize, is experiencing a security issue within its network, resulting in some stores’ digital network being down.
Ahold Delhaize said its teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. The company said that includes taking some systems offline to help protect them.
It is unclear whether any information was compromised.
The Hannaford website and app are currently down. Hannaford said customers will be refunded for any unfulfilled orders placed through its website or app.
Hannaford stores and pharmacies remain open.
Company statement
Ahold Delhaize released the following statement: “Ahold Delhaize is experiencing a security issue within its network. Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them. At this time, our stores are open and serving customers. Protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates and partners is a top priority. We apologize for any inconvenience this issue may have caused customers and partners.”
Hannaford External Communication Manager Caitlin Cortelyou said “Hannaford stores remain open and continue to welcome customers. We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate our customers’ patience and understanding. We’ll provide an update once the issue has been resolved.”
Website and app message
The following message currently appears on the Hannaford website and app: “Our Hannaford website and app are currently unavailable. We are working to restore service as quickly as possible. Any unfulfilled orders placed through Hannaford.com or the Hannaford app will be refunded. Hannaford stores and pharmacies remain open during normal business hours. We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate your patience.”

title: OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly hiding a 'sophisticated recording device' in its office
text:
OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly hiding a ‘sophisticated recording device’ in its office
OpenAI discovered a "sophisticated recording device" in one of its offices planted by an employee who has been arrested, the company said Tuesday.
The employee, who has since been dismissed by the company, is a Saudi national and has been identified by the U.S. Department of Justice as 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan.
Video above: 'Tremendous self-policing': Trump unveils voluntary AI safety accord with tech leaders
The device was discovered on Sept. 30 during a regular sweep of a conference room where the device was found inserted into a USB port on the back of a television screen and "concealed in toilet paper," according to the DOJ.
OpenAI has determined the device was in the conference room for about two days before it was discovered. Alfozan, who had been an engineer on the product team since July 2025, the DOJ said, was arrested on Oct. 9 and remains in federal custody.
CNN has reached out to Alfozan for comment.
OpenAI said the device was for monitoring audio, had advanced encryption, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring. Alfozan had been seen on security cameras accessing the meeting room, where "highly confidential" discussions took place. The DOJ said a backpack belonging to Alfozan was found to have other similar recording devices, and OpenAI said it has evidence he intended to deploy more recording devices throughout their offices.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in a statement. "We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance."
The DOJ alleged that Alfozan used a "productivity tool" to find information about OpenAI's meeting rooms, calendars and the locations of its leadership. A chatbot associated with Alfozan's wife was found to have submitted prompts about building an encrypted audio recording device.
A LinkedIn page listed under Alfozan's name showed previous positions at Meta as a senior systems engineer for around five years, as well as at a company called Nash. The profile says that Alfozan attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. He's also a partner in Raed, a Saudi-based venture capital firm. CNN has reached out to the firm for comment.
In a statement, U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said the protection of U.S. technology companies is "a matter of national security."

title: Federal audit reviews MaineCare oversight, fraud safeguards
text:
MAINE (WABI) - Federal officials confirmed they are auditing MaineCare to review oversight in areas considered high risk.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said the audit will examine safeguards against fraud, waste and abuse—including how the state identifies risks, refers suspected fraud and handles improper payments.
States are responsible for maintaining Medicaid program-integrity controls and providing CMS with timely, accurate information.
CMS said it works with states to assess those controls and may coordinate with inspectors general and law enforcement when appropriate.
The agency said it can’t discuss details of the ongoing audit and has no additional updates.

title: A freed man faces life back in prison after a Supreme Court ruling on the First Step Act
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two years after his release from prison, Patrick Dewayne Smith spends Sundays with his family in a modest brick church with a white steeple in rural Tennessee. He works two jobs. He goes to ball games to cheer for nieces and nephews he had never met. After serving 13 years for a nonviolent drug conviction, he is trying to rebuild his life.
Now Smith could be sent back to prison for the rest of it.
A federal judge released him in 2024 under rules adopted after Congress passed the First Step Act, a landmark criminal justice law during President Donald Trump’s first term. But the Supreme Court ruled in May that people sentenced under older, harsher laws cannot rely on the disparity between their sentences and current penalties to seek early compassionate release.
“Every time I get a call, I’m hoping it’s some good news. Or, you know, at least not no bad news,” said Smith, a tall, soft-spoken 47-year-old whose beard is now flecked with gray.
Smith is among about a dozen people nationwide who could be returned to prison because of the ruling, according to FAMM, a sentencing reform group formerly Families Against Mandatory Minimums. Without clemency from the White House, the group says, second chances could disappear for those people.
The First Step Act opened a path to freedom
The First Step Act was the most significant rewrite of federal sentencing laws in a generation. Among other changes, it reduced some lengthy mandatory minimum sentences, particularly for nonviolent drug crimes. Trump said the law would “make our communities safer and give former inmates a second chance at life after they have served their time.”
The law was championed by Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and senior adviser who had a personal connection to the issue: Kushner’s father had spent time in federal prison when Kushner was younger.
Thousands of people have been released from prison in the years since the law was passed, but some recent Supreme Court rulings have made it harder for other people already serving long sentences to argue for their release. For Smith and others like him, competing interpretations have created a high-stakes legal limbo.
“They’re doing everything that they should be doing. They’re reestablishing relationships with families. They’re volunteering in their communities. They’re working,” said Shanna Rifkin, FAMM’s general counsel. “Having them reincarcerated is so unjust given that they have demonstrated their rehabilitation.”
Without a grant of clemency from the White House, Rifkin says their second chance could be snatched away.
Trump remains proud of signing the First Step Act, and the administration is actively reviewing developments, said a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the issue.
Supreme Court ruling narrows options for people serving long sentences
In 2023, the U.S. Sentencing Commission adopted new rules for people serving unusually long sentences. Judges could sometimes consider changes to the law when deciding whether to grant compassionate release to inmates who had served at least 10 years.
Not everyone agreed.
The Department of Justice argued the new rules went beyond what the First Step Act allowed. Judges nevertheless agreed to free dozens of people across the country after considering legal changes and other factors, FAMM found.
The dispute eventually went all the way to the Supreme Court, which handed down a 6-3 decision in May. It found that sentencing disparities from decades past are not “extraordinary and compelling” reasons to grant compassionate release.
“It is hard to see how Congress’s deliberate decision not to extend newly reduced penalties to those already sentenced could be a convincing reason that ‘warrant(s)’ a reduction,” Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote for the conservative majority.
The decision was one of two during the last Supreme Court term that narrowed the options for people serving long sentences, said Daniel Harawa, a law professor at New York University. “I worry a lot about what this means for federal criminal justice reform,” he said.
For Smith and about a dozen other people around the country, it could mean they have to finish serving a sentence that would not be handed down today.
Prior convictions meant a life sentence
Smith grew up in a small town in rural northern Alabama and became addicted to drugs as a teenager, his lawyers said in court documents. At 17 he was arrested for twice selling crack cocaine to an informant. A pair of marijuana convictions followed a few years later. He served about three years in prison. After his release he worked as a construction worker and a janitor.
In 2010, he got involved with a drug ring selling crack cocaine and marijuana on the Tennessee-Alabama line, prosecutors said. Caught on phone calls recorded by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, he was convicted of drug conspiracy and money laundering after he pulled out of a plea deal that called for 12 years to 14 years in prison in exchange for his cooperation.
His lawyers called his involvement “unremarkable,” but the federal conviction combined with his prior record triggered a life sentence.
The judge questioned whether the punishment fit the crime, but said the laws tied her hands. It was the longest sentence linked to the 20-person case, exceeding even the ringleader’s.
Smith said he resolved to keep his head down behind bars, working prison jobs and avoiding infractions.
“What kept me sane was that faith, that belief in God,” he said.
He missed little things, like sleeping in a full-sized bed and taking a bath after a long day. He missed big things, too: His mother died during his first year in prison and he couldn’t ask his family to shoulder the $1,000 it would cost for him to travel home for the funeral.
After 13 years, Smith got his second chance
After the Sentencing Commission adopted its new compassionate release rules following the First Step Act, Smith asked a judge for a reduction to time served. It took nearly a year, but the court agreed he should go free.
He returned to Alabama and moved in with his sister and her daughter.
Last month, prosecutors filed court documents challenging his release and they pointed to the Supreme Court decision. They argued he would be subject to a mandatory-minimum sentence of 25 years, even under current laws, and called the judge’s decision to release him “difficult to justify.”
A Justice Department official speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing case said the Supreme Court decision means his release is no longer valid, and the department cannot agree to a sentence below what the law requires.
The prospect of a return to prison is a bitter pill for his father, James Smith, a mainstay at the Willow Grove Missionary Baptist Church.
“When you got rapists and murderers and you get this guy on a nonviolent case and you want him for life,” he said, “it doesn’t sit well with me.”

title: Archbishop of US military says Catholic soldiers should not serve on Hasan’s firing squad
text:
(AP) - Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Church’s pastoral services to Catholics in the U.S. military, is condemning the proposed livestream of the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan.
Broglio, in a statement Monday, also stipulated that any Catholic soldier assigned to the U.S. Army firing squad should ask to be excused from that duty, which he described as contrary to the teachings of the church. He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the livestream plans.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.
Broglio recalled that he presided over the funeral of Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack.
The crime committed by Hasan “was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” Broglio asked.
“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio added. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?”

title: Woman charged with OUI after crash involving Bonny Eagle school bus
text:
Westbrook woman charged with OUI after crash involving Bonny Eagle school bus
Crash happened Friday morning on Route 22
Westbrook woman charged with OUI after crash involving Bonny Eagle school bus
Crash happened Friday morning on Route 22
A Maine woman has been charged with operating under the influence after police said she crashed an SUV into a Bonny Eagle school bus in Westbrook.
Annemarie Napolitano, 40, of Westbrook, was also charged with aggravated criminal mischief and violating conditions of release in connection with Friday's crash on Route 22.
The Westbrook Police Department said the crash happened at about 9:30 a.m. Friday, Oct. 9, in the area of 93 County Road.
A Maine's Total Coverage photographer captured video of the crash scene, which shows the crash happened near Haven's Candies.
Police said there were 19 children, ages 4 to 12, and five staff members on the school bus at the time of the crash. A few of the children complained of pain and were evaluated at the scene by members of the Westbrook Fire Department, but police said no children or staff members needed to be taken to a hospital.
Investigators determined that an SUV, which was being driven by Napolitano, crossed the center line of County Road and crashed into the front driver's side corner of the school bus. The SUV then continued on and struck the side of the bus before nearly hitting another vehicle and eventually winding up on the side of the road, according to police.
Video from the scene shows the school bus sustained serious damage as a result of the collision, which sent the SUV off the road and into a ditch.
The area of County Road where the crash happened remained closed while both vehicles were removed from the scene.

Glenburn

title: How to access home healthcare for older Mainers
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Maine’s aging population means that more older adults will be seeking home healthcare — either through skilled nursing, help with daily tasks or a combination.
Home healthcare is a patchwork of services that can be paid for through Medicare, Medicaid or out-of-pocket, depending on the need.
Maine has the highest median age in the nation, at 44.9 years, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. The state’s 65-and-older age group is expected to grow 11.4% from 2027-32, according to the Maine Office of the State Economist projections.
Often the care sought from home health agencies is done in conjunction with family caregivers who are taking on the responsibility of helping an older relative age in their home, experts in the field say.
According to a 2025 review of research by Johns Hopkins University, “profound demographic shifts” will lead to greater demand for services in the U.S. over the next decade or longer for home health and other long-term health services.
Patty Buiocchi, chief operating officer of post-acute care at MaineHealth, said the demand is “only going to get higher and higher. Will the supply also become higher? That remains to be seen.”
“Home health is so increasingly important to the healthcare system, because when people are getting care in their home, it reduces unnecessary hospital visits,” Buiocchi said.
What are the different types of home healthcare?
Buiocchi, who oversees MaineHealth’s Home Health and Hospice, said that in general, Medicare pays for skilled nursing care needed in the home. Examples include recovering from a surgery or an illness where the patient requires the assistance of skilled nurses while recuperating at home.
Medicare is the federally funded health insurance program for those 65 and older, while Medicaid serves lower-income and disabled populations.
If an older person doesn’t need skilled nursing, but needs help with tasks for daily living, such as cooking, cleaning, remembering to take medications, groceries and laundry, they could qualify for those services under Medicaid, or if they don’t qualify, could purchase them out-of-pocket from an agency, Buiocchi said.
Medicare services are typically shorter-term, for instance rehabilitating at home after surgery, she said.
How can I access services?
Because services are in great demand, Buiocchi advised older Mainers who need help or their caregivers to educate themselves on what’s available.
“Be proactive,” Buiocchi said. “Don’t wait until someone has an acute incident. Call organizations to see what they provide and when they provide it. Get an assessment, and see what your insurance will cover.”
Noël Bonam, Maine AARP’s state director, said a good first step is to call 211 or reach out to your local Agency on Aging.
“They will do an assessment to see what are the needs in this caregiving situation, what kind of support is needed and what kind of resources are available,” Bonam said.
One of the first steps that can be taken is to look up caregiver support groups. For instance, the Southern Maine Agency on Aging offers caregiver training and support groups.
Some may qualify for help under Medicaid, known as MaineCare in the state. The first step is to get an assessment by filling out the long-term care application or calling 833-525-5784.
Catherine Dorrington, owner of Coastal Care Solutions in South Portland, said their business doesn’t provide Medicare or Medicaid home health services. But agencies such as Coastal Care can offer a number of out-of-pocket services to help older adults, such as respite care for caregivers, moving into new housing, and assistance with daily tasks.
“As you age, you can often continue to do things, but you may have to do them in a different way or with additional support,” Dorrington said.
If I’m a caregiver, do I have to follow the new Medicaid work requirement rules?
Most caregivers with Medicaid insurance are exempt from the work requirements that will require Medicaid recipients to work, volunteer or attend school for at least 80 hours per month starting in 2027.
Olivia Umoren Ezeuko, director of public policy and advocacy for USAging, a national association that supports state agencies on aging, said it’s important for caregivers to know about this exemption so they fill out the paperwork properly to prove their status. If not, people risk becoming uninsured.
“A lot of people are going to go to their next doctor’s appointment and find out they don’t have coverage anymore,” Umoren Ezeoko said during a public briefing on the topic. She said states are trying to make the process of maintaining Medicaid insurance as seamless as possible by linking employers with Medicaid eligibility documentation so that many workers do not need to obtain proof of employment.
Where can I go for help?
There are several good resources online, including at the Southern Maine Agency on Aging, which offers help for family caregivers. Or call 800-427-7411.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has a guide to help families determine whether they qualify for home healthcare services through Medicaid. Under Medicaid, one of the first steps is to fill out the long-term care application. In addition to asking about what type of help is needed, Medicaid will need financial information, such as income and assets. Families can also call 833-525-5784 and to see what services they may qualify for.
The Maine AARP also has a guide on home- and community-based services. Call 866-554-5380 for more information.
Caregivers can also call 211, which will connect them to resources.

title: Here’s what Cumberland voters will see on November’s ballot

Access to health options, affordable housing, and quality education across the state are foundational for a strong society and economy. title: Broadway Bridge Replacement Enters Final Stretch On I-95 Near Bangor Through End Of Year
text:
Traffic in the area of the Broadway Bridge in Bangor will get a little trickier this week, as crews get ready for the final phases of the bridge replacement project.
What And When Will This All Happen?
According ot the Maine Department of Transportation, crews will be working on shoulder reconstruction along with milling and pavement in the southbound area of I-95 near Broadway beginning on Friday, October 16th and running through the weekend.
This means the traffic pattern will be changing to accommodate the work, so motorists are asked to use caution and be aware.
How Will The Work Impact Travel?
Officials with the Maine DOT say the work will be done in phases, in order to prepare for the transition from the temporary bridge to the new permanent one.
Phase 1:
"The southbound high-speed lane will be closed to traffic while crews complete milling and paving at both ends of that lane."
We're told the southbound travel lanes will stay open, along with the on and off ramps in the area, so motorists will still have access to those avenues.
Phase 2:
"The southbound high-speed lane will be opened to traffic across the new bridge. The southbound travel lane and the Exit 185 southbound off-ramp will be closed while crews complete excavation, milling, and paving at the north end of the travel lane and ramp."
Read More: Maine Fall Fun: Take Amtrak to Celtics & Bruins Games
During that time, drivers should follow the signs for the detour, which will take them to the Stillwater Exit (186) and down Stillwater Ave to Broadway, so they can bypass all of the work.
Phase 3
Once crews have completed the milling, paving, and excavation, they will start Phase 3 by reopening the Exit 185 southbound off-ramp.
"The southbound high-speed lane will remain open to traffic across the new bridge, and the southbound travel lane will remain closed."
Read More: Llewellyn Estes Bridge Removal Work Begins In Old Town
They may have to close the on-ramp temporarily to finish up work on the ends of the ramp and travel lane.
If that happens, motorists will be detoured down Broadway to Stillwater Ave and will have access to the interstate via the on-ramp at Exit 186.
Phase 4:
All of the new southbound lanes and ramps will open across the new bridge.
The Maine DOT says they will have plenty of message boards, signs, and cones around the area, letting folks know of the upcoming transitions and helping to guide them through the changes.
If we all just slow down, stay alert, exercise a little patience and understanding, and cooperate with the changes, knowing they're important and necessary, we'll all hopefully get through this weekend without incident.
The Broadway Bridge Project broke ground in 2023 and is scheduled to officially wrap up by the end of this year.

title: Mainers are in for a harsh winter— thanks to Republicans
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rep. Chellie Pingree is the U.S. congresswoman for Maine’s 1st District.
Between the mountains of snow, the waves of bitter cold and the occasional Nor’easter, we
Mainers are no strangers to harsh winters.
This winter could be one of the hardest in recent memory. And not because of the weather. The statewide average price of heating oil just hit a record $6.02 a gallon. As of Sept. 28, it was still averaging $5.96 — up nearly 79% from the same week last year. At today’s price, a 250-gallon fill-up costs about $1,490 — an expense many Maine families will face more than once this winter.
Meanwhile, gas prices are hovering around $4.40 per gallon as of Sept. 25, according to
Maine Public.
As if all this wasn’t awful enough, the number of Mainers receiving assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has fallen by 13% — 13,000 people in all, including 7,000 children. Another 31,000 Mainers are projected to lose MaineCare coverage over the next year.
Add it all up and this winter is going to put an enormous strain on Maine families — especially those who can least afford it.
This looming crisis is the result of choices President Trump and congressional Republicans made. Choices they continue to defend.
Let’s back up to July 4, 2025, when the president signed his hallmark legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, into law.
The “Big Ugly Bill” is a more accurate name. It slashed Medicaid by $1.2 trillion and SNAP by $211 billion over the next decade, all while handing hundreds of billions of dollars in tax breaks to the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations.
Far from offsetting those devastating cuts, the Big Ugly Bill’s ludicrous tax breaks are projected to increase federal deficits by $4.6 trillion, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also handed $175 billion to the Department of Homeland Security, helping turbocharge the Trump administration’s cruel immigration enforcement agenda and bringing chaos and violence to communities across the country. That includes Maine, where an ICE agent shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13.
The young father was not the target of ICE’s operation that morning. He had no criminal history, and we don’t have body camera footage of the shooting. His family has still not been contacted by the federal government and is still waiting for a full accounting of what happened.
This bill will go down as one of the most irresponsible, destructive, and costly pieces of legislation in American history. Not just in terms of its fiscal recklessness, but its human toll as well: nearly 13 million fewer people enrolled in Medicaid by 2034 and roughly 2.4 million fewer people receiving SNAP in an average month, according to CBO estimates. Its consequences will reach every community in America, in shuttered rural hospitals, overwhelmed food banks and increased costs for state and local governments.
The Big Ugly Bill alone would have been devastating enough for Maine. Then Trump’s reckless, unauthorized war of choice in Iran has kicked every one of these crises into overdrive. In the nearly eight months since the war began — a conflict Trump insisted wouldn’t last more than a few weeks — the global economy has been thrown into turmoil.
The on-again, off-again closure of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, has sent energy prices skyrocketing — and disrupted the flow of goods around the world. When the world’s energy supply gets squeezed, everyone pays more. In a state like Maine, where a colder-than-average winter can mean the difference between keeping the heat on and putting on extra layers just to stay warm, the potential consequences are catastrophic.
None of this had to happen. These crises have been created or made worse by Trump’s policies — and by congressional Republicans’ refusal to push back on the president and stand up for their constituents.
And now, with Americans staring down record energy costs, Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home early for a seven-week campaign recess. Rather than staying to work on the many challenges facing our nation, Republicans tucked tail and left.
Republicans could’ve chosen to help you. They chose to help the already-rich get even richer — and to give an army of masked, heavily armed and utterly unaccountable ICE agents virtually unlimited resources to terrorize our communities.
My Democratic colleagues and I have been fighting them every step of the way. We’ve voted against these devastating cuts. We’ve introduced legislation to protect healthcare and food assistance. We’ve demanded accountability for an administration that continues to put its deeply unpopular agenda ahead of the people it’s supposed to serve.
And we are demanding action on the heating crisis: end the war in Iran, protect the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, reverse changes to the Home Owner Managing Energy Savings Rebates and High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate programs and reinstate the energy efficiency tax credits Republicans eliminated. Speaker Johnson should call the House back to Washington so Congress can get to work.
We will keep fighting — at every turn, and for as long as it takes. Because Mainers deserve better. They deserve a government that makes their lives more affordable — not one that cuts their healthcare and food assistance, sends energy prices through the roof and hands massive tax breaks to the people who need them least.
Mainers have survived plenty of hard winters. But the hardships coming this winter are the result of decisions made by Republicans in Washington, who would rather leave town than fix the problems they created.

title: CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle Justice Department case over opioid prescriptions
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday.
The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of prescribing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.”
It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis.
“Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement.
CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.”
The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing.
The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids.
The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden’s administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills,” or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose.
It alleged that poor staffing levels coupled with performance metrics and incentive compensation policies implemented by the company led to pharmacists racing to fill prescriptions without confirming they were legitimate. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says.
Under the settlement, CVS must also “implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement.
Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently.
Most of the settlements — and dollars — have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart.
___
Associated Press reporter Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report from Philadelphia.

title: Employee arrested after listening device found in OpenAI conference room, FBI and the company say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.
The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden in the conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.
The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.
“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.
The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications.
Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room, according to the complaint.
Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a camera at the time it was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on a half-dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, the complaint says.
The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device was installed, according to the FBI.
The complaint also he also used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left an unattended bag in a different room in the building that included his wallet, identification and another recording device.

title: How to find real deals at outlet malls, according to an expert
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Outlet malls can still offer real savings, but only for shoppers who know certain tricks, according to Kyle James, a writer for ConsumerAffairs.
James said outlet malls are skilled at creating the appearance of a great deal.
“You see these huge signs everywhere, 60% off, close-out sale — well, the thing is, you show up next week or a month from now, the signs are still there collecting dust,” James said. “So it’s important to be aware of that, and a lot of the products you’re going to find at these outlet malls are stuff that’s made specifically for the outlet mall, and so a lot of times the quality isn’t as good.”
James said if a store has every size and color of an item in stock, that item was likely manufactured specifically for the outlet rather than being overstock from a regular retail location. Items that are harder to find in every size are more likely to be genuine overstock from the main store.
James recommends skipping the merchandise displayed at the front of an outlet store.
“When you first walk into one of these outlet stores, the stuff in the front that’s going to be all close to full price — the stuff they’re trying to make the most money on,” James said. “So I like to give the tip of shopping the store backwards. Go to the back of the store or the backside of the store, that’s where the clearance items are.”
James said shoppers can save even more by checking an outlet mall’s website and customer service desk for coupon books or hidden coupon pages. An extra 10% to 15% off can make a meaningful difference on larger purchases.

title: Augusta utility sues 4 paper mills over toxic PFAS in drinking water
text:
The Greater Augusta Utility District has filed a federal lawsuit against four upstream paper manufacturers to recover millions spent filtering toxic “forever chemicals” out of the capital city’s public drinking water supply.
The utility is asking the court to hold the mills responsible for polluting the Kennebec River watershed rather than forcing ratepayers and taxpayers to absorb the cost of complex water treatment.
The outcome could set a legal blueprint for public water systems across Maine and nationwide.
The dispute centers on Augusta’s Riverside wells, where pumps pull groundwater from an aquifer connected to the Kennebec River. Officials shut the wells down after testing in 2021 showed unsafe levels of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
Water from these wells contained 23.3 parts per trillion of the six PFAS compounds that Maine measures to establish drinking water safety. The state limit is 20 parts per trillion. To picture that scale, one part per trillion equals one drop of water in 20 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
While that sounds exceedingly small, state and federal environmental regulators emphasize that even trace amounts of these manmade chemicals can pose human health risks, with long-term exposure linked to kidney cancer, liver damage, high cholesterol and immune system disruption.
To protect its 13,750 customers, the utility invested $2 million — much of which came from grants — to build an ion-exchange treatment facility. Water began flowing safely this summer, but the utility argues that the financial burden belongs to the polluters.
The lawsuit marks a crucial strategic shift in environmental litigation.
Most PFAS cases target the chemical creators, like 3M or DuPont. Maine has filed two lawsuits against major chemical companies, alleging they willfully introduced toxic chemicals into Maine’s environment while concealing their known health and environmental risks.
In its lawsuit filed last week, the Augusta district is going after the paper mills that used PFAS while making grease-resistant paper and disposable dishware, including: Sappi North America Inc., which operates a mill in Skowhegan; Huhtamaki Inc., which makes Chinet products in Waterville; Kimberly-Clark Corp., which had a plant in Winslow; and American Tissue Corp. and its subsidiary, American Tissue Mills of Maine, which operated a mill in Augusta. The Winslow and Augusta mills have been closed for several years.
A similar legal strategy succeeded in Michigan in 2022, where footwear manufacturer Wolverine Worldwide paid $54 million to the state, two local communities and residents after dumping PFAS-contaminated leather-treatment waste.
However, while Wolverine involved a single isolated disposal dump, proving causation along Maine’s 30-mile Kennebec River corridor could be far more complex because discharges from multiple mills commingle in the water.
But federal law offers a powerful legal tool: the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, or Superfund, which establishes the mechanisms needed to force responsible parties to pay for environmental cleanup costs.
“Liability is strict, retroactive and joint and several,” said Anthony Moffa, an environmental law professor at the University of Maine School of Law. Under that law, defendants can be held responsible for cleanup costs even if they complied with all of their permits, Moffa said.
This legal framework resolves a question that hung over the Greater Augusta Utility District’s recent project opening, where officials said there was no single “smoking gun” to blame for its PFAS spike. In its suit, the district claims mill discharges blended together over decades to form an indivisible toxin.
But under federal Superfund regulations, plaintiffs do not have to isolate individual chemical molecules to establish liability. They only need to prove an upstream mill discharged hazardous waste into the watershed. And for that, they turned to state-run water, leachate and fish testing.
The district cites PFAS spikes in paper mill discharge, landfill runoff and fish tissue as its proof.
“Defendants, and not the district, its taxpayers, or its customers, should bear the past, present, and future costs of investigating, monitoring, treating, and remediating PFAS contamination affecting the district’s drinking water,” the district said in its Oct. 7 suit in U.S. District Court.
The litigation builds on a wave of class-action litigation by central Maine landowners and farmers, who are suing some Maine paper mills after their sludge spread as fertilizer contaminated private wells and tainted farm fields across Somerset and Kennebec counties.
Unlike some national settlements reached with chemical creators, none of the Maine lawsuits targeting paper mills has been settled, according to court records, with regional class actions still working their way through federal and state dockets as the paper mills mount vigorous defenses.
Because the spreading of industrial sludge was state-permitted, Maine maintains historical records of its use. From those records, the state estimated eight paper companies spread at least a half million cubic yards of paper mill waste in Maine between 1989 and 2016.
But Maine has no such records for industrial PFAS discharges into public water bodies. For decades, state and federal discharge permits regulated things like suspended solids or pH, but they did not require monitoring of PFAS compounds.
However, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection conducted a 10-month statewide study testing industrial and municipal wastewater effluent in 2022. The agency calculated that regulated facilities discharge roughly 30 pounds of PFAS into Maine waters every year.
Maine now requires all who discharge into public waters to monitor and report PFAS levels.
Upstream paper companies and industry leaders have argued the mills operated within the law.
A spokeswoman for Sappi said the company is reviewing the lawsuit. She said Sappi complies with environmental regulations, operates within its state and federal discharge permits and doesn’t knowingly use PFAS in products.
Neither Huhtamaki nor Kimberly-Clark responded to requests for comment. American Tissue has ceased operations and filed for bankruptcy in 2001. Under federal law, if a responsible party cannot pay, the financial burden shifts to the solvent co-defendants remaining.
Industry leaders echoed that defense and cautioned against penalizing law-abiding businesses.
The executive director of the Maine Wood Products Council, Krysta West, stressed that mills work hard to apply current science. “It is always concerning when lawsuits are filed against companies in any sector who operated in accordance with state and federal permits,” West said.
The lawsuit lands amid Maine’s broader reckoning with legacy chemical pollution.
For decades, state-approved programs encouraged paper mills and wastewater plants to spread their leftover sludge on local fields as free fertilizer. The practice has contaminated almost 100 farms, ruined dairy herds and fouled hundreds of private drinking wells in central Maine.
The public outcry prompted Maine to become the first state to ban sludge-based fertilizer use.
Public health advocates said mills cannot claim ignorance after decades of scientific warnings.
“Industries choosing to create or use PFAS in spite of that should not be surprised when consumers, regulators, and other impacted groups … seek compensation for the harms,” said Emily Carey Perez de Alejo, executive director of Portland-based Defend Our Health.

title: Cornell bans fraternity parties in wake of gang rape allegation
text:
(AP) — Cornell University suspended parties at fraternity houses until next year and is giving state police a role in investigating reports of sexual assault on campus in the school’s latest response to outrage over its handling of a gang rape allegation.
The measures announced Tuesday by Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff include a suspension of all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses through the end of the 2026-27 academic year and a new “zero tolerance” policy that would immediately suspend chapters for violations.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.
Cornell has more than 20 active Interfraternity Council fraternities. The council did not immediately respond to an email request for comment. It’s unclear whether the restrictions extend to off-campus parties.
It’s not the first time Cornell has cracked down on fraternity parties. The university temporarily suspended them in 2022 after reports of a sexual assault and students being drugged at fraternity-affiliated housing.
Cornell also tightened fraternity safety rules in 2019 after freshman Antonio Tsialas was found dead in a gorge following an alleged hazing incident. A year earlier, a fraternity was placed on probation over a contest in which members competed to have sex with women they considered overweight.
Cornell plans alternatives to fraternity parties
Cornell said it will solicit input about “the development of safe social alternatives” to Greek life party culture and direct university resources toward those alternatives.
Kotlikoff also committed to adding a case manager to the school’s Office of Civil Rights to help those who report sexual misconduct on the Cornell campus navigate the process, and to working with New York State Police to allow its criminal investigators — who are independent of Cornell — to investigate allegations.
Crimes reported on Cornell’s campus are generally investigated by campus police, a department that has full law enforcement powers but is controlled by the university.
The campus police force operates independently from municipal police in Ithaca, New York, where the university is located. Its officers investigated the 2024 gang rape allegations and presented their initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to prosecute within weeks of the woman making her first report to police.
New York’s governor removed the district attorney from the case this month after a public outcry over the lack of charges.
The investigation is now being led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, while Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent review of the university’s response.
A state police spokesperson declined to comment.
A gang rape allegation sparks scrutiny of Cornell’s response
In a lawsuit filed in September, the woman alleged that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024.
She said she was pressured to use drugs and that other men entered the room while she was incapacitated. She also alleges that Snapchat messages describing her as sexually available to anyone at the house circulated among fraternity members without her knowledge.
Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students following an internal investigation, but no criminal charges have been filed. The seven men accused in the woman’s lawsuit have all denied her allegations, either saying that the sexual activity was consensual or that they weren’t involved.
Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for one of the men accused in the woman’s lawsuit, criticized the restrictions announced Tuesday as a sweeping response to problems that extend beyond fraternities, arguing that universities promote Greek social life but distance themselves from it when controversies arise.
“Greek life has become the convenient target,” he said in an emailed statement. He warned that parties could simply move off campus, where there would be less oversight. “Changing the address doesn’t change the behavior.”
Cornell faces broader pressure for reform
Kotlikoff’s announcement came a day before Cornell’s Faculty Senate was to take up a proposed resolution expressing no confidence in the administration’s ability to effectively address sexual assault on campus.
Paul Ortiz, a Cornell labor history professor who is the lead sponsor of the resolution, said Tuesday that he welcomed the new measures but regretted that it took student protests, media coverage and the suffering of people like the woman suing the university over an alleged gang rape to prompt action.
“That the administration is only acting the day before they might be held accountable in the faculty senate is deeply troubling,” Ortiz said in an email to The Associated Press, adding that he believes the no-confidence resolution is “more important than ever.”
“The key point to understand is that scores of students, staff, faculty and alumni have approached the sponsors of the resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but the tip of the iceberg,” he continued. “Students and alumni have shared experiences of being raped at Cornell.”
“These women testify that they were frightened to report assaults because they felt that Cornell has at times treated rape as more of a ‘PR problem’ than a heinous crime,” Ortiz said.
In his Tuesday letter, Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk.
Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programs, he said, calling the actions “first steps toward systemic change on our campus.”
“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said.

title: A more balanced Congress requires Democrats
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In most midterm elections, voters are looking for candidates that will balance the power in Washington, D.C. This is more critical than ever this year, after two years of domination by President Trump and the Republicans.
More than half of the citizens in our country have no real representation in the U.S. Congress today; Democrats have been silenced and Republicans are not allowed to disagree with the White House.
The high prices and hardships Mainers are facing today are a direct result of the president’s whims and decisions. Nothing will change if we don’t send enough Democrats to Congress in November to balance the decision-making.
If we don’t slow down Trump’s administration, it will leave us with an economic, environmental, cultural and geopolitical mess that will take many years to clean up.
Please consider what’s at stake for Maine and our country when we vote in the midterms.
Beverly Wood
North Berwick

title: With high fuel costs, people seeking early help from River Valley Wood Bank
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
RUMFORD — With the price of heating oil at a record high, River Valley Wood Bank volunteers say people are already turning to them for help and winter hasn’t even started yet.
Shannon Glover, Gary Dolloff and Jacob Hickey were busy Oct. 8 removing a half-cord of seasoned firewood donated by Matt Pingree from Dolloff’s pickup.
“I’m already getting calls from people worried about oil,” Glover said. “‘I can’t afford oil and it’s getting cold.'”
Since 2023, the River Valley Wood Bank has served as a community-run emergency firewood initiative, operating similarly to a food pantry, with its objective to assist locals on a temporary basis who have exhausted their wood supply usually in the middle of winter.
“People are turning to us and we really don’t have that,” Dolloff said. “We try to get somebody from point A to point B in a week or so.”
He said they delivered about seven cords of donated wood last winter to around 18 families in the River Valley.
“We don’t fill the basements, but I have noticed that a lot of times it was when people run out of wood,” Glover said. “I guess it’s hard to get in the middle of winter … It’s usually about half a truck load to drop off and get them by for three or four days.”
Dolloff and Glover agree that it’s going to get crazy within the next month or so.
Dolloff, executive director/manager of the Greater Rumford Community Center, helps a lot of people on fixed incomes.
“Six years ago, I was helping people that needed a little bit (of heating oil) right around Christmastime and I’d give them a hundred gallons,” Dolloff said. “That was back when it was like $1.62.”
Glover, a community volunteer for the Red Cross, said, “Now, 100 gallons … I just got some last week, was $638, better than a third of a tank.”
Dolloff added, “That’s the whole check (Social Security) for the month. For a hundred gallons, you can’t even get through two weeks.”
The wood bank was started by Glover and Dolloff.
“What gave me the idea was all the things he (Dolloff) was posting about people looking. It blew my mind,” Glover said. “He posted at least twice a week about people in need of wood. That’s when I read about the wood bank in Bethel. And I thought, can we get one here?”
The wood donated by Pingree was already split and was added to the stockpile in a 6x12x8-foot shed built by Region 9 School of Applied Technology students in 2023.
The shed, which holds about four cords of wood, was named Bumpa’s Wood Shed by Glover in honor of her father, with whom she used to split wood as a child.
Glover noted they try to keep the location of the wood shed private for security reasons. Still, there were people that have helped themselves to the wood at times. There are now security cameras set up in that area.
For that reason, Glover said she and Dolloff are the only people who pull wood from the shed.
Glover said her husband and children volunteer to help out at times. Dolloff said a group of middle school kids also volunteered last winter.
Dolloff and Glover are already getting requests from people seeking wood to heat their homes.
“Looking for seasoned wood for the wood pantry in the River valley, we have some but (we’re) thinking this is going to be a very tough heating season,” Dolloff said.
Dolloff said that if loggers have a cord or half-cord to donate, he’ll find someone to split it.
People in need of wood assistance can contact Glover or Dolloff through Facebook or by calling Dolloff at 207-369-9906.
“We supply enough wood to get you through a few weeks until you can get back on your feet,” Dolloff said.
FOOD PANTRY
Glover, who is also manager of the Old School Food Pantry in Mexico, said that the first week of the month is usually the slowest at the pantry, but October has already seen more people than expected.
“We had 70 people by 5 o’clock,” she said. “I had to stop filling boxes; I ran out of food. They said ‘I either have to get heat, food or medicine.'”
Glover said that kind of rush never happens. “Our normal number for the first of the month is about 30 people,” she said.
She said the produce side still had some food left, but from the other shelves, “they wiped us out.”
“I have just peanut butter, mustard and pinto beans that nobody wants left on my shelf right now,” Glover said. “Delivery happens next week.”
With limited income from Social Security and the additional costs of medications, food, heating oil, gas for their vehicles, many seniors are seeking help.
“That’s why you’re seeing so many older adults back at work because they can’t survive off their Social Security,” she said. “It’s scary.”
