title: What’s on the Lewiston ballot?
text:
LEWISTON — From City Council elections to a needle ordinance amendment, residents are already voting early ahead of the Nov. 3 election on a plethora of city and state candidates and five ballot questions for the city.
The general and municipal elections will be held Tuesday, Nov. 3. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
The polling location for Wards 1 and 3 is the Lewiston Armory at 65 Central Ave.; Ward 2 at Montello School, 407 East Ave.; Wards 4, 5 and 7 at Longley School, 145 Birch St.; and Ward 6 at The Green Ladle, 156 East Ave. on the Lewiston High School campus.
Voters who wish to cast their ballots before Election Day can do so on the first floor of City Hall from Tuesday, Oct. 13m through Thursday, Oct. 29, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. However, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, voting will be from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Absentee ballots became available Oct. 5. Voters can request a ballot online through the state’s absentee ballot request service and can download an application or contact the City Clerk’s office at 1-207-513-3124. Applications can be mailed or delivered to City Hall, faxed to 1-207-777-4621 or emailed to [email protected].
Absentee ballots can be mailed or cast in person now through Thursday, Oct. 29, at the City Clerk’s office on the second floor of City Hall at 27 Pine St.
Sample ballots for ward and district can be found on the city website.
City elections
The candidates for mayor are incumbent Carl Sheline, Rick LaChapelle, Brian Beaulieu, Jay Rodrigue and Charles Soule. The mayor presides over the City Council.
There are seven candidates vying for the City Council from Wards 2, 4 and 6. They are:
Ward 2: incumbent Susan Longchamps and Rebecca J. Long.
Ward 4: incumbent Michael Roy, Matthew D. Agren and Chandra L. Sasseville.
Ward 6: Robert C. Glaspy Jr. and Hollie Anne Niemi. Incumbent David Chittim did not seek reelection.
The council, which has seven members, makes policy decisions.
There are five candidates for four seats on the School Committee, with only one of those seats being contested. They are:
Ward 1: committee Chair Jean Phoenix Irons McLaughline.
Ward 3: incumbent Emily S. Leavasseur.
Ward 5: Nicole Johnson and Marcel Leclair.
Ward 7: Amran M. Osman.
Ballot questions
Residents will vote on five ballot questions pertaining to city government.
Question 1 reads: “Shall the city ordinance pertaining to the Lewiston Syringe Service Program be amended to mandate a strict 1:1 needle exchange with a 20-syringe daily limit per person, require each provider to operate from one fixed location, and prohibit all mobile exchange units?”
A yes vote establishes the new 1:1 needle exchange mandate. A no vote retains the city’s existing ordinance.
Question 2 reads: “Shall a Charter Commission be established for the purpose of establishing a New Municipal Charter?”
A yes vote will establish a charter commission. A no vote would reject the creation of a new charter commission to formulate a new charter.
Questions 3, 4 and 5 are described by city officials as “housekeeping items” focusing on procedural language changes in the city charter.
“All three of these are to correct errors and omissions in the charter that were oversights by the previous Charter Review Committees in 2012 and 2021. They are all housekeeping in nature,” City Clerk Kathy Montejo wrote in an email.
The proposed changes correct outdated references in the city charter after previous revisions removed or renumbered provisions, but neglected to change references to those provisions elsewhere in the charter, Montejo said.

title: While helping Maine, Susan Collins failed the nation
text:
John P. Dionne of Bangor formerly worked in construction and spent the last 20 years prior to retirement as the facility manager for a residential vocational training program.
I’ve lived most of my life in Maine, raised on a potato farm in the St. John River Valley in northern Maine. I spent four years in Connecticut going to college, which opened a huge
window of awareness of the world and its complex demographics, some beautiful, others
heartbreaking. 
The year I spent in Iowa as a VISTA volunteer exposed me to dichotomies and similarities of different regions in the United States. While there, I worked with a community action agency, helping the less fortunate and many aged folks to winterize their homes, building and installing passive hot air solar panels to provide them with relief from high energy costs. That was in 1980 and 1981.
Now, 45 years later, we find ourselves facing the same challenges and tribulations we faced when I was a mere 23-year-old spirit looking forward to a good life.
I did vote for Sen. Susan Collins more than once, believing she would uphold these values and advocate for the people of Maine and the United States. Over the last 10 years, however, my respect for her service to this country, its people and international security and prosperity has dwindled.
Whenever I return to northern Maine, where both Sen. Collins and I grew up, I am saddened by the desolation, depression and lack of vitality. Such a crisis exists in many rural areas in this country.
The United State Senate provides equal representation for states regardless of size or demographics. U.S. senators’ primary objective and mission should be to create policies that support the well-being, health, safety and prosperity of the entire nation. Sen. Collins might have thrown a few perks our way, but she and many others have failed the nation.
Sen. Collins has failed to protect the social and civic institutions legally established to benefit the advancement and well-being of Americans. The scaling back of equal opportunity for women is abusive. There are many good public institutions endorsed by altruistic leaders over the past century that are being gutted and attacked.
Sen. Collins has failed to erect guardrails against big business pilfering earthly resources, big- money brokers that celebrate greed over humanitarian values, campaign contributions that soil elections and politics that purposely stoke division instead of embracing national and world harmony.
Sen. Collins and many others have failed to acknowledge the disastrous impact of world climate change and to begin implementing measures to not only mitigate the pain we will suffer but also address how societies can work together to change the momentum and prepare.
Climate change is as much a threat as the risk of nuclear arsenals. It scales worse because eradication of people and communities will happen over time, we will watch, and we will be helpless. What just happened in Nepal is proof, more than 1,400 killed, more than 5,000 people still missing, drowned or buried under a wall of mud. Who’s next?
Sen. Collins has failed to smother the culture of war that persists in this country and across the world. It is still evident in the games our children and even their parents play, glamorized in theaters, marketed by the military-industrial complex as good for the economy, propped up by people of power in the interest of national security to feed fear and retain their influence.
And to our neighbors, friends and family, north, south, east and west, Sen. Collins has compromised American goodwill and common purpose across the world.We can thank Sen. Collins for the early days of her service to the state of Maine.
Obviously, her influence and voice toward righteousness for the nation has been diminished to a whisper. We will need immense corrective action over the next decade and it’s time for better leadership to replace her and many others from both parties.

title: Scarborough volleyball wins gritty match against talented York squad
text:
YORK — Scarborough High’s volleyball team knew it was in for a series of tests to end the regular season.
The Red Storm passed a difficult exam Tuesday, beating Class B power York in five games, 25-18, 20-25, 21-25, 25-12, 15-10.
“It was really nice to win a fifth set because we haven’t won a fifth set at all this year,” said Scarborough’s high-flying outside hitter Caleb Atwood.
Scarborough, ranked eighth in the latest Varsity Maine poll, improved to 8-4 and will finish its Class A schedule against Kennebunk on Thursday and then No. 1 ranked Thornton on Monday.
“We end with a really difficult schedule,” said Scarborough coach Nicole Petherbridge. “We play a lot of tough opponents. It could hurt us in the standings, but I think it’s preparing us to peak at the right time.
York (9-3), the Class B runner-up the past two years, is ranked fifth in the poll. All of the Wildcats’ losses have been in five-game matches against top teams, including Thornton and defending Class B champion Washington Academy. York finishes its season at Greely, the only team to beat Washington Academy this season.
BIG POINT
York utilized an all-senior lineup on Senior Night in the first game. Neither team was particularly sharp to start, with Scarborough overcoming eight service errors to win the game.
The Wildcats went to their regular starting lineup, featuring junior outside hitter Evie Martin, and held sway in the next two games. Martin notched seven kills in Game 2 and Elizah Roe had three, including a powerful hit from the back row. In the third game, Ava Walker keyed a separating 9-0 York run with three service aces.
York took an early 3-1 lead in the fourth game when it won the longest rally of the entire match, one that featured numerous defensive digs by both teams. In that moment, York appeared ready to close out the match.
Instead, Scarborough won nine of the next 10 points and never really looked back.
“That is the beauty and the horror of volleyball,” said York coach Deanna Martin. “It’s all in the momentum, and it’s very, very mental. As teams get runs and points, it’s very hard mentally as an athlete to respond to that, and it takes a lot of work to learn that skill.”
DIVERSIFY
In York’s second- and third-game wins, both teams’ attack flowed primarily through one person; Martin for York and Atwood for Scarborough.
It was when Atwood’s supporting cast found their groove in the final two games that Scarborough got the upper hand. Middle hitters Lexi Cowie and Calli Juhring were both strong defensive presences, with Cowie notching three kills and block point in the fifth game. Right-side hitter Elena Pijunovic had been swinging big with intent throughout the match and found the spots for kills in the fourth game. Ani Perkins used tips and hits to keep York’s defense guessing.
Overall good defense, i.e., the first pass, led to consistently on-target sets from Natalie Philibert.
UNSUNG HERO
Scaroborough sophomore Sophy Jin was used as a serving specialist and shined, particularly in the final two games. Jin had five service points in each of the last two games and three total aces. In the momentum-swinging fourth game, Jin also had a backset to find Atwood in her favorite position on the far left that Atwood buried to the court for a 4-3 lead, igniting the pivotal run.
Suzann Link was another Scarborough serving standout, with 11 total points.
STATISTICS
• Scarborough: Caleb Atwood, 18 kills, one ace; Lexi Cowie, 10 kills, three blocks; Elena Pijunovic, eight kills; Ani Perkins, six kills.
• York: Evie Martin, 16 kills; Elizah Roe, 5 kills; Ava Walker, five aces; Sophie Coite, three kills, two blocks.

title: Cornell suspends fraternity parties, gives state police role in investigating campus assault reports
text:
Cornell University is suspending parties and other social events at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year and will give the New York State Police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus, university officials announced Tuesday, amid mounting outrage over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.
The measures announced by Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff include a suspension of all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses through the end of the 2026-27 academic year and a new “zero tolerance” policy for violations that would result in the immediate emergency suspension of a chapter.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.
The university president said the school would begin conversations with students and faculty experts about “the development of safe social alternatives” to Greek life party culture and invest money to get those initiatives off the ground.
He also committed to adding a case manager to the school’s Office of Civil Rights to help those who report sexual misconduct on the Cornell campus navigate the process, and to working with the New York State Police to allow its criminal investigators — who are independent of Cornell — to investigate allegations.
Crimes reported on Cornell’s campus are generally investigated by campus police, a department that has full law enforcement powers but is controlled by the university. The campus police force operates independently from municipal police in Ithaca, New York, where the university is located. Its officers investigated the 2024 gang rape allegations and presented their initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to prosecute within weeks of the woman making her first report to police.
New York’s governor removed the district attorney from the case this month after a public outcry over the lack of charges.
The investigation is now being led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, while Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent review of the university’s response. New York State Police sometimes handle major crime investigations for small municipal police agencies, bringing in expertise that isn’t available locally.
Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk.
Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programs, including education aimed at encouraging bystanders to intervene, he said, calling the various actions announced Tuesday “first steps toward systemic change on our campus.”
“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said.

title: State says infection control issues at CMMC in Lewiston could jeopardize Medicare agreement
text:
In an investigation of sterile processing contamination issues at Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston in late August, state and federal officials found ongoing infection control deficiencies and said the hospital could be terminated from the Medicare program if they are not resolved by early January.
On Aug. 21, during an investigation of several complaints at the hospital, the state declared that CMMC’s failure to address contamination issues posed an immediate risk to patients. Officials had observed an unknown orange and yellow substance inside four sterile surgical instrument trays marked “ready for use.” All instrument trays that go through the sterile processing department were stained with the same substance, staff confirmed.
This “had been a known issue since 2023,” the department’s staff told state officials.
The Lewiston hospital sent some surgical patients to other hospitals after the state’s finding. The immediate jeopardy situation, “in which a recipient of care has suffered or is likely to suffer serious injury, harm, impairment or death,” was resolved by the afternoon of Aug. 24, but officials from the Maine Department of Health and Human Services and the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) continued investigating the facility and interviewing staff and management about observed issues.
In a written notice to CMMC CEO Allen Stefanek on Oct. 8 detailing the results of that investigation, a CMS enforcement official said “substantial noncompliance remains” with three conditions that allow hospitals to participate in the federal Medicare program, including deficiencies with CMMC’s infection control stewardship, physical environment and governing body.
If the hospital does not comply with the conditions by Jan. 6, 2027, CMS may terminate its Medicare agreement. A CMMC spokesperson said Tuesday the hospital has implemented a plan of correction that includes updated policies, quality audits and ongoing monitoring.
Even so, they said, “we have no evidence that any instrument used in patient care at CMMC was non-sterile or contaminated. CMMC routinely monitors its sterilization processes and equipment, and its surgical site infection rate has consistently remained below the national average.”
According to the investigation report, hospital leadership failed to implement an infection prevention and control program, maintain a clean and sanitary environment, and address infection control findings.
Specifically, officials said, CMMC failed to ensure that supplies used during surgical procedures were sterile, that operating room tables “were free of rust and chipped paint” and that expired supplies were removed from patient care areas, including operating room tubing, tube clamps and airway devices that expired in 2024.
Sanitary issues impacted six out of seven operating rooms, two cardiac operating rooms, the cardiac catheterization lab, the emergency department, common areas and four hospital units, including a rehabilitation ward, the report said.
Staff in the sterile processing department told state investigators they had observed staining in the sterile surgical instrument trays since 2023. When asked how many trays had been returned from the operating room to be reprocessed due to contamination, the department’s manager said: “None, no one turns the trays away. We would have to close the doors due to the prevalence of the issue.”
These issues, and the hospital’s failure to correct them, are of “such character as to substantially limit the hospital’s capacity to furnish adequate care and/or as to adversely affect the health and safety of patients,” the CMS notice said.
The Central Maine Healthcare system includes CMMC, hospitals in Bridgton and Rumford, and several physician practices.
The health system’s infection prevention plan for fiscal year 2025 flagged contamination issues as “high risk” for CMMC’s sterile processing department, also called perioperative services, according to the investigation report.
The health system flagged the same issue in its fiscal year 2026 infection plan.
In 13 CMMC board of directors meetings from fiscal year 2026, there was no discussion of infection control concerns, according to the state’s review of meeting minutes. The most recent meeting was in July. The chair of the board had been absent for three out of five meetings, the state found.
“Regarding concerns in the perioperative and sterile processing department of this magnitude,” the chair told the state in an Aug. 26 interview, “I learned about it during this survey. It came to my knowledge last week.”
Central Maine Healthcare was acquired by California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation in February. In a statement on Sep. 9, a spokesperson said the nonprofit had committed more than $50 million toward replacing Central Maine Healthcare’s electronic medical records system, rebuilding the workforce and improving infrastructure and recruitment.
The spokesperson at the time did not note any investments in the sterile processing department, but said Tuesday that “CMMC continues to invest” in the department and provide oversight as part of an ongoing commitment to quality and safety.
The hospital’s operating rooms are no longer on diversion and have returned to normal operations, the spokesperson said.
The state also identified standard-level deficiencies at Central Maine Healthcare’s outpatient practices, including at Central Maine Obstetrics-Gynecology, where front office staff said they were instructed to turn pregnant patients away due to short staffing and other issues. The state said this was a failure by Central Maine Healthcare to communicate waitlist expectations and provide care to patients in need, as mandated by hospital bylaws.
It’s not uncommon for the state to investigate complaints at Maine’s hospitals. Over the last two years, the state has investigated CMMC 14 other times and identified a handful of standard-level deficiencies, as opposed to the condition-level deficiencies found in August. A complaint investigation from late 2025 even concluded that CMMC was in substantial compliance with infection prevention and control standards.
MaineHealth Maine Medical Center was investigated by the state for complaints 25 times in the same two-year timeframe. St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston was investigated nine times and on one visit the state identified noncompliance with Medicare conditions related to the hospital’s medical staff bylaws.
Noncompliant hospitals have the opportunity to correct deficiencies, but in the meantime, the federal government considers the hospital to be unaccredited and grants full jurisdiction to the state agency to oversee all accreditation complaints and monitoring visits.
This “standard CMS process” is happening at CMMC, said Lindsay Hammes, Maine DHHS spokesperson.
“We are committed to maintaining rigorous sterilization standards, addressing identified opportunities for improvement and ensuring patients receive care in an environment focused on quality and safety,” a CMMC spokesperson said.

title: Bobby Charles wants to cut crime and taxes if elected governor
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bobby Charles, former assistant secretary of state under Colin Powell, seeks Maine governor's office
The Republican candidate won a seven-way contest in the June primary after a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
Bobby Charles, former assistant secretary of state under Colin Powell, seeks Maine governor's office
The Republican candidate won a seven-way contest in the June primary after a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles, who won a seven-way primary in June, now has his eyes set on the Blaine House.
Charles was up by double digits in the crowded GOP primary field, but the race was ultimately decided by a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
"I asked my team to look at all the jurisdictions that have ever done ranked choice, including in Europe, and there was no jurisdiction where someone had been up in a field of eight, or even like that, by 17 or 18 points and didn't prevail," Charles said.
This information is what led Charles to declare victory even before the tabulation was complete.
Now, it's all eyes on the Nov. 3 general election and his two opponents: independent candidate Rick Bennett and Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree.
"I think the contrast is starker, which makes it, in my view, a little more enjoyable because you're not trying to split hairs," he said.
Charles has been vocal about Pingree, even before the two won their respective primaries.
Specifically because of Pingree's role in the Mills administration, where she served as the leader in the state on issues like climate and housing, Charles blames her for the issues the state is facing.
"Bottom line, up front, Hannah Pingree is the carbon copy and bears responsibility for the Janet Mills policies," Charles said.
Charles' campaign slogan is "cut crime, cut taxes, no nonsense."
"One of the things that people don't talk about is the policies that have encouraged crime to multiply," he said. "The cashless bail. The fact that you just have a rotating door; someone gets arrested and they're immediately let go again."
Charles said there are drug cartels that bring illegal substances to Maine, so he has what he calls a 20-point accountability plan that will do things like enforce strict criminal accountability.
When it comes to taxes, Charles wants to cut property taxes.
"I want to give a $100,000 homestead exemption to every single Mainer and, very important side point, I want it to be 100% reimbursed," he said.
The current homestead exemption is $25,000. Charles said he would raise it to $50,000 in his first two-year budget and raise it to $100,000 in his second biennium.
He also wants to eliminate the income tax.
"There are 11 states that have no income tax. I think that is a great goal," Charles said. "Ronald Reagan, for whom I worked, cut the income tax at the federal level by 25% and immediately generated 18 million jobs."
Charles said this will put more money in people's pockets.
He also said he wants to tackle healthcare and housing, adding that the two go hand in hand because healthcare workers need affordable housing, and without those workers, Maine will continue to see healthcare closures.
"I don't want to lose young people. I want them to stay here. I don't want to lose older people. I want them to come back here. Healthcare and housing are two key parts of that," Charles said.
The son of a school teacher, Charles grew up in the town of Wayne in Kennebec County. He got an Ivy League education, served in the Navy, worked under President Ronald Reagan and founded a lobbying and consulting firm in Washington, D.C.
Charles said that with all of his experience, it's time to give back to the state that raised him, and that's why he wants to be Maine's next governor.
"Right here in this town, that little general store over there was run by a World War II vet. We had World War II vets all over this town. They gave me everything I have, together with my mom," Charles said. "At a certain point in time, you get to an age and you say, 'You know what? I need to start giving back the skill sets that I've got to give back in.'"

title: Aging Untold: Feeling “off” could be a vitamin deficiency
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we look at how nutrient absorption changes as we age, what warning signs to watch for and the key vitamins to keep on your radar.
We also explore the mental health benefits of spending time solo and how embracing “me time” can boost your confidence and mood.
Then, we examine a concerning rise in cancer among younger adults and what early detection means for families.
When someone does not feel quite like themselves, a handful of nutrient deficiencies could be behind it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Two common deficiencies are vitamin B12 and vitamin D, she said.
Rogers said a check of your blood levels is a good first step, but it has limits.
Spending some time alone can be empowering.
For some, it’s a choice. Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said she needs and wants more solo time as she gets older.
For others, being alone is an adjustment after the loss of a loved one.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommends turning to a friend for support and taking small steps by combining something you enjoy with doing it alone, like a walk.
Brittany Auclair’s baby boy was just 8 months old when she first noticed an issue while breastfeeding.
“He decided that he favored one side over the other,” she said. Then, while pumping milk, she noticed a lump.
Auclair was 29 when she was diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer.
Cancer is increasing in people under 65, and women are now more likely than men to develop it, according to the American Cancer Society.
Under a large red boot sign on Lower Broadway in Nashville, you will find Robert’s Western World.
The bar has operated for more than 30 years and plays only traditional country music.
The walls are covered with photos of some of country music’s biggest names, who have been regulars at the bar, including Dolly Parton and Waylon Jennings.
You will find no televisions inside. Cans of beer start at $2.50.

title: Double OT, a Hat Trick and a First Career Goal Highlight Monday Soccer
text:
The County Scoreboard: Double-OT Drama and a Caribou Hat Trick Highlight Monday Soccer
Monday delivered close finishes, late-game drama and one big offensive performance as Aroostook County soccer teams continued through the final stretch of the regular season.
Presque Isle and John Bapst needed double overtime to settle a nine-goal girls matchup, Caribou answered with six goals in a win over Ellsworth, and Houlton's Will Baillargeon scored his first high school goal with three and a half minutes remaining to help the Shires earn a boys soccer tie with Ashland.
Here is a look at Monday's action.
Girls Soccer
John Bapst 5, Presque Isle 4, 2OT
Presque Isle and John Bapst played one of the day's most entertaining games, combining for nine goals before the Crusaders came away with a 5-4 victory in double overtime.
Emily Collins scored twice for the Lady Wildcats.
Delanie Cyr and Eily Hallett each added a goal, while Breanne Burlock and Carrlyn Buck recorded assists for Presque Isle.
The Wildcats battled John Bapst throughout regulation and into the second overtime before the Crusaders finally found the deciding goal.
Caribou 6, Ellsworth 2
Carly Levesque led a big offensive day for Caribou with a hat trick as the Lady Vikings defeated Ellsworth 6-2.
Quinn Corrigan was involved throughout the attack, finishing with a goal and three assists.
Shayna Pelletier and Peyton West also scored for Caribou as the Vikings put six on the board.
Boys Soccer
Houlton 1, Ashland 1
Houlton found the equalizer late in regulation to earn a 1-1 tie with Ashland.
Will Baillargeon scored with approximately three and a half minutes remaining, and the goal was a memorable one. It was the first high school goal of Baillargeon's career.
Neither side was able to find another before the game ended even.
John Bapst 4, Presque Isle 2
John Bapst completed the varsity sweep of Presque Isle with a 4-2 victory in the boys matchup.
The Wildcats put two goals on the board but could not overcome the Crusaders' four-goal performance.
Ellsworth 3, Caribou 1
Ellsworth earned a 3-1 victory over Caribou in Monday's boys matchup.
The result gave Caribou and Ellsworth a split of their varsity contests after the Lady Vikings earned a 6-2 victory earlier in the day.

Easton came out with a 6-1 victory over PCS.
Mason Pelletier led the charge with a 2 goal, 3 assist afternoon, Anthony Toompkins added in two goals of his own, with Josiah Ellis and Aaden Tibbets adding in scores for the Bears.

title: Both of Maine's senators oppose Trump's diesel deal with Putin
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Both of Maine's senators, Collins and King, oppose Trump's diesel deal with Putin
Sen. Susan Collins and Sen. Angus King, both of Maine, are among the members of Congress who have expressed opposition to the deal President Donald Trump reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import tons of Russian diesel to the United States.
Collins, a Republican, is one of 12 senators who sent a letter to Trump on Tuesday that calls on the president to rescind the Russian diesel deal.
"Congress and the American people support ending the Russia-Ukraine war, which has cost hundreds of thousands of lives over the last four and a half years because Russia chose to invade its neighbor," the senators said in the letter. "A brokered peace, however, must be on just terms. It must uphold democratic values, the sovereignty and security of Ukraine, and their people's right to choose their future."
"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war," the senators continued. "This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded."
Collins, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.), Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) also urged Trump to implement sanctions authorized by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which the president signed into law last month.
"Both chambers passed the legislation with resounding, bipartisan votes, clearly demonstrating our intent and granting you the authorities to broker a just and fair peace. These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," the senators concluded.
The letter comes two days after Collins, Shaheen, Blumenthal, Murkowski, Tillis, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) issued a joint statement opposing Russian diesel fuel imports to the United States.
King, an independent, issued a statement on Saturday in response to Trump's agreement with Putin, calling the deal "a fraud." He then wrote an opinion piece with retired U.S. Army Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling, the Army's former commander in Europe, that was published in the New York Times on Monday. In the op-ed, King and Hertling argued that the White House and Pentagon are putting global stability at risk.
On Tuesday, King appeared on CNN News Central and was asked about Trump's diesel deal with Putin.
"Unfortunately, it's just one more nail in the coffin of our foreign policy for the past 80 years, which has been deterrence, particularly against aggressors," King said. "The only beneficiary of this so-called deal that the president has announced is Vladimir Putin. It's not going to do a damn thing about the price of diesel. It's going to undermine Ukraine, where they're trying to save their country from an aggressive and murderous dictator. And it's basically going to give Putin more money to bomb hospitals, the electric grid and civilians in Ukraine."
King also pointed to a law passed in 2022 that explicitly bans Russian energy imports in an effort to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's war against Ukraine.
"(The deal is) illegal. It's wrong. It's immoral, and the only real beneficiary is Vladimir Putin," King said in the CNN interview. "It's just not going to move the needle on diesel prices. It's a political stunt."
Trump has held fast to his deal with Putin and lashed out, blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for America's high diesel costs and asserting he should step aside — something Ukraine's leader has no intention of doing.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

title: Celebration of Life for Anne Butler
Louise C. Vannah Brown
text:
Louise C. Vannah Brown, age 82, of Jefferson, passed away peacefully on the evening of Oct. 3, 2026, at MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta.
Born on July 28, 1944, to George and Elisabeth (Fitch) Vannah, she was the eldest of four children. Louise attended local schools and graduated from Waldoboro High School in 1962, later attending beautician school in Portland. On Sept. 12, 1966, she married Nelson Brown, of Jefferson, while he was home on leave from Vietnam. Louise was employed for many years at GE Sylvania in Waldoboro and later worked for the state of Maine’s Bureau of Taxation, retiring in 1996.
Animals were woven into the very fabric of Louise’s life. She found immense joy in her beloved horses — Bo Jangles, Lacey, and Topper — and her many dogs, including Heidi, Sara Lee, Kojak, Digger, Molly, Dobe, Jesse, and Brandy. Her creativity shone brightly through her artwork, her floral arrangements, and the perennial gardens she tended with such devotion.
Her family extends their deepest gratitude to Whitney Fraser, Emily Sprague, and Betsy Woodard for the extraordinary kindness and gentle care they provided to Louise.
Louise was predeceased by her parents; her husband, Nelson; her sister, Nancy; and her nephew, Tommy.
Louise is survived by her sister, Bonnie Orff and her husband Burton; her brother, Ernest Vannah and his wife Colleen; and her sister-in-law, Sharon Brown. She also leaves behind her beloved dog, Sara Lee, as well as many nieces, nephews, great-nieces, great-nephews, and cousins.
Per Louise’s request, there will be no public services.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home, Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the Brown family, please visit Louise’s Book of Memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Woman charged with criminal homicide after 3-year-old, father found dead at resort
text:
POCONO TOWNSHIP, Pa. (WFMZ) — A woman has been charged with criminal homicide after a 3-year-old boy and his father were found dead in a guest room at a Great Wolf Lodge in Pocono Township, Pennsylvania.
The Monroe County district attorney said 27-year-old Metallica Harrison was charged in the deaths.
Police said Harrison called 911 and told authorities her son and husband were already dead.
When officers arrived at the room, they noticed injuries to Harrison’s wrist and neck.
The criminal complaint says officers found that both the boy and man were deceased and appeared to have suffered stab wounds.
“This was a violent domestic tragedy in which two people, the boy and the father, lost their lives. There are charges filed now against the woman who was actually the caller,” said Mike Mancuso, the Monroe County district attorney.

title: ICE takes over Susan Collins-Troy Jackson debate 3 months after Biddeford killing
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins acknowledged Tuesday that President Donald Trump’s administration deployed too many immigration agents without proper vetting, as Democrat Troy Jackson closed their third debate by saying she “paid for the bullets” in a fatal shooting in Biddeford.
The debate, hosted by WABI and WAGM, was the third of four in 10 days. It fell three months after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, a Colombia native who was not the target of a warrant. Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash, holds a narrow polling lead in the crucial race.
Collins’ comments echoed reforms she has pushed since the shooting, but they were among her sharpest on the agency following the July shooting. Jackson’s campaign previewed his ICE attack hours before the debate, and he closed on a line that appeared to be written in advance.
“Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump’s command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger,” Jackson said in his closing statement.
He was referring to the June immigration funding package Collins voted for weeks before the shooting, which Democrats have made a centerpiece of their attacks on her. Jackson again said it gave ICE $70 billion without reforms, a figure he has repeatedly overstated. ICE got about $38 billion, with most of the rest going to Customs and Border Protection. Collins secured money for training and oversight, though not mask bans and warrant requirements Democrats wanted.
Collins, a Republican seeking a sixth term, restated that ICE needs reform but should not be abolished. She cited $20 million she secured for body cameras, a 17% budget increase for the Homeland Security inspector general and more money for de-escalation training.
“I think what happened is far too many ICE officers were hired and deployed without adequate vetting and training,” Collins said.
Jackson, who wants to abolish ICE and move its work to CBP, an agency prevalent in border areas including Aroostook County, seized on the admission and called ICE a rogue agency doing Trump’s bidding.
In a rejoinder, Collins tried to outflank Jackson by countering that the agents who fatally shot Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January were from CBP. Jackson conceded some may have been but blamed a culture he said ICE created.
Collins’ argument was that her clout gets results for Maine. Through an hour dominated by energy costs, healthcare and Trump’s tariffs on Canada, she said several times that she and Jackson would have voted the same way on the Iran war, the tariffs and Trump’s tax-and-spending law, but that only she could deliver. She pointed to nearly $37 million in federal heating aid released early after she lobbied the administration, and to tariff exemptions for Canadian pulp, concrete and road salt.
“Our Constitution guarantees that regardless of population, each state has two senators, but it does not guarantee that all 100 senators will have the same knowledge, experience, and clout,” Collins said in her closing statement.
Jackson said he would not give her credit for pulling a few items off the tariff list “when we should have never had a list.” He also argued that Democrats need control of the Senate to end the Iran war, after Collins said there were not enough votes to do so.
The exchanges grew testy as the night went on. Collins said Jackson had “repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long,” and she attacked him for not yet filing a campaign finance report. His first one is due Thursday because he replaced former nominee Graham Platner after the last quarterly deadline. He promised to release it Wednesday morning, a day early.
The candidates meet a final time Thursday at the Gracie Theater in Bangor, in a debate hosted by News Center Maine, The Portland Press Herald and Maine Public. It will be the only one with a live audience and questions from voters.

title: Police confiscate robot that groped 16-year-old girl, probe whether young men were at the controls
text:
COLOGNE, Germany (AP) — German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said.
Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot’s suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault.
They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online.
Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot’s movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time.
Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said.
“We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was ”new territory for us.”
Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men’s mobile phones were confiscated.
North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground.
The robot, said to be 120 cm (about 3 ft 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache.
Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street.
One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area.
On the police’s Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticized inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim.

title: Cautious optimism for job market outlook ahead of election
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. labor market appears to have stalled. Several recent months have seen negative job growth, and just 29,000 jobs were created last month.
The Bank of America Institute looked into their job data, and believes, despite poor top line numbers, there is reason for optimism.
“Our overall impression is things are not too bad. Now obviously we had a weak payrolls just last week, print from last week, but actually in our data, it’s consistent really with fairly decent employment growth overall,” said David Tinsley, Bank of America Institute senior economist.
The Bank of America Institute notes lower income household wages are starting to catch up to higher income household wages. Also, more people are switching jobs, with July showing the highest rate of job changes in more than three years.
“One of the things we also see in our data is that the raises people get when they switch has moved higher over the last year or so,” Tinsley said.
Economists believe there are many components leading to lower job creation, but the idea that AI is leading to mass layoffs is currently overblown.
“We just don’t see that yet. I mean the data is not playing out to back that up,” said Sean Murphy, with the Bipartisan Policy Center.
Murphy said one issue is that Americans don’t have the skillset for the kinds of skilled trade jobs that are in demand.
“And many of those are really good paying family wage type of jobs, but we just don’t necessarily have the workforce to fill them,” Murphy said.
Murphy believes Congress could improve the situation by supporting legislation that funds job training to set Americans up for success for the jobs of tomorrow.
“Really thinking about how do we get more strategic about how do we connect the talent to opportunity moving forward,” Murphy said.
The economy and employment have consistently topped polls of voters’ concerns.

title: Is Maine’s moose permit lottery truly fair?
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
In Maine, the annual moose permit lottery is a high-profile event. For many big game hunters, winning a permit means a chance at the hunt of a lifetime. But with thousands of permits available and far more applicants than permits, the odds of being selected can be formidable.
Maine allocated 3,631 moose hunting permits to residents and nonresidents in 2026. Last year, 76,217 people applied for a permit.
Every year, there are far more unsuccessful applicants than winners, and some skeptics who follow the list of winners ask the same questions: “Is the lottery really fair?” “I have been applying for more than 20 years unsuccessfully, yet my neighbor has been drawn three times? How can that be fair?” Or, “I know a family that got three permits the same year.”
To address these concerns, the Northwoods Sporting Journal asked the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife how it accounts for every paid chance, including additional chances purchased by nonresidents, and who independently verifies the drawing. The questions also addressed software audits, recordkeeping and whether an outside auditor has certified that the lottery follows its published rules.
The lottery is administered through a rigorous, impartial and carefully verified process, with multiple levels of review and safeguards in place to ensure that the rules are applied consistently, applicant information is accurate and every eligible applicant has an equal opportunity in the drawing, the department said.
“We spend weeks checking and rechecking the data, the program, the results, and after the lottery is complete,” the department said.
As a public agency in Maine, MDIFW is audited by the Maine State Auditor every three to five years, the department said. Because it receives federal funds, it also undergoes additional oversight. Multiple department employees review the lottery process, and the final applicant and chance database is independently reconciled. The department said checking and vetting the database takes several weeks.
The lottery process works by assigning a random number to each purchased chance and each preference point associated with an application. The lowest random number drawn is assigned to the application. After every application has a random number, the applications are sorted, and permits are assigned to those with the lowest numbers.
The computer program used to conduct the lottery is independently tested in multiple ways, both as a complete program and through tests of its individual components, the department said. Multiple people repeatedly test the program to ensure it functions as intended and that the lottery is conducted accurately. After the lottery, the results are retained and reviewed to ensure the drawing was conducted properly.
However, the department did not address several questions about independent oversight, including who verifies the drawing, whether an independent auditor has certified that the lottery follows its rules and whether records are kept to allow the drawing to be independently reproduced. It also did not provide the requested totals for the chances entered in the resident and nonresident drawings.
MDIFW said it welcomes questions about the lottery. Contact Mary Ellen Wickett at 207-215-6974 or maryellen.wickett@maine.gov for more information.

title: Partial demolition of collapsed bridge in Old Town begins Tuesday morning
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - Starting Tuesday, a bridge in Old Town that collapsed during construction almost two months ago will be partially demolished.
The replacement Llewelyn Estes bridge spanning the Stillwater River collapsed in August when crews were pouring concrete as part of a years-long construction project, injuring three workers.
Crews will start the process of removing impacted spans of the bridge Tuesday morning between the hours of 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. Work could continue into next week.
Workers will separate the damaged span from the pier and abutment, making the pieces smaller before removing them from the river.
Maine DOT says the temporary bridge will be closed for periods while crews work, although exact times are fluid.

title: Deborah Ann (Moody) Cunningham
text:
Deborah Ann (Moody) Cunningham, 73 of Nobleboro, passed away at her home with her loving husband and sons by her side. Born in Waldoboro on May 27, 1953, she was the daughter of Donald A. and Mavis M. (Lewis) Moody.
Deborah grew up in Newcastle and graduated from Lincoln Academy in 1971. On Dec. 20, 1975 she married Owen Cunningham and the couple started a family. Throughout the years, she worked for Chapman & Chapman Insurance and Waldoboro Family Medicine, but her most important role was as homemaker and mother to their two boys.
Deborah loved sewing, quilt making, and camping. More than anything though, she enjoyed spending time with her family.
She is survived by her husband, Owen Cunningham; her son, Mathew Cunningham and his wife, Jennifer; son, Jason Cunningham; two grandchildren, Spencer and Carolyn; a sister, Donna McNally and her husband Robert; and brother, Donald Moody and his wife Doreen.
A private graveside service will be held for her family in the Dunbar Cemetery in Nobleboro. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in her memory to Pope Memorial Humane Society, P.O. Box 1294, Rockland, ME 04841.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for his family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: Man accused of killing 2 family members with a chainsaw, decapitating both
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - A 47-year-old Alabama man was arrested Monday in connection with the murder of two family members.
According to the Mobile Police Department, Thomas Steele was taken into custody after officers found two women dead inside a home when they were responding to a death investigation Monday afternoon.
Police allege Steele intentionally killed the two women. According to court documents, Steele used a chainsaw in the killings, decapitating both.
The 47-year-old was arrested and booked into Mobile County Metro Jail, where records show he was charged with two counts of murder.
The identities of the victims were being withheld pending notification of next of kin.
Anyone with further information regarding the investigation has been urged to contact the Mobile Police Department at 251-208-7211.

title: State says infection control issues at CMMC in Lewiston could jeopardize Medicare agreement
text:
In an investigation of sterile processing contamination issues at Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston in late August, state and federal officials found ongoing infection control deficiencies and said the hospital could be terminated from the Medicare program if they are not resolved by early January.
On Aug. 21, during an investigation of several complaints at the hospital, the state declared that CMMC’s failure to address contamination issues posed an immediate risk to patients. Officials had observed an unknown orange and yellow substance inside four sterile surgical instrument trays marked “ready for use.” All instrument trays that go through the sterile processing department were stained with the same substance, staff confirmed.
This “had been a known issue since 2023,” the department’s staff told state officials.
The Lewiston hospital sent some surgical patients to other hospitals after the state’s finding. The immediate jeopardy situation, “in which a recipient of care has suffered or is likely to suffer serious injury, harm, impairment or death,” was resolved by the afternoon of Aug. 24, but officials from the Maine Department of Health and Human Services and the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) continued investigating the facility and interviewing staff and management about observed issues.
In a written notice to CMMC CEO Allen Stefanek on Oct. 8 detailing the results of that investigation, a CMS enforcement official said “substantial noncompliance remains” with three conditions that allow hospitals to participate in the federal Medicare program, including deficiencies with CMMC’s infection control stewardship, physical environment and governing body.
If the hospital does not comply with the conditions by Jan. 6, 2027, CMS may terminate its Medicare agreement. A CMMC spokesperson said Tuesday the hospital has implemented a plan of correction that includes updated policies, quality audits and ongoing monitoring.
Even so, they said, “we have no evidence that any instrument used in patient care at CMMC was non-sterile or contaminated. CMMC routinely monitors its sterilization processes and equipment, and its surgical site infection rate has consistently remained below the national average.”
According to the investigation report, hospital leadership failed to implement an infection prevention and control program, maintain a clean and sanitary environment, and address infection control findings.
Specifically, officials said, CMMC failed to ensure that supplies used during surgical procedures were sterile, that operating room tables “were free of rust and chipped paint” and that expired supplies were removed from patient care areas, including operating room tubing, tube clamps and airway devices that expired in 2024.
Sanitary issues impacted six out of seven operating rooms, two cardiac operating rooms, the cardiac catheterization lab, the emergency department, common areas and four hospital units, including a rehabilitation ward, the report said.
Staff in the sterile processing department told state investigators they had observed staining in the sterile surgical instrument trays since 2023. When asked how many trays had been returned from the operating room to be reprocessed due to contamination, the department’s manager said: “None, no one turns the trays away. We would have to close the doors due to the prevalence of the issue.”
These issues, and the hospital’s failure to correct them, are of “such character as to substantially limit the hospital’s capacity to furnish adequate care and/or as to adversely affect the health and safety of patients,” the CMS notice said.
The Central Maine Healthcare system includes CMMC, hospitals in Bridgton and Rumford, and several physician practices.
The health system’s infection prevention plan for fiscal year 2025 flagged contamination issues as “high risk” for CMMC’s sterile processing department, also called perioperative services, according to the investigation report.
The health system flagged the same issue in its fiscal year 2026 infection plan.
In 13 CMMC board of directors meetings from fiscal year 2026, there was no discussion of infection control concerns, according to the state’s review of meeting minutes. The most recent meeting was in July. The chair of the board had been absent for three out of five meetings, the state found.
“Regarding concerns in the perioperative and sterile processing department of this magnitude,” the chair told the state in an Aug. 26 interview, “I learned about it during this survey. It came to my knowledge last week.”
Central Maine Healthcare was acquired by California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation in February. In a statement on Sep. 9, a spokesperson said the nonprofit had committed more than $50 million toward replacing Central Maine Healthcare’s electronic medical records system, rebuilding the workforce and improving infrastructure and recruitment.
The spokesperson at the time did not note any investments in the sterile processing department, but said Tuesday that “CMMC continues to invest” in the department and provide oversight as part of an ongoing commitment to quality and safety.
The hospital’s operating rooms are no longer on diversion and have returned to normal operations, the spokesperson said.
The state also identified standard-level deficiencies at Central Maine Healthcare’s outpatient practices, including at Central Maine Obstetrics-Gynecology, where front office staff said they were instructed to turn pregnant patients away due to short staffing and other issues. The state said this was a failure by Central Maine Healthcare to communicate waitlist expectations and provide care to patients in need, as mandated by hospital bylaws.
It’s not uncommon for the state to investigate complaints at Maine’s hospitals. Over the last two years, the state has investigated CMMC 14 other times and identified a handful of standard-level deficiencies, as opposed to the condition-level deficiencies found in August. A complaint investigation from late 2025 even concluded that CMMC was in substantial compliance with infection prevention and control standards.
MaineHealth Maine Medical Center was investigated by the state for complaints 25 times in the same two-year timeframe. St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston was investigated nine times and on one visit the state identified noncompliance with Medicare conditions related to the hospital’s medical staff bylaws.
Noncompliant hospitals have the opportunity to correct deficiencies, but in the meantime, the federal government considers the hospital to be unaccredited and grants full jurisdiction to the state agency to oversee all accreditation complaints and monitoring visits.
This “standard CMS process” is happening at CMMC, said Lindsay Hammes, Maine DHHS spokesperson.
“We are committed to maintaining rigorous sterilization standards, addressing identified opportunities for improvement and ensuring patients receive care in an environment focused on quality and safety,” a CMMC spokesperson said.

title: Vatican says pope’s lung nodule surgery was successfully completed
text:
Vatican says Pope Leo XIV has lung cancer, had lower lobe of his right lung removed
Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery Tuesday that confirmed that he has lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican said.
The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The statement made no mention of treatment going forward, and the Vatican said doctors were not currently speaking of chemotherapy or other therapies. The Vatican press office noted the medical statement spoke of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer.
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about three hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.
Leo had walked into Rome’s Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
Oncologists said prior to the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20.
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Video below: Doctor talks the Pope's recent surgery announcement
Recovery could allow November travel to South America
There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
Oncologists often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery — which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery.
The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.
Pope was hospitalized for typhoid fever in 1985
This is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome — a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for “Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.”
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the “horrible” pain of the fever. “I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’
“Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, 'Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here — the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.' I never looked back.”

title: Avery Cochrane Is Bringing Camp, Chaos and Big Pop Energy to Her Debut Album [Exclusive]
text:
Avery Cochrane Went From Caddying to Chasing Pop Stardom – Now She’s Ready for Her Close-Up [Exclusive]
Avery Cochrane is gearing up for her next pop era, and she's doing it on her own terms.
The rising pop singer will release her debut album, Vengeance Through My Omnipresence, on Jan. 29, 2027, following the success of her debut EP Male Validation and Other Drugs.
With more than 20 million streams to her name and "Shapeshifting on a Saturday Night" surpassing 46 million views on social media, Cochrane is building a colorful, campy pop universe all her own.
She's also hitting the road on the Weapons of Iridescence Tour, which includes 13 cities nationwide, with stops in Washington, D.C., New York, Chicago, and West Hollywood's historic Troubadour.
Meanwhile, her fan-favorite COCH-TOBER celebration is bringing daily surprises tied to the new album.
Ahead of this next chapter, Cochrane spoke with PopCrush about her self-made pop star journey, the sonic surprises waiting on her new album, and the deeply personal reason connecting with listeners means so much to her.
Avery Cochrane Talks New Album, Tour and Her Pop Star Journey
You literally worked odd jobs to fund the dream of becoming a pop star. Now you’re releasing your debut album. When you look at the version of yourself who was caddying and singing at a seafood restaurant to pay for studio time, what do you think would surprise her most about where you ended up?
I don’t think she’d be surprised by anything, honestly. Quite literally everything I’ve been manifesting for myself the last five years has come true, which makes me explode with gratitude.
I’m still the same scrappy and determined songwriter I’ve always been… just with slightly more budget and a bigger team. The plan has always been to move to LA and do music full time. Now that I’m here, I’m trying to figure out my next milestone.
"Toy Gun” is part of this new era, and even the title feels like it comes with a little danger and a lot of personality. What’s something about this album that you think people will not see coming based on what they know about you so far?
I’m throwing a lot of sonic surprises at everyone. As always, the project mostly prioritizes my lyrics, but the producers I’ve created it with are so incredibly skilled and creative, and the sounds we come up with in the studio together are just too good to not include in these records.
I’m excited to hear what people think of the little vocal chops and synth lines.
You’ve built such a distinct world around your music, from the campy visuals to COCH-TOBER and the whole “self-made pop diva” thing. At what point did you realize you weren’t just making songs anymore; you were building an entire universe for people to step into?
I realized I was world-building around the release of my song “Existential Crisis at the Tennis Club.” That was the first song of mine that had any sort of traction on socials, which was extremely exciting for me. I wrote the song existing in a made-up universe in which I went on to marry a boring rich man, instead of the love of my life. The aesthetics that came with that were so inspiring to me, and when it came to shooting the cover art, I wanted what I saw in this made-up universe to be reflected in it.
When I had the budget to create my first real music video (Shapeshifting), the director and I threw around the campy word a lot. The release of that song and music video felt like a debut single (though I had been releasing music for 4 years prior) because it was my first baby step into the pop world. I knew I had a bit of an audience by that point, and I really wanted to keep their attention.
You’ve spent years essentially betting on yourself before there was any guarantee that the rest of the world would catch up. Now that the album, tour, and all of this momentum are happening at once, what part of the dream still feels the most surreal to you?
Maintaining belief in myself was easy, but trying to get others to see the vision was complicated. I spent 4 years debating whether or not I was just delusional and untalented, and was told by my daydreamer parents that I was a star too many times as a kid. Yes, I wanted the pop stardom, but more than anything I wanted to be a writer.
As an ex-willfully-idiotic-teenage-girl (for the bit), nobody, including myself, took my intellect seriously. Once I dropped the act and started really writing, a skill I always suspected I had, everything clicked. Seeing people singing my overthought and hyper-specific lyrics back to me challenges the deep-seated belief I had in my incompetence. I didn’t know I had the power to connect with others through my words. That’s the most surreal part.

title: Spruce Mountain schools target fourth grade math decline as scores improve
text:
JAY — Math scores are improving among younger students in Regional School Unit 73, but a decline in performance beginning in fourth grade has prompted a closer examination of classroom instruction, curriculum consistency and teacher training.
Chris Hollingsworth, the district’s curriculum and technology coordinator, presented three years of assessment data during the Oct. 8 board of directors meeting, highlighting gains in third grade math performance while identifying challenges as students advance to more complex material.
“We actually have shown growth in math over the last three years,” Hollingsworth said.
Third-grade assessment scores increased from 1495 to 1499 and then to 1501 over the three years, approaching the state benchmark of 1505, according to figures Hollingsworth presented.
He also reported that the percentage of third grade students in a performance category identified as green increased from 42% to 55% between the first two years reviewed, compared with statewide figures of 48% and 49%, respectively.
Despite those gains, Hollingsworth said students struggle to maintain their progress as they move into fourth grade, when instruction introduces more challenging concepts and additional word problems.
“The bad news is things seem to go well until the end of third grade and then we kind of hit a cliff,” he said.
The findings have prompted a review of how teachers use Math in Focus, the district’s mathematics curriculum. Hollingsworth said conversations with elementary school teachers revealed considerable variation in the instructional resources being used across classrooms.
He is working with building principals to align Math in Focus lessons with the district’s established scope and sequence, which outlines the progression of mathematical skills students are expected to master before reaching high school algebra.
The effort is intended to provide more consistent instruction across classrooms while making better use of curriculum materials the district already purchases. Hollingsworth said he plans to review the curriculum and identify lessons that correspond with the instructional sequence.
Principals will work with teachers to ensure classroom lessons follow that progression. The district hopes to use existing professional development periods and other scheduled staff time to complete the alignment work. Providing additional training to help teachers implement the curriculum effectively, however, remains a challenge.
“Unfortunately we’re not a district that has a lot of professional development money,” Hollingsworth said. He explained that funding allocated for teacher stipends associated with committee work reduces the money available for professional development. Training costs have also increased, making it difficult to bring in outside specialists.
RSU 73 participates in a regional educational collaborative that offers professional development opportunities, but Hollingsworth said relatively few neighboring districts use Math in Focus, limiting access to training tailored to the program.
He is contacting the collaborative’s director to explore opportunities for additional support, including training focused on elementary mathematics instruction.
The district’s approach involves two related efforts: aligning existing curriculum materials with instructional expectations and identifying affordable ways to give teachers the training needed to use those materials effectively.
Hollingsworth said much of the curriculum alignment can be completed through planning and collaboration with principals, while additional training will depend on available funding. He expects the work to continue throughout the school year, with principals taking a central role in coordinating instructional changes across buildings.
The district also plans to revisit professional development needs during upcoming budget discussions, when the costs and potential benefits of additional training can be considered. Hollingsworth cautioned that the challenges facing RSU 73 are not unique to Spruce Mountain schools, pointing to broader concerns about math achievement across Maine.
“It’s not a Spruce Mountain issue,” he said. “It’s a whole state issue.”
While the district works to address declining performance in higher grades, Hollingsworth emphasized the importance of making full use of the resources already available. “When we’re paying for Math in Focus, we want to make sure that we’re getting everything out of that as well,” he said.
RSU 73 includes Jay, Livermore and Livermore Falls.

title: One seriously injured in Auburn crash after attempted traffic stop
text:
One seriously injured in Auburn, Maine, crash after attempted traffic stop
Officials say the crash happened after driver failed to stop for sheriff's deputy.
One seriously injured in Auburn, Maine, crash after attempted traffic stop
Officials say the crash happened after driver failed to stop for sheriff's deputy.
Authorities say one person was seriously injured in an Auburn crash that happened after a driver failed to stop for an Androscoggin County Sheriff's deputy.
The Sheriff's Office said that the deputy attempted to stop a vehicle for a traffic violation shortly after 10:40 p.m. Monday, but the vehicle continued into Auburn on Minot Avenue.
The vehicle then crashed in the 1600 block of Minot Avenue, and members of the Auburn Police and Fire departments responded to the scene.
The Sheriff's Office said a female who was in the vehicle was initially taken to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston and later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland with serious injuries.
It is unclear if the injured person was the driver of the vehicle.
The crash is being investigated by the Auburn Police Department, but the Sheriff's Office noted that it is working with Auburn police to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.

title: Police investigating embezzlement allegations related to South Portland youth soccer club
text:
South Portland police investigating embezzlement allegations related to Strikers youth soccer club
South Portland Police Chief Dan Ahern confirmed that the police department is investigating allegations of embezzlement related to the South Portland Strikers, a popular youth soccer club.
Hundreds of local children are involved with the Strikers, who play home games at the Wainwright Recreation Complex.
The president of the club, Gabe Harp, sent an email to parents Monday night, saying: "The South Portland Strikers Board of Directors is aware of an ongoing matter that involves the potential unauthorized use of club funds in 2025 and 2026 by a former member of our board."
Ahern would not provide any additional information about the case, including who is being investigated or the amount of money that was embezzled.
"We take our fiduciary responsibilities seriously, have engaged an external financial professional, and are implementing improved financial controls and governance practices," Harp said in his email to parents.
Harp's email to parents went on to say that because this is an active legal matter, the organization will not share specifics and the priority is to cooperate with law enforcement.
The Cumberland County District Attorney's Office said it could be two to three weeks before the case ends up in the DA's office and charges are filed.

title: Maintenance worker dies after being hit by truck at gas station
text:
LOUISA, Ky. (WSAZ/Gray News) - A maintenance worker was struck and killed by a semitruck at a Kentucky gas station Monday morning.
The Louisa Police Department said a worker at a gas station along U.S. 23 told police they noticed a body around 5:50 a.m. and reported it.
A few minutes after the first report, a customer came across the body, realized the victim was dead and called 911 again.
Louisa Police Chief Steven Wilburn said the maintenance worker was checking his diesel containers due to the rain. That is when a semitruck, pulling out after pumping gas, unknowingly hit the worker.
Police said the victim was kneeling in front of the truck just before he was hit.
The worker died at the scene, Wilburn said.
Police say they watched footage and were able to find the trucking company and call the truck driver back. The driver immediately returned to the scene.
The victim’s name is not being released at this time, police said.
According to the Louisa Police Department, no charges have been filed at this time.
The incident is still under investigation.
