title: What to know as Pope Leo XIV prepares for surgery to remove lung nodule
text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery Tuesday that confirmed that he has lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican said.
Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The statement made no mention of treatment going forward, and the Vatican said doctors were not currently speaking of chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests. The Vatican press office noted the medical statement spoke of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer.
Leo’s lymph nodes also would have been removed and tested, to determine if the cancer had spread, and there was no word yet on those test results.
“Adenocarcinoma is the most common (type of lung cancer), also with the most favorable prognosis,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. “While we know the diagnosis we now need to know the stage.”
“We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?” Liu said.
If the cancer has spread, more tests will be needed to determine what kind of therapy to pursue, he said. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy or targeted therapy, which involves oral pills for specific cancers.
The Vatican says the surgery was successful
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about three hours, the Vatican statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.
“The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said, adding that the pope later returned to his room.
The right lung is divided into three sections or lobes while the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the remainder of the lung can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy and physically active people.
Leo had walked into Rome’s Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
Oncologists said prior to the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis would be “excellent” since it would have been removed at an early stage.
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20.
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Recovery could allow November travel to South America
There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
Oncologists often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery — which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery.
The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
“He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.
Pope was hospitalized for typhoid fever in 1985
This is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome — a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for “Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.”
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the “horrible” pain of the fever. “I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’
“Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ’Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here — the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”
___
Barry reported from Milan. Associated Press writer Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Father of 5 killed in home by bullet believed fired by hunter, deputies say
text:
SWEET HOME, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A 54-year-old man was killed Saturday when a bullet passed through his home, according to authorities in Oregon.
The Linn County Sheriff’s Office believes the shot came from a nearby hunter.
Deputies found a partially dressed deer near where the shots were fired, Sheriff Michelle Duncan said.
The hunter left the scene. It is unclear whether the hunter knew Robert Church had been hit.
Church leaves behind five children. His daughter, Shy, said her father “was one of a kind” and “loved his children more than anything in the world.”
Neighbors said the area is popular for hunting and that the shooting happened on private property. They urged hunters to follow the rules and be aware of where they are shooting.
Duncan said investigators do not believe the shooting was intentional and urged the hunter to come forward so Church’s family can get answers and closure.
Church’s family started an online fundraiser to help with funeral expenses. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Linn County Sheriff’s Office.

title: Mainers are in for a harsh winter— thanks to Republicans
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rep. Chellie Pingree is the U.S. congresswoman for Maine’s 1st District.
Between the mountains of snow, the waves of bitter cold and the occasional Nor’easter, we
Mainers are no strangers to harsh winters.
This winter could be one of the hardest in recent memory. And not because of the weather. The statewide average price of heating oil just hit a record $6.02 a gallon. As of Sept. 28, it was still averaging $5.96 — up nearly 79% from the same week last year. At today’s price, a 250-gallon fill-up costs about $1,490 — an expense many Maine families will face more than once this winter.
Meanwhile, gas prices are hovering around $4.40 per gallon as of Sept. 25, according to
Maine Public.
As if all this wasn’t awful enough, the number of Mainers receiving assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has fallen by 13% — 13,000 people in all, including 7,000 children. Another 31,000 Mainers are projected to lose MaineCare coverage over the next year.
Add it all up and this winter is going to put an enormous strain on Maine families — especially those who can least afford it.
This looming crisis is the result of choices President Trump and congressional Republicans made. Choices they continue to defend.
Let’s back up to July 4, 2025, when the president signed his hallmark legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, into law.
The “Big Ugly Bill” is a more accurate name. It slashed Medicaid by $1.2 trillion and SNAP by $211 billion over the next decade, all while handing hundreds of billions of dollars in tax breaks to the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations.
Far from offsetting those devastating cuts, the Big Ugly Bill’s ludicrous tax breaks are projected to increase federal deficits by $4.6 trillion, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also handed $175 billion to the Department of Homeland Security, helping turbocharge the Trump administration’s cruel immigration enforcement agenda and bringing chaos and violence to communities across the country. That includes Maine, where an ICE agent shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13.
The young father was not the target of ICE’s operation that morning. He had no criminal history, and we don’t have body camera footage of the shooting. His family has still not been contacted by the federal government and is still waiting for a full accounting of what happened.
This bill will go down as one of the most irresponsible, destructive, and costly pieces of legislation in American history. Not just in terms of its fiscal recklessness, but its human toll as well: nearly 13 million fewer people enrolled in Medicaid by 2034 and roughly 2.4 million fewer people receiving SNAP in an average month, according to CBO estimates. Its consequences will reach every community in America, in shuttered rural hospitals, overwhelmed food banks and increased costs for state and local governments.
The Big Ugly Bill alone would have been devastating enough for Maine. Then Trump’s reckless, unauthorized war of choice in Iran has kicked every one of these crises into overdrive. In the nearly eight months since the war began — a conflict Trump insisted wouldn’t last more than a few weeks — the global economy has been thrown into turmoil.
The on-again, off-again closure of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, has sent energy prices skyrocketing — and disrupted the flow of goods around the world. When the world’s energy supply gets squeezed, everyone pays more. In a state like Maine, where a colder-than-average winter can mean the difference between keeping the heat on and putting on extra layers just to stay warm, the potential consequences are catastrophic.
None of this had to happen. These crises have been created or made worse by Trump’s policies — and by congressional Republicans’ refusal to push back on the president and stand up for their constituents.
And now, with Americans staring down record energy costs, Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home early for a seven-week campaign recess. Rather than staying to work on the many challenges facing our nation, Republicans tucked tail and left.
Republicans could’ve chosen to help you. They chose to help the already-rich get even richer — and to give an army of masked, heavily armed and utterly unaccountable ICE agents virtually unlimited resources to terrorize our communities.
My Democratic colleagues and I have been fighting them every step of the way. We’ve voted against these devastating cuts. We’ve introduced legislation to protect healthcare and food assistance. We’ve demanded accountability for an administration that continues to put its deeply unpopular agenda ahead of the people it’s supposed to serve.
And we are demanding action on the heating crisis: end the war in Iran, protect the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, reverse changes to the Home Owner Managing Energy Savings Rebates and High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate programs and reinstate the energy efficiency tax credits Republicans eliminated. Speaker Johnson should call the House back to Washington so Congress can get to work.
We will keep fighting — at every turn, and for as long as it takes. Because Mainers deserve better. They deserve a government that makes their lives more affordable — not one that cuts their healthcare and food assistance, sends energy prices through the roof and hands massive tax breaks to the people who need them least.
Mainers have survived plenty of hard winters. But the hardships coming this winter are the result of decisions made by Republicans in Washington, who would rather leave town than fix the problems they created.

title: Man who fell to his death while riding Six Flags roller coaster identified
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - Police have identified the man who died on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia Monday afternoon.
Cobb County police identified the victim Tuesday as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta. According to witnesses, the man fell to his death from the Goliath roller coaster, which goes at 70 miles per hour and drops twice — once at 170 feet and the other at 175 feet.
EN ESPAÑOL | Autoridades identifican al hombre que murió tras caer de montaña rusa de Six Flags
Logan Conner, who said he was on the ride with his fiancée, reported watching the man come out of his seat.
“The man started levitating in the air sideways,” Logan Conner told NBC. “We made direct eye contact with him.”
According to police, Kariem was thrown from the ride, hitting other patrons as he fell. His body was found on a nearby roof.
Britny Landry, who was waiting in line to ride the coaster a second time, said she saw somebody “fly out” but at first wasn’t sure what she saw.
“Maybe somebody had a bag or something,” she told KTVU-TV.
Several other people were injured. The exact number of victims and the extent of their injuries are unknown.
Riders were stuck on the roller coaster following the incident and had to be helped to the ground.
Six Flags Over Georgia was shut down after the incident and remained closed on Tuesday. The park will reopen on Friday, according to its website.
Kariem worked for the Atlanta Public Schools, the district confirmed on Tuesday. APS said he worked at Wesley International Academy, a K-8 charter school. It is not known what his exact role was, but his social media pages refer to him as an IT manager.
“He was a cherished member of the Wesley International Academy and APS families whose presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched. Our thoughts are with everyone mourning his loss during this difficult time,” APS said in a statement.
Six Flags has temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six parks “out of an abundance of caution.” Officials said the affected attractions are similar to Goliath, which only uses a lap bar to secure riders.
In a statement, Six Flags said it’s cooperating with the police investigation.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected,” the spokesperson said. “Out of respect for the family’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time.”
Before Monday’s incident, Six Flags Over Georgia has had at least seven deaths since its opening in 1967, according to The Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park deaths.

title: Man injured after stepping in front a vehicle in Palermo
text:
A man was taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries Tuesday after he stepped into the path of an oncoming vehicle on Route 3 in Palermo.
Shortly after 5:30 a.m., Maine State Police troopers responded to the report of a vehicle versus pedestrian crash near Level Hill Road, Shannon Moss, public information officer with the state Department of Public Safety, wrote in a news release.
Level Hill Road intersects with Route 3 between Greeley Corner and East Palermo.
The preliminary investigations shows that the man, who Moss did not identify, had parked his vehicle on the side of Route 3 and stepped out of it. The man then intentionally walked into the roadway and was struck by an oncoming vehicle.
The man, Moss said, suffered life-threatening injuries and was taken by Liberty Ambulance to Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor.
The driver of the vehicle was not injured.
Also responding were the Waldo County Sheriff’s Office, several area fire departments and Ready Road Towing.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Matt Dunlap criticizes Jared Golden in his final sprint against Paul LePage
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
State Auditor Matt Dunlap sharply criticized U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, the outgoing Democrat whose 2nd District seat he’s trying to win, at an Orono event last week.
Dunlap faulted the more moderate Golden for questioning his viability last year and for several votes in which Golden sided with the Republican House majority.
The comments showed Dunlap’s willingness to take a more progressive stand while knocking a fellow Democrat whose swing voters could help him fend off former Gov. Paul LePage in a tight race for the conservative-leaning district. The Republican’s team seized on them to paint Dunlap as out of step, and Golden said the remarks said the Democrat looks “scared of losing.”
“I don’t think he’s going to endorse me,” Dunlap said of Golden, according to audio of the event at the University of Maine in Orono obtained by the Bangor Daily News. “In fact, he probably has gone through several cases of Matt Dunlap voodoo dolls, tearing limbs off them.”
His comments at the event traced the months between Dunlap airing a primary bid against Golden last spring, his October decision to run citing the four-term congressman’s vote for a Republican-backed bill requiring proof of residency at the polls and Golden’s November decision to not seek another term.
Dunlap told attendees that he’d been approached about challenging Golden about a year and a half ago after the congressman “kind of went [missing in action]” and Democratic supporters were concerned “he might lose the next election.”
After he announced last year he was exploring a run to make sure the support behind him was genuine, it “blew up and Jared said a lot of things to the press about my viability.” Just after Dunlap announced he was exploring a run, Golden said he “has a small chance of beating me, but zero chance of beating Paul LePage.”
National Democrats backed state Sen. Joe Baldacci, D-Bangor, in the June primary. But Dunlap won, and party leaders in Maine and in Washington eventually rallied behind him in what is shaping up to be a strong year for the party. He is now in their “Red to Blue” program.
At the Orono event, Dunlap went on to say Golden had received “a pass” on many votes because of the makeup of the district. But he said Golden went too far by becoming the deciding vote against two Iran war powers resolutions, not doing enough to preserve healthcare subsidies and often being “the only Democrat voting with Republicans on their agenda.”
“It’s no secret that Matt and Jared don’t see eye to eye on everything,” Dunlap spokesperson Harry Burke told the BDN. “But as these comments show, Matt Dunlap is laser focused on ensuring Maine has a representative who will fight to lower gas prices by ending the Iran War, and lower health care costs by extending the ACA tax credits. Matt is an independent voice who isn’t afraid to criticize members of either party when he thinks they’re out of line with the district.”
In a statement, Golden replied to Dunlap’s remarks by saying a candidate usually knows who they’re running against by now and that the nominee is “running against Paul LePage, not me.”
“This comes across as someone scared of losing, and seeding the ground to shift the blame if he does,” he said.
The Democrat remains generally seen as an underdog in the race with LePage, a former two-term governor. Decision Desk HQ, the BDN’s national election results partner, sees the Republican as having a 64% chance of winning.
LePage has been under fire from Dunlap over his alignment with President Donald Trump, his age and his failure to file his required financial disclosure on deadline. In a debate last week, Dunlap mostly avoided attacking the president directly but criticized the administration on high costs, Iran, immigration enforcement and Medicaid while arguing Congress should be a check on the White House.
“It’s just one more example of how extreme Matt Dunlap is that Jared Golden isn’t liberal enough for [him],” LePage adviser Brent Littlefield said of the Democrat’s criticism of Golden. “He’s so far to the left, he’s out of step with the district.”

title: A man falls to his death from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia
text:
Police are investigating after a man fell to his death from a roller coaster at a Six Flags near Atlanta, watched by other visitors to the amusement park as he was catapulted from the ride.
Officials have not confirmed how the man died Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia in Austell, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta. No information has been released about the condition of several others who were hurt.
Cobb County Police Department major crimes unit detectives are investigating.
Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the ride associated with the man’s death, but local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath roller coaster.
Logan Conner said he was on the Goliath with his fiancée when he saw the man come out of his seat.
“The man started levitating in the air sideways,” he told NBC. “We made direct eye contact with him.”
Britny Landry had been on the ride earlier Monday and was waiting in line to go again. She could see part of the Goliath track.
“We just look, and I just see somebody fly out,” she told KTVU-TV. She said she wasn’t sure if that’s what she saw at first. “Maybe somebody had a bag or something.”
Six Flags Entertainment Corporation temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks, “out of an abundance of caution,” according to a company spokesperson, who said staff members and local authorities responded immediately and that the park is cooperating with the investigation.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said, adding that the company is providing support to guests and staff who were impacted.
Police and Six Flags did not immediately respond to messages seeking additional information Tuesday. A message seeking comment also was sent to the state Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner.
Goliath, which was opened in 2006, reaches a top speed of 70 mph (113 kph) with a height of 200 feet (61 meters), according to the park’s website.
During about 3 1/2 minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills,” the website says.
Lisa Cupid, Cobb County Board of Commissioners chairwoman, said next of kin of the man who died have been notified.
“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” Cupid said. “We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories.”
The park is a major part of the county’s tourism and brings in visitors from across the Southeast, Cupid said.
The death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tallies amusement park accidents and represents victims.
It also comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California announced the retirement of its famous X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. The park settled one wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.
Last year, a 32-year-old man died from blunt impact injuries after riding a high-speed roller coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. His death was ruled accidental.
—-
Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack contributed to this report.

title: Longtime Portland boys basketball coach Joe Russo retires
text:
Joe Russo has retired as Portland High’s boys basketball coach.
Russo, 69, had been weighing the decision to retire for months — his friends and fellow coaches would say years. On Tuesday he made it public.
“I handed in my resignation. I sat and had a good conversation with Spencer (Allen, the Portland athletic director),” Russo said Tuesday evening. “Something is telling me this is the right time.
“The truth is, I still enjoy it. I wish I could do it forever. But I knew I would have to give it up sometime. When do I pass the torch? And I just said, ‘maybe this is the time.'”
A Portland native, Russo coached the Bulldogs for 36 seasons and won his sixth state championship with the program in February, guiding a gritty, defense-oriented team that lost six regular-season games while dealing with injuries, sickness, and players staying away from practice during a large-scale immigration enforcement operation.
“There’s not many leaders out there who could have navigated all of that and keep teenagers focused,” said South Portland boys basketball coach Kevin Millington.
Millington said he used to joke that “this was the 15th straight year (Russo) had said he was done but I always felt this year was different. Not because they had won (the championship) but because of the way he said it.”
Russo said that his final game being a state championship win had little to do with his decision.
“I never really coached for championships. I always coached to be competitive, for the players to be the best they can, and give a good effort,” Russo said. “When I do look back, it won’t be the last year I won. It will be that I’ve been very fortunate to have 36 great years,” at Portland.
Russo’s boys basketball teams won 517 games, including 11 over his first three seasons at Bonny Eagle. At Portland, he also helped start and coach the Portland girls volleyball program.
In 2018, the same year Russo was inducted into the Maine Basketball Hall of Fame, he overcame non-Hodgkin Large B Cell Lymphoma cancer. Russo was back coaching both volleyball and boys basketball in the 2018-19 school year.
Russo said he is healthy and that was not a factor in his decision to retire.
Russo won his 500th game in a AA North quarterfinal in 2025. That made him the 10th coach in Maine high school basketball history to reach the mark. He is now sixth on the all-time wins list.
After the Bulldogs defeated Camden Hills to win the 2026 Class A title, Russo indicated to friends, peers, and other acquaintances that he had probably just coached his last game.
He had made similar statements for at least a decade, usually in the muted light of a Cross Insurance Arena hallway after Portland had been eliminated. Russo would look tired and worn down. Then he would take a couple of weeks to think about it and by the next season would be back on Portland’s sideline.
Last season felt different. The Bulldogs won a state title and Russo was beaming. In mid-summer, Russo was still waiting to make his retirement final but also saying he was 98% sure he was done. He was letting his assistant coaches run the summer program.
As late as mid-September, Allen, the Portland AD, said he figured each day that passed increased the odds that Russo would return as Portland’s coach. Allen joked that on the days Russo was at the high school as a part-time physical education teacher he would try to avoid crossing paths with Russo.
“If he doesn’t see me he can’t give me his resignation,” Allen said.
As recently as last week, Russo said he was tempted to keep coaching, “because our freshmen are dynamite.”
The first day of practice for the 2026-27 season is Nov. 16, less than five weeks away.
Possible in-program successors as head coach would be top assistant Dan LeGage, a former head coach at Westbrook, and long-time assistant Joe Johnson. Russo’s longest tenured assistant Joe Giordano has indicated previously that he planned to step aside whenever Russo retired.
Russo said there are a “lot of qualified people,” who could succeed him, including several in “our own building.” He added that because he’ll likely know so many of the candidates he doesn’t want to be involved in the hiring process.
Russo was born on Dec. 7, 1956, the same day as Boston Celtics legend Larry Bird. Russo and his family moved from a different Portland neighborhood to Munjoy Hill when he was in third grade. The new house had a basketball hoop.
“So I started playing it. I played all the way through college and rec leagues. I studied the game,” Russo said. A point guard known for his defense, Russo said he was often referred to as “peppery,” by Portland sportscaster Frank Fixaris.
After graduating from Portland High in 1975, Russo earned a degree and played basketball at UMaine Presque Isle. He started his teaching and coaching career at Bonny Eagle, a job he enjoyed, but he and his wife Donna, who met in junior high and began dating as high school juniors, both wanted to stay in Portland. The Russos have been married 46 years. They have three grown children and nine grandchildren.
After his 500th win, Russo talked about what it meant to him to teach and coach at Portland High.
“When this job (at Portland) came, it was the dream job, pretty much,” Russo said. “Mainly because being from Portland and going to Portland High, you’re happy for the players. I was just like them growing up. So it means a lot when you’re doing it for the school you grew up in. I’m happy for the city and the school and the kids.”
Russo’s Portland teams won state championships in 1999, 2004, 2014, 2016, 2017, and 2026, and finished as state runner-up in 2007, 2015, and 2023.
The 2016, 2017, and 2023 state finals were against South Portland.
“From a basketball perspective, Joe’s teams were always an elite defensive team,” Millington said. “The other thing he’s really elite at is, he’s very patient. Maybe that comes with age. He wasn’t trying to win the state championship in the first game or the fifth game and they were always much better at the end of the year than they were in the beginning.”

title: Two killed in head-on crash involving wrong-way driver on I-95
text:
MEDWAY, Maine (WABI) - Two people are dead following a crash involving a wrong-way driver in a stolen car on I-95 in northern Penobscot County.
According to Maine State Police, drivers reported seeing a car traveling south in the northbound lanes in Island Falls just before 9:30 Monday night.
Officials say an East Millinocket police officer encountered the car near mile marker 248 when it was traveling more than 100 miles per hour. The officer attempted a traffic stop, but the driver, Luis Mendoza, 20, of Indian Township, continued at a high rate of speed, police say.
The car then entered a construction zone just south of exit 244 in Medway and struck another car head-on, according to officials. The construction zone had concrete barriers separating northbound and southbound traffic.
Mendoza and the driver of the second car, Sandra Lacombe, 67, of Medway, both died at the scene. Each car had one occupant.
During the search for the wrong-way driver, authorities discovered the car that Mendoza was driving had been stolen from a Hannaford in Houlton, police say.
The crash site was closed for several hours Monday night, causing traffic delays.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Stolen Vehicle Chase Ends In Head-on Collision On I-95 Near Medway
text:
Two Killed In Medway After Driver, Trying To Evade Police In Allegedly Stolen Car, Enters Construction Zone The Wrong Way
There was a massive police presence in Medway Monday evening authorities tried to piece together how two people ended up dead following a police chase.
How Authorities Say It All Started
According to the Maine State Police, the incident began in the how of Houlton, when a 2011 Toyota Camry was stolen from the Hannaford parking lot there.
The man driving the stolen Camry, 20-year-old Luis Mendoza of Indian Township, headed south upon allegedly stealing the car. Reports of a wrong-way driver started to come into dispatchers around 9:21 PM. Callers reached out to the Bangor Regional Communications Center stating a car was driving south bound in the north bound lanes in the area of Island Falls.
Read More: Bangor Broadway Bridge Project Final Phases Start October 16
State and local law enforcement agents began to head in that direction. They did not yet know the car was stolen from Houlton, just that it was driving the wrong way.
What Happened Next
According to authorities, Mendoza kept travelling south to the Millinocket, where it was reported that he was driving southbound on the interstate at speeds upwards of 100 miles an hour. A member of the East Millinocket Police Department came across the vehicle at around mile marker 248 at 9:48 PM.
When the officer, who at this point had turned around and caught up with the speeding Camry, attempted to stop the vehicle, the situation went from dangerous to deadly.
"The officer continued south and began entering the crossover at mile marker 244 to enter the correct flow of traffic. The wrong-way vehicle continued south in the northbound lanes and entered a construction zone on a bridge in Medway just south of Exit 244. Due to construction, southbound traffic is diverted onto the northbound bridge, with concrete barriers separating one lane of northbound traffic from one lane of southbound traffic. The wrong-way vehicle entered the construction zone traveling south in the northbound lane and struck another vehicle head on."
The end result of the crash
Mendoza was killed. The collision also killed the driver and sole occupant of the other car involved, 67-year-old Sandra Lacombe of Medway.
Read More: Maine Man Shot And Killed In Indian Township, Suspect Arrested
Authorities had the area shut down for several hours trying to figure out what happened. Later it was determined that the car had been stolen in Houlton. The investigation is still ongoing.

title: Store says AI-generated receipt was used to secure fraudulent purse refund
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ALICE, Texas (KIII) — Employees at Horseshoes Western Wear said they are learning a new lesson about protecting the business after a fake, apparently AI-generated receipt was used to obtain a warranty refund.
Manager Inez Almaraz said the store’s owner learned from a distributor that a receipt appearing to be AI-generated was used to get a warranty refund for a purse.
“We’ve never had anything or any of this happen, especially with something that we carry. For them to produce or generate a fake AI receipt is something that’s just not tolerated,” Almaraz said.
Distributor fell victim to fake receipt
Almaraz said the purse involved was a Consuela designer purse, which the store carries and sells.
“Consuela is a designer purse, and we are fortunate to be able to carry it and sell it,” Almaraz said.
The distributor fell victim to the fake receipt before it was identified as fraudulent.
A comparison of the real receipt and the fake showed differences, including the wrong address.
Retail seller Angel Ramos said employees found the discrepancy because the store did not carry the purse listed on the fake receipt.
“Just be more cautious. Look at your receipts. Pay attention to your systems. Just keep track of your inventory because we didn’t carry that purse,” Ramos said.
Better Business Bureau says AI making fakes harder to detect
The Better Business Bureau says artificial intelligence is making it easier for scammers to create convincing documents, meaning businesses can’t always rely on obvious mistakes to spot a fake.
Katie Galan with the Better Business Bureau said scammers rely on urgency to avoid detection.
“What they want is for you to rush and to not have the time to verify, to ask questions, to look at that receipt a little closer. So, that’s what they prey on, is us being in so much of a rush that we don’t have time to double-check things,” Galan said.
Almaraz said she hopes sharing the store’s experience will help other small businesses avoid the same situation.
“We never thought it would happen to us, and we didn’t even know something like that even existed. If it happened to us, it can happen to anybody,” Almaraz said.

A promise to mom, a century-old farm: How these families kept developers at bay
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Home ownership has been the bedrock of the American dream, mainly driven by single homeowners.
But corporate buyers are changing that landscape, according to The Lincoln Institute of Land Policy and the Center for Geospatial Solutions. In a 2025 report, the group wrote that “this trend is reducing the housing stock available to individual homebuyers.”
In order to buck that trend as well as preserve the environment, there’s a non-profit in South Carolina working with homeowners who wish to protect their properties from development long after they’re gone.
Two Upstate South Carolina families have placed more than 250 acres under conservation easements through Upstate Forever, permanently restricting development on land that has been in their families for generations.
The announcement is part of a broader milestone for the organization, which now protects more than 40,000 acres across a 10-county area.
A conservation easement
Under a conservation easement, landowners retain ownership of their property. The easement places legal restrictions on what can ever be built there, shielding the land from future development regardless of who owns it.
Scott Park of Upstate Forever said the arrangement functions as a charitable donation.
“Conservation easements, they’re in essence a charitable donation, so that’s why Upstate Forever can be a grantee of these conservation easements,” Park said. “So the landowner is the grantor; they grant those restrictions to Upstate Forever. We are the forever steward, so we’re almost a partner in the pocket of that landowner now for as long as that landowner owns that piece of property.”
The properties
Ed Lomas’s Moore Farm, located near Horsepen Creek in Greenville County, spans 110 acres and has been in his family for more than 100 years. The property, once used for cotton farming, has been used for raising cattle since around the 1950s. It is now surrounded by new neighborhoods.
“Twenty years ago, you would wait for cars to come by maybe every few minutes,” Lomas said. “Now it’s a constant stream, especially first thing in the morning.”
Lomas said the easement process took about a year and a half. He said he pursued it after watching other families lose their land.
“I actually had a phone call from a family friend about a year ago saying they had exactly that scenario,” Lomas said. “They were older, they couldn’t take care of it, it was going to be left to the children, it was going to be a big mess. They felt that was their only option, just to sell the land.”
Lomas said the property will be safe and family members “will not be able to be pressured into selling it as a development.”
Alice Smith’s property, Duck Haven, is a 146-acre tract in Pickens County with rolling fields that connect to the Saluda River. Her grandparents purchased the land in the 1940s, and Smith said she made a promise to her mother to keep it intact.
“I made a promise to my mother that I would find a way to keep the land together,” Smith said.
Smith said she chose conservation over development offers.
“My grandparents bought it in the 40’s, and it was actually most, from what I’ve discovered, it was mostly farmland when they bought it,” she said.
‘Salt of the earth’
Park said the organization is seeing growing demand from landowners facing development pressure.
“You meet landowners like Ed and Alice that are just salt of the earth,” Park said. “They just want to protect their property. They see the development pressure that’s coming around them and they are pretty much, they are laser focused on getting these properties protected, and we’re happy to be a partner in that.”
Both Lomas and Smith said they want other families to know the option exists.
“There are opportunities and ways to protect and conserve the property you may have,” Lomas said.
“I’m not well-to-do, I’m not really well connected, but if for some reason I can plant a seed in anyone, that if I’m able to do this, they can too,” Smith said.
Smith said the easement ensures the land will remain as it is beyond her lifetime.
“What your family sacrificed and worked so hard for did not go to waste and a developer is not going to be able to ever touch it, and even when I’m gone, it’s still going to stay like this,” she said.

title: UMaine Extension offers virtual backyard bird learning series for kids
text:
University of Maine Cooperative Extension will offer “Introduction to Project Feeder Watch,” a 10-session online series for Maine youth ages 10-14, from 3:30 to 4:30 p.m. on select Mondays from Nov. 2, 2026, through April 12, 2027. Sessions will be held via Zoom.
Participants will learn to identify common backyard birds while exploring bird beaks, diets and habitats, and developing observation and documentation skills through regular feeder observations. No previous bird identification experience is required. The series will be led by Carolyn Reece, leader of the Pollinator Protectors 4-H club, and Erin McDonald, a 4-H Youth Development Professional in York County. The sessions are modeled after the national Project Feeder Watch program. Families have the option to participate in that program for an additional fee, however it’s not required.
Participation is free; registration is required by 11 p.m. on Oct. 19. Enrollment is limited to 10 participants, with a wait list available after capacity is reached. For event information and registration, visit the program webpage.
If reasonable accommodation is needed, please contact Sarah Sparks at 207.581.8206 or sarah.sparks@maine.edu by October 19, 2026.
Support for 4-H Virtual Learning programs is provided by the Maine 4-H Foundation.

title: Breeze Airways adds another non-stop option from Portland

text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - Breeze Airways is once again expanding its footprint at the Portland International Jetport (PWM).
The airline announced on Tuesday that it will start offering direct flights between Portland and Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. The flights will be on Thursdays and Sundays starting on May 27, 2027.
Breeze already offers so-called Breeze Thru service from Portland to Myrtle Beach, providing same-plane, one-stop flights. That service started in July.

Breeze currently operates more than 300 year-round and seasonal routes to 95 cities in the United States, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

title: Man who fell to his death while riding Six Flags roller coaster identified
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - Police have identified the man who died on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia Monday afternoon.
Cobb County police identified the victim Tuesday as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta. According to witnesses, the man fell to his death from the Goliath roller coaster, which goes at 70 miles per hour and drops twice — once at 170 feet and the other at 175 feet.
EN ESPAÑOL | Autoridades identifican al hombre que murió tras caer de montaña rusa de Six Flags
Logan Conner, who said he was on the ride with his fiancée, reported watching the man come out of his seat.
“The man started levitating in the air sideways,” Logan Conner told NBC. “We made direct eye contact with him.”
According to police, Kariem was thrown from the ride, hitting other patrons as he fell. His body was found on a nearby roof.
Britny Landry, who was waiting in line to ride the coaster a second time, said she saw somebody “fly out” but at first wasn’t sure what she saw.
“Maybe somebody had a bag or something,” she told KTVU-TV.
Several other people were injured. The exact number of victims and the extent of their injuries are unknown.
Riders were stuck on the roller coaster following the incident and had to be helped to the ground.
Six Flags Over Georgia was shut down after the incident and remained closed on Tuesday. The park will reopen on Friday, according to its website.
Kariem worked for the Atlanta Public Schools, the district confirmed on Tuesday. APS said he worked at Wesley International Academy, a K-8 charter school. It is not known what his exact role was, but his social media pages refer to him as an IT manager.
“He was a cherished member of the Wesley International Academy and APS families whose presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched. Our thoughts are with everyone mourning his loss during this difficult time,” APS said in a statement.
Six Flags has temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six parks “out of an abundance of caution.” Officials said the affected attractions are similar to Goliath, which only uses a lap bar to secure riders.
In a statement, Six Flags said it’s cooperating with the police investigation.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected,” the spokesperson said. “Out of respect for the family’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time.”
Before Monday’s incident, Six Flags Over Georgia has had at least seven deaths since its opening in 1967, according to The Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park deaths.

title: Las Vegas Sassy Seniors bring community service across the valley
text:
LAS VEGAS (InvestigateTV) — A Las Vegas group called the Sassy Seniors has spent the past year showing up to community events across the valley dressed in pink and carrying pom-poms.
The group was founded by a woman named Kathy Yanke, who wanted to find others her age to do community work alongside. She has since recruited about a dozen women who rotate in and out of events throughout the Las Vegas Valley.
In their first year, the group logged 4,000 hours of community service.
For a lot of those who volunteer, it gives them a sense of belonging.
The Sassy Seniors do not limit themselves to a single cause or organization. They have worked with veterans, participated in community and highway cleanups, and supported heart health initiatives in February through the Red Cross and other organizations.
Yanke initially connected the group to causes she had personal ties to, but organizations have since begun reaching out to her directly because of the group’s social media presence.
One member of the group works on a program that takes old wedding dresses and repurposes them for babies born sleeping — a term used to describe stillborn infants. The woman involved in the program had experienced infant loss herself.
It’s emotional work, but with that comes a joy because the group feels like they are making a difference.
The group is scheduled to travel to Hawaii to participate in a ceremonial anniversary event for Pearl Harbor Day, where they will present World War II veterans.
Membership in the Las Vegas Sassy Seniors is open to women generally 50 and older. Prospective members are asked to be available Tuesday nights for planning meetings and rehearsals, and to commit to at least 10 hours of community service per month.
The group can be found on Facebook or Instagram by searching Las Vegas Sassy Seniors.

title: Witnesses detail moment man fell to his death from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia
text:
ATLANTA (AP) - Witnesses watched in horror as a man riding a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia was ejected from his seat, almost seeming to hover above the car before hitting several people and falling to his death.
The nightmarish death prompted Six Flags to temporarily close nine similar coasters across North America.
Police and a state agency that oversees ride inspections are investigating, but many questions remained Tuesday, including how the man fell out and whether there were problems with his restraints.
The man, a school employee from Atlanta, was killed Monday while riding Goliath, the park’s tallest roller coaster with a first hill of 200 feet (61 meters).
“It looked like he was hovering because the car was moving underneath him,” said Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead.
The man fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, then was ejected from the ride on its final turn.
“It felt like slow-motion, but it happened in an instant,” Mendenhall said. “I was just praying in those moments. I was praying: ‘God, please let him stay in that car.’”
Goliath towers above the entrance at Six Flags Over Georgia just outside Atlanta with a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down. There are no seat belts. Instead, riders are restrained with lap bars that pull down over their legs and waist.
In a theme park industry that it is constantly introducing new thrills, it’s far from the world’s tallest, fastest or wildest coaster.
One family watched as the man flew out of the roller coaster
The man who died was 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, according to Cobb County police. Investigators and park employees told investigators that he was thrown from the coaster before striking other patrons.
Officials have not released any other information about the people who were hurt.
Kariem worked as the information technology manager at a public charter school and before that was a technology teacher.
In a statement, the Wesley International Academy said it was devastated, saying Kariem’s “dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did.”
Summer Bates, who was at the park with her husband and three children, saw Kariem fall. “One thing I think that will stick with us is the sound of his body coming down,” she said.
Bates said she and her family rode Goliath earlier in the day.
“My older two children rode on the cart ahead of us,” she said. “I noticed they kept trying to push theirs down tighter. I assured them that they were OK. But once my husband, youngest child and I loaded our cart and headed up the incline, I quickly understood why my older two were messing with theirs. It just didn’t feel secure and tight.”
Amusement ride oversight varies by state
In the U.S., roller coasters and other rides at major amusement parks such as Six Flags are not regulated by the federal government. That responsibility falls to states.
Georgia’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees annual ride inspections, is “conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review,” of what happened, said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson.
In California, the state approves new rides and ones that have been modified and either directly inspects them or relies on an annual inspection by the owner. Florida’s largest theme parks are exempt from state safety inspections, unlike smaller venues and fairs. Instead, the largest theme parks like Walt Disney World and Universal conduct their own inspections and have their own protocols.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to change the federal law that allows U.S. safety officials to regulate mobile rides but exempts major amusement parks.
Opponents of federal oversight say serious injuries and fatalities on amusement park rides are rare and often the result of riders not following rules.
Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the industry has multiple layers of inspection.
Six Flags closes roller coasters elsewhere
Six Flags Entertainment Corp. temporarily shut down roller coasters at six of its theme parks in the U.S. and Canada. The parks were already scheduled for seasonal midweek closures on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Those rides include a second coaster named Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California; Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Illinois; Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey; Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds in North Carolina; and the rides Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada’s Wonderland in Ontario, Canada.
The company did not say why those specific rides were shut down or what would be done before they reopen.
Bolliger & Mabillard, the Swiss company that manufactured the coaster and many others worldwide, said it is actively investigating and won’t comment “until we have a better understanding of what happened.”
“Our thoughts are with the family and those affected,” it said.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia; McCormack from Concord, New Hampshire; and Seewer from Toledo, Ohio. Associated Press writers Sudhin Thanawala in Atlanta; Michael Biesecker in Pittsburgh; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed.

title: Children among 6 killed in flooding from Hurricane Simon, Tropical Storm Rachel remnants
text:
ENSENADA, Mexico (AP) — The death toll from Hurricane Simon and the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel rose to six Tuesday after heavy rains triggered flooding and landslides along Mexico’s Pacific coast, authorities said.
Simon was a Category 1 storm before strengthening Tuesday night and was nearly a major hurricane again, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami. Off Mexico’s Pacific coast, Simon was bringing heavy rain to Nayarit and Sinaloa states, where authorities remained on alert for rising rivers and flooding. Over the weekend, the hurricane brought heavy rain to the southern state of Guerrero, killing one person.
But the worst damage was reported farther north, in the coastal city of Ensenada, Baja California, where flooding caused by Rachel’s remnants killed at least five people.
The victims included a 13-year-old girl whose body was found Sunday, two women ages 30 and 35 and a 4-year-old boy whose bodies were recovered Monday, and an unidentified person found near a stream Tuesday, the state prosecutor’s office told The Associated Press.
Five others remained missing in Baja California, including three in Ensenada and a father and son who went fishing Saturday in San Felipe, on the Gulf of California, and never returned.
About 300 military personnel, police and rescue workers searched along Ensenada’s El Pipila stream Tuesday, while the Mexican Navy continued looking for the missing fishermen, state civil protection authorities said.
Floodwaters swept away vehicles, damaged homes and cut off access to some communities.
Johana Nuriulu, a resident of Ensenada’s Buena Vista community, said the flooding began overnight, shortly after heavy rain knocked out electricity.
“We heard a loud noise that sounded like ocean waves, but very intense,” she said. When she stepped outside, she discovered a nearby stream had overflowed.
“The water was sweeping everything away; it took a cabin ... animals, everything.”
Elsewhere near Ensenada, Mexican soldiers used helicopters to rescue 32 people, including 13 minors, from Rancho Genesis, a camp for orphans staffed by missionaries.
The army said 22 of those rescued were foreign nationals. Baja California Security Secretary Gen. Laureano Carrillo said they included Americans and Germans.
Hurricane Simon moves along Pacific coast
Simon was moving parallel to Mexico’s Pacific coast Tuesday, threatening more rainfall in Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa.
The hurricane was about 125 miles (200 kilometers) west of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco, with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 kph), according to the hurricane center. The storm may strengthen overnight, but forecasts show gradual weakening Wednesday.
In southern Guerrero state, Simon’s heavy rains toppled trees and utility poles, blocked roads and flooded homes in coastal communities, including the resort city of Acapulco, Gov. Evelyn Salgado said.
A 71-year-old person died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo, the state capital, she said.
Authorities also took preventive measures in the port city of Mazatlan, Sinaloa, ahead of the storm, national Civil Protection Coordinator Laura Velázquez said Monday.
Meanwhile, conditions were improving in the tourist destination of Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, where residents began resuming normal activities as the rain subsided.
State authorities ordered schools to reopen Tuesday, while operations at Puerto Vallarta’s airport gradually resumed.
Tropical Storm Trudy was forecast to rapidly intensify into a hurricane Wednesday and a major hurricane by Friday in the Pacific Ocean, the hurricane center in Miami said Tuesday night. The storm was about 440 miles (705 km) south-southeast of Acapulco, Mexico, with maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (75 kph).
___
Silva Rey reported from Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. Associated Press writer Fabiola Sánchez contributed from Mexico City.
___
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: ‘Sophisticated recording device’ found in OpenAI conference room, FBI and the company say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.
The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.
The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.
“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.
The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.
“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.
Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.
The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.
Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.
The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.
The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

title: Officers save 2-year-old girl’s birthday after scam leaves her father broke
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - Two Phoenix police officers responded to reports of a scam that left a father penniless days before his 2-year-old daughter’s birthday – then used their own money to buy her presents, moving him to tears.
Officers Alessandro Figuccio and Tanner Schnieder, partners at the Phoenix Police Department’s Cactus Park Precinct, have worked together for about a year. Their paths to policing were different: Figuccio said becoming an officer was a childhood dream, while Schnieder was a truck driver before he decided to change careers.
About two months ago, the officers reviewed their call log and saw a call that stood out. A man who said he worked for DoorDash got a call that appeared to come from the company, Figuccio said. The caller told him his account had been deactivated and directed him to enter a code at a kiosk to reactivate it.
Soon after, the man’s last paycheck was gone.
Officers step in to help
Figuccio and Schnieder went to the man’s house to take his report on the scam, and after hearing his story, they decided to do something more for him. The interaction was caught on their body-worn cameras.
The man told the officers he had just paid his rent and car payment and had nothing left, Figuccio said. His 2-year-old daughter’s birthday was the next day.
“He had his daughter sitting there in a high chair, eating, and he’s just starting to break down to us,” Schneider said. “I look in, see his daughter, and then, it hits me.”
The officers drove to a store, where they filled a cart with clothes and toys for the toddler. They also picked out a small pink bicycle with tassels for her to ride when she gets older.
“We just started throwing stuff in the cart,” Schnieder said. “We’re like, dude, if I was his daughter, I’d be happy as heck.”
The officers paid for the items themselves and brought them back to the family’s home. Schnieder said the father began to cry when he saw the bicycle. He then gave the officers a hug.
“It’s rewarding, especially since I knew he had no money left,” Figuccio said.
For Schnieder, the gesture was personal. He said his family had been in a difficult position before, and he wanted to help someone who needed it.
The officers’ response was a small act of kindness in a difficult moment and another way to serve their community together.
