title: Dispute over a driveway in Greenville drags neighbors into a years-long legal battle
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
Along Lily Bay Road, a Greenville street that hugs picturesque Moosehead Lake, there’s a narrow driveway tucked between two homes that’s littered with fencing materials and no parking signs.
The barriers, which also include concrete blocks and a cattle gate, are among the outward signs of a years-long legal battle between neighbors over a shared driveway that still hasn’t reached a resolution.
On one side are Carl and Denise Chretien, who own a second home on the road. The property includes a main driveway on one side of the house and a narrow second driveway on the other, which they occasionally use to access a rear entrance and maintain the property’s backyard.
Meanwhile, their neighbors to the north, Emily Patrick and Aaron Crossman, bought their home in 2020, two years after the Chretiens moved in. Patrick and Crossman’s home doesn’t have its own driveway, but it does have a deeded easement to use the shared driveway between the two properties to access a small parking area behind their house.
Previous owners of the neighboring homes created the easement, a legal allowance for someone to use land they don’t own for a specific purpose, in 1982. It gives the owner of Crossman and Patrick’s home the right to use a 24-foot-wide strip of land that runs 125 feet from the center line of Lily Bay Road, according to legal documents.
Disagreements over where the property line between the two homes lies, how much of the driveway Crossman and Patrick can use and how the shared driveway should be maintained started years ago. Those arguments have since escalated to the Chretiens blocking portions of the driveway to restrict Crossman and Patrick’s access to it.
The dispute is an example of the gamble homeowners can take when buying a property that includes an easement, especially if the neighboring properties get sold to new families who don’t see eye-to-eye. Those agreements about how to share property, even if penned decades prior, can become a point of contention when new neighbors disagree on the terms and ignite years of expensive litigation.
“Emotions can run pretty hot in many property disputes between neighbors,” said Chris Uphouse of Veridian Law, the Chretiens’ attorney. “Like any fight, this started with small disagreements that snowballed.”
The Chretiens declined to speak with the Bangor Daily News directly. Uphouse was previously a legal consultant for the BDN.
Throughout the dispute, Patrick has maintained that the shared driveway must remain clear so an ambulance can pull up to their home if their youngest child, who has a rare genetic kidney disorder and mild cerebral palsy, has a medical emergency.
The fight appears to have started when Crossman allegedly performed some work to improve drainage along the side of the communal driveway that abuts his house without receiving permission from the Chretiens first, according to Patrick and Uphouse.
On another occasion, Crossman trimmed trees that the Chretiens believed belonged to them, though it was later determined the trees sat on Crossman’s property, Uphouse said.
The Chretiens then began installing markers and barriers, such as metal chains, posts and a cattle fence, to identify where they believed the line between the two properties was and where Crossman and Patrick’s easement ended. The overall intention, Uphouse said, was to prevent their neighbors from parking their vehicles in the driveway and blocking the Chretiens’ access to a rear entrance and their backyard.
“The genesis of [the fight] is a difference of interpretation or understanding about where the right of way is in the driveway,” Uphouse said. “The core dispute is the neighbors believe the surface of the driveway itself, the length of it, is how far the right of way extends.”
The dispute came to a head when Crossman and Patrick arrived home from vacation in 2023 to find a 6-foot wall made of concrete blocks lining a portion of the driveway, cutting off their access to their home, Patrick said.
The family filed a lawsuit against their neighbors and a judge granted an injunction ordering the Chretiens to remove “all fencing including concrete fencing and barricade that is located within or in any way impedes access to the paved or gravel driveway” by May 19, 2024, according to court records obtained by the BDN.
The Chretiens eventually removed portions of the barriers and pushed them back, but never hauled everything away, according to Patrick.
Still, the legal battle between the neighbors continues, as both parties have accused the other of poor conduct, trespassing and harassment throughout the fight, according to documents from Piscataquis County Superior Court.
The Chretiens have accused Crossman of dismantling fence materials and throwing them into a retention pond behind the Chretiens’ home, as well as hitting the barriers with his vehicle, plowing snow against the fence, and allowing others to park in the driveway, blocking it.
Patrick said she and Crossman have both accidentally backed their vehicles into the barriers due to the space constraints they create. On one occasion, Patrick said Crossman damaged a taillight this way.
“These illegal barriers have caused a lot of damage to our personal vehicles, and that night Aaron did lose his temper and remove the gate and throw it in their pond,” she said.
In other cases, Patrick said the family has allowed friends to park in the driveway during gatherings, but this only happened when the Chretiens weren’t home.
“The gate and blocks create a natural barrier where snow piles up, and Aaron does his best to clear snow as close to it as possible because we need as much space to turn around as we can,” Patrick said.
The Chretiens have installed motion-activated cameras pointed at the area between the two homes, which Patrick believes is an invasion of privacy. Uphouse said the cameras are in place to capture any bad behavior from the Chretiens’ neighbors.
“Our house is like a prison for so many different reasons,” Patrick said.
Earlier this year, the court ruled that Crossman was in contempt of court because he “violated the preliminary injunction by repeatedly, blatantly and systematically impeding Defendants’ use of the right-of-way, and by harassing Defendants,” according to legal documents.
Today, a barrier the Chretiens made between the two properties, constructed primarily of concrete blocks, a cattle gate, planters and plastic poles used to mark driveways for snow removal, still exists.
This gives Crossman and Patick enough room for roughly one car to pass by the barriers at a time to park next to their home. Patrick worries it still isn’t enough space for larger vehicles, including ambulances and delivery trucks that drop off medication for her son monthly.
Crossman and Patrick also want more space so they can turn their vehicles around rather than back down the narrow driveway onto the busy road.
“It feels like we’re losing ground all the time,” Patrick said. “We just want to be able to back up safely.”
Patrick also argues the various iterations of the fence violate Maine’s spite fence law.
The Greenville code enforcement office also issued the Chretiens a violation notice informing them the barriers violate the town’s fence ordinance, according to documents provided to the BDN. The notice instructed the family to remove the concrete blocks and cattle fence, then apply for a fence permit, but Patrick said town officials are neglecting to enforce the violation.
Mike Roy, Greenville’s town manager, did not respond to a request for comment. Uphouse did not respond to a request for comment about the violation notice.
Mediation attempts have proven unsuccessful, both Uphouse and Patrick said.
Patrick said their attorney has withdrawn from the case and the family can’t afford a new lawyer, as they’ve already paid tens of thousands of dollars in legal fees. These expenses also limit their ability to purchase a new home to escape the battle.
Earlier this month, Patrick said her family is leaning toward accepting a proposed settlement, the terms of which are confidential. If that happens, Patrick said she and Crossman will likely put their home on the market and pursue buying elsewhere, as the family can’t afford another home in Greenville that’s large enough to hold their five children.
If a settlement fails, the case will head to a jury trial, but that likely wouldn’t start until 2028, according to Uphouse.
“If we settle, I cannot bear to stay here next to these neighbors and we can’t afford to buy here in the hometown we love with the market being what it is,” Patrick said. “We are in purgatory at the moment, waiting to hear what is next.”

title: Federal prosecutors may be delaying local efforts to crack down on MaineCare fraud
text:
Federal prosecutors may be delaying local efforts to crack down on MaineCare fraud
A leaked document reveals that the Maine Attorney General's Office is waiting for a response from federal prosecutors
Federal prosecutors may be delaying local efforts to crack down on MaineCare fraud
A leaked document reveals that the Maine Attorney General's Office is waiting for a response from federal prosecutors
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has opened an audit of MaineCare, examining how the state oversees the program to see whether it has proper safeguards to prevent waste, fraud and abuse.
As the Trump administration continues to claim that Maine is a hotbed of Medicaid fraud, 8 Investigates has learned that federal prosecutors may be delaying the state’s efforts to crack down on fraudulent MaineCare billing.
Last week, 8 Investigates reported that a supervisor in the Maine attorney general’s office accidentally sent a 45-page document providing updates on dozens of open cases to dozens of people, including members of the media.
The document mentions two cases of alleged MaineCare fraud. Both companies are suspected of submitting “phony” bills, billing for services not covered by the program and employing providers who are not certified.
The memo says the companies’ potential theft amounts to nearly $1.98 million in taxpayer funds.
The document also notes that the Attorney General’s Office is waiting to hear back from the U.S. Attorney’s Office to learn whether the two cases will be pursued federally. "After multiple inquiries, we remain awaiting an update from the U.S. Attorney's Office regarding whether this matter, along with a group of other matters/investigations with similar allegations, will be pursued federally (civilly or criminally)."
The Maine Attorney General’s Office has not responded to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Maine said that, under U.S. Department of Justice policy, the office does not comment on the existence or progress of ongoing investigations.
While the U.S. Attorney's Office doesn't dictate which Medicaid fraud cases move forward, it does work collaboratively with state attorneys general.

title: BRHS field hockey vs. Oak Hill rescheduled
Supreme Court refuses to toss out fees for lawyers who sought hand count in Arizona election
text:
PHOENIX (AP) — The U.S. Supreme Court has refused to toss out $122,000 in legal costs that lawyers for former Arizona gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake were ordered to pay for false and misleading statements they made in a lawsuit that sought to require a hand-count of all ballots in the 2022 midterm elections.
The nation’s highest court on Tuesday denied a request from Andrew D. Parker, an attorney who represented Lake in the lawsuit, to review a lower-court decision over the legal costs arising from the unsuccessful litigation.
The lawsuit by Lake and state lawmaker Mark Finchem sought to ban electronic tabulation devices. It was dismissed by a judge who found Lake and Finchem lacked standing to sue and that their lawsuit was filed too close to the election.
In 2022, Lake lost the governor’s race to Democrat Katie Hobbs and Finchem was defeated in the secretary of state’s race by Democrat Andrian Fontes. Both Republicans had promoted the narrative that the 2020 election was marred by fraud.
Maricopa County had sought sanctions against Lake, Finchem and their lawyers, alleging they broke a court rule by making unfounded allegations and by not conducting the necessary research before filing the lawsuit.
U.S. District Judge John Tuchi later concluded the lawsuit’s claims lacked an adequate basis in fact, that the standard inquiry attorneys must make before pressing litigation hadn’t been done and that the lawyers acted recklessly in seeking a court order based on frivolous claims.
The requirement to pay the legal fees applies to the lawyers who pressed the lawsuit, not to Lake and Finchem.
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected appeals over the lawsuit’s dismissal and the awarding of the legal fees.
The Associated Press left phone and email messages Tuesday for Parker, whose firm is based in Minneapolis.
Earlier this year, Parker asked the Supreme Court to throw out the requirement to pay Maricopa County’s legal fees in the case, arguing such sanctions would deter attorneys from bringing aggressive or novel legal claims.
Maricopa County said lawyers for Lake and Finchem had disregarded a letter that identified false allegations they had made in their lawsuit and relied on some of those claims in a later court filing. The county’s attorneys said those who brought the lawsuit failed to present evidence to support their allegations and falsely alleged that Arizona didn’t use paper ballots and that its electronic voting systems hadn’t been subjected to expert analysis.

title: He waited 30 years to hunt a Maine moose. It was over in 18 minutes.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
At 6:35 a.m. Monday, Mark Boudreau spotted a bull moose standing directly in front of him on a logging road. He and his nephew had barely started driving into their hunting area when they came face to face with the animal they had spent days scouting for. Just 18 minutes after legal shooting time, Boudreau’s long-awaited hunt was over.
Boudreau, 53, of Sidney, had been applying for a Maine moose permit since he was 23. After three decades of waiting, he finally drew one this year, having accumulated 40 bonus points along the way.
His nephew Nick Cummings was at the moose lottery in Acton when he heard his uncle’s name announced.
“I called him as fast as I could dial my phone, and the countdown was on,” Cummings said.
Boudreau hunted in Wildlife Management Districts 14 and 17 with his nephew Noah Cummings as his subpermittee. The family has hunted from its camp nearby since 1962, building a longstanding tradition around Maine’s moose hunt.
Together, they’ve participated in 22 moose hunts since 2014 and have yet to come home empty-handed.
Years of experience helped them prepare for Boudreau’s long-awaited hunt. They scouted nearly every weekend, using trail cameras to monitor moose activity. Having hunted the same area in previous years, they already had a good idea of where to look.
In the four days before the hunt, they repeatedly saw moose in a recent cut where Boudreau would eventually take his bull.
Their plan was straightforward: drive to the spot where they had seen the moose. If the animals were gone, they would try calling to draw in a mature bull.
They waited at the end of the road until shooting time, then started driving at 6:31 a.m.
Four minutes later, they spotted the bull standing directly in front of them.
Boudreau and his nephew got out, loaded their firearms and had a quick, 10-second conversation before deciding the bull was the one they wanted.
Both hunters fired once. When the bull turned and stumbled away, they each fired again, and the moose fell.
The bull weighed 846 pounds and had a 46-inch antler spread.
For Boudreau, the moment marked the culmination of 30 years of hoping for a chance to hunt a moose of his own. Until then, he had served as a subpermittee on just one other hunt.
“He had a very emotional moment,” Cummings said.

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off in latest debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Troy Jackson versus Susan Collins round three is here.
The latest meeting in a flurry of debates between Maine’s candidates for U.S. Senate starts Tuesday at 7 p.m. Tonight’s event is the penultimate matchup between the two, with the last coming Thursday. (That event will be brought to you by Maine Public, NEWSCENTER Maine and the Portland Press Herald.)
Collins and Jackson’s debate tonight will be hosted by WABI and WAGM. You can watch a livestream below and follow along with our live commentary on the event.
-Despite that, we saw some new stuff, such as Jackson’s promise to deliver his campaign finance report Wednesday morning.
-Overall, there were few followers.
We’ll see you Thursday for the last debate!
-Kirby Wilson
Collins pushed back on that, noting that CBP officers killed two people in Minneapolis.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins noted the various ICE reform measures that she’s supported over the years, including de-escalation training and mandatory body-worn cameras.
Jackson has called for ICE to be abolished altogether.
Read our story about how the candidates would handle immigration enforcement here. We did a nice deep dive.
-Kirby Wilson
A note on candidates’ style
Both Jackson and Collins have seemed more emotional at times, with Jackson essentially telling Collins at one point not to lecture him on the difference between Medicare and Medicaid. At another point, Collins seemed vexed by Jackson’s barbs about her personal integrity.
-Kirby Wilson
“Troy has repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long,” Collins fired back. “I just cannot continue to ignore these attacks on my integrity.”
Collins then noted that she supported a measure that would regulate data centers such that they have no impact on electric rates.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson disagreed with this assessment, noting that he has a good relationship with the Canadians.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson once again criticized Collins for not doing enough to stop the tariffs.
-Kirby Wilson
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning,” Jackson said. “How bout that?”
-Kirby Wilson
“Sen. Collins is not going to stand there and school me on what I know,” Jackson said. “Don’t sit here and tell me about these things.”
And she said the government needs to do a better job fighting fraud in the healthcare program.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson criticized Collins for voting to advance Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins said she agreed with her opponent, and she criticized the Republican president.
“I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and I don’t think that that was well anticipated,” Collins said.
She said her ideal end to the war would be an agreement from Iran that they’d stop pursuing the enrichment of uranium.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins bashed Jackson for policies he supported in Augusta as the state Senate president, saying they are the reason electricity is so expensive here.
Who will voters believe? Whose record will they be more skeptical of? That question could decide the race.
-Kirby Wilson
So far, we’re treading familiar ground — all of this was addressed in each of the first two debates.
-Kirby Wilson
“Nobody should have to choose between keeping warm and buying groceries or other necessities,” Collins said.
The senator then criticized Jackson, whose leadership she said led to higher energy prices when compared to the rest of New England.
-Kirby Wilson
The 58-year-old former logger and state Senate president has been teasing this line of attack on social media today, since it’s the three-month anniversary of immigration agents killing Johan Sebastián Guerrero in Biddeford.
Collins, 73, parried similar attacks at last week’s debates, calling the shooting horrific and calling for an impartial investigation. She has also defended the need to preserve U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a federal agency Jackson wants to abolish.
Beyond that, it will be interesting to see if Jackson can recapture the energy and sharpness he displayed during their first meeting last Tuesday. He was able to put Collins on the defensive and deliver memorable lines that have had long tails in social media. Can he do it again?
Collins, meanwhile, was much sharper during their second debate last Thursday. She fully displayed her knowledge and experience, while putting Jackson on the defensive on issues like abortion and his leadership at the State House. Does she have any surprises in store?
Polling shows a tight race and it’s not clear that either candidate has said or done anything to change that — at least so far.
-Randy Billings

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Old Orchard Beach
text:
Voting is now open for the Nov. 3 municipal and state elections in Old Orchard Beach. Mainers statewide will chime in on state legislative races and high-profile elections for governor and U.S. Senate.
In Old Orchard Beach, voters will decide on various local races, including Town Council, School Board and town clerk, as well as one referendum.
Here’s what you need to know:
TOWN COUNCIL
Voters will choose from four candidates for three two-year terms on the Town Council: Kenneth Blow, Lori Gramlich, Shawn O’Neill and Michael Tousignant. Gramlich, a member of the Maine House, is the only newcomer on the council ballot; the other three are incumbents.
Blow, a local business owner, is a lifelong resident of Old Orchard Beach who has served on the Town Council for 13 years and is the current vice chair. He is simultaneously seeking the House District 151 seat.
In his responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Blow said his priorities include providing essential services and infrastructure upgrades in town and maintaining one of the lowest mill rates in southern Maine. He also highlighted the importance of bringing more affordable housing to Old Orchard Beach.
Gramlich, O’Neill and Tousignant did not respond to the voter guide survey.
SCHOOL BOARD
Three candidates are vying for two seats on the school board: David Boudreau, Peter Flaherty and Donna Moutsatos.
Flaherty and Moutsatos, the incumbents, did not respond to the voter guide survey.
Boudreau, director of sales at a local business, previously served on the school board for nine years, including seven as chair. In his responses to the voter guide, Boudreau said his priorities are fiscal responsibility, planning for a new school without burdening taxpayers, and maintaining staff retention through fair, sustainable contracts.
TOWN CLERK
Kim McLaughlin, the incumbent, is the only candidate running for town clerk. She was first elected to the position in 2024.
During her time as town clerk, McLaughlin received the Lorraine Fleury award from the Maine Senate for her election security preparations, her close work with the police department and her dedication to providing a safe, secure polling place.
COMMUNICATIONS CENTER BOND
Voters will also weigh in on a $3.3 million bond referendum to support the proposed replacement of an outdated radio communications system used by the public safety, public service and school departments of Old Orchard Beach and Scarborough.
The upgrade would improve communications between departments, which firefighters and police officers in both municipalities say have been a problem.
If voters reject the bond in November, the town would be responsible for finding a new funding source and returning the question to voters at a later election.
STATE AND COUNTY RACES
Old Orchard Beach residents are tasked this November with choosing their state representatives.
In Senate District 31, which includes Saco, Old Orchard Beach and Buxton, voters will choose between incumbent Democrat Donna Bailey and Republican challenger Scott Eccleston.
In House District 131, which covers Old Orchard Beach, voters will choose between Blow and Democrat Robert Kelly. Gramlich, running for Town Council, is termed out of office and thus not seeking reelection.
Voters across York County will also weigh in on a referendum that would abolish a county treasurer position and elect a sheriff.

title: Political candidates must value an effective and ethical justice system
text:
Jason Cherry, a Maine attorney with a practice focused on data privacy and criminal law, is a former special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. While at the FBI, he served as an assistant section chief for more than 430 employees and a budget of $150 million as well as a legal instructor.
I am interested in voting for a U.S. Senate candidate who understands the importance of an objective, professional and efficient U.S. Justice Department. Presidents from both political parties have shown overt favoritism to donors and other individuals in exchange for favors or to appease allies.
The Clinton administration was notorious for the 11th-hour pardon of 140 people, to include Marc Rich, a serial fraudster. On the other side, the Trump administration has granted over 1,900 pardons (and counting) across his terms in office.
The extensive list of pardons includes several fraudsters who have stolen hundreds of millions of dollars. These acts of “clemency” raise costs in healthcare, defense and other industries if the perpetrators of the fraud can expect to be freed by their political connections and influence. They fear no repercussions, so their behavior will continue onward.
In addition, these political indulgences send an extremely demoralizing message to everyone working diligently to establish an objective, professional and efficient justice system in their town, county, state and nation. Furthermore, the legitimacy of the entire justice system is at stake as these political indulgences send an alarming message to the public. Why should anyone obey the laws if they can get use their political influence to avoid any repercussions?
It is unclear why the U.S. Congress has not acted to restore legitimacy to the federal system of justice by restricting these apparent pay-to-pardon schemes. Perhaps, like many states, it is time to consider forming bipartisan clemency boards to prevent the executive branch from engaging in political indulgences.
As an FBI special agent, I took an oath to uphold the U.S. Constitution and to protect and serve the public. The acronym and motto of the FBI (Fidelity, Bravery and Integrity) used to mean only one thing — service and protection of my neighbors, my community, state and nation. Given the rampant rise in political indulgences, particularly the enabling of lawlessness in D.C., fidelity to whom? Bravery for whom? Integrity to whom and for what?
In his farewell address of Sept. 19, 1796, President George Washington described the importance of our justice system: “The due administration of justice is the firmest pillar of good government, I have considered the first arrangement of the judicial department as essential to the happiness of the country, and to the stability of its political system.”
The need for federal and state legislators to function as a true check and balance to restore legitimacy to our national justice system is long overdue. Instead, what is happening is a number of blank checks are being written in exchange for pardons galore.
I find it difficult to vote for a political party or politician who does not understand the importance of an objective, professional, efficient and ethical justice system, but merely stands aside or even enables the practice of unethical behaviors like these modern-day political indulgences.

title: Eastern Iowa veterans travel to Washington to see memorials built in their honor
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Eighty-seven Eastern Iowa veterans traveled to Washington, D.C., Tuesday to visit the memorials built in their honor.
The first Eastern Iowa flight of this kind took off in the 1990s. There have been 61 flights since then.
Among the 87 veterans on board was Joe Latham Jr., who flew missions from the cockpit during the Vietnam war. He was one of the first pilots to shoot down a Soviet-designed MiG fighter jet.
“101 missions, a lot of night missions bombing, a lot of day missions, bombing. We were just lucky to get out alive,” Latham said.
Not everyone survived. Three men Latham flew with are listed on the wall, including his best friend.
“My very best friend, three of the guys that I flew with are on the wall, including my very best friend. It was he and I were roommates together and everything else. We flew in two different flights the same night. I was one hour later night bombing low altitude North Vietnam. And he didn’t come back,” Latham said.
Latham has lived a full life since returning from war. The names of his loved ones are engraved on the wall in Washington.
“Memories and I’ll be tearing up but this is this wonderful,” Latham said.
The wall is not the only place in Washington tied to Latham’s friends.
“Of course, Arlington, and I have very good friends buried in Arlington... that I flew with, and eventually I’ll be there too,” Latham said.

title: 10 Terrifying Ghost Stories That Are Uniquely Maine
text:
10 Terrifying Ghost Stories That Are Uniquely Maine
Since we are right in the middle of Spooky Season, it only makes sense that we should highlight some of the most common Maine ghost stories.
Considering the state has been inhabited by European settlers for about 400 years, and by Native Americans for thousands of years longer than that, it should not be a surprise that there are a few ghostly hotspots throughout the Pine Tree State.
We've put together a list of some of the wildest, most Maine, ghost stories. These stories take place in a variety of locations including a lighthouse (shocker!), a hotel, a college dorm, and even in an old movie theater.
Check Out These 10 Stories Of Haunted Maine
What other stories need to be added to our list? Let us know by sending a message using our app.
As you saw from the list, Maine has several spooky legends involving tragic deaths, unexplained disappearances, and spirits that supposedly still haunt the places where these events occurred. One tale involves a lighthouse on a 35-acre island about a mile offshore, where a young man reportedly shot and killed his landlord during a confrontation involving a rifle. Overcome with grief and remorse, the young man took his own life later that night, and legend says his spirit still haunts the lighthouse. In Randolph, near Gardiner, the Old Narrow Gauge trail is rumored to be haunted by a man who disappeared while riding his bicycle. Neither his body nor his bike was ever found, and visitors reportedly experience strange orbs, see spirits, and hear frightening screams telling them to leave. Another famous legend comes from Bucksport, where town founder Colonel Jonathan Buck allegedly had a woman burned as a witch after refusing to provide financial support for their son. Before her death, the woman's son reportedly retrieved one of her legs and buried it as a memorial. After Buck died, a stain resembling a leg supposedly appeared on his tombstone and remained even after the stone was replaced. Each story blends Maine history with tragedy, mystery, and supernatural folklore, keeping these eerie legends alive for locals and paranormal enthusiasts.

title: Store says AI-generated receipt was used to secure fraudulent purse refund
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ALICE, Texas (KIII) — Employees at Horseshoes Western Wear said they are learning a new lesson about protecting the business after a fake, apparently AI-generated receipt was used to obtain a warranty refund.
Manager Inez Almaraz said the store’s owner learned from a distributor that a receipt appearing to be AI-generated was used to get a warranty refund for a purse.
“We’ve never had anything or any of this happen, especially with something that we carry. For them to produce or generate a fake AI receipt is something that’s just not tolerated,” Almaraz said.
Distributor fell victim to fake receipt
Almaraz said the purse involved was a Consuela designer purse, which the store carries and sells.
“Consuela is a designer purse, and we are fortunate to be able to carry it and sell it,” Almaraz said.
The distributor fell victim to the fake receipt before it was identified as fraudulent.
A comparison of the real receipt and the fake showed differences, including the wrong address.
Retail seller Angel Ramos said employees found the discrepancy because the store did not carry the purse listed on the fake receipt.
“Just be more cautious. Look at your receipts. Pay attention to your systems. Just keep track of your inventory because we didn’t carry that purse,” Ramos said.
Better Business Bureau says AI making fakes harder to detect
The Better Business Bureau says artificial intelligence is making it easier for scammers to create convincing documents, meaning businesses can’t always rely on obvious mistakes to spot a fake.
Katie Galan with the Better Business Bureau said scammers rely on urgency to avoid detection.
“What they want is for you to rush and to not have the time to verify, to ask questions, to look at that receipt a little closer. So, that’s what they prey on, is us being in so much of a rush that we don’t have time to double-check things,” Galan said.
Almaraz said she hopes sharing the store’s experience will help other small businesses avoid the same situation.
“We never thought it would happen to us, and we didn’t even know something like that even existed. If it happened to us, it can happen to anybody,” Almaraz said.

title: Down East ambulance service to close after 60 years
text:
A volunteer ambulance service in Down East Maine is closing after 60 years, and it’s unclear who will cover the communities losing aid.
Dennys River Volunteer Ambulance service will close Nov. 30, Capt. Wayne Seeley said. Seeley, who is in his 80s, runs the service alongside his wife, Roberta. The EMS provider has struggled for years to find volunteers, he told the Bangor Daily News.
It covers the towns of Dennysville and Pembroke, and the unorganized townships of Cathance, Edmunds and Marion.
The ambulance service closing in rural Washington County will likely exacerbate the area’s already thin emergency coverage. This comes just over a month after the BDN reported on how Maine has failed for years to ensure residents have EMS coverage, especially in rural areas. That failure has left ambulances on the financial brink and risks longer wait times for Mainers experiencing medical emergencies.
The municipalities have just over a month to figure out who will provide EMS to residents. Maine law does not require the service be provided. The BDN could not reach Dennysville and Pembroke clerks Tuesday.
Maine EMS is working with the ambulance service as it goes through its licensure termination process, Director Wil O’Neal said.
The EMS runs with only four to six volunteers, which means it can’t provide 24-hour coverage, Seeley said. For years, it has tried to get more volunteers, but no one was willing to take the unpaid positions, he said. The closure coincides with the service’s license expiring in late November.
“It feels horrible, terrible,” Seeley said. “One of the worst things I’ve ever had to do. I really enjoyed doing it, but I guess there comes a time that you have to stop.”
Dennys River runs around 100 to 150 calls a year, Seeley said. They weren’t enough to generate revenue and pay people, he said.
Downeast EMS covers calls that Dennys River is unable to go to, Seeley said. The quasimunicipal ambulance service is aware of the pending closure, a staff member told the BDN. Downeast’s service director did not immediately respond to request for comment.
There are tentative plans and discussions happening to find new coverage for the unorganized townships, Unorganized Territories Administrator Heron Weston said. He said it’s likely that the coverage will be split between multiple agencies to try to keep response times lower.
“It’s a real blow to that area,” Weston said.
Nearby townships are serviced by Downeast EMS and Pleasant River Ambulance Service, according to coverage map in Washington County’s unorganized territories. Eastport, Lubec and Machias also have ambulance services, O’Neal said.

title: 'Breaking Bad' Star RJ Mitte's Cause of Death Confirmed
text:
‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death Confirmed at 34 [Report]
RJ Mitte, best known for playing Walter White Jr. on Breaking Bad, died at 34, and new details have emerged about the circumstances surrounding his death.
The actor’s death was confirmed Monday (Oct. 12), prompting an outpouring of sadness from those remembering his work on the hit AMC drama and his advocacy for people with disabilities.
Now, his representative has confirmed a key detail about the actor’s cause of death.
What Was RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death?
Mitte died by suicide Monday, his representative confirmed to Page Six.
READ MORE: ‘Breaking Bad’ Named Best TV Show of 21st Century
His manner of death will be determined by a medical examiner following an autopsy. A judge said there appeared to be no signs of foul play.
Who Was RJ Mitte on 'Breaking Bad'?
Mitte was best known for playing Walter “Flynn” White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston’s Walter White, on Breaking Bad. The acclaimed AMC series ran for five seasons from 2008 to 2013.
The actor brought personal experience to the role. Diagnosed with cerebral palsy at age 3, Mitte helped bring greater visibility to the disability through his work on the show.
READ MORE: Chad Lowe’s Daughter Fiona Dead at 13: ‘She Was the Light of Our Lives’
Outside of acting, Mitte was a passionate disability rights advocate. He served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s, as well as a Screen Actors Guild spokesperson for actors with disabilities.
He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives.
Following news of his death, his representative asked the public to respect the privacy of his family and loved ones.
If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 800-273-TALK (8255) or text the Crisis Text Line at 741741.

title: Houlton Car Theft Leads to Double Fatal Crash
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) -What began as a car theft from the Hannaford parking lot in Houlton ended in a deadly wrong-way crash on I-95.
According to Houlton Police, on Monday Oct. 12th around 9:10 p.m. a woman reported that her black 2011 Toyota Camry had been stolen from the Hannaford parking lot. Police say she had left the keys inside the vehicle. At 9:21 p.m., the Bangor Regional Communications Center received a report of a wrong-way driver near Island Falls. Police later confirmed the wrong way driver was driving the stolen Camry. Troopers responded to the area. About 17 minutes later, an East Millinocket police officer spotted the Camry near mile marker 248, still traveling the wrong way at speeds topping 100 miles per hour. The officer tried to stop the driver, but the vehicle continued south. The officer followed, then used the crossover at mile marker 244 to get back into the proper lanes of travel.
Police say the Camry entered a construction zone on a bridge in Medway, just south of Exit 244. Southbound traffic is currently diverted onto the northbound bridge, where concrete barriers separate one lane in each direction. The wrong-way driver entered the construction zone and crashed head-on into another vehicle. Police identified the wrong way driver as 20-year-old Luis Mendoza of Indian Township. The other vehicle was being driven by 67-year-old Sandra Lacombe of Medway. Both drivers died in the crash. I-95 was closed near the crash scene for several hours. The investigation remains ongoing.

title: Children among 6 killed in flooding from Hurricane Simon, Tropical Storm Rachel remnants
text:
ENSENADA, Mexico (AP) — The death toll from Hurricane Simon and the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel rose to six Tuesday after heavy rains triggered flooding and landslides along Mexico’s Pacific coast, authorities said.
Simon was a Category 1 storm before strengthening Tuesday night and was nearly a major hurricane again, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami. Off Mexico’s Pacific coast, Simon was bringing heavy rain to Nayarit and Sinaloa states, where authorities remained on alert for rising rivers and flooding. Over the weekend, the hurricane brought heavy rain to the southern state of Guerrero, killing one person.
But the worst damage was reported farther north, in the coastal city of Ensenada, Baja California, where flooding caused by Rachel’s remnants killed at least five people.
The victims included a 13-year-old girl whose body was found Sunday, two women ages 30 and 35 and a 4-year-old boy whose bodies were recovered Monday, and an unidentified person found near a stream Tuesday, the state prosecutor’s office told The Associated Press.
Five others remained missing in Baja California, including three in Ensenada and a father and son who went fishing Saturday in San Felipe, on the Gulf of California, and never returned.
About 300 military personnel, police and rescue workers searched along Ensenada’s El Pipila stream Tuesday, while the Mexican Navy continued looking for the missing fishermen, state civil protection authorities said.
Floodwaters swept away vehicles, damaged homes and cut off access to some communities.
Johana Nuriulu, a resident of Ensenada’s Buena Vista community, said the flooding began overnight, shortly after heavy rain knocked out electricity.
“We heard a loud noise that sounded like ocean waves, but very intense,” she said. When she stepped outside, she discovered a nearby stream had overflowed.
“The water was sweeping everything away; it took a cabin ... animals, everything.”
Elsewhere near Ensenada, Mexican soldiers used helicopters to rescue 32 people, including 13 minors, from Rancho Genesis, a camp for orphans staffed by missionaries.
The army said 22 of those rescued were foreign nationals. Baja California Security Secretary Gen. Laureano Carrillo said they included Americans and Germans.
Hurricane Simon moves along Pacific coast
Simon was moving parallel to Mexico’s Pacific coast Tuesday, threatening more rainfall in Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa.
The hurricane was about 125 miles (200 kilometers) west of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco, with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 kph), according to the hurricane center. The storm may strengthen overnight, but forecasts show gradual weakening Wednesday.
In southern Guerrero state, Simon’s heavy rains toppled trees and utility poles, blocked roads and flooded homes in coastal communities, including the resort city of Acapulco, Gov. Evelyn Salgado said.
A 71-year-old person died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo, the state capital, she said.
Authorities also took preventive measures in the port city of Mazatlan, Sinaloa, ahead of the storm, national Civil Protection Coordinator Laura Velázquez said Monday.
Meanwhile, conditions were improving in the tourist destination of Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, where residents began resuming normal activities as the rain subsided.
State authorities ordered schools to reopen Tuesday, while operations at Puerto Vallarta’s airport gradually resumed.
Tropical Storm Trudy was forecast to rapidly intensify into a hurricane Wednesday and a major hurricane by Friday in the Pacific Ocean, the hurricane center in Miami said Tuesday night. The storm was about 440 miles (705 km) south-southeast of Acapulco, Mexico, with maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (75 kph).
___
Silva Rey reported from Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. Associated Press writer Fabiola Sánchez contributed from Mexico City.

title: Video shows theft of returnables that were donated to Maine fire department
text:
Video shows theft of returnable bottles and cans that were donated to Maine fire department
Officials say thieves stole returnable bottles and cans that had been donated to two volunteer fire departments in Maine, and one of the thefts was caught on camera.
The Liberty Fire and Rescue Department said that at about 2:30 a.m. on Oct. 5, at least two people drove up to the fire station on West Main Street and stole the returnables from the donation bin that is located outside the station.
The department shared video of the Oct. 5 incident. The video shows a pickup truck pulling into the fire station parking lot and someone getting out on the passenger's side. That person is then seen putting multiple bags into the bed of the truck.
"Unfortunately, we have not been able to identify the individuals involved. We are asking our community to please keep an eye and ear out," Liberty Fire and Rescue said in a Facebook post. "If you have heard anything, know something, or have heard anyone talking about this incident, we would appreciate you reaching out to us."
In a follow-up Facebook post, Liberty Fire and Rescue said that the Montville Fire Department also had donated returnables stolen from it on the same night. Officials said police reports have been filed in connection with the incidents.
Liberty Fire and Rescue did share a photo in the follow-up post that showed its donation bin was overflowing by 6 a.m. Monday.
Liberty Fire and Rescue noted that it will be keeping its returnables donation bin outside of the station for now.
"This is the first time something like this has happened, and we sincerely hope it does not happen again," the department said. "We refuse to let the actions of a few discourage us from continuing a project that has been supported by so many wonderful people in our community."
Liberty Fire and Rescue also said that people can bring returnables directly to 10-4 Redemption on Route 3 in Montville, and let them know that the proceeds are for Liberty Fire and Rescue.

title: Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
text:
Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
President Donald Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she’ll “vigorously defend” herself against “false” allegations.
Trump's administration said Tuesday it had asked her to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”
Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to the AP over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct.
“Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.”
Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week.
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly. But in a statement released late Sunday, her lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations."
The allegations began surfacing weeks ago
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
There was no immediate response to Zacharia's statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.
Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.
Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president's daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa’s “Dance the Night,” from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie “Barbie.”
Democrats call for an investigation
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California’s Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

title: Inside the Maine unit investigating online child exploitation
text:
VASSALBORO, Maine (WABI) - A specialized unit in the Maine State Police investigates online child exploitation and works to educate the public about it.
Unit changed name last year
The unit shifted last year from the Computer Crimes Unit to the Major Crimes Unit–Special Victims. Investigators say the name is more appropriate for the type of investigations they conduct.
“We’re partnered up with agencies from all the way to Madawaska and Fort Kent all the way down to Kittery,” said Lt. Taylor Bagley, of the Special Victims Unit, Maine State Police.
The unit works in cooperation with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which facilitates cybertips. Those tips have increased in recent years.
“With 4,000 cyber tips coming in over the course of a year, we have to find creative ways because we can’t staff our way out of that particular issue,” Bagley said.
The unit also manages the Northern New England Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, known as ICAC. Its mission is to identify, arrest and prosecute anyone who uses the internet to produce or share child sexual abuse material, including anyone who uses the internet to lure minors into illicit relationships.
“We’re still working with child pornography on the ICAC side but the increase in just the chat cases that we’re seeing and sextortion related offenses throughout the state has grown substantially. That has taken a toll on our resources in the lab,” Bagley said.
“We have nine analysts with two supervisors, and they will usually go out with every search warrant to help assist with examining devices,” said Sgt. Joshua Lander, of the Special Victims Unit, Maine State Police.
A forensic investigator with the unit described the process. “We work off our forensic images, so we’ll make a forensic copy of the evidence which we then process and look for artifacts relevant to the case.”
Dog trained to detect electronic devices
In addition to technology, the unit is also utilizing a dog. Marley is Maine’s first electronic storage detection K-9.
“There have been multiple cases over the last two years that detectives have not found devices. I bring Marley in. Marley finds the device. In multiple cases, that was the only device that Marley found had the CSAM (child sexual assault material) on the device. Had it not been for Marley finding that device, the suspect would not have been charged,” said Sgt. Christopher Crawford, of the Special Victims Unit, Maine State Police.
Crawford said Marley has also been an asset in other investigations. “He has found cell phones that were thrown out that were critical for a homicide investigation.”
Investigators urge parents to talk with children
Investigators say the single most important thing parents can do is talk to their kids about their online activity.
“Anytime a person online is starting to ask those personal questions about like how old they are, where they go to school – those are the red flags that you really want the kids to know about,” Lander said.
The Major Crimes Unit–Special Victims is headquartered in Vassalboro, with satellite offices in Bangor and Gray.

title: Waldoboro High School under "do not drink" order due to high lead levels
Augusta utility sues 4 paper mills over toxic PFAS in drinking water
text:
The Greater Augusta Utility District has filed a federal lawsuit against four upstream paper manufacturers to recover millions spent filtering toxic “forever chemicals” out of the capital city’s public drinking water supply.
The utility is asking the court to hold the mills responsible for polluting the Kennebec River watershed rather than forcing ratepayers and taxpayers to absorb the cost of complex water treatment.
The outcome could set a legal blueprint for public water systems across Maine and nationwide.
The dispute centers on Augusta’s Riverside wells, where pumps pull groundwater from an aquifer connected to the Kennebec River. Officials shut the wells down after testing in 2021 showed unsafe levels of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
Water from these wells contained 23.3 parts per trillion of the six PFAS compounds that Maine measures to establish drinking water safety. The state limit is 20 parts per trillion. To picture that scale, one part per trillion equals one drop of water in 20 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
While that sounds exceedingly small, state and federal environmental regulators emphasize that even trace amounts of these manmade chemicals can pose human health risks, with long-term exposure linked to kidney cancer, liver damage, high cholesterol and immune system disruption.
To protect its 13,750 customers, the utility invested $2 million — much of which came from grants — to build an ion-exchange treatment facility. Water began flowing safely this summer, but the utility argues that the financial burden belongs to the polluters.
The lawsuit marks a crucial strategic shift in environmental litigation.
Most PFAS cases target the chemical creators, like 3M or DuPont. Maine has filed two lawsuits against major chemical companies, alleging they willfully introduced toxic chemicals into Maine’s environment while concealing their known health and environmental risks.
In its lawsuit filed last week, the Augusta district is going after the paper mills that used PFAS while making grease-resistant paper and disposable dishware, including: Sappi North America Inc., which operates a mill in Skowhegan; Huhtamaki Inc., which makes Chinet products in Waterville; Kimberly-Clark Corp., which had a plant in Winslow; and American Tissue Corp. and its subsidiary, American Tissue Mills of Maine, which operated a mill in Augusta. The Winslow and Augusta mills have been closed for several years.
A similar legal strategy succeeded in Michigan in 2022, where footwear manufacturer Wolverine Worldwide paid $54 million to the state, two local communities and residents after dumping PFAS-contaminated leather-treatment waste.
However, while Wolverine involved a single isolated disposal dump, proving causation along Maine’s 30-mile Kennebec River corridor could be far more complex because discharges from multiple mills commingle in the water.
But federal law offers a powerful legal tool: the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, or Superfund, which establishes the mechanisms needed to force responsible parties to pay for environmental cleanup costs.
“Liability is strict, retroactive and joint and several,” said Anthony Moffa, an environmental law professor at the University of Maine School of Law. Under that law, defendants can be held responsible for cleanup costs even if they complied with all of their permits, Moffa said.
This legal framework resolves a question that hung over the Greater Augusta Utility District’s recent project opening, where officials said there was no single “smoking gun” to blame for its PFAS spike. In its suit, the district claims mill discharges blended together over decades to form an indivisible toxin.
But under federal Superfund regulations, plaintiffs do not have to isolate individual chemical molecules to establish liability. They only need to prove an upstream mill discharged hazardous waste into the watershed. And for that, they turned to state-run water, leachate and fish testing.
The district cites PFAS spikes in paper mill discharge, landfill runoff and fish tissue as its proof.
“Defendants, and not the district, its taxpayers, or its customers, should bear the past, present, and future costs of investigating, monitoring, treating, and remediating PFAS contamination affecting the district’s drinking water,” the district said in its Oct. 7 suit in U.S. District Court.
The litigation builds on a wave of class-action litigation by central Maine landowners and farmers, who are suing some Maine paper mills after their sludge spread as fertilizer contaminated private wells and tainted farm fields across Somerset and Kennebec counties.
Unlike some national settlements reached with chemical creators, none of the Maine lawsuits targeting paper mills has been settled, according to court records, with regional class actions still working their way through federal and state dockets as the paper mills mount vigorous defenses.
Because the spreading of industrial sludge was state-permitted, Maine maintains historical records of its use. From those records, the state estimated eight paper companies spread at least a half million cubic yards of paper mill waste in Maine between 1989 and 2016.
But Maine has no such records for industrial PFAS discharges into public water bodies. For decades, state and federal discharge permits regulated things like suspended solids or pH, but they did not require monitoring of PFAS compounds.
However, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection conducted a 10-month statewide study testing industrial and municipal wastewater effluent in 2022. The agency calculated that regulated facilities discharge roughly 30 pounds of PFAS into Maine waters every year.
Maine now requires all who discharge into public waters to monitor and report PFAS levels.
Upstream paper companies and industry leaders have argued the mills operated within the law.
A spokeswoman for Sappi said the company is reviewing the lawsuit. She said Sappi complies with environmental regulations, operates within its state and federal discharge permits and doesn’t knowingly use PFAS in products.
Neither Huhtamaki nor Kimberly-Clark responded to requests for comment. American Tissue has ceased operations and filed for bankruptcy in 2001. Under federal law, if a responsible party cannot pay, the financial burden shifts to the solvent co-defendants remaining.
Industry leaders echoed that defense and cautioned against penalizing law-abiding businesses.
The executive director of the Maine Wood Products Council, Krysta West, stressed that mills work hard to apply current science. “It is always concerning when lawsuits are filed against companies in any sector who operated in accordance with state and federal permits,” West said.
The lawsuit lands amid Maine’s broader reckoning with legacy chemical pollution.
For decades, state-approved programs encouraged paper mills and wastewater plants to spread their leftover sludge on local fields as free fertilizer. The practice has contaminated almost 100 farms, ruined dairy herds and fouled hundreds of private drinking wells in central Maine.
The public outcry prompted Maine to become the first state to ban sludge-based fertilizer use.
Public health advocates said mills cannot claim ignorance after decades of scientific warnings.
“Industries choosing to create or use PFAS in spite of that should not be surprised when consumers, regulators, and other impacted groups … seek compensation for the harms,” said Emily Carey Perez de Alejo, executive director of Portland-based Defend Our Health.
