title: President Trump campaigns for Republicans as some push back on certain policies
text:
President Trump campaigns for Republicans as some push back on certain policies
President Trump is intensifying his campaign efforts for Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections, even as some members of his own party push back against parts of his agenda.
President Trump campaigns for Republicans as some push back on certain policies
President Trump is intensifying his campaign efforts for Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections, even as some members of his own party push back against parts of his agenda.
With three weeks until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump is ramping up his campaign travel to support Republican candidates, some of whom are challenging his policies.
Speaking at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday, Trump addressed criticism from within his party regarding his Russia diesel deal.
"It's a deal for the world. It's not a deal for us. It's a way of getting a lot of oil out to the world," Trump said.
The deal temporarily eases U.S. sanctions to allow Russian diesel exports in an effort to bring down soaring diesel prices.
"You know the oil deal brought down prices. That's a world deal, not a USA deal," Trump said.
When asked whether his policies might make it harder for Republicans to win in November, Trump did not respond.
Among the Republicans pushing back on the deal is Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan, whom the president traveled to Alaska to campaign for Tuesday. Sullivan's campaign told The New York Times that the senator "believes American energy dominance is the answer to high prices," adding that means producing more energy in Alaska, "not importing it from Russia."
The criticism extends well beyond Sullivan. A dozen senators, including six Republicans, sent Trump a letter Tuesday urging him to rescind the agreement. The lawmakers argued the deal would provide Russia with additional money to finance its war in Ukraine while offering little relief to American consumers.
Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is also facing a competitive reelection race, was among those signing the letter. Collins had already joined Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina in calling on Trump to reverse course on the deal. Republican Sens. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma and John Cornyn of Texas also signed Tuesday's letter.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania has gone further, announcing legislation aimed at blocking purchases of Russian oil and saying he will try to force a House vote on the measure.
The divisions extend to other policies and other competitive races.
"Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers said in a campaign ad.
Rogers, who has been endorsed by Trump, is campaigning to end the president's tariff fight with Canada after also breaking with Trump over the war in Iran.
Despite those divisions, Trump said Republican enthusiasm is "way up" as he continues a series of campaign rallies.
However, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 48% of voters who supported Kamala Harris in 2024 said they were very enthusiastic about voting in the midterms, compared with 30% of Trump voters.
Vice President JD Vance acknowledged the historical challenges facing the party in power during midterm elections.
"We know that we're swimming against some serious historical trends here, but I think that we have as good a chance as I've ever seen to really defy those historical trends," Vance said.
Trump says he is now holding about one rally a day. He is campaigning in Alaska Tuesday, with rallies scheduled in Arizona and Montana Wednesday as Republicans fight to maintain control of Congress.
Meanwhile, the White House has a new face behind the briefing room podium. Katie Zacharia replaced Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary and held her first briefing Tuesday. Zacharia previously served as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group and briefly as a spokesperson at the Department of Homeland Security.
During her first briefing, Zacharia confirmed that the White House had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign.
"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said.
Guilfoyle, a former prosecutor and television personality who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr., has faced allegations of improper conduct. Reports alleged she offered access to Trump administration officials in exchange for money, gifts or favors. One allegation involved a businessman who said Guilfoyle sought help paying a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for access. Other reports alleged she threatened to use U.S. influence against the Greek government. Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Trump told reporters Tuesday that Guilfoyle had been doing a good job but said, "we didn't like what we were reading." The White House has not announced who will replace her.
In another controversy, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from using additional taxpayer money for television advertisements featuring the president and promoting his agenda.
The Department of Homeland Security had allocated $20 million for the advertising campaign. The White House has defended the spots as public service announcements, while lawsuits challenging them argue they amount to an unlawful use of taxpayer money for political promotion.
The criticism has also been bipartisan, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune saying the ads should not be paid for with taxpayer dollars.
Trump has said MAGA Inc. would pay for future ads instead. That has sparked a separate Federal Election Commission complaint from Common Cause alleging that Trump, as a federal officeholder, is unlawfully directing the super PAC's spending.
A White House official said there are no immediate plans to reimburse taxpayers for money already spent on the advertisements.

title: How to access home healthcare for older Mainers
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Maine’s aging population means that more older adults will be seeking home healthcare — either through skilled nursing, help with daily tasks or a combination.
Home healthcare is a patchwork of services that can be paid for through Medicare, Medicaid or out-of-pocket, depending on the need.
Maine has the highest median age in the nation, at 44.9 years, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. The state’s 65-and-older age group is expected to grow 11.4% from 2027-32, according to the Maine Office of the State Economist projections.
Often the care sought from home health agencies is done in conjunction with family caregivers who are taking on the responsibility of helping an older relative age in their home, experts in the field say.
According to a 2025 review of research by Johns Hopkins University, “profound demographic shifts” will lead to greater demand for services in the U.S. over the next decade or longer for home health and other long-term health services.
Patty Buiocchi, chief operating officer of post-acute care at MaineHealth, said the demand is “only going to get higher and higher. Will the supply also become higher? That remains to be seen.”
“Home health is so increasingly important to the healthcare system, because when people are getting care in their home, it reduces unnecessary hospital visits,” Buiocchi said.
What are the different types of home healthcare?
Buiocchi, who oversees MaineHealth’s Home Health and Hospice, said that in general, Medicare pays for skilled nursing care needed in the home. Examples include recovering from a surgery or an illness where the patient requires the assistance of skilled nurses while recuperating at home.
Medicare is the federally funded health insurance program for those 65 and older, while Medicaid serves lower-income and disabled populations.
If an older person doesn’t need skilled nursing, but needs help with tasks for daily living, such as cooking, cleaning, remembering to take medications, groceries and laundry, they could qualify for those services under Medicaid, or if they don’t qualify, could purchase them out-of-pocket from an agency, Buiocchi said.
Medicare services are typically shorter-term, for instance rehabilitating at home after surgery, she said.
How can I access services?
Because services are in great demand, Buiocchi advised older Mainers who need help or their caregivers to educate themselves on what’s available.
“Be proactive,” Buiocchi said. “Don’t wait until someone has an acute incident. Call organizations to see what they provide and when they provide it. Get an assessment, and see what your insurance will cover.”
Noël Bonam, Maine AARP’s state director, said a good first step is to call 211 or reach out to your local Agency on Aging.
“They will do an assessment to see what are the needs in this caregiving situation, what kind of support is needed and what kind of resources are available,” Bonam said.
One of the first steps that can be taken is to look up caregiver support groups. For instance, the Southern Maine Agency on Aging offers caregiver training and support groups.
Some may qualify for help under Medicaid, known as MaineCare in the state. The first step is to get an assessment by filling out the long-term care application or calling 833-525-5784.
Catherine Dorrington, owner of Coastal Care Solutions in South Portland, said their business doesn’t provide Medicare or Medicaid home health services. But agencies such as Coastal Care can offer a number of out-of-pocket services to help older adults, such as respite care for caregivers, moving into new housing, and assistance with daily tasks.
“As you age, you can often continue to do things, but you may have to do them in a different way or with additional support,” Dorrington said.
If I’m a caregiver, do I have to follow the new Medicaid work requirement rules?
Most caregivers with Medicaid insurance are exempt from the work requirements that will require Medicaid recipients to work, volunteer or attend school for at least 80 hours per month starting in 2027.
Olivia Umoren Ezeuko, director of public policy and advocacy for USAging, a national association that supports state agencies on aging, said it’s important for caregivers to know about this exemption so they fill out the paperwork properly to prove their status. If not, people risk becoming uninsured.
“A lot of people are going to go to their next doctor’s appointment and find out they don’t have coverage anymore,” Umoren Ezeoko said during a public briefing on the topic. She said states are trying to make the process of maintaining Medicaid insurance as seamless as possible by linking employers with Medicaid eligibility documentation so that many workers do not need to obtain proof of employment.
Where can I go for help?
There are several good resources online, including at the Southern Maine Agency on Aging, which offers help for family caregivers. Or call 800-427-7411.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has a guide to help families determine whether they qualify for home healthcare services through Medicaid. Under Medicaid, one of the first steps is to fill out the long-term care application. In addition to asking about what type of help is needed, Medicaid will need financial information, such as income and assets. Families can also call 833-525-5784 and to see what services they may qualify for.
The Maine AARP also has a guide on home- and community-based services. Call 866-554-5380 for more information.
Caregivers can also call 211, which will connect them to resources.

title: Maine plans winter survey to study impacts of offshore wind development
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine announces additional marine life surveys near proposed offshore wind development
Researchers will examine fish and other marine life in the Gulf of Maine ahead of potential wind turbine construction
Maine announces additional marine life surveys near proposed offshore wind development
Researchers will examine fish and other marine life in the Gulf of Maine ahead of potential wind turbine construction
The Maine Department of Marine Resources announced on Tuesday that it plans to conduct another round of research in the Gulf of Maine to study marine life near a proposed offshore wind development.
The winter bottom trawl survey is scheduled to begin the week of January 11, 2027, and continue through Feb. 28. The department notes that the project could be extended into March depending on weather conditions.
A 55-foot trawling vessel, the Northern Lights, is set to depart from Portland and conduct approximately 37 sampling tows over nine days.
Researchers are set to examine fish and invertebrate populations to establish baseline data that they will then compare with findings collected during the construction and operation of Maine's proposed offshore wind research array.
According to the state, the research is intended to help scientists understand the effects of offshore wind development on marine ecosystems as well as commercial fishing.
Officials do not plan to ask fishermen to move their gear during the survey. However, the department says additional notices will be issued if fishing gear is set to interfere with research operations.
The survey is part of Maine's broader effort to study the environmental and fishing-industry impacts of offshore wind energy before commercial development.
In a separate announcement on Wednesday, DMR said it will also conduct plankton and larval lobster surveys in the Maine Research Array Wind Energy Area between Jan. 1 and March 31, 2027.
The surveys will be conducted in partnership with Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences and will take place up to two days per month aboard the R/V Maine. The plan is for researchers to monitor zooplankton and the distribution of lobster larvae to establish baseline data prior to potential offshore wind development.

title: Hunter facing charges after stray bullet hits, kills pet donkey, officials say
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - South Carolina authorities say a hunter has been charged after a donkey was shot and killed over the weekend.
According to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, officers were called to a property in Anderson County after a report of a shooting involving a pet donkey named Angelique.
Officials said the hunter fired a gun at a deer but missed, and the stray bullet hit the donkey.
Joann Kelly, founder of Hasty’s Haven where Angelique lived, said the donkey’s death feels like a nightmare and that her entire rescue team has been left traumatized.
“Angelique came to us several years ago, along with her other three herd members,” the rescue shared. “They were previously therapy donkeys for special needs children and we have used them for education in the community. They were always the first to greet anyone and gentle in nature.”
Neighbors were seen on Monday adjusting a hunting stand near where officials said the bullet came from.
South Carolina officials said the hunter involved in the shooting was charged with negligent use of a firearm and hunting within 300 yards of a residence.
“This unfortunate incident serves as an important safety reminder,” the Department of Natural Resources said. “Hunters must always positively identify their target, be aware of what lies beyond it, and ensure they are shooting in a safe direction.”
The rescue said they hope other hunters learn from what occurred.
“I just hope this doesn’t happen to anyone else. I hope that other hunters take note and be respectful,” Kelly said.

title: Ryan Coogler’s ‘The X-Files’ Picked Up for Series By Hulu
text:
Ryan Coogler’s ‘The X-Files’ Picked Up for Series By Hulu
It’s time to reopen The X-Files.
Disney announced today that the pilot for the new revival of The X-Files overseen by Black Panther and Sinners director Ryan Coogler will move forward and become a full-fledged series on the company’s Hulu streaming service.
The new version of the classic ’90s conspiracy thriller is described as a “reimagining” which follows “two highly decorated but vastly different FBI agents who form an unlikely bond when they are assigned to a long-shuttered division devoted to cases involving unexplained phenomena.” The stars of Coogler’s X-Files are Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel.
Original X-Files creator Chris Carter is an executive producer on the new show.
READ MORE: The Worst American TV Remakes of Foreign Shows
Here was Coogler’s comment on the news:
I’ve loved ‘The X-Files’ for a long time, so getting the chance to write and direct the pilot has meant a great deal to me. What Chris Carter created is special, and we wanted to honor everything that made the original series connect with so many people while also finding our own way into that world.
The old X-Files aired on Fox from 1993 to 2002, and starred David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson as FBI Agents Mulder and Scully, who are assigned to investigate cases of the strange and the supernatural. After the initial nine-season run dense with an elaborate alien invasion mythology, the show was brought back for a two-season revival with Duchovny and Anderson in 2016 and 2018.
The duo also starred in two big-screen X-Files movies, one in 1998, while the show was still on the air, and one, The X-Files: I Want to Believe, in 2008 that was sort of an epilogue to the show — at least until Fox greenlight that prior revival with Duchovny and Anderson. (Carter was still tinkering with that last X-Files movie as recently as last summer, when a new director’s cut of it debuted on Hulu.)
It’s not clear if or when Mulder and Scully may appear on Coogler’s X-Files. But one imagines that if the show is popular at all, it’s only a matter of time.

title: A brief briefing: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia makes debut
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia’s first press briefing operated much differently from a standard Karoline Leavitt briefing.
The press conference lasted 14 minutes and included questions from only three outlets - Breitbart News Network, The Daily Mail, and FOX News.
FOX news asked whether her role includes making things less tough for Republicans in the midterms. Zacharia said she hoped to amplify the president’s agenda.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” she said.
During the briefing, Zacharia said U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to resign. She also said Trump would step up his midterm campaign appearances.
“You can expect more of the midterm blitz. Just now we’ve added Kentucky, and we have a few other stops as he goes down to Florida. So it will be Georgia, Kentucky and Florida,” Zacharia said.
Zacharia described Trump as the administration’s best spokesman. She ended the briefing after answering a question about balancing family and work responsibilities.
“So thank you for that question. In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska. And we can ask him all of the questions out there.”

title: Obituary: William H. Harmon
text:
SUMNER – William H. Harmon, 91, passed away peacefully on Friday Oct. 9, 2026, at Cindy and Mike’s home where he resided for the past month. He was born on March 29, 1935, in Mexico, a son of the late Leon and Bessie (Sotman) Harmon.
He graduated from the local school system and went on to work at Puiia’s Hardware and Lumber working his way up to the foreman position for 44 years. And after retirement he worked part-time at the Buckfield/Sumner Transfer Station for 25 years, retiring in March of this year.
He married Rosemarie “Tibby” Mercier Porter on Oct. 15, 1988, at South Arm, and they were married for 13 years before she passed in April of 2001.
Bill developed a lifelong passion for the outdoors at an early age. He would head to the woods as soon as school was done. He was always hunting, fishing, and trapping. He was self-taught on how to mount horns and making his famous pack baskets, which he has made so many of them and was always willing to donate for a good cause. Bill was always ready to tell a story or two, about pretty much anything. He was full of knowledge and always willing to tell you, “That’s not how I would have done it.”
He loved to spend time with his family and friends, especially his children and grandchildren.
He is survived by his significant other Martha Dunn; children, Brian (Jody) Harmon and Karen Harmon; loving stepchildren, Cindy (Michael) Stevens, Kathy D’Agostino, Timothy (Candace) Porter, David (Kelly) Porter, and Martha’s two sons Ted (Vivian) Dunn and John (Kathy) Dunn. As well as, his sister Joan Robichaud; several grandchildren and great- grandchildren, along with nieces and nephews.
He was predeceased by his loving parents; his wife Tibby Harmon; son Michael Harmon; sister Jeannette Cormier; and granddaughter Jo-Ann Rioux.
In keeping with Bill’s wishes, there will be no services. He will be laid to rest at St. John’s Cemetery in Rumford.
The family would thank the wonderful staff at Andwell so we were able to keep him home.
Arrangements are under the care of Chandler Funeral Home and Cremation Services, 45 Main St., to make an online condolence please visit http://www.chandlerfunerals.com
In lieu of flowers donations can be given to Andwell Health Partners or Operation Reboot.

title: Candidates for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District answer your questions
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
To put the focus on the topics and concerns that matter most to you, the BDN opinion section asked subscribers for their questions for the candidates for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House. Today, we’re sharing answers from the candidates for the U.S. House for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, Republican former Gov. Paul LePage and State Auditor Matt Dunlap, a Democrat. Visit bangordailynews.com/candidates-questions to see the responses in other races.
What measures would you vote for to ensure that all Mainers have access to affordable healthcare? Should all Americans have access to the same coverage, at the same cost, as members of Congress? Do you support Medicare-for-all or another form of universal health care? If so, how would you pay for it? If not, why not.
Matt Dunlap, Democrat
I will fight with every chance I get to fix our broken health care system and make it better for every Mainer, and that means taking every opportunity possible to vote to make sure Mainers have access to affordable health care. Healthcare is too expensive, but Paul LePage spent more time passing tax cuts for billionaires than doing anything to fix it. I will take on Big Pharma and the insurance companies that are making millions while too many families can’t afford lifesaving care.
LePage may call Medicare and Medicaid cuts “the greatest thing that can happen to the Maine people,” but as your representative, I will vote to restore the Medicaid cuts, expand tax credits to make health insurance premiums more affordable, and fight for Medicare for All (which would be $1 trillion dollars cheaper than our current system).
Paul LePage, Republican
Mainers deserve affordable care, more choices and the freedom to choose their doctors. Those with pre-existing conditions should have coverage. I support more competition in our insurance marketplace, transparent pricing and removing bureaucracy, which simply adds cost to patients without any beneficial health outcomes. Under Obamacare, insurance companies have gotten rich. Insurance companies should have to compete for your business and they should be forced to justify the prices they charge for premiums. Congress should live under the same rules as the people it represents. As governor, I signed Public Law (PL) 90, which expanded insurance options and lowered premiums for Mainers. This reform was touted by The Wall Street Journal because it actually lowered health insurance premiums.
I oppose completely government-run healthcare. First, it would force every Mainer to lose their health plans including union plans, employer plans, or other types of healthcare plans, which would be eliminated. Second, government-run healthcare will cost all Mainers as tens of trillions of dollars gets eaten by an inefficient system which would force across-the-board tax increases on Maine families, including the middle class. Very importantly, government-run healthcare would put bureaucrats in charge of your healthcare decisions and take those decisions away from you and your doctor.
What specific steps do you support to preserve the financial stability of Social Security? Would you support raising the payroll tax on higher incomes? Raising the full retirement age? Reducing benefits, particularly to those with high incomes? Should government spending be reduced in other areas?
LePage
First of all, I myself receive Social Security. I have always, always supported Social Security and Medicare. It is time we have an honest conversation about the Social Security cap, which shields wealthy individuals from having to pay more Social Security tax. Adjusting the cap so high-income earners pay more may help with solvency. People paid into this program throughout their working lives, and Washington must honor that commitment.
As governor, I lowered taxes for Maine seniors so they could keep more of their retirement income in their pockets. Washington should start by controlling spending elsewhere, cracking down on improper payments and strengthening an economy that supports more workers paying into Social Security. We need to eliminate fraud within the system because it undermines benefits for people who earned them. Lastly, any long-term reform must protect those already counting on it.
Dunlap
What’s best for our seniors is best for everyone, and that means I will work hard every single day to lower your costs and protect Social Security. LePage has called Social Security “welfare, pure and simple” but I know that when you’ve paid into the system your whole life, you’ve earned it.
When he was governor, LePage passed tax cuts for the wealthy and made seniors pay for it by slashing senior nutrition assistance like Meals on Wheels, blocking affordable housing for seniors, and even refusing federal funding for dementia and Alzheimer’s programs. As your congressman, I’ll remove the cap on Social Security contributions, a bipartisan proposal that will keep Social Security solvent for years to come, ensuring the system works for future generations.
Do you believe that climate change is real and made worse by burning fossil fuels? If not, why not? If so, what specific actions would you support to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to ensure the U.S. reengages with international partners to address climate change? How would you support the transition to cleaner energy sources? How would you stand up to the president to move a climate-focused agenda forward?
Dunlap
Climate change is real, and it’s affecting all of us here in Maine — warmer winters affect our hunting and fishing game and our winter sports tourism economy. Sea level rise from climate change has a big impact on our coastal communities, and even slight increases in ocean temperature can lead to more severe storms and fewer lobsters for our fisherman. I support greater efforts to use renewables to power our grid, including in partnership with international allies like our neighbors to the north.
LePage
My energy policy starts with what Mainers pay to heat their homes, fill their tanks and keep the lights on. Now is not the time to wage war on certain fuels or impose an expensive so-called Green New Deal that increases costs. I support any energy source that can reliably lower the cost of heating your home or lowers your electricity bill. Cleaner technology should earn its place by being affordable and dependable. We should unleash American energy production and remove unnecessary barriers to building energy infrastructure. I will judge proposals from any president or international organization by whether they serve Maine people and lower costs. Families deserve affordable energy and practical solutions. We will never strengthen or revitalize our economy without more affordable energy.
How will you make sure our laws, including the Constitution, are enforced equally for everyone, including members of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the president? What laws should be enforced or changed to hold the president accountable and to ensure the survival of our democracy? Is this a top priority for you? What steps will you take to protect mail-in voting?
LePage
Upholding the Constitution is a fundamental responsibility. Everyone must be held to the law. Congress already has constitutional tools for oversight and accountability, and I would use them when the facts warrant it. Regarding law enforcement, we can support officers while demanding transparent investigations when something goes wrong.
While we’re on the topic of the rule of law, we should also hold fraudsters accountable. The same scrutiny should be held when it comes to credible allegations of government waste, fraud and abuse.
I believe we should restore confidence in our elections through widely supported, common-sense measures such as voter ID. We are asked for our IDs almost everywhere and there is no reason they should not be used to ensure we protect our elections. I support ensuring only citizens of the United States are voting. These positions are common-sense.
I support Maine’s absentee ballot system, especially because so many elderly people depend on it to cast their vote. Eligible citizen voters should have access to absentee voting and confidence that our elections are secure.
Dunlap
In America, no man is above the law. As state auditor, my job is to be politically neutral and ensure that government is working for you, and that taxpayer dollars are wisely spent. But that only works if you’re willing to look beyond partisan politics. There are times where both parties have been annoyed by my audit findings, but at the end of the day the job is about protecting taxpayers not appeasing politicians. I’ll approach my role in Congress the same way: Is this good for Mainers, or is it good for Washington, D.C.? That means enforcing the laws, no matter whether it’s about the president or a member of my own party.
In terms of ensuring the survival of our democracy, here are a few changes I support: a ban on congressional stock trading so that you know politicians are working for your best interest rather than their own; and getting money out of politics so that billionaires and corporate interests don’t control who wins. My campaign doesn’t take a cent of corporate PAC money.
As a former secretary of state, I strongly support Mainers’ right to vote. Fortunately, the Supreme Court recently ruled to support the right to vote by mail, and prevented federal overreach into what is ultimately a state process.
What are your top 3 accomplishments as a lawmaker?
Dunlap
I have dedicated my entire career in government service to the people of Maine, having led the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine and putting people first as secretary of state and state auditor. My top accomplishment in the Legislature was helping to establish the Lifetime Hunting and Fishing License Endowment, which allowed us to make sure our outdoor heritage survived and thrived for future generations.
As secretary of state, I implemented the first-in-the-nation statewide ranked-choice voting election for the people of Maine.
I have never been beholden to a particular political party or its interests, and I’m proud to have called out fraud and corruption from both parties. In the Legislature, I also helped establish OPEGA (Office of Program Enforcement and Government Accountability) as the only Democrat to support that.
LePage
As governor, my proudest accomplishments include saving healthcare, especially rural healthcare, by paying off a massive $750 million debt owed to Maine’s hospitals when I became governor; lowering taxes for working Mainers including the working poor; and stopping automatic gas tax increases. I also am proud we brought accountability to Maine’s welfare system by ending illegal immigration sanctuary city policies and cracking down on fraud that saw EBT cards used at strip clubs, casinos, and liquor stores.
Why should we trust you?
LePage
Maine voters know me. Not every voter will agree with me all of the time but I will make the tough decisions needed to make life here more affordable and revitalize our economy. Maine built me, and I have spent my life giving back to the state that gave me everything.
Dunlap
I’m like you: Born on a farm near Bar Harbor and deeply proud of where I come from. I went to the University of Maine and have worked as a proofreader, dishwasher, bartender, and even a fur trapper. Like you, I respect hard work and am on the side of working people. I’m a Mainer and pay taxes here, which is more than my opponent can say. And I will fight for Maine because I myself am a Mainer.

title: Man accused of shooting at teens in homecoming prank says they drove toward him
text:
ADDIS, La. (WAFB/Gray News) — A man accused of firing a shot at high school students during a homecoming prank says he feared for his safety and did not know the people outside his home were teenagers.
Josiah Arrington was arrested and charged with aggravated assault with a firearm following the incident Tuesday night, Oct. 6, at the Riverboat Trailer Park in Addis.
According to the police chief, the teenagers were participating in homecoming festivities when they mistakenly went to Arrington’s home, believing it belonged to a friend.
The chief said Arrington came outside and yelled at the teenagers, who then tried to leave. As they were driving away, the chief said Arrington fired a shot that struck their vehicle.
No one was injured.
However, Arrington said there is more to what happened before he pulled the trigger.
Arrington says teens drove toward him
Arrington said he was preparing to step outside to smoke a cigarette and drink coffee when he encountered two or three people dressed in all black and wearing masks near his porch.
He said he had no idea who they were or why they were on his property.
“I just kept screaming, ‘What are you doing in my yard? What are you doing in my yard? What are you doing in my yard?’” Arrington said.
Arrington claims that as he approached the road, the individuals got into their vehicle and accelerated toward him, forcing him to jump out of the way.
“So as I met the road, they jumped into drive and sped towards me. I jumped to the side, and I fired one shot, expecting it to be a warning shot, not to injure anybody, not to hit the vehicle,” Arrington said.
Arrington acknowledged firing the shot but insisted he was not trying to strike the vehicle or hurt anyone. He said he did not realize the bullet had struck the car.
The police chief described the teenagers as trying to flee when Arrington fired. The chief did not mention a vehicle driving toward Arrington.
‘I didn’t know they were high school students’
Arrington repeatedly emphasized that he did not know the people outside his home were teenagers.
He said the darkness, their clothing, and the masks prevented him from identifying them.
“I didn’t know they was high school students, man. Please put it out there. I didn’t know that they were high school students, man. I wouldn’t hurt no kids,” Arrington said.
Arrington said his daughter recently graduated from high school and that he has young children in his life. He insisted he would never intentionally hurt children.
He also expressed regret over the incident and apologized to the teenagers and their families, acknowledging that the experience could have been traumatic for them.
“I’m sorry that happened to them because I know that could be traumatic to their life too. So I also want to apologize to them,” Arrington said.
Despite his explanation, Arrington was charged with aggravated assault with a firearm.
Police chief warns homecoming pranks are going too far
The shooting comes after police received several reports of homecoming pranks going too far in the area.
The police chief said what started as a tradition of students toilet-papering their friends’ homes has escalated in some cases to property damage.
He said students have worn masks and all black to disguise themselves, which he advises against. He said police have received reports of students throwing ketchup, mustard, and barbecue sauce on cars, garage doors, and concrete. Police have also received reports of paintball guns being used, leaving damage to homes.
The chief said he issued a warning Monday night, one day before the shooting, urging students to stop damaging property and encouraging parents to keep track of what their children are doing.
While he stressed that not all students participating in homecoming traditions are causing problems, he said some have taken things too far.
He also warned homeowners to understand the laws surrounding the use of firearms, emphasizing that people fleeing a property does not, by itself, justify shooting at them.
The chief said Tuesday’s incident could have ended much differently, adding that he is thankful no one was injured.
“And I beg that anybody that has kids or whatever, please don’t, you know, don’t fire a shot at kids or towards kids or anything like that, especially if they’re trying to just get away and run off,” the chief said.
The chief encouraged parents to know where their children are, what they are doing and to make sure homecoming traditions do not turn traumatic.

🎃👻 MAINE’S SPOOKIEST LEGEND? The Mysterious Cursed Tomb in Bucksport!
text:
Bucksport, Maine, Is Home to a Spooky Cursed Tomb Legend
This is such an exciting time of year! Fall really is the best, especially here in Maine. Between the beautiful foliage, crisp air, and all the Halloween-themed events happening across the state, there's no shortage of ways to get into the spooky spirit. And when it comes to creepy stories and local legends, it's hard to beat Bucksport!
Honestly, this is the perfect time of year to explore Bucksport. The fall scenery, historic charm, and spooky stories make it a fun destination for anyone looking to get out and enjoy the season.
One of Maine's greatest spooktacular days is almost here! Be sure to mark your calendar for Bucksport's 17th Annual Ghostport, Saturday, October 17th, from 10am-10pm.
Ghostport offers a full day of Halloween and fall-themed fun along the waterfront walkway!
Read More: Bucksport, Maine Transforms Into "Ghostport" For One Spooky Day
Did you know that Bucksport is home to one of Maine's most famous spooky legends: The Cursed Tomb of Colonel Buck. If you've never heard the story, prepare to enjoy a scary treat!
The tomb features a mysterious stain that looks quite a bit like a woman's stocking-clad leg and foot. Some people say it looks more like a boot, but either way, it's certainly not something you would ever expect to see on a memorial!
According to local legend, Colonel Jonathan Buck ordered a woman accused of witchcraft to be burned at the stake. As the story goes, one of her legs rolled out of the fire, and before her death, she placed a curse on the colonel. Then the strange leg-shaped stain later appeared on his tomb as a reminder of that curse.
Of course, it's a legend, but the story has been passed down through generations, making the tomb one of Bucksport's most talked about attractions.
If you're looking for a fun fall adventure in Maine, why not add Bucksport to your list? You can enjoy the autumn scenery, explore the town's historic charm, and check out the legendary tomb, it really is a perfect Halloween season adventure. Just don't forget to look for that mysterious stain!

text:
Ernest Manton Barter, 77, of Boothbay Harbor, passed away on Oct. 8, 2026 at Togus VA in Augusta just 10 days shy of his 78th birthday.
Ernest was born on Oct. 18, 1948 in Boothbay Harbor to Warren Stanley Barter and Florence Elaine (Emerson) Barter. He grew up in the Boothbay region and graduated from Boothbay Region High School. He continued his education at the University of Maine at Fort Kent and later attended the Maine Criminal Justice Academy.
Ernest proudly served his country in the United States Army from 1970-1972, attaining the rank of specialist five (SP5).
Throughout his working years, Ernest held a variety of positions within his community. His employment included Blake’s Boatyard, C+B Marina, Ocean Point Marina, the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, and G+G Towing. His diverse career reflected his wide range of skills and experiences.
Outside of work, Ernest enjoyed spending time hunting, woodworking, reading, and playing video games. Whether working with his hands, enjoying the outdoors, or settling in with a good book or favorite game, Ernest appreciated the hobbies that brought him enjoyment throughout his life.
Ernest was predeceased by his beloved wife, Eileen Diann (Brewer) Barter; his son, Cory Allan Barter; his parents, Warren and Florence Barter; and his siblings, Samuel, Thomas, Elaine, and Roxanne.
He is survived by his sons, Brian Keith Barter and Brent Stephen Barter and his wife, Elizabeth, of Whitefield; and his daughter, Michele Erin Barter-Ripley and her husband, Nicholas, of East Boothbay; and his siblings, Gregory and Terry. He also leaves behind his grandsons, Cody, Colin, Stephen, Cole, and Gabe; his granddaughters, Courtney, Allyson, Madeleine, and Isabelle; and great-grandchildren, Josie, Beau, Walker and Maisyn, Charlie and Lucy, Presley and Ridge, Jameson and Sterling.
Ernest will be remembered by his family and those who knew him for the many roles he held throughout his life, from his service to his country and community to his role as a father and grandfather. Friends are welcome to join the family for a time of visitation from 6-8 p.m. on Oct. 19 at the Hall Funeral Home, at 975 Wiscasset Road in Boothbay. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Tuesday ordered a halt to tree-cutting at the East Potomac Golf Course until Oct. 26, putting a further pause on work at the historic D.C. course that has been part of President Donald Trump's plans to remake the city.
Reyes issued the order one day after a tense three-hour hearing in which she harshly criticized the government for having deceived her with its actions over the holiday weekend.
At that hearing, Reyes ordered a 24-hour pause that could be extended to 14 days if necessary. title: Letter: Why I no longer support Susan Collins
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For 18 years, I supported Susan Collins.
I was proud to support a moderate, pro-choice Republican woman from Maine. I respected her work ethic, bipartisan instincts and independence. I believed her growing seniority would translate into greater benefits for Maine.
Over time, I began to see the limits of that bargain.
Collins has been exceptionally effective at bringing federal money home. That matters. But too often it has looked like spackle on a state with deep structural cracks.
Maine has lost much of the value-added economy that once turned our natural resources into good jobs: paper, shoes, textiles, manufactured housing, wood products and food processing. We have spent decades managing the consequences.
A state in decline needs a strong social safety net. Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, food assistance, rural health care and education are essential. But survival is not an economic strategy.
Maine also needs federal policy aimed at rebuilding prosperity: infrastructure, energy, housing, workforce development, research, manufacturing and industries that create good jobs.
After nearly three decades in office, I wanted Collins’ seniority to mean more than appropriations and occasional independence.
Her vote for Brett Kavanaugh became a turning point for me.
Troy Jackson is imperfect. I will not agree with him on everything. But he comes from the Maine economy I am describing and understands economic insecurity from the ground up.
I support Troy Jackson, warts and all, because Maine needs more than help managing decline. We need leadership determined to reverse it.
Brenda Garrand
Rockland

title: Las Vegas Sassy Seniors bring community service across the valley
text:
LAS VEGAS (InvestigateTV) — A Las Vegas group called the Sassy Seniors has spent the past year showing up to community events across the valley dressed in pink and carrying pom-poms.
The group was founded by a woman named Kathy Yanke, who wanted to find others her age to do community work alongside. She has since recruited about a dozen women who rotate in and out of events throughout the Las Vegas Valley.
In their first year, the group logged 4,000 hours of community service.
For a lot of those who volunteer, it gives them a sense of belonging.
The Sassy Seniors do not limit themselves to a single cause or organization. They have worked with veterans, participated in community and highway cleanups, and supported heart health initiatives in February through the Red Cross and other organizations.
Yanke initially connected the group to causes she had personal ties to, but organizations have since begun reaching out to her directly because of the group’s social media presence.
One member of the group works on a program that takes old wedding dresses and repurposes them for babies born sleeping — a term used to describe stillborn infants. The woman involved in the program had experienced infant loss herself.
It’s emotional work, but with that comes a joy because the group feels like they are making a difference.
The group is scheduled to travel to Hawaii to participate in a ceremonial anniversary event for Pearl Harbor Day, where they will present World War II veterans.
Membership in the Las Vegas Sassy Seniors is open to women generally 50 and older. Prospective members are asked to be available Tuesday nights for planning meetings and rehearsals, and to commit to at least 10 hours of community service per month.
The group can be found on Facebook or Instagram by searching Las Vegas Sassy Seniors.

title: Maintenance worker dies after being hit by truck at gas station
text:
LOUISA, Ky. (WSAZ/Gray News) - A maintenance worker was struck and killed by a semitruck at a Kentucky gas station Monday morning.
The Louisa Police Department said a worker at a gas station along U.S. 23 told police they noticed a body around 5:50 a.m. and reported it.
A few minutes after the first report, a customer came across the body, realized the victim was dead and called 911 again.
Louisa Police Chief Steven Wilburn said the maintenance worker was checking his diesel containers due to the rain. That is when a semitruck, pulling out after pumping gas, unknowingly hit the worker.
Police said the victim was kneeling in front of the truck just before he was hit.
The worker died at the scene, Wilburn said.
Police say they watched footage and were able to find the trucking company and call the truck driver back. The driver immediately returned to the scene.
The victim’s name is not being released at this time, police said.
According to the Louisa Police Department, no charges have been filed at this time.

title: A freed man faces life back in prison after a Supreme Court ruling on the First Step Act
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two years after his release from prison, Patrick Dewayne Smith spends Sundays with his family in a modest brick church with a white steeple in rural Tennessee. He works two jobs. He goes to ball games to cheer for nieces and nephews he had never met. After serving 13 years for a nonviolent drug conviction, he is trying to rebuild his life.
Now Smith could be sent back to prison for the rest of it.
A federal judge released him in 2024 under rules adopted after Congress passed the First Step Act, a landmark criminal justice law during President Donald Trump’s first term. But the Supreme Court ruled in May that people sentenced under older, harsher laws cannot rely on the disparity between their sentences and current penalties to seek early compassionate release.
“Every time I get a call, I’m hoping it’s some good news. Or, you know, at least not no bad news,” said Smith, a tall, soft-spoken 47-year-old whose beard is now flecked with gray.
Smith is among about a dozen people nationwide who could be returned to prison because of the ruling, according to FAMM, a sentencing reform group formerly Families Against Mandatory Minimums. Without clemency from the White House, the group says, second chances could disappear for those people.
The First Step Act opened a path to freedom
The First Step Act was the most significant rewrite of federal sentencing laws in a generation. Among other changes, it reduced some lengthy mandatory minimum sentences, particularly for nonviolent drug crimes. Trump said the law would “make our communities safer and give former inmates a second chance at life after they have served their time.”
The law was championed by Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and senior adviser who had a personal connection to the issue: Kushner’s father had spent time in federal prison when Kushner was younger.
Thousands of people have been released from prison in the years since the law was passed, but some recent Supreme Court rulings have made it harder for other people already serving long sentences to argue for their release. For Smith and others like him, competing interpretations have created a high-stakes legal limbo.
“They’re doing everything that they should be doing. They’re reestablishing relationships with families. They’re volunteering in their communities. They’re working,” said Shanna Rifkin, FAMM’s general counsel. “Having them reincarcerated is so unjust given that they have demonstrated their rehabilitation.”
Without a grant of clemency from the White House, Rifkin says their second chance could be snatched away.
Trump remains proud of signing the First Step Act, and the administration is actively reviewing developments, said a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the issue.
Supreme Court ruling narrows options for people serving long sentences
In 2023, the U.S. Sentencing Commission adopted new rules for people serving unusually long sentences. Judges could sometimes consider changes to the law when deciding whether to grant compassionate release to inmates who had served at least 10 years.
Not everyone agreed.
The Department of Justice argued the new rules went beyond what the First Step Act allowed. Judges nevertheless agreed to free dozens of people across the country after considering legal changes and other factors, FAMM found.
The dispute eventually went all the way to the Supreme Court, which handed down a 6-3 decision in May. It found that sentencing disparities from decades past are not “extraordinary and compelling” reasons to grant compassionate release.
“It is hard to see how Congress’s deliberate decision not to extend newly reduced penalties to those already sentenced could be a convincing reason that ‘warrant(s)’ a reduction,” Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote for the conservative majority.
The decision was one of two during the last Supreme Court term that narrowed the options for people serving long sentences, said Daniel Harawa, a law professor at New York University. “I worry a lot about what this means for federal criminal justice reform,” he said.
For Smith and about a dozen other people around the country, it could mean they have to finish serving a sentence that would not be handed down today.
Prior convictions meant a life sentence
Smith grew up in a small town in rural northern Alabama and became addicted to drugs as a teenager, his lawyers said in court documents. At 17 he was arrested for twice selling crack cocaine to an informant. A pair of marijuana convictions followed a few years later. He served about three years in prison. After his release he worked as a construction worker and a janitor.
In 2010, he got involved with a drug ring selling crack cocaine and marijuana on the Tennessee-Alabama line, prosecutors said. Caught on phone calls recorded by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, he was convicted of drug conspiracy and money laundering after he pulled out of a plea deal that called for 12 years to 14 years in prison in exchange for his cooperation.
His lawyers called his involvement “unremarkable,” but the federal conviction combined with his prior record triggered a life sentence.
The judge questioned whether the punishment fit the crime, but said the laws tied her hands. It was the longest sentence linked to the 20-person case, exceeding even the ringleader’s.
Smith said he resolved to keep his head down behind bars, working prison jobs and avoiding infractions.
“What kept me sane was that faith, that belief in God,” he said.
He missed little things, like sleeping in a full-sized bed and taking a bath after a long day. He missed big things, too: His mother died during his first year in prison and he couldn’t ask his family to shoulder the $1,000 it would cost for him to travel home for the funeral.
After 13 years, Smith got his second chance
After the Sentencing Commission adopted its new compassionate release rules following the First Step Act, Smith asked a judge for a reduction to time served. It took nearly a year, but the court agreed he should go free.
He returned to Alabama and moved in with his sister and her daughter.
Last month, prosecutors filed court documents challenging his release and they pointed to the Supreme Court decision. They argued he would be subject to a mandatory-minimum sentence of 25 years, even under current laws, and called the judge’s decision to release him “difficult to justify.”
A Justice Department official speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing case said the Supreme Court decision means his release is no longer valid, and the department cannot agree to a sentence below what the law requires.
The prospect of a return to prison is a bitter pill for his father, James Smith, a mainstay at the Willow Grove Missionary Baptist Church.
“When you got rapists and murderers and you get this guy on a nonviolent case and you want him for life,” he said, “it doesn’t sit well with me.”
___
Associated Press video journalist Kristin M. Hall in Nashville, Tenn., contributed to this report.

title: Here’s what Yarmouth voters will see on November’s ballot
text:
Absentee voting is underway leading up to Maine’s Nov. 3 election. On Election Day, Yarmouth residents can vote in person at the Yarmouth High School gym from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.
In addition to federal, gubernatorial and district attorney races, here’s what Yarmouth voters will decide on their ballots. To see the complete ballot and dive more into candidate responses, explore the 2026 Maine Voter Guide.
SCHOOL RECREATION PROJECT BOND
Yarmouth voters will decide whether to borrow $2 million to fund several recreation facilities projects at Yarmouth schools.
If approved, the district would replace the synthetic turf field and track at Yarmouth High School, both of which are deteriorating, according to the Yarmouth School Committee. The playground at the Yarmouth Elementary School, which is 25 years old and has no available replacement parts, would be fully replaced. The project would also expand the recreation opportunities at Harrison Middle School and make the play space more accessible.
The school department estimates that the total cost of the project will be $3.14 million, but due to $1.1 million already reserved for the turf and track replacement, only $2.05 million needs to be borrowed.
CUMBERLAND COUNTY COMMISSIONER, DISTRICT 3
The Board of Cumberland County Commissioners is comprised of five commissioners who are elected for a four-year term. The Board oversees the financial operations, approved budgets and manages county property. Yarmouth residents, part of Cumberland County’s 3rd district, will choose between two candidates:
Amy Leshure, Democrat
What are your top three priorities?
1) Responsible budgeting and the county’s long-term fiscal stability. 2) Building stronger partnerships with municipalities and the state to share services, reduce duplication and secure sustainable funding. I will aim to have county government delivering essential services efficiently and transparently. 3) Right-sizing the county jail by strengthening behavioral health, substance-use and public safety services.
Why are you running?
I am running because county government has a meaningful impact on our communities. I bring more than 20 years of financial and operational experience and a collaborative leadership style. I will use this experience to strengthen fiscal oversight, increase transparency and help Cumberland County work more effectively with municipalities to solve our regional challenges.
Robert P. Vail, Independent
What are your top three priorities?
The expansion of county services to reduce local taxes. Ensure that training for first responders are standardized across the county. Include school departments with regionalization to offset rising costs.
Why are you running?
The challenges facing us today, whether housing, social issues, job creation, aging, childcare, lack of a workforce in our police, fire, rescue and public works departments need to have different approaches, and I believe I can contribute to that end.
MAINE STATE SENATE
Yarmouth residents in State Senate District 25 will see that Teresa S. Pierce of Falmouth is uncontested in her bid for reelection. Voters in State Senate District 23 will choose between two candidates:
Mattie Daughtry, Democrat
What are your top three priorities?
Affordability: Too many Mainers are struggling to afford the basics. We need to lower costs for housing, food, healthcare and energy. Healthcare: Protect local hospitals and providers, especially in rural Maine. Childcare: Build on clearing the state waitlist by making quality childcare more affordable and accessible for every Maine family.
Why are you running?
I’m running for my final term in the Senate because Maine is facing extraordinary financial and political pressures. I want to use these next two years to protect what makes our state special while building a future where every Mainer, no matter where they live or what they earn, has a fair shot at their version of the Maine dream.
Bernard Porter, Republican
Did not respond.
MAINE HOUSE DISTRICT 103
Former Yarmouth Town Council Chair Karin Orenstein, Democrat, is running uncontested for Maine House District 103, which covers Yarmouth.

title: Woman accused of nearly running over deputy when fleeing from Harpswell traffic stop

Deputies stopped Pennell, who was wanted on a warrant out of Cumberland County, near Harpswell and Gurnet roads in Harpswell about 12:21 p.m.

title: Hannaford app, website offline as parent company addresses security issue
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford’s website and mobile app have been temporarily shut down as the supermarket chain’s parent company addresses a cybersecurity issue.
Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch company that owns the Scarborough-based grocer, said in a brief news release Monday that it was experiencing an internal network issue and had taken some systems offline to protect them.
That includes the Hannaford app and website, both of which carried messages Tuesday morning that they were unavailable.
Stores remain open as usual, and any unfulfilled online orders will be refunded.
The company said Tuesday that the measures were precautionary and that, although the investigation is ongoing, there is no evidence to suggest that customer or employee data was compromised.
A November 2024 breach of Ahold Delhaize’s systems affected more than 95,000 Mainers — most of them current or former employees, Hannaford said — and over 2 million people worldwide.
Ahold Delhaize did not provide a timeline for when online service was expected to be restored but said teams are “working with urgency” and were starting controlled relaunches of some systems. A Hannaford spokesperson reiterated that the company is working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.
“We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate our customers’ patience and understanding,” Hannaford spokesperson Caitlin Cortelyou said in a written statement Tuesday.
Ahold Delhaize says it has contacted outside cybersecurity experts to help with its response and is “engaging with the appropriate authorities” as necessary.
“As the investigation is ongoing, we are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts,” the company added.
If the cybersecurity issue is deemed to have been a data breach, then Maine law requires it to be reported to the Office of the Maine Attorney General. The office did not immediately respond to an email Tuesday asking whether it had received any reports about this issue.
Ahold Delhaize is one of the world’s largest food retailers and operates more than 2,000 U.S. stores under several brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant Food.

title: Victim releases video of co-worker convicted of poisoning her
text:
BERKELEY, Calif. — A Berkeley engineer is speaking out after a judge expunged a felony conviction against the co-worker who poisoned her on the job nearly a decade ago.
Rong Yuan said she could not believe what she saw when she discovered her co-worker pouring something into her water bottle. The substance was later identified as a toxic chemical.
“Shocked. I don’t know why,” Yuan said when asked what she thought when she saw it.
Symptoms began in 2017
In 2017, Yuan started experiencing symptoms including vomiting and hair loss. For more than two years, she visited doctors seeking answers.
Her mother then noticed her water bottle smelled strange. After a deep cleaning failed to resolve the issue, Yuan set up a small camera at her work desk.
“I never expected that I could capture anybody,” Yuan said.
A sample of the water found 3.5 million times the federal level for cadmium. Yuan and her parents tested positive for cadmium poisoning.
Co-worker pleaded guilty
Yuan’s co-worker, David Xu, was charged with premeditated attempted murder. In a plea deal, he pleaded guilty to poisoning and received two years of probation.
“I don’t think he deserves a second chance. A second chance for a lot,” Yuan said.
Despite an objection from the district attorney’s office, the court agreed to expunge Xu’s felony conviction.
“They couldn’t find out this criminal record,” Yuan said.
Yuan said she still does not know exactly why Xu poisoned her, but she recalled that he had not let her work in the lab and had referred her to other jobs.
“He’s a nobody. He’s a coward,” Yuan said.
Father died last year
Yuan said her father’s health declined after he cooked using her water bottle. He died last year from heart failure. Yuan said she is speaking out in his honor.
“To come out of my comfort zone, to be interviewed about you, to tell the public what kind of effect it had on my family, and how broken the system is,” Yuan said.
Yuan said she continues to experience effects from the poisoning and is only able to work part-time. She requested $500,000 in restitution but has received $7,000.

title: Brittany Renee Barton
text:
Brittany Renee Barton, 41, of Edgecomb, passed away peacefully on Sept. 23, 2026 at Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor with her loving family by her side.
Brittany was born on July 26, 1985 in Damariscotta to Carol (Wall) Curtis and Christopher Barton. She grew up in Nobleboro and attended local schools before graduating from Lighthouse Academy.
Throughout her life, Brittany held a variety of jobs that allowed her to connect with people and share her talents. She worked in clothing stores, at Subway in Waldoboro, Dunkin’ in Connecticut, and Mr. Ribs. She also worked at Kings Korner Daycare and at a travel agency in Nobleboro.
Brittany was someone who found happiness in the simple things in life. Growing up, she enjoyed ballet, swimming, and being a Brownie and later a Girl Scout. She loved butterflies, watching movies, ice skating, and sliding in the winter. She especially enjoyed spending time outdoors and had a great love for animals.
Brittany also loved shopping and cooking, but perhaps most of all, she cherished time spent with her family and friends. Those who knew her will remember her for the love she gave so freely and the memories she created with the people who meant the most to her.
Brittany’s greatest joy was her family, and she leaves behind her children, Orianna Barton and Omarion Calel, both of Edgecomb; her mother and stepfather, Carol and Elijah Curtis, of Edgecomb; and her father and stepmother, Christopher and Beth Barton, of Augusta; brother James Libby, of Damariscotta; niece Alexandria Libby, of Damariscotta; nephews Nicholas Lamar, of Waldoboro, and Jacoby Peaslee, of Windsor; aunt Mary Calison, of Ottisfield, along with several cousins. She will also be lovingly remembered by many extended family members and friends whose lives she touched.
She was predeceased by her sister, Nicole Barton Peaslee; her maternal grandparents, Martin and Lillian Wall; her paternal grandparents, Thelma and Harold Barton; and her uncles, Edward Wall and Stanley Wall.
Brittany will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved her. Her memory will live on through her children, her family, her friends, and the many special moments shared throughout her life.
A memorial service to celebrate Brittany’s life will be held on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026 at 2 p.m. at Faith Baptist Church, at 144 Mills Road in Newcastle.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home, Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the Barton family, please visit Brittany’s Book of Memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Archbishop of US military says Catholic soldiers should not serve on Hasan’s firing squad
text:
(AP) - Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Church’s pastoral services to Catholics in the U.S. military, is condemning the proposed livestream of the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan.
Broglio, in a statement Monday, also stipulated that any Catholic soldier assigned to the U.S. Army firing squad should ask to be excused from that duty, which he described as contrary to the teachings of the church. He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the livestream plans.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.
Broglio recalled that he presided over the funeral of Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack.
The crime committed by Hasan “was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” Broglio asked.
“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio added. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?”

title: Hannaford website down after parent company reports cybersecurity incident
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The website for Hannaford supermarkets displayed an “unavailable” message on Tuesday afternoon, following an announcement by the regional supermarket chain’s parent company of a cybersecurity incident.
Ahold Delhaize, the Netherlands-based multinational holding company that owns Hannaford, announced on Monday that it is “experiencing a security issue within its network.”
“Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue,” the company said. “This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them. At this time, our stores are open and serving customers.”
Hannaford.com on Tuesday displayed a message stating that stores remain open during business hours, and the company is working to restore online service
“Any unfulfilled orders placed through Hannaford.com or the Hannaford app will be refunded,” the message said.
