title: 3 takeaways from the 3rd Maine Senate debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The third U.S. Senate debate between Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican incumbent Susan Collins didn’t break much new ground, though the candidates did sharpen their responses to questions about affordability, the Iran war and tariffs.
But Tuesday’s debate did provide a few striking moments, and some new substance. Both Collins and Jackson further elucidated their stances on data centers, saying they supported some form of regulation on where the centers could be located, and on how much water and electricity they use.
Polls show a tight race between the 73-year-old Collins and 58-year-old Jackson in Maine’s pivotal Senate race.
Here are three moments that stood out from their third meeting in a week. They will meet again Thursday for their final debate.
1. They got under each other’s skin
Collins provoked a strong reaction from Jackson about halfway through the debate. The Republican said “once again, Troy is confusing the Medicaid program with the Medicare program.” She proceeded to lecture him about the difference: Medicare largely goes to the elderly; Medicaid largely goes to the poor and sick.
Jackson grew visibly agitated in his response, saying that he understood the issue well because he had visited four birthing centers that have closed recently.
“Don’t act like I don’t know what I’m talking about, because I do,” Jackson said.
At another point, Jackson returned the favor. After Collins raised the issue of Medicaid fraud, the Democrat brought up recent ProPublica reporting about the FBI investigating whether Collins’ orbit was steering federal funding to a defense contractor and donor.
“I’m shocked that you’re talking about fraud, because there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the FBI,” he said. (The ProPublica story said that the FBI had been gearing to investigate Collins, but the bureau has never accused her of fraud.)
Collins didn’t respond at the time, but brought it back up later after Jackson said she does the bidding of billionaires.
“Troy has repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long,” she said. “He lied when he said that I was under investigation and found to have committed fraud by the FBI. And I just cannot continue to ignore these attacks on my integrity.”
At yet another point, Collins noted that Jackson has not yet filed a campaign finance report, which would show who his donors are. (Jackson entered the race after the last quarterly reporting period ended on June 30.)
The next round of reports are due by midnight on Thursday, but Jackson offered to release his early.
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning. How about that? Is that enough?” Jackson said. “Because we see yours and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me … I’ll give you the report tomorrow and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday.”
2. Collins finds differences in agreement
At several points, Collins deployed a new strategy to highlight her experience — and it came when the candidates seemed to agree on an issue.
Jackson has repeatedly hit Collins for advancing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which extended tax cuts for the wealthy and slashed $1 trillion in public health funding. Many of the cuts will take effect after the midterms.
But Collins noted that she voted against enacting the bill, which became law in 2025 after Vice President JD Vance broke a tie in the Senate. Despite her vote, she touted her ability to ensure that a $50 billion fund was included to help rural hospitals.
“Troy would have never been able to get that into the bill,” Collins said.
Jackson noted that the funding Maine would receive because of Collins’ amendment pales in comparison to the cuts.
Collins deployed the same tactic later when it came to Canadian tariffs, which both candidates oppose.
“The bottom line is that Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs,” she said. “But here’s the key difference: I’ve been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list. Troy would have gotten nothing.”
Jackson protested, noting that he’s been in contact with the Canadian ambassador and the consulate in Boston. But Collins made it clear she was referring to the Trump administration.
“Well, it wasn’t the Canadians that started this problem — it was the Trump administration,” she said.
3. Jackson leans into ICE shooting in Biddeford
Jackson came into the debate planning to make an issue of Collins’ votes to fund U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Tuesday was the three-month anniversary of federal agents fatally shooting Johan Sebastián Guerrero in Biddeford.
But he had to wait for the end of the debate to do it.
Jackson criticized Collins for supporting $70 billion in new funding for ICE and other agencies. He called ICE a “rogue agency” that needs to be abolished, with immigration enforcement being shifted to U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the FBI.
Collins, however, noted that she was able to include several reforms in the funding bill, including $20 million for body-worn cameras and de-escalation training.
“But more needs to be done,” she said.
Jackson pounced on Collins’ contention that some ICE agents are properly vetted and trained.
“I don’t know how you could stand up here and argue that it’s a good thing to let them out onto our population, out onto the American public, when we’ve seen consistently that they will murder people if you don’t comply explicitly with them,” Jackson said.

title: Police identify Atlanta man killed after being ejected from Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster
text:
Police identify Atlanta man killed after being ejected from Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster
Police have identified the man who died after being ejected from a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta.
Preliminary findings from witness and employee interviews indicate Kariem struck other patrons before falling beneath the ride, according to the Cobb County Police Department. Investigators are still examining what happened.
Officers working at the park responded around 3:58 p.m. and found Kariem beneath the attraction, unresponsive and not breathing. His family has been notified, police said.
Kariem worked as an IT manager at Wesley International Academy, a charter school in southeast Atlanta.
Atlanta Public Schools extended condolences to Kariem's family, friends and loved ones, describing him as a cherished member of the school and district communities.
"His presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched," an APS spokesperson said. "Our thoughts are with everyone mourning his loss during this difficult time."
Witnesses describe seeing a man fly out of the roller coaster
Logan Conner said he was on Goliath with his fiancée when he saw the man come out of his seat.
"The man started levitating in the air sideways," he told NBC. "We made direct eye contact with him."
Britny Landry had been on the ride earlier Monday and was waiting in line to go again.
"We just look, and I just see somebody fly out," she told KTVU-TV. She said she wasn't sure at first what she saw. "Maybe somebody had a bag or something."
Lisa Cupid, Cobb County Board of Commissioners chairwoman, said the man's next of kin have been notified.
"I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," Cupid said. "We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories."
Six Flags closes roller coasters elsewhere
Six Flags said in a statement that it has temporarily shut down nine similar roller coasters at six of its theme parks in the U.S. and Canada. Those parks were already scheduled for seasonal midweek closures on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The affected rides include a second coaster named Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California, Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Illinois, Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey, the coasters Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds in North Carolina and the rides Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada's Wonderland in Ontario.
Six Flags Entertainment did not immediately respond Tuesday to emailed questions seeking more information on why those specific rides were shut down and what would be done before they reopen.
Georgia's Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees ride inspections, is "conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review," said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson.
Goliath, which opened in 2006, reaches a top speed of 70 mph with a height of 200 feet, according to the park's website. The park in suburban Atlanta opened in 1967.
Riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills" during the more than 3-minute ride, the website says.
Other recent roller coaster deaths and safety claims
The death is at least the seventh at the Georgia park since 1989, including two people who were in restricted areas and struck by roller coasters and two who died in auto accidents, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tallies amusement park accidents and represents victims.
In 2006, a man died after likely having a heart attack on the Goliath coaster, the law firm said.
The latest death comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California announced the retirement of its X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious brain injuries. The park settled one wrongful-death lawsuit with the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.
Last year, a 32-year-old man died from blunt impact injuries after riding a high-speed roller coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. His death was ruled accidental.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis gets 40 years to life in prison in Tupac Shakur’s murder case
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — Duane “Keffe D” Davis has been sentenced in the 1996 shooting death murder case of Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas.
On Tuesday, Judge Carli Kierny sentenced Davis to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of Shakur.
A jury found Davis guilty on Aug. 31 after less than three hours of deliberations on charges that included first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.
Davis had already been in police custody since his arrest in September 2023.
Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars.
Shakur’s killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir.
According to DiGiacomo, Davis was trying to profit off a killing that he committed, and for that he does not deserve the minimum sentence.
“In my mind he deserves the maximum possible sentence,” DiGiacomo added.
Davis’ lawyer, Michael Sanft, said he plans to appeal the verdict.

title: Washington resident charged with conspiracy in Canada shool shooting is ordered detained
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — A Washington state resident charged with conspiracy in one of the worst school shootings in Canada’s history has been ordered detained pending further hearings in the case.
Melody Bryant, also known as James Cody Bryant, of Bellingham, Washington, was charged this month with conspiring to murder people in a foreign country. Investigators said she provided assistance to Jesse Van Rootselaar, who killed eight people and wounded 27 in the mountain community of Tumbler Ridge in February.
Bryant declined to report Van Rootselaar’s plans, agreed to distribute a livestream of the attack, provided money and shared advice on how to delete online messages to keep the plot a secret, according to a criminal complaint filed this month in U.S. District Court in Seattle.
At a detention hearing Tuesday, Magistrate Judge Mary Alice Theiler said she did not believe there were any conditions — such as internet restrictions — that could ensure the safety of the community if Bryant were to be released pending trial.
Bryant has not entered a plea, and her public defender, Greg Murphy, said in court he has not yet been provided with evidence needed to evaluate the government’s case against her.
Murphy argued for her release pending trial, noting that federal agents first interviewed Bryant just days after the attack and allowed her to remain free in the ensuing seven months.
Even after filing the complaint against her on Oct. 2, the government waited for four days to take her into custody, Murphy noted.
“There is no evidence that suggests any new danger to the communty in the last seven months since the government first interviewed her,” Murphy said.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Todd Greenberg told the judge that the criminal charge carried a presumption that Bryant would be detained.
“The defendant was, over the course of months, in daily communication with someone who was planning a mass murder event in British Columbia,” Greenberg said. “Bryant chose not to intervene.”
Authorities say Van Rootselaar killed her mother and stepbrother at home before attacking a nearby secondary school in Tumbler Ridge, killing five children ages 12 and 13 as well as an educational assistant. Van Rootselaar was later found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Tumbler Ridge in the Canadian Rockies is more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) northeast of Vancouver, British Columbia, near the provincial border with Alberta. The provincial government website lists Tumbler Ridge Secondary School as having 175 students from Grades 7 to 12.
The families of victims are suing artificial intelligence company OpenAI in U.S. federal court, seeking to hold the ChatGPT maker responsible for failing to alert police to the shooter’s alarming interactions with the chatbot.

title: The power of ‘me time’ — why solo time is a gift
text:
(Aging Untold) — A little “me time” isn’t selfish — it can be empowering.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing why solo time gets easier — and more necessary — as we get older, and how to turn alone time into one of life’s most confident experiences.
Why alone time matters more as we age
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck shared a simple benefit of solitude.
“The biggest benefit is you don’t offend anybody else. The biggest benefit is nobody’s going to get mad at you while you’re alone,” Cradduck said.
She emphasized that being alone and feeling lonely are not the same experience.
“You have to understand that being alone and feeling lonely are totally opposite. They’re not the same thing,” Cradduck said.
Even as a self-described extrovert, Cradduck said solo time has become something to look forward to.
“I’m a huge extrovert. I love to be around people, but I actually like being alone. And I embrace the time when I can. And I’m finding the older I get, the more alone time I actually need and want,” she said.
Adjusting to life alone after loss
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke pointed to the example of a long-married couple facing life alone after the death of a spouse.
The transition can come with real anxiety, she said, offering a starting point for anyone adjusting to being on their own.
“I think, what would I tell someone that was in that position — and I’ve had people in that position — is just to ask a friend to help you adjust to life on your own and take really small steps with combining something you enjoy and doing it alone, like if it’s a walk or something,” O’Rourke said.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added that stepping outside a routine built around another person can feel intimidating at first, but that solo time can also offer a kind of relief from the pull of daily obligations.
“Sometimes being able to be alone is really refreshing, you know? Because sometimes I feel like I’m being pulled in all these different areas, so to just be able to have some me time, reflect, it’s really a cool thing,” Rogers said.
A childhood lesson in self-reliance
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose shared a personal story about learning to be comfortable alone at age 10, after walking to a restaurant by herself near a new school.
“I would give myself a pep talk that throughout all my life I would have myself and that I would always be OK alone. Like, promise me you’ll be OK alone and still have fun and still enjoy your life,” Ambrose said.
She said that early habit shaped how she thinks about relationships and independence later in life.
“No matter who’s in the room when you’re born and who’s in the room where you die, you have yourself on the journey. So you may have a spouse, but you really have yourself, and you need to be your own best friend,” Ambrose said.
She also encouraged getting out and trying new things alone as a way to meet people, not avoid them.
“If you go out and you just go out and discover things and do things, you never know when you might meet your next best friend outside yourself. So you’ve got to get out there and mix it up,” Ambrose said.
During a trip by herself to San Francisco, Ambrose started to feel alone, but remembered how she coached herself as a child.
“But my 10-year-old self came through, and I’m like, you’re going to get out there and walk the streets of San Francisco and have a great time. And I did, I made the most out of it,” Ambrose said.
O’Rourke said enjoying alone time isn’t about avoiding people — it’s about self-confidence.
Key takeaways
- Alone and lonely aren’t the same thing. Enjoying solo time doesn’t mean you’re isolated or sad.
- The need for alone time can grow with age. Even committed extroverts may find they want more solo time as they get older.
- Start small when adjusting to life alone. Pairing an enjoyable activity, like a walk, with solo time — and leaning on a friend for support — can ease the transition after a major life change such as losing a spouse.
- Confidence, not avoidance, is the goal. Comfort with solitude is about self-assurance, not about withdrawing from people or relationships.
- Being your own best friend is a lifelong asset. You’re with yourself for the entire journey, even when a spouse or loved ones are present.
- Trying new things alone can open doors. Going out and exploring on your own can lead to unexpected new friendships.

title: Another top swap in Varsity Maine boys soccer poll
text:
What is a voter to do? On Sept. 29, Brunswick eked past Lewiston 3-2 and last week became the unanimous No. 1 in the Varsity Maine boys soccer poll, a week after the Dragons took over the top spot by one point over the Blue Devils. Easy enough. But then last Thursday, Lewiston turned the tables with a 1-0 overtime win over Brunswick.
The teams split their two matches. Both teams have scored three goals in those two games. How do you split that difference? Most Varsity Maine voters appear to have gone with the “latest is the greatest” approach, giving the top spot back to the Blue Devils after they were ranked second the previous two weeks following two weeks at No. 1.
Lewiston still has a matchup with rival and ninth-ranked Edward Little on its schedule. Brunswick, which earned its second five-goal victory over the Red Eddies on Saturday (winning 7-2), has three games against Class A North playoff contenders: Mt. Blue, Messalonskee and Mt. Ararat.
Behind the Blue Devils and the Dragons in the poll are four Class A South squads, who are also the top four teams in their region, in the same order: Thornton Academy, Deering, Gorham and Scarborough. Those four teams don’t play each other in the final week of the regular season, but Portland, the fifth-place team in A South, has a chance to play spoiler with games against Thornton and Scarborough.
Fryeburg is back in the rankings at No. 10, the same spot they held in the Sept. 22 poll.

title: Here’s what Falmouth voters will see on November’s ballot
text:
Absentee voting is underway leading up to Maine’s Nov. 3 election. On Election Day, Falmouth residents can vote in person at the Falmouth High School gym from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
In addition to federal, gubernatorial and county races, here’s what Falmouth voters will see on their ballots. To see the complete ballot and dive more into candidate responses, explore the 2026 Maine Voter Guide.
MAINE STATE HOUSE
Falmouth residents in State House District 111 will see that Amy Kuhn (D-Falmouth) is running uncontested to be reelected to the Maine House of Representatives. Voters in District 112 will decide between two candidates:
Sean Mahoney, Democrat
What are your top three priorities?
We need more housing and we have to make it more efficient and economical to build and buy it. We need electricity that is affordable, is generated with the least amount of impact on our natural resources and is delivered in a manner that is transparent and understandable. We need to strike the balance at the municipal level of providing good schools for our children, necessary services for our community and ensuring that the costs of those services are reasonable and fair.
Why are you running?
First, I love Maine, and have since I first crossed the Piscataqua River Bridge in 1982. Second, now is not the time to be on the sidelines criticizing those working in Augusta. I want to be part of addressing the challenges facing Maine today. I have experience with the Legislature, experience to know progress is made when people are willing to work together even if they don’t agree on every issue, when results are more important than posturing and when the work is done with humility.
Lauren Jones, Republican
What are your top three priorities?
1. Make Maine more affordable by lowering taxes and unnecessary regulatory costs. 2. Protect parental rights, individual liberty and local control. 3. Expand housing and economic opportunity by removing barriers that make it harder to build, work, start a business and raise a family in Maine.
Why are you running?
I’m running because I don’t want Maine to become a place our children have to leave in order to afford a home, build a career or raise a family. As a mom and real estate broker, I see firsthand how taxes, housing costs and overregulation are squeezing Maine families. I want a government that spends less, listens more, respects parents and protects the individual freedoms that make Maine worth calling home.
MAINE STATE SENATE DISTRICT 25
Teresa S. Pierce is running unopposed for reelection to represent Falmouth in the State Senate.

title: Cat café in Gardiner launches nonprofit rescue, seeks donations

text:
GARDINER, Maine (WABI) - Bonnie Caspersen, owner of The Cat’s Familiar, a cat café in Gardiner, has started a nonprofit rescue called Kitty Coven.
The nonprofit’s first initiative is to rescue four litter mates currently in foster care for vetting and to put them up for adoption at the café.
Caspersen said $97 has been raised toward a $994 goal.
“This is something that Gardiner has needed for a very long time, to have a place for people to gather that is safe and we are safe for everybody,” Caspersen said. “In order for us to continue, we have to have kitties because that’s the big draw. If just one dollar, people gave one dollar, all my friends that I know, one dollar, we’d hit it in no time.”
To donate, people can search “kittycoven318″ on Venmo, call The Cat’s Familiar at 207-620-5080, or message the café on Facebook.

title: Inside Robert’s Western World: Nashville’s classic honky tonk
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — Lower Broadway is known for high-rise honky tonks and rooftop bars that draw crowds late into the night. Under a large red boot sign sits Robert’s Western World, a bar that plays only traditional country music.
Robert’s Western World has operated for more than 30 years. The bar sells cans of beer starting at $2.50.
“We’ve left it alone. It’s not broke. Don’t fix it,” owner Emily Jones said.
A time capsule on Broadway
Jones and her husband, JesseLee, own Robert’s Western World and are working to keep its legacy going.
“A time capsule when people walk in here,” Emily Jones said. “We are in a society where people are longing for something tangible. They want to know the history.”
JesseLee Jones moved to Nashville from Brazil and worked at Robert’s Western World before getting the chance to buy it.
“Do what’s in your heart, because if you do what’s in your heart, you don’t work a day in your life,” he said.
No distractions
JesseLee Jones said the bar does not have a television inside.
“You come in here and it’s like stepping back into the 50s, and the 60s, and the 70s, the heydays of country music,” he said.
The walls are covered with photos of some of country music’s biggest names, who have been regulars at the bar, including Dolly Parton and Waylon Jennings.
“They just want to tuck in the crowd, have a beer and just be human and take in the vibe,” Emily Jones said.
The bar was named one of USA Today’s best bars in the country.
Expansion plans
Emily and JesseLee Jones have bought the building next door and plan to expand Robert’s Western World.
“But it will still be Nashville. It will still be real,” JesseLee Jones said. “And that is what’s missing nowadays. Believability.”

title: 2 cats believed dead after Maine house fire
text:
Two cats are believed dead after a Sunday morning house fire in Durham.
The fire broke out about 3:01 a.m. at the two-story Cape-style home on Stieg Road, according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
When firefighters arrived, they found the attached two-car garage engulfed in flames and a burning vehicle in the driveway.
No one was injured in the fire, but two cats are believed to have died.
Investigators have been unable to determine the cause and origin of the fire because of the extensive damage.
The fire remains under investigation.

title: Newport restaurant hosts fundraiser for Partners for Peace in honor of late coworker
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEWPORT, Maine (WABI) - A Newport restaurant is turning a night out into a way to support domestic violence survivors.
In honor of Domestic Violence Awareness Month, Angler’s Seafood will donate 10 percent of its sales Tuesday, between 4 and 8 p.m., to Partners for Peace.
For Angler’s, it’s personal.
Staff are honoring their late coworker, Amy Nickerson, who was killed in a domestic homicide in Searsmont in 2023.
“They were a big part of when Amy had passed away. They were a big support when we had done a candlelight vigil here. They were always there. They reached out with extra materials and have given us things to support other people. It feels very good. It’s a very sentimental thing. It’s something that really struck a lot of the employees here, so it’s just a way to kind of give back and just remember,” said Connor Grindal, general manager of Angler’s Newport.
Partners for Peace has spent more than 50 years supporting survivors in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties.
Staff expect a busy evening and encourage customers to make a reservation.

title: Tres meses después de la muerte de Johan Sebastián, seguimos luchando por la verdad
text:
Sean P. Murphy fue fiscal en el Bronx y fiscal federal, combatió el crimen organizado y ayudó a dirigir la investigación del Departamento de Justicia sobre el ataque del 6 de enero al Capitolio. Criado en Vermont y hoy abogado de Gideon Asen en Maine, representa a la familia de Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
Hace casi tres meses, en la madrugada del 13 de julio de 2026, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero salió de su casa. Pensaba, como cada mañana, en el momento en que volvería para abrazar a su esposa, Karolina, y a su pequeña hija.
La noche anterior había sido como cualquier otra. Karolina dobló la ropa. Johan dijo que se iba a acostar. Se dieron un beso. Ninguno de los dos imaginó que sería el último.
Nunca tuve la fortuna de conocer a Johan en vida. Hay algo extraño y hermoso en llegar a conocer a alguien solo a través de quienes lo amaron y hoy tienen que vivir sin él.
Lo conocí a través de sus padres, Omar y Dora, quienes viajaron desde Colombia para reclamar el cuerpo de su hijo. En la funeraria de Portland, salí de la sala, pero los gritos de dolor de una madre ante el cuerpo de su hijo asesinado atravesaron las paredes. Fue un lamento que nunca hubiera querido escuchar y que jamás quiero olvidar.
Lo conocí a través de Daniela, su hermana, quien fue la primera de la familia en llegar a Estados Unidos. Como le pasaría a cualquier hermana mayor, carga con una culpa que no le corresponde. Daniela, nada de esto fue culpa tuya. Sabemos quién es responsable.
Y lo conocí a través de Karolina y de la hija que tuvieron juntos. Me asombra la fortaleza de Karolina. Este país les ha arrebatado demasiado. Lo siento de corazón. Basta pasar dos minutos con esa niña para saber que la llama de su papá sigue viva en ella.
Desde julio, mi socio Ben Gideon y yo hemos luchado por Johan. Hace poco nos reunimos con representantes de la oficina del fiscal general del estado de Maine, la primera y única entidad gubernamental que ha confirmado que investiga el uso de fuerza letal por parte de un agente federal.
En esa reunión nos devolvieron varios objetos que habían sido considerados sin valor probatorio. Pero faltaba uno: la silla de seguridad de su hija para el carro. Karolina preguntó por qué. Le dijeron que una bala disparada por un agente federal la había atravesado, así como otras balas disparadas por un agente federal habían matado a su esposo.
Las primeras versiones decían que su hija iba con él en el carro. Gracias a Dios, no era así. Pero la temeridad salta a la vista, y cuesta siquiera imaginar el horror de lo que pudo haber ocurrido. Una sola tragedia ya era demasiado.
La única justificación que han dado para la muerte de Johan ha sido la «seguridad pública». ¿Saben qué protege de verdad a la gente? No dispararles a padres de familia inocentes, que cumplen la ley y cuyo único sueño es darles una vida mejor a los suyos.
Hablemos claro sobre lo que pasó aquí. Este gobierno tomó la infame decisión de quitarle la vida a Johan y, ante las consecuencias, ha guardado silencio. Un presidente que quiere ser rey ha decidido que cualquiera de nosotros puede ser sacrificado con tal de imponer su agenda. Tiene que dejar de violar nuestro derecho a la vida, y tiene que hacerlo ya.
Johan no tenía la ciudadanía estadounidense, pero encarnaba lo mejor de lo que significa ser estadounidense. Trabajaba, amaba a su familia y soñaba. Quien justifique que lo hayan matado no puede llamarse patriota.
Y Johan no es el único. Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good, Alex Pretti y Lorenzo Salgado Araujo forman parte del mismo club, uno al que nadie querría pertenecer y cuya cuota se paga con la vida. A sus familias les deben respuestas, no excusas.
Pero de poco sirve la indignación si perdemos la esperanza. Quien haya vivido un invierno en Maine sabe que incluso el frío más crudo termina por cederle el paso a la primavera. Ahora que se acercan las elecciones de mitad de período en Estados Unidos, espero y le pido a Dios que nuestro país empiece a abrirse camino hacia esa primavera.
Esto no es lo que somos los estadounidenses. Tenemos que ser mejores.
Tres meses después, la familia de Johan sigue esperando verdad, justicia y que los responsables rindan cuentas. No dejaremos de luchar hasta que eso ocurra.

title: New Trenton dental hygienist business looking to spread smiles
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
TRENTON — Those looking for new dental care options in Hancock County can smile wide. Shoreline Dental Hygiene just opened last month in Trenton, and unlike many area dentists’ and dental hygienists’ practices, owner and dental hygienist Melanie Liles said the waiting list is still short, and her team is ready for a continued influx of first-time customers.
“I have well over 100 patients already; I’m super excited about that,” Liles said. Originally from Georgia, she moved to Maine to be closer to family and establish her longtime goal of running her own practice.
Unlike dentists, who are licensed doctors responsible for diagnosing and treating oral diseases and performing procedures such as extractions and root canals, dental hygienists focus primarily on preventive oral care with things such as cleanings and patient education.
And while Liles said there will be no laughing gas or intricate surgical procedures at her practice, dental hygienists are just as vital in keeping their community healthy and teeth pearly white.
“The core of the work is just helping and informing others — we can have a patient come in that was raised all their life without being told to take care of their teeth; they fail to see the connection oral care and their head has with the rest of the body,” she said. “People don’t know things like periodontal (gum) disease are linked to diabetes and heart diseases — all the bacteria in your mouth can run through your entire system.”
“We’re not just teeth cleaners; we are highly educated,” she added. “We take the same classes dentists take.”
Liles emphasized preventive care and proper education are essential aspects of the trade, the latter something she stresses in interactions with her patients.
“We are big on education here at the practice,” she said. “When people come in, we teach them oral health instructions for brushing and flossing, do nutritional counseling and ask them what their diet is like — do they eat a lot of sugar, or eat before going to bed, for example.” She said informing patients can make a major difference in the trajectory of their oral health — gingivitis, for instance, is reversable with consistent daily oral hygiene.
Liles said the dental care industry in the Ellsworth area has been welcoming, and she looks forward to establishing connections when referring patients for more in-depth care outside the purview of dental hygienists.
“When you come in and start your own practice, you try not to step on any toes,” she said. “However, everybody’s been super welcoming and said they are excited to have us. I even had a couple of dentists since we opened that have lost their hygienists and are sending people our way. We are very grateful for that.”
Available dental services at Shoreline Dental Hygiene include cleanings, oral health assessments, periodontal care, oral cancer screenings, teeth whitening and more. Liles said she can also perform temporary crown cementing and fillings until a patient is seen by a licensed dentist.
Shoreline Dental Hygiene provides services for both children and adults, and the clinic is in-network with MaineCare and Delta Dental. It also has wheelchair accessibility, and the practice is open to helping others with special needs.
Currently, Liles is part of a three-person team alongside another dental hygienist and office clerk. She hopes to grow her staff and her customer base in the near future. Finding dental hygienists in particular is difficult, she said, as many have retired or moved from the area since the pandemic, and many more have become burned out by the physical and emotional demands of the job.
“When you are in the same position for eight to nine hours a day, it’s hard on your body,” Liles explained.
She said part of her patient care philosophy centers around addressing “dental anxiety,” uncomfortableness exhibited by people visiting dental care facilities ranging from general anxiety to outright phobia. Liles said everything about her care approach as well as the clinic itself is designed to put patients at ease — from her “bedside manner” to the calming teal colors and sea tones decorating the facility.
“I want people to be relaxed. We have things like blankets and noise-cancelling headphones to help those uncomfortable,” she said. “I don’t just wheel up with no hello and start taking x-rays of a patient. I go to them at eye level and have a conversation, asking things like ‘How are you doing today?’ and ‘What brings you in?’ We establish a relationship and start knocking down the barriers of anxiety.” Liles said there will be no surprise procedures during a visit, as she explains every step of the process.
Located at 1164 Bar Harbor Rd. in Trenton, the busy route to Mount Desert Island, Liles said she has already met people from all over the country and world in her first weeks of operation.
She highlighted she’s looking forward to meeting more people and welcoming new regulars at the business.
“I’m a people person; I love people,” Liles said. “I want every patient that comes to this practice to know that we are there for them. Every patient’s needs are different, and you will be treated as an individual.”

title: Maine’s public universities offer $250 scholarships to 24,500 Alfond Grant recipients
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — As part of broader efforts to keep more Maine students in the state for college and careers, the University of Maine System will offer $250 scholarships to 24,500 Alfond Grant recipients who are now in high school and even beginning to graduate, supporting their educational attainment and upward mobility while strengthening Maine’s workforce.
Alfond Grant recipients born in the 2008 pilot year at MaineGeneral and those born statewide 2009-2012 who enroll at Maine’s public universities are eligible for the one-time $250 scholarship, which is being funded by UMS, in large part using slot machine revenue it receives through the state.

title: A brief briefing: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia makes debut
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia’s first press briefing operated much differently from a standard Karoline Leavitt briefing.
The press conference lasted 14 minutes and included questions from only three outlets - Breitbart News Network, The Daily Mail, and FOX News.
FOX news asked whether her role includes making things less tough for Republicans in the midterms. Zacharia said she hoped to amplify the president’s agenda.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” she said.
During the briefing, Zacharia said U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to resign. She also said Trump would step up his midterm campaign appearances.
“You can expect more of the midterm blitz. Just now we’ve added Kentucky, and we have a few other stops as he goes down to Florida. So it will be Georgia, Kentucky and Florida,” Zacharia said.
Zacharia described Trump as the administration’s best spokesman. She ended the briefing after answering a question about balancing family and work responsibilities.
“So thank you for that question. In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska. And we can ask him all of the questions out there.”

title: When Does Roseanne Barr’s New Show ‘Meemaw’ Premiere?
text:
Roseanne Barr Has Filmed 8 Episodes of ‘Meemaw’ – When Does It Premiere?
Roseanne Barr has filmed eight episodes of a new sitcom, but there's one big question hanging over the project: Where will it air?
The comedy, titled Meemaw, was filmed in Austin, Texas, and features Barr as the matriarch of a family of preppers.
But despite having a completed season, the show reportedly hasn't found a network or streaming platform willing to pick it up.
That leaves Barr with a finished comeback project and an uncertain path to television.
Where Will Roseanne Barr's New Show 'Meemaw' Air?
According to Naughty But Nice, ABC, NBC and CBS aren't interested in the sitcom, while major streaming platforms have also been reluctant to take it on.
Roseanne couldn't get a network to finance her comeback, so she went ahead and made the show herself. Now she's got eight episodes and no buyer. That's a very expensive gamble.
Newsmax is reportedly being explored as a potential home for Meemaw, but no deal has been announced. For now, there's no confirmed network, streaming platform or premiere date for the series.
READ MORE: Roseanne Barr Was Told Her Heart Is ‘Damaged’ — and She Wants Nothing to Do With Surgery
The independently produced comedy also stars Randy Quaid, Tony Hinchcliffe, Drea de Matteo and Jon Lovitz.
Barr plays the grandmother at the center of a survivalist family whose plans include an extravagant bat mitzvah.
Why Is Roseanne Barr's Comeback Facing Challenges?
Barr's return to television comes eight years after ABC canceled the revival of Roseanne in 2018 following her social media post about former President Barack Obama adviser Valerie Jarrett.
READ MORE: Roseanne Barr Turned Down ‘The Conners’ Ghost Cameo: 'Not Dead'
The network later continued the family sitcom without Barr as The Conners. Now, the industry appears hesitant to take a chance on her latest project, despite her continued fan base.
“Roseanne still has fans,” the insider added. “But fans aren't television executives.”
Barr's new sitcom has been filmed, but until a buyer steps forward, its future remains uncertain. For viewers wondering when they can watch Meemaw, there's no release date to circle on the calendar just yet.

title: Leeds family appeals after unvaccinated student’s request to attend school denied
text:
The family of a Leeds student is appealing a judge’s decision to keep the partially unvaccinated child out of school while a court case is decided.
The student’s father, James Childs, filed a request for injunctive relief in August, which would have allowed his son to attend Tripp Middle School in Turner while the case plays out in court.
District Judge Stacey Neumann denied those requests on Sept. 8, citing an “absence of a strong showing on the merits and Plaintiffs’ own delay in seeking relief.” Childs should have known nearly a year before the start of the 2026 school year about the district’s vaccination policy, Neumann wrote, and yet he did not seek court action until Aug. 12 of this year.
Neumann is weighing a request from the state to dismiss the entire case and has until Tuesday to do so.
An attorney for Childs said Oct. 8 that they filed an appeal that day to the U.S. Court of Appeals regarding Neumann’s order on the family’s request for emergency relief. If granted, the appeal would allow the child to attend school while the court case is ongoing.
“If we lose here, the next stop is the U.S. Supreme Court,” said Brian Festa, vice president and co-chair of We the People USA Inc., the law firm suing on Childs’ behalf.
Childs sued Cari Medd, superintendent of Maine School Administrative District 52, and Pender Makin, commissioner of the state’s Department of Education, in July. He alleges that Medd and Makin are forcing him to vaccinate his child through threats of “expulsion and ultimatums.”
Because of state law, his son, who is now in eighth grade, cannot attend school until he receives the Tdap (tetanus , diphtheria and pertussis) and meningococcal vaccinations.
Makin’s countersuit says that the child has received his required vaccinations up until the sixth grade. In September 2025, the child was permitted to start his seventh grade year on the condition that he would receive his vaccinations for that year within 90 days.
The agreement was solidified in writing by the child’s mother, the filing says, and as the year went on, the family ensured school officials that the child would receive his vaccinations by the start of his eighth-grade year. Medd made it clear that he would not be allowed to start the 2026-27 school year without his up-to-date vaccinations.
When a preliminary injunction is filed, irreplaceable harm must be proven.
Childs alleges that denying his son the ability to attend school “completely deprives his educational opportunities.”
Neumann is in agreement that Childs’ son will miss educational opportunities each day he is absent, but said that it’s not because of Maine’s vaccination laws.
Childs chooses not to vaccinate his son for religious beliefs and believes that mandating the vaccinations challenges his First Amendment and parental rights, according to the lawsuit. We The Patriots is a nonprofit parental rights organization that has sued other school districts across the country, including for other vaccination cases.
Until 2019, parents could claim religious exemptions in Maine, but state law changed in 2021 after officials noticed declining vaccination rates.
“The Free Exercise Clause ‘does not relieve an individual of the obligation to comply
with a valid and neutral law of general applicability on the ground that the law proscribes
(or prescribes) conduct that his religion prescribes (or proscribes),'” Neumann wrote.
Makin has previously denied requests for a statement, citing the ongoing lawsuit.
MSAD 52 includes the towns of Greene, Turner and Leeds.

title: Jury selection to begin in federal hate crimes trial over Buffalo, N.Y., supermarket shooting
text:
For Wayne Jones, discussing the horrific supermarket shooting in Buffalo, N.Y., in which a white supremacist killed 10 people, including his mother Celestine Chaney, has taken over much of his life these past four years.
He can numbly list talking points for media and gun violence panels. But thinking about her absence each day is one reason why Jones would not want to see the shooter sentenced to death.
“I really think that he should just sit and have to think about it year after year after year and just be miserable,” said Jones, who plans to attend the trial. “When I was younger, I probably was more prone to say ‘kill him.’ But, at this point, I mean, he’s still got well another 20-30 years of appeals.”
Jury selection is set to begin Tuesday in the federal trial in which Payton Gendron faces a potential death penalty. The attack at the Tops Friendly Market in 2022 is believed to be the deadliest hate-motivated shooting targeting Black people by a lone gunman in the last century.
Gendron is facing over two dozen federal hate crime charges and more than a dozen firearms charges. He is already spending life in prison after pleading guilty to state murder charges in a 2023 trial where he tearfully admitted to the crimes and renounced his past views.
His defense team is not going to dispute his guilt. Their sole objective is to ensure Gendron is spared from execution.
“Nothing will change the fact that Payton Gendron will die in prison,” the federal public defender office said in a statement. “At trial, we will offer mitigating evidence about Payton that the jury needs to consider in making its decision. Nothing we say or do is intended to be disrespectful or insensitive to the victims, the survivors, or their loved ones.”
Some victims’ family members, however, are not totally against the death penalty.
“I’ve never been like out here like, ‘Yay! Go for the death penalty.’ That’s never been me,” said Buffalo Common Council member Zeneta Everhart, who ran for office over a year after her son, Zaire, survived the shooting. “Ten people died that day in an egregious way and in an awful, terrible, traumatic way.”
Her son, now 25, and the two other survivors have had their lives irrevocably altered, she added.
How racist conspiracy theories played a role in the attack
On May 14, 2022, a then-18-year-old Gendron drove over 200 miles (320 kilometers) from his home in Conklin, a predominantly white and rural town, to Buffalo. He fired around 60 shots from a semiautomatic rifle at employees and shoppers. Video revealed Gendron apologized to a white store worker after shooting him in the leg. He surrendered to police as he exited the supermarket.
Investigators found past social media posts and other writings by Gendron dedicated to planning an attack to frighten people who were non-white and non-Christian into leaving the U.S. He also promoted a baseless “great replacement theory” that people of color will replace white people through higher birth rates and immigration.
The victims who were killed were all Black and between ages 32 and 86. Besides Chaney, they included Geraldine Talley, Katherine Massey, Pearl Young, Andre Mackneil, church deacon Heyward Patterson, Ruth Whitfield, Roberta Drury, Margus Morrison and Aaron Salter, a retired Buffalo police officer who was working as a security guard.
Under President Joe Biden, the U.S. Justice Department in 2024 decided to pursue a death sentence. It was the first capital case overseen by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland, who had previously put a moratorium on the death penalty.
Gendron and his legal team relayed that he would only plead guilty in his federal case in exchange for a life sentence. The Justice Department rejected that proposal.
Anti-Black crimes still lead in hate crime data
The 2022 shooting stands apart as one of the deadliest acts of anti-Black violence in modern U.S. history. It also reflects a grim reality represented in national bias crime statistics.
Black people have comprised the “no. 1 numerical target” annually since the FBI began collecting data in 1991, hate crime analyst Brian Levin, of the California Association of Human Relations Organizations, said. The record high was 3,670 anti-Black bias incidents in 1996.
According to FBI data released in August, law enforcement agencies reported over 2,800 anti-Black hate crime incidents in 2025, nearly three times the number targeting Latinos. The FBI also reported a 7% decline in hate crime incidents from 2024 to 2025.
The Buffalo shooting and the 2015 Charleston, S.C., church shooting, in which a white gunman killed nine Black churchgoers, show how online radicalization makes this a terrorism matter as well.
“Unfortunately, he (Gendron) fits the pattern of young, mostly white males undertaking targeted massacres which are then justified by manifestos, which are also part of a continuing chain that references prior attacks often but seeks to encourage future ones,” Levin said.
Everhart, whose son still has shrapnel in his body after being shot in the neck, says hate crime enhancements might be the only deterrent.
“This isn’t a shooting over a robbery or a domestic violence situation. This is domestic terrorism,” Everhart said. “It is important we go after the death penalty in this case. But if he doesn’t end up getting it, I know that justice will be served.”
Garnell Whitfield lost his 86-year-old mother Ruth in the shooting. He has no thoughts on whether capital punishment should be issued because “this is the federal government doing what they deem they have to do.”
He’s spent the past four years honoring his mother’s memory by working with church groups, victims’ rights groups, gun lobbyists and others to address white nationalist movements and racial violence.
Whitfield said he hopes trial testimony reveals more about “the support that he (Gendron) might have had, the radicalization, social media and societal ills that caused people to hate and be violent that are inherent in our society” that preceded the killing.
“Those are the things that I care about,” he said.

title: SK Tours brings King’s Bangor to life (If you dare!)
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - During spooky season, there might not be a more popular stop in Bangor than Stephen King’s house on West Broadway. Did you know traces of King and his work can be found throughout the Queen City?
One local business sees a jump-scare in attendance around Halloween as it showcases uneasy Easter eggs from the king of horror himself.
Like Pennywise coaxing little Georgie into the sewers, bringing folks deeper into the storied streets is SK Tours of Maine.
“It’s a 2 1/2 hour driving, narrated tour about Stephen’s life, his writing, his books, some of the philanthropy from the Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation, and a bit of Bangor history as well,” explains James Tinker, owner of SK Tours.
Started by Tinker’s father 15 years ago, he says carrying on the business after his father’s retirement was an easy choice because of his longtime love of King.
“The first [King] book I ever read was ‘The Eyes of the Dragon,’” Tinker recalls. “I was hooked on King, and then I just started reading everything I could get my hands on.”
Offering public and private tours, an upwards of 4,000 bone-chilling bookworms and frightening film fanatics load into its Pennywise van every year to dissect local landmarks that inspired King.
“We’ve had people come from as far as Siberia, New Zealand, all over the world to take the tour and kind of immerse themselves into the King experience. They’re thrilled to be able to see the landmarks, like the Paul Bunyan statue or the standpipe,” Tinker describes. “Since the Thomas Hill standpipe is the only one of its kind, a lot of people, when they read the book It, they don’t know what it is, so they don’t know what it looks like.”
Beyond the horrors King has imagined happening here, Tinker adds it is important to them to highlight the scare and care King has brought to Bangor.
“The Kings have been so good to my family from way back when my father owned Betts Bookstore in downtown Bangor all the way to starting the tour business. He’s been so good to us that we need to give that back,” says Tinker. “We need to share the stories of how good he is to us and our city and our whole state and share those with people who otherwise wouldn’t know about the foundation or their charitable works.”
That includes showcasing spots like Hayford Park, where Stephen and Tabitha King have supported the stadium, aquatic center and playground.
SK Tours say it’s booked through Halloween.
With their new SK Tours app, a $5 yearly membership unlocks all King-related landmarks to visit independently - if you dare!

title: Trump says he cares for Americans. They think he's more focused on his wealth, an AP-NORC poll finds
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Most Americans think Donald Trump is profiting off the presidency in unethical or illegal ways and is focused more on his wealth than helping people like them, a new AP-NORC poll finds.
As Trump’s family business pulls in record money from new ventures helped by his policies, the survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that when it comes to allegations that Trump is profiting from the presidency, about 6 in 10 U.S. adults believe he is either illegally profiting or doing something unethical but not illegal. Only about 2 in 10 think the Republican president is doing nothing wrong, while a similar share say they don’t know enough to say.
At the same time, just over half of Americans say Trump has prioritized his personal financial interests “a lot” since returning to the White House, while only about one-quarter say he puts the same emphasis on the country as a whole. Few U.S. adults, about 1 in 10, say he’s focused “a lot” on people like them.
“His wealth increases,” said Barbara Thaxton, 87, an independent from Summerfield, Florida, “but the people in the country are just barely getting by.”
Trump derided the issue of conflicts of interest at the start of his second term, telling The New York Times that “I found out that nobody cared.” Unlike in his first term, he’s lifted a self-imposed ban on his family striking private-sector deals overseas and started several new crypto businesses.
The poll results suggest that most U.S. adults think growing his personal fortune has been a focus for Trump in his second term, at least to some extent. Only about one-quarter of U.S. adults say he’s prioritizing his personal business interests “only a little” or “not at all,” including less than half of Republicans.
The White House says Trump is not profiting, but most Americans see red flags
The White House has repeatedly dismissed accusations that Trump and his family business are benefiting financially from his office as a fake problem, stating categorically that he has zero conflicts and acts only in the interest of the country.
In a required federal disclosure of his financial holdings that Trump filed in June, he reported taking in more than $1 billion from new crypto businesses after he loosened regulation on the industry.
One of his biggest crypto ventures got a half-billion-dollar investment after he was elected from a United Arab Emirates business tied to the royal family. It also got help from a cryptocurrency company founded by a Chinese billionaire in trouble with the law in the U.S.
On the real estate side of the business, the Trump Organization has struck eight foreign deals in the first year of his presidency, including many in authoritarian or one-party states with influence over private business and eager to keep Trump happy, U.S. tariffs low or the U.S. military protecting it — or all three.
Overall, about 4 in 10 U.S. adults say Trump is doing something illegal, while about 2 in 10 think he’s doing something unethical but not illegal. Democrats are especially likely to believe he has broken the law, with about 8 in 10 saying that.
Oscar Delgado, a 50-year-old Democrat who voted for Trump in 2024 because he thought he could improve things, now accuses Trump of “turning greedy.”
“He’s not putting the country first,” said Delgado, who lives in Lansing, Michigan, and works in a Ford metal stamping factory. “I wanted a change, but I didn’t expect this change.”
Republicans are less convinced Trump is doing something wrong
Independents and Republicans are much less convinced than Democrats that Trump is breaking the law. Only about 3 in 10 independents and about 1 in 10 Republicans say he’s doing something illegal. About 2 in 10 independents and a similar share of Republicans think his behavior is unethical but not illegal.
Most Republicans think he is doing nothing wrong or say they don’t know enough to judge.
“His family has probably benefited, but I don’t think he has,” said Republican Audra Pelsue, 52, dismissing Trump critics as too angry to see straight. “It’s Trump derangement syndrome.”
Pelsue, a manager at a laundry machine maker from Syracuse, New York, sees a double standard among Trump critics, pointing to what she says was insufficient outrage over President Joe Biden’s son.
“Look at Hunter Biden!” she said, referring to his position as director at Ukrainian energy company Burisma when his father, a Democrat, was vice president. “It was OK for Biden kids to benefit, but it’s not OK for Trump’s?”
Most Americans think Trump puts his financial interests ahead of the country’s
Even if they don’t think his behavior is illegal, Americans are much likelier to say Trump is prioritizing his personal business interests, compared with the country overall or people like themselves.
Just over half, 56%, of U.S. adults say Trump has put “a lot” of emphasis on his personal businesses since taking office again, while a similar share, 54%, say this about the business interests of his friends and family.
In contrast, only about one-quarter of Americans say he’s prioritized the country as a whole “a lot” since returning to the White House, and even fewer, about 1 in 10, say he’s focused “a lot” on people like them.
Republicans are likelier to think Trump has prioritized the country, with about half saying he’s put “a lot” of emphasis on this since taking office, while about one-quarter say he’s given that amount of focus to his personal business interests. But only about one-quarter of Republicans say he’s emphasized people like them “a lot.”
John Bartus, of Twin Falls, Idaho, notes that Trump has agreed to donate his salary, which comes to $400,000 a year.
“It seems like his business interests are a part of his life, but it doesn’t seem like he lets that interfere with what’s going on in the country,” said Bartus, who’s 67. “He puts it on the back burner.”
But Lisa Fernandez, a Democrat from Edinburg, Texas, said Trump is using the power of the presidency but not in ways to help others.
“He’s exploiting it for his own needs and his family and making a profit off the people who he is supposed to be serving,” said Fernandez, 57, a retired math teacher. “His whole reason for being is to enrich himself and take what he can take without consequences.”
___
Thomson-DeVeaux reported from Washington.
___
The AP-NORC poll of 2,140 adults was conducted Sept. 24-28 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

title: Husband charged after pregnant wife’s bloodied, beaten body found in their garage
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KOLD/Gray News) - Court documents have revealed gruesome new details after a man allegedly beat and stabbed his pregnant wife to death in their Arizona home.
Warning: This article contains disturbing details that may be upsetting to readers.
Deputies with the Pima County Sheriff’s Department responded to a home in Vail on Friday after 49-year-old Joseph Clark called saying he killed his wife, 39-year-old Noelle Clark. Upon arriving on the scene, they immediately detained Joseph Clark as he tried to walk out of the home’s front door.
Inside the home, deputies found Noelle Clark’s bloodied and beaten body covered with a blanket in the garage. She was pregnant and appeared to be in her second or third trimester, investigators say.
Two children, ages 2 and 5, were found unharmed on the stairs inside the home.
What the evidence shows
Investigators allege Joseph Clark beat his wife with his hands and a belt before stabbing her in the chest in their children’s bedroom. He later allegedly ran her over with a car after dragging her body through the home and putting her in the garage.
Deputies say Noelle Clark’s body showed signs of blunt force trauma to her head and face, a deep stab wound in the middle of her chest and marks on her back that matched a belt found in the children’s bedroom. A bloody knife, a pool of blood and blood splatter were also found in the bedroom.
Deputies say bloody drag marks led from the bedroom to the garage. There were tire marks on Noelle Clark’s arms and bloody tire marks on the garage floor, indicating her arms were run over by a car, according to investigators.
Based on the evidence at the scene, investigators allege Joseph Clark also had plans to dispose of his wife’s body.
Suspect claims his wife had ‘tortured’ him
Joseph Clark was arrested on two counts of second-degree murder, and his bond was set at $1 million.
He claimed that his wife had been electrically torturing him, and that’s why he killed her. He said he had been “tortured, shocked over a couple of years” and that all his teeth “popped out from being zapped.” Investigators said they found no visible or obvious injuries on his body.
Joseph Clark is scheduled to appear in court again next Tuesday.

title: Susan Collins still working with operatives tied to straw donation scheme
text:
When the investigative news outlet ProPublica reported on Sen. Susan Collins’ ties to a disgraced convicted fraudster, the outlet wrote about how Scott Reed, a key figure in Collins’ political orbit, may have been aware of a scheme to direct an illegal straw donation to the Republican senator from Maine.
But Reed, who heads the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results Super PAC, wasn’t the only Collins ally who may have known of the plan.
MacKenzie Dolan, who co-founded The Morning Group, worked in 2020 with the 1820 PAC, the main pro-Collins Super PAC.
A federal investigator said both Dolan and Reed received an email sent Dec. 13, 2019, from the fraudster, Navatek CEO Martin Kao, updating them on his plans to create a shell company to make a donation to the PAC.
The investigator said in court documents that Kao sent the email from an address associated with a “navatekllc.com.”
“I just received confirmation from our bank that the new account for the Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers will be up and ready to go by early next week,” Kao wrote. “I’ll be in touch next week re getting 1820 a check by year end.”
The group sent a $150,000 check to the PAC about two weeks later, ProPublica reported.
This cycle, Collins for Senator has paid Dolan’s firm, The Morning Group, at least $300,000 for fundraising services in 2025-26. And the firm has received at least $1.1 million from Pine Tree Results PAC. The Morning Group was also hired by Reed and the 1820 PAC during the 2020 cycle.
Neither Reed, Dolan nor Collins has been accused of or charged with wrongdoing by authorities during their investigation into Kao, who is currently in prison for money laundering and bank fraud. Kao pleaded guilty to charges relating to the illegal contribution in 2022.
But Collins’ ongoing relationship with Reed and Dolan may give critics more fodder in their attempts to cast Collins as corrupt in the closing weeks of Maine’s closely watched and tight U.S. Senate race against Democrat Troy Jackson.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a written statement that Reed and Dolan were “thoroughly investigated” and “cleared by the FBI in 2021.”
“Martin Kao was the guilty party and he was sentenced to seven years in federal prison,” Kernen said. “Martin Kao tried to get his sentence reduced by blaming Senator Collins, her staff, Scott Reed and MacKenzie Dolan for his criminal conduct. The FBI, the Biden Department of Justice, and the Federal Election Commission didn’t believe him and the judge did not offer him any leniency.”
A spokesperson for The Morning Group declined to speak with a reporter on Monday.
Democrats are working to keep the ProPublica story in the headlines. The Senate Majority PAC, which is tied to Democratic Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., issued a Sept. 29 memo outlining its plan to tie political corruption to increased living costs in an effort to sway a small number of undecided voters. And they’ve put millions behind an ad campaign here highlighting the ProPublica story.
Local Democrats held a press conference outside of Collins’ office in response to the report. And a Democratic attorney has filed a formal ethics complaint against Collins.
Collins has also leveled corruption allegations against her opponent, former Senate President Troy Jackson, accusing him of using his influence to help his son, who was an Augusta lobbyist while Jackson was in power. Jackson has denied that his son had any influence over his legislative agenda.
But much of the focus has been on Collins’ orbit, with the candidate getting questions about Kao at each of last week’s two Senate debates.
Numerous outlets have reported that Reed, who was the leader of the 1820 PAC that secured Kao’s illegal donation, is leading Pine Tree Results.
Reed is also a close friend of Collin’s husband, Tom Daffron, who was paid for consulting work last year by Reed’s firm, Chesapeake Enterprises.
FEC records show that the Collins Victory Committee has joint fundraising agreements with Pine Tree Results and with other Collins committees — her principal campaign committee (Collins for Senator) and her leadership committee (Dirigo PAC.)
But the ties between the 2020 donation and Dolan have received less scrutiny.
A federal search warrant from April 7, 2021, said that Reed and Dolan were “associated with the 1820 PAC,” and that they received the email from Kao about the bogus Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers group.
As a federal contractor, Kao was prohibited from making political contributions.
ProPublica’s investigation cited emails showing that Kao had told Reed he was working with his attorney to create the Young Women Scientists group to obscure the donation.
“Very smart,” Reed replied, according an email reviewed by ProPublica.
Collins campaign manager Steve Abbott dismissed that exchange when speaking to reporters last month, though he said he did not have any firsthand knowledge of the conversation between Kao and Reed.
“I might also say the same thing if I were trying to do something and had consulted with my attorney,” Abbott said. “I would also say that that is very smart, but I have no idea what any of their conversations were or what was said.”
ProPublica reported that a staffer for the 1820 PAC requested contact information for Kao on Collins’ behalf so she could thank him. Abbott said Collins’ office has no record that Collins made such a call.
Collins’ campaign has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and accused ProPublica of trusting a convicted felon‘s word. The investigation was based in part on what Kao told federal investigators in an effort to earn a lighter sentence.
But the outlet has pushed back, saying that federal investigators corroborated some of Kao’s claims and wanted to launch a wider probe — a move that was thwarted when Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

title: Breeze Airways will offer direct flights between Portland and Myrtle Beach
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Breeze Airlines will add nonstop, year-round flights next year between the Portland International Jetport and Myrtle Beach International Airport in South Carolina.
The airline started offering that route this year with one stop, where passengers do not need to change planes. Now, the flights will be direct on Thursdays and Sundays starting May 2027.
“Every route we add to our network starts with the same question: Where can Breeze’s direct service bring travelers a convenience they don’t already enjoy today?” said David Neeleman, founder and CEO of Breeze Airways, said in a news release. “These new routes and destinations now bring Breeze’s high-value, low-cost service to these cities, making affordable travel to great destinations more convenient than ever.”
Breeze Airways currently offers 15 destinations with 11 nonstop options from Portland.
Last year was the busiest year ever for the jetport, with nearly 2.6 million passengers. Nine airlines provided service to 27 nonstop destinations in 2025. American Airlines carried more than 726,000 people, nearly one-third of all travelers in and out of Portland.
Breeze, which had added several new destinations in recent years, accounted for 180,000 travelers, or more than 7%, according to jetport officials.
In the first six months of 2026, the total number of passengers was lagging slightly behind the same period last year, according to the jetport’s website.
