title: Real estate agents turn to AI to make listings shine. When is it ‘house fishing?’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tom Landry had been trying to find his clients a home on one of Maine’s unbridged islands for over a year, when the listing popped up.
It was ideal. The rustic, classic cottage with its screened-in porch was charming, but the real showstopper was the backyard. A string of cafe lights hung over a ring of Adirondack chairs and a striking stone fireplace.
But when Landry and his clients made it to the 900-square foot house, listed for $579,000, they did a double take. The porch was less rustic and more dilapidated. The backyard scene built for entertaining didn’t exist at all. The house’s best features had been AI-generated.
“You arrive and it’s literally falling down,” said Landry, owner of Benchmark Real Estate in Portland. “There were parts of the house you couldn’t even walk through. It was laughable.”
It’s a concept known as “house fishing” — the real estate version of “catfishing,” or making something appear better online than it does in reality.
As AI becomes more advanced and accessible, real estate agents are increasingly using the technology to touch up photos, virtually stage a room or write listings.
Landry said agents have an obligation to make things look as good as possible for their clients, but when does it become deceptive or false advertising?
“It is a bit of an ethical quandary here,” Landry said.
AI DISCUSSIONS INCREASING
That sentiment is growing locally and nationally.
“We are definitely looking into AI and the proper ways to be using AI in real estate,” said Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors.
Members at the organization’s recent conference had a three-hour class about AI use in the industry, and AI guidelines will be included as a “core course” that The Maine Real Estate Commission requires licensees to take every two years, she said.
AI was the central topic of the Maine Real Estate and Development Association’s annual Forecast Conference in February, and it will also be a major focus of the National Association of Realtors “NTX” conference next month.
“Everybody is dealing with it,” Oberg said.
Legislators in Wisconsin and California have passed laws requiring that digitally altered photos in listings be clearly labeled and that the unedited photos also be included. Lawmakers in New Jersey and New York are considering similar restrictions.
The National Association of Realtors’ code of ethics recommends that members “refrain from exaggerating, misrepresenting or concealing pertinent facts” and to present a “true picture” in advertising and marketing.
‘OVER AND ABOVE’
Real estate agents have been known to add a little spin to spruce up a listing. A house in disrepair is waiting for “a little TLC,” from “an investor with a vision.” Creative camera angles can make a shoebox-sized living room look spacious.
It’s also commonplace for agents to touch up photos. They might digitally remove a trash can blocking the garage or some clutter the seller didn’t put away. The lights might be brightened to create an inviting atmosphere, or a sunset enhanced. A fire might even be added to the fireplace.
“Some things are up for grabs,” Landry said, “but this has gone over and above.”
A discerning buyer could have spotted that some things in the listing weren’t quite right. One porch photo looked a little shabbier, and was missing the rug, the string lights and the potted plants that brightened up the other. The aerial shots of the backyard didn’t show the fireplace.
But the porch photos weren’t next to one another, making side-by-side comparisons harder, and the listing didn’t disclose that any photos had been edited, nor were the altered shots labeled.
“People were doctoring photos before AI,” but the ease, speed and intensity with which people can change things now is “mind-boggling,” said Steve Weikal, Industry Chair of the Real Estate Transformation Lab at the MIT Center for Real Estate.
“We’ll have to figure out a way to police that,” he said. “How do we trust what we’re seeing and who we’re interacting with? … AI is opening up the Pandora’s box.”
Weikal, however, believes AI can be a powerful tool for the industry, and said it could help solve the problem as more time and money is invested in verification technology.
THE IMPORTANCE OF TRUST
Matt Pouliot, owner of Pouliot Real Estate in Augusta, said labeling will be key moving forward.
“It’s critical that consumers know that the property they’re buying looks as close as possible to what’s online,” he said.
Trust is crucial in the business, he added, and “we need to maintain that by not putting in a swimming pool where there isn’t one.”
Pouliot said his company recently adopted an AI policy based on the National Association of Realtors’ best practices. He sees the technology as a boon, provided there are still human-centered checks and balances.
Writing listings has never been faster, Pouliot said, and AI often comes up with zippy turns of phrase that he wouldn’t have.
It can eliminate a lot of back-and-forth administrative work, help with scheduling, respond to emails or draft social media posts.
“Automate the part that’s drudgery, that prevents you from being out in the field and out meeting with people and out networking and taking people on tours,” said Weikal, at MIT.
‘A FUNDAMENTAL TRUST PROBLEM’
Not all real estate agents have jumped on the bandwagon.
Andy Mooers, owner of Mooers Realty in Houlton, said using AI in listings is not only lazy, but also dangerous.
“Anyway you slice and dice it, AI slop is a fundamental trust problem,” he wrote in a blog post on his website.
Mooers said in an interview that he’d rather his clients see “the good, the bad and the ugly” — that the house is on a busy road, that the living room is small or that there are power lines over the roof.
Choosing to show a property as it really is, rather than what it could be, ultimately saves everyone time and energy, he said.
“AI makes everything perfect … and life isn’t like that,” he said.
AGENTS OBSOLETE?
AI is also helping clients become more informed. They’re doing research ahead of time and asking more and smarter questions.
A 2025 Realtor.com survey found that of 1,000 people in various stages of the market, 82% had used AI for real estate insights.
In some cases, the technology is helping sellers cut out agents altogether.
New platforms like Ridley offer AI software packages to help people sell their homes for a flat fee instead of paying a sellers’ commission.
A New York Times reporter recently wrote about selling his house with the help of an AI chatbot, and reportedly received a higher selling price.
But Weikal doesn’t think agents are going to be out of a job anytime soon.
People thought online listing platforms like Zillow and Redfin would also put agents out of work. The job has just adapted.
“The role is changing to a more advisory role,” Weikal said.
Landry, at Benchmark, said people still want human advice.
“When you’re negotiating over the most consequential life and financial decision you’re going to face … do you really want to chance it?”
The public’s trust in real estate agents is still high, Pouliot said.
“It only stays that way if we stay dedicated to accuracy.”

title: Vatican says pope’s lung nodule surgery was successfully completed
text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery Tuesday that confirmed that he has lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican said.
Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The statement made no mention of treatment going forward, and the Vatican said doctors were not currently speaking of chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests. The Vatican press office noted the medical statement spoke of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer.
Leo’s lymph nodes also would have been removed and tested, to determine if the cancer had spread, and there was no word yet on those test results.
“Adenocarcinoma is the most common (type of lung cancer), also with the most favorable prognosis,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. “While we know the diagnosis we now need to know the stage.”
“We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?” Liu said.
If the cancer has spread, more tests will be needed to determine what kind of therapy to pursue, he said. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy or targeted therapy, which involves oral pills for specific cancers.
The Vatican says the surgery was successful
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about three hours, the Vatican statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.
“The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said, adding that the pope later returned to his room.
The right lung is divided into three sections or lobes while the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the remainder of the lung can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy and physically active people.
Leo had walked into Rome’s Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
Oncologists said prior to the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis would be “excellent” since it would have been removed at an early stage.
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20.
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Recovery could allow November travel to South America
There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
Oncologists often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery — which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery.
The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
“He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.
Pope was hospitalized for typhoid fever in 1985
This is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome — a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for “Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.”
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the “horrible” pain of the fever. “I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’
“Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ’Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here — the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”
___
Barry reported from Milan. Associated Press writer Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report.
___

title: Fake Denzel Washington quote appears on Trump’s Truth Social account
text:
(CNN) - A fake quote attributed to actor Denzel Washington appeared on President Trump’s Truth Social account.
Monday’s post allegedly quotes Washington supporting the president and calling him a great friend.
A spokesperson for Washington confirmed the quote was not real.
It is unclear if Washington and the president have ever met.
Media outlets say similar fake endorsements of the president have previously appeared on social media, linking actor Matthew McConaughey and singer Mick Jagger to the same comments attributed to Washington.

title: Check your medicine cabinet: More than 112,000 bottles of acetaminophen recalled
text:
(CNN) - More than 112,000 bottles of Extra Strength Acetaminophen sold on Amazon have been recalled.
The pills are made by Aurobindo Pharma but sold under Amazon’s private label.
It is not clear if anything is actually wrong with the 500-milligram caplets. The recall is based on consumer complaints that some of them are discolored.
The Food and Drug Administration has not assigned a health risk classification to the recall.
Acetaminophen is a common pain reliever frequently referred to as Tylenol, and paracetamol in most countries outside the U.S.
Customers who have the medication are asked to contact Amazon customer service for a remedy.

title: Breeze Airways will offer direct flights between Portland and Myrtle Beach
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Breeze Airlines will add nonstop, year-round flights next year between the Portland International Jetport and Myrtle Beach International Airport in South Carolina.
The airline started offering that route this year with one stop, where passengers do not need to change planes. Now, the flights will be direct on Thursdays and Sundays starting May 2027.
“Every route we add to our network starts with the same question: Where can Breeze’s direct service bring travelers a convenience they don’t already enjoy today?” said David Neeleman, founder and CEO of Breeze Airways, said in a news release. “These new routes and destinations now bring Breeze’s high-value, low-cost service to these cities, making affordable travel to great destinations more convenient than ever.”
Breeze Airways currently offers 15 destinations with 11 nonstop options from Portland.
Last year was the busiest year ever for the jetport, with nearly 2.6 million passengers. Nine airlines provided service to 27 nonstop destinations in 2025. American Airlines carried more than 726,000 people, nearly one-third of all travelers in and out of Portland.
Breeze, which had added several new destinations in recent years, accounted for 180,000 travelers, or more than 7%, according to jetport officials.
In the first six months of 2026, the total number of passengers was lagging slightly behind the same period last year, according to the jetport’s website.

title: Maine’s governor’s race ‘sleepy’ according to political science professor
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - There will not be a fifth debate in the Maine governor’s race.
University of Maine Political Science Chair Mark Brewer thinks Pingree’s campaign not wanting to do a fifth debate is strategic.
Polling shows she has a substantial lead over Rick Bennett and Bobby Charles.
He thinks the Pingree campaign sees the path to victory as staying the course and avoiding a major gaffe on the campaign trail.
“Rick Bennett’s campaign for whatever reason hasn’t gained a whole lot of traction, despite some people, including myself thinking he had the potential to shake things up. So far he hasn’t really done that. It’s hard to say that the governor’s race is sleepy, because our gubernatorial races aren’t sleepy, but, it’s kind of sleepy,” said Brewer.
The three candidates will be taking part in a debate Wednesday night with our media partner WMTW at 8 p.m.
We will be streaming that debate on our website and Facebook page.

title: Saco father detained by ICE at jetport on way to visit deaf son
text:
Nguinamau Celestino’s wife dropped him off at the Portland jetport at 3 a.m. to catch an early flight to Washington, D.C. He was on his way to visit Abel, his youngest son, who had just begun his first semester at a high school for the deaf.
Nguinamau never arrived.
Celestino’s daughter, Margarida, 24, said her brother checked their father’s location on his phone after his flight was scheduled to land. He was at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Scarborough.
Margarida, a medical technician based in Auburn, woke at 6 a.m. to two missed calls from her dad, which she returned, but he didn’t pick up. She was on her way to work when her mom called; Margarida told her employer there was a family emergency and headed to Saco, where her parents live, to put the pieces together.
“Usually we see videos of people being taken, but unfortunately, everything with my dad was so silent,” she said. “Nobody said anything.”
The Celestino family — which includes Nguinamau, his wife Sukombo, their eldest Margarida and three sons, Lionel, 21, Nludi, 18, and Abel, 15 — are originally from Angola, later lived in Namibia and came to the U.S. in 2017 as asylum seekers. Their application is still ongoing. Only Margarida has a green card.
Early on Friday, Oct. 9, Margarida said her father walked into the airport and went straight to security. He saw ICE agents around, but didn’t have any reason to think they were there for him. But when he showed his ID to a TSA agent, she said, ICE agents looked at his picture, said they were there for Celestino, and detained him.
Immigration enforcement has been ramping up at airports nationwide, and local advocates said there were several detentions at the jetport in August, including of asylum seeker and registered nurse Debora Kapisha, who has since been released.
Margarida said her father has no criminal history, but agents told him he had overstayed his visa.
An ICE spokesperson confirmed Tuesday that Nguinamau was arrested during “targeted operations” last week, and said that he entered the country legally but violated the terms of his lawful admission and “remained in the U.S. illegally for nearly eight years.”
He was processed at the Scarborough facility, but by the time Margarida’s husband arrived at 9 a.m., Nguinamau had already been transferred out of the state. Margarida’s husband, a U.S. citizen, had come to bring Nguinamau a jacket, because she heard from another detained family member that the facility is chilly, and Nguinamau gets cold easily.
The agency’s online detainee locator showed Tuesday that Celestino is now being held at the Strafford County Corrections facility in Dover, New Hampshire.
Margarida said her father has been in touch every day via phone, and seems to be doing alright. The family organized a GoFundMe, which has raised nearly $30,000, and they’ve transferred some funds to him. He was able to keep his medications, but she said his work authorization card, Social Security card and Angolan ID were all missing from his wallet when they picked up his belongings.
Nguinamau works in plumbing and HVAC for Pine State Services, and got his associate’s degree at Southern Maine Community College. All of the Celestino children attended Portland Public Schools, including King Middle and Casco Bay High.
Their youngest sibling, Abel, received special services at East End Community School and played for the Baxter Seagulls, an ASL basketball team for students with the Maine Educational Center for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing.
The center announced Nguinamau’s detention on Facebook over the weekend, describing him as a beloved member of the Greater Portland and center community.
“Our Deaf and Hard of Hearing community has always been strengthened by the connections we build, the families we support, and our willingness to stand together when someone is in need. This is a time to put those values into action,” center co-directors Steve Connolly and Catherine Lushman wrote in the post.
Connolly and Lushman said they were drafting letters to Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, asking them to intervene on behalf of the Celestino family.
For now, Margarida is worried about the impact Nguinamau’s detention will have on the rest of her family. Her mom has lupus and high blood pressure, and travels to Boston every three weeks for treatment, which she worries could be impacted by her husband’s detention.
Abel, who was awaiting his father’s visit in D.C., had to leave his school for the long weekend, and the family scrambled to find a friend in the city to look after him. The friend stepped up to the challenge, Margarida said, but it wasn’t the same as Abel spending the weekend with his father.

title: Eastern Iowa veterans travel to Washington to see memorials built in their honor
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Eighty-seven Eastern Iowa veterans traveled to Washington, D.C., Tuesday to visit the memorials built in their honor.
The first Eastern Iowa flight of this kind took off in the 1990s. There have been 61 flights since then.
Among the 87 veterans on board was Joe Latham Jr., who flew missions from the cockpit during the Vietnam war. He was one of the first pilots to shoot down a Soviet-designed MiG fighter jet.
“101 missions, a lot of night missions bombing, a lot of day missions, bombing. We were just lucky to get out alive,” Latham said.
Not everyone survived. Three men Latham flew with are listed on the wall, including his best friend.
“My very best friend, three of the guys that I flew with are on the wall, including my very best friend. It was he and I were roommates together and everything else. We flew in two different flights the same night. I was one hour later night bombing low altitude North Vietnam. And he didn’t come back,” Latham said.
Latham has lived a full life since returning from war. The names of his loved ones are engraved on the wall in Washington.
“Memories and I’ll be tearing up but this is this wonderful,” Latham said.
The wall is not the only place in Washington tied to Latham’s friends.
“Of course, Arlington, and I have very good friends buried in Arlington... that I flew with, and eventually I’ll be there too,” Latham said.

title: How often do roller coaster injuries happen?
text:
Are roller coaster injuries common? Here’s what to know
Six Flags said it has temporarily closed nine rides at six parks across the country after a man died and several others were injured on Monday in a roller coaster incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.
The man who died was 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, according to the Cobb County police. The identities of those injured have not been released by officials.
The incident comes weeks after a lawsuit was filed against Six Flags, after more than 100 riders allege sustaining brain injuries from the roller coaster X2.
With the recent incident in Georgia, questions about roller coaster safety are under scrutiny. The Get the Facts Data Team looked into how often roller coaster injuries occur at North America parks.
Are serious injuries common on amusement rides?
In 2024, an estimated 118 serious injuries occurred at amusement parks in North America, according to the National Safety Council’s 2024 amusement ride safety report for the IAAPA. That’s about 8% of all logged injuries, the same share reported for 2023.
The National Safety Council considers an injury "serious" if it results in a hospitalization for more than 24 hours for medical observation or results in death. NSC estimates are based on surveys sent to more than 400 amusement facilities in the U.S. and Canada. About 227 facilities responded to the latest survey for 2024.
Is the rate of getting injured on a ride high?
"The chance of being seriously injured on a fixed-site ride at a U.S. amusement park is 1 in 15.5 million rides taken," according to IAAPA's website.
The rate of getting injured on a roller coaster in 2024 was 1.27 per million rides, according to NSC.
That was an increase from 2023, when the rate was 0.88 per million rides, but the chances of injury remain slim.
Most of the ride injuries, about 60%, are attributed to guest-related factors, like not following the rules or having a medical condition, the report found.
Other injury factors were attributed to technical or operational factors, at 15% and 9%, respectively.

title: Federal agents raid Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. home
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Federal agents carried out a pre-dawn raid Monday at the Washington home of Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar.
The exact location is not being disclosed out of respect for her privacy.
It is not immediately clear what homeland security agents were looking for, but the Department of Justice says the raid is part of a federal criminal investigation.
Background on targeting
Omar, who is Somali-born, has frequently been a target of the Trump administration.
Last January, President Trump criticized her hours before an assailant attacked her with a syringe that ended up containing vinegar.
Last week, Vice President JD Vance accused her of immigration fraud, a claim that has not been substantiated.
Omar responds
Omar responded to the raid in a post on X.
“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar said. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
Timing questions raised
Questions about the timing of the raid are being raised.
A memorandum issued in 2024 under Attorney General Merrick Garland established that public raids and investigations could not be carried out with the purpose of hurting or discrediting a candidate close to an election.
The raid comes 22 days before the midterm elections. Omar is on the ballot.

title: How to access home healthcare for older Mainers
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Maine’s aging population means that more older adults will be seeking home healthcare — either through skilled nursing, help with daily tasks or a combination.
Home healthcare is a patchwork of services that can be paid for through Medicare, Medicaid or out-of-pocket, depending on the need.
Maine has the highest median age in the nation, at 44.9 years, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. The state’s 65-and-older age group is expected to grow 11.4% from 2027-32, according to the Maine Office of the State Economist projections.
Often the care sought from home health agencies is done in conjunction with family caregivers who are taking on the responsibility of helping an older relative age in their home, experts in the field say.
According to a 2025 review of research by Johns Hopkins University, “profound demographic shifts” will lead to greater demand for services in the U.S. over the next decade or longer for home health and other long-term health services.
Patty Buiocchi, chief operating officer of post-acute care at MaineHealth, said the demand is “only going to get higher and higher. Will the supply also become higher? That remains to be seen.”
“Home health is so increasingly important to the healthcare system, because when people are getting care in their home, it reduces unnecessary hospital visits,” Buiocchi said.
What are the different types of home healthcare?
Buiocchi, who oversees MaineHealth’s Home Health and Hospice, said that in general, Medicare pays for skilled nursing care needed in the home. Examples include recovering from a surgery or an illness where the patient requires the assistance of skilled nurses while recuperating at home.
Medicare is the federally funded health insurance program for those 65 and older, while Medicaid serves lower-income and disabled populations.
If an older person doesn’t need skilled nursing, but needs help with tasks for daily living, such as cooking, cleaning, remembering to take medications, groceries and laundry, they could qualify for those services under Medicaid, or if they don’t qualify, could purchase them out-of-pocket from an agency, Buiocchi said.
Medicare services are typically shorter-term, for instance rehabilitating at home after surgery, she said.
How can I access services?
Because services are in great demand, Buiocchi advised older Mainers who need help or their caregivers to educate themselves on what’s available.
“Be proactive,” Buiocchi said. “Don’t wait until someone has an acute incident. Call organizations to see what they provide and when they provide it. Get an assessment, and see what your insurance will cover.”
Noël Bonam, Maine AARP’s state director, said a good first step is to call 211 or reach out to your local Agency on Aging.
“They will do an assessment to see what are the needs in this caregiving situation, what kind of support is needed and what kind of resources are available,” Bonam said.
One of the first steps that can be taken is to look up caregiver support groups. For instance, the Southern Maine Agency on Aging offers caregiver training and support groups.
Some may qualify for help under Medicaid, known as MaineCare in the state. The first step is to get an assessment by filling out the long-term care application or calling 833-525-5784.
Catherine Dorrington, owner of Coastal Care Solutions in South Portland, said their business doesn’t provide Medicare or Medicaid home health services. But agencies such as Coastal Care can offer a number of out-of-pocket services to help older adults, such as respite care for caregivers, moving into new housing, and assistance with daily tasks.
“As you age, you can often continue to do things, but you may have to do them in a different way or with additional support,” Dorrington said.
If I’m a caregiver, do I have to follow the new Medicaid work requirement rules?
Most caregivers with Medicaid insurance are exempt from the work requirements that will require Medicaid recipients to work, volunteer or attend school for at least 80 hours per month starting in 2027.
Olivia Umoren Ezeuko, director of public policy and advocacy for USAging, a national association that supports state agencies on aging, said it’s important for caregivers to know about this exemption so they fill out the paperwork properly to prove their status. If not, people risk becoming uninsured.
“A lot of people are going to go to their next doctor’s appointment and find out they don’t have coverage anymore,” Umoren Ezeoko said during a public briefing on the topic. She said states are trying to make the process of maintaining Medicaid insurance as seamless as possible by linking employers with Medicaid eligibility documentation so that many workers do not need to obtain proof of employment.
Where can I go for help?
There are several good resources online, including at the Southern Maine Agency on Aging, which offers help for family caregivers. Or call 800-427-7411.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has a guide to help families determine whether they qualify for home healthcare services through Medicaid. Under Medicaid, one of the first steps is to fill out the long-term care application. In addition to asking about what type of help is needed, Medicaid will need financial information, such as income and assets. Families can also call 833-525-5784 and to see what services they may qualify for.
The Maine AARP also has a guide on home- and community-based services. Call 866-554-5380 for more information.
Caregivers can also call 211, which will connect them to resources.

title: Man stopped his truck and walked into road where another driver hit him in Palermo
text:
A man who pulled his truck over and then walked into the road was hit by another driver Tuesday morning in Palermo.
The man, whose identity hasn’t been made public, pulled over on Route 3, near Level Hill Road, about 5:35 a.m. and then walked into the road, where another driver hit him, according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
He was taken to Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor, where he was being treated for life-threatening injuries.
The other driver wasn’t injured.
The crash remains under investigation.
Palermo is west of Belfast.

title: Wiscasset’s voter guide to Nov. 3 local questions
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
From wiscasset.gov:
At the Nov. 3 referendum, Wiscasset voters will consider four proposals: an ordinance amendment concerning the Ordinance Review Committee; a new Fire Department Cost Recovery Ordinance; a temporary moratorium on new or expanded data center development; and a temporary moratorium limiting certain mobile home park lot rent increases. The ballot also contains a non-binding referendum question regarding a regional high school.
Ordinance Review Committee (ORC): Wiscasset has had difficulty recruiting volunteers for several boards and committees. This is not unique to Wiscasset. Communities elsewhere in Maine (are) also struggling to fill committee vacancies. Work, family responsibilities, and other commitments can limit the time residents have in preparing for and attending meetings. For the ORC, difficulty filling its six seats and obtaining the four members required for a quorum has delayed ordinance review. Lack of a quorum caused the ORC to cancel several meetings. These delays prevented the land use ordinance changes needed to comply with Maine's new housing law, LD 1829, from being placed on the Nov. 3 ballot as planned. The Town must bring its ordinances into compliance by July 1, 2027. A November vote would have allowed time to address voters' concerns, revise the amendments, and submit them for another vote if they were rejected. Waiting until June leaves little time before the compliance deadline.
The proposed amendment would eliminate the ORC and shift its duties to town staff. Town staff would prepare draft ordinances and amendments, with review and discussion by the Selectboard at public meetings.
The Town's stated reason for the change is that it now has sufficient professional, paid staff to research and draft ordinances, with legal review as needed. Selectboard meetings, in place of ORC meetings, would provide a forum for residents to ask questions, raise concerns, and suggest revisions. Applicable public hearing requirements and voter approval requirements would remain. Most of the Selectboard feel this change would result in higher public participation in the process.
Fire Department Cost Recovery: The cost of providing fire protection has risen sharply. Wiscasset has spent more than $ 1.3 million on new fire apparatus in recent years, representing a substantial investment by taxpayers. Nationally, documented municipal purchases show apparatus price increases of approximately 60% to 90% since 2020. Protective gear and other essential equipment have also become more expensive.
This ordinance would authorize the Town to recover actual Fire Department response costs for specified incidents through insurance claims or direct billing. Its stated purpose is to offset expenses for certain types of calls otherwise paid through the Fire Department budget. Similar ordinances are used in Maine and other state municipalities.
Covered incidents include hazardous materials and hazardous-waste cleanup; vehicle and aircraft crashes or fires; water-related emergencies within buildings (for example, flooded basements, broken sprinklers); utility-line standby resulting from vehicle crashes; and the third and subsequent false fire or sprinkler alarm at the same location (nuisance alarms caused by improper use of maintenance).
The Fire Chief, in consultation with the Town Manager, would decide whether to assess all, some, or none of an eligible response's costs. Fees would be established by the Selectboard and based solely on actual Town costs. A third-party agency could handle billing and collection, with invoices payable within 30 days of receipt.
Fire Department services would not be denied or withheld because of a lack of insurance or refusal to pay.
Data Center Moratorium: This ordinance would temporarily stop the Town from accepting, processing, reviewing, or approving applications for new, enlarged, or expanded data centers. It would expire six months after enactment unless lifted earlier or extended under its stated conditions. It would apply to applications filed on or after Nov. 3, 2026.
The stated purpose is to allow the Town time to study potential impacts of data centers and determine whether additional local zoning and building standards are needed. The moratorium identifies electricity demand, water supply, wastewater capacity, noise, lighting, traffic, visual character, and municipal finances as subjects for review.
Town staff, appropriate committees, and outside resources would review existing ordinances and study these issues. Staff would report findings and recommended ordinance amendments to the Selectboard which would make the report public and determine whether and when to submit the proposals to the Planning Board for public hearings and before a Town Meeting.
The moratorium would not permanently prohibit data centers. It excludes equipment incidental to another business, routine maintenance or equipment replacement that does not expand an existing data center, and government information technology infrastructure used for governmental purposes. Extensions of no more than 180 days each would require findings that the need for the moratorium continues and reasonable progress is being made.
No proposals for a data center are under consideration at this time.
Mobile Home Park Rent Increase Moratorium: The proposed moratorium grew out of a request for a permanent ordinance regulating mobile home park lot-rent increases. In July, Eric Fleischmann of the Maine Labor Climate Council approached the Selectboard on behalf of park residents concerned about rising rents. He submitted a proposed rent-stabilization ordinance based on a state-developed model.
The Selectboard discussed the proposal at its Aug. 25 workshop. Members identified questions and concerns that required further review before a permanent ordinance could be put before voters. Following that discussion, the Town sought legal assistance in preparing a temporary moratorium that would limit covered rent increases while the issue was studied.
Park owners also asked to participate. Nick and Samantha Beers, owners of Maplewood Hill, described substantial expenditures to repair and improve aging infrastructure. They questioned whether restrictive rent limits would allow owners to cover operating costs and finance necessary improvements. They also disputed some statements made about their park's rent increases and maintenance.
The Board welcomed that feedback and clarified that it needed more time to hear the pros and cons of a permanent ordinance before presenting a permanent ordinance to the voters. The moratorium would provide time to examine residents' and owner's concerns, accept public comment, and determine whether any permanent local regulation is actually needed.
This moratorium would temporarily prohibit covered lot rent increases exceeding 3% above the rent charged on Sept. 1, 2026. It would cover tenants living in a park when the ordinance is enacted, including increases previously announced.
It provides for retroactive application to Sept. 1 and would expire six months after enactment unless extended under its stated conditions.
The stated concern is that large lot rent increases may displace residents who own their homes but rent the land beneath them. Moving a manufactured home can be expensive or impractical, limiting residents' alternatives.
The proposal excludes leases covering both a landlord-owned home and its lot, and resident-owned cooperative parks whose elected boards approve increases. Lot rent includes mandatory fixed fees but excludes utility, telephone, and broadband expenses. The Town Manager would enforce the moratorium; violations could result in a $200 fine per offense and an order to refund improperly charged increases. Each affected lot would (be a) separate offense. Adoption would not automatically establish permanent rent control.
Non-binding Referendum Question: Should Wiscasset explore the possibility of a single high school serving students from multiple area towns?
In recent years, there has been growing discussion in Wiscasset and neighboring communities about whether greater regional collaboration could help address some of the challenges facing our schools, including declining enrollment, rising costs, and the desire to provide students with a broad range of educational opportunities.
Wiscasset and the Boothbay Region previously worked together on an application to the Maine Department of Education to explore a consolidated grades 9-16 school. Although that particular proposal did not move forward, the process demonstrated enough interest in regional approaches that some community members and officials felt it was worth asking residents more broadly whether the conversation should continue. Wiscasset's own Future of the Schools Committee has also identified regionalization as one possible path toward long-term sustainability, while recognizing that it would require significant planning, collaboration, and community input.
That is the purpose of the non-binding question on Wiscasset's November ballot: "Should Wiscasset explore the possibility of a single high school serving students from multiple area towns?" This is a survey, or "straw vote," and does not authorize the consolidation of Wiscasset's schools, commit the town to a particular partner or location, or approve any spending or specific plan. Rather, it is intended to provide a clearer picture of whether Wiscasset residents are interested in having conversations with neighboring communities about what a regional high school might look like, whether it could expand opportunities for students, and whether there could be potential financial or operational benefits from working together. Any actual proposal that might emerge from those conversations would require considerably more study, public discussion, and the appropriate approval process before moving forward.

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off in latest debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Troy Jackson versus Susan Collins round three is here.
The latest meeting in a flurry of debates between Maine’s candidates for U.S. Senate starts Tuesday at 7 p.m. Tonight’s event is the penultimate matchup between the two, with the last coming Thursday. (That event will be brought to you by Maine Public, NEWSCENTER Maine and the Portland Press Herald.)
Collins and Jackson’s debate tonight will be hosted by WABI and WAGM. You can watch a livestream below and follow along with our live commentary on the event.
-Despite that, we saw some new stuff, such as Jackson’s promise to deliver his campaign finance report Wednesday morning.
-Overall, there were few followers.
We’ll see you Thursday for the last debate!
-Kirby Wilson
Collins pushed back on that, noting that CBP officers killed two people in Minneapolis.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins noted the various ICE reform measures that she’s supported over the years, including de-escalation training and mandatory body-worn cameras.
Jackson has called for ICE to be abolished altogether.
Read our story about how the candidates would handle immigration enforcement here. We did a nice deep dive.
-Kirby Wilson
A note on candidates’ style
Both Jackson and Collins have seemed more emotional at times, with Jackson essentially telling Collins at one point not to lecture him on the difference between Medicare and Medicaid. At another point, Collins seemed vexed by Jackson’s barbs about her personal integrity.
-Kirby Wilson
“Troy has repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long,” Collins fired back. “I just cannot continue to ignore these attacks on my integrity.”
Collins then noted that she supported a measure that would regulate data centers such that they have no impact on electric rates.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson disagreed with this assessment, noting that he has a good relationship with the Canadians.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson once again criticized Collins for not doing enough to stop the tariffs.
-Kirby Wilson
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning,” Jackson said. “How bout that?”
-Kirby Wilson
“Sen. Collins is not going to stand there and school me on what I know,” Jackson said. “Don’t sit here and tell me about these things.”
And she said the government needs to do a better job fighting fraud in the healthcare program.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson criticized Collins for voting to advance Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins said she agreed with her opponent, and she criticized the Republican president.
“I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and I don’t think that that was well anticipated,” Collins said.
She said her ideal end to the war would be an agreement from Iran that they’d stop pursuing the enrichment of uranium.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins bashed Jackson for policies he supported in Augusta as the state Senate president, saying they are the reason electricity is so expensive here.
Who will voters believe? Whose record will they be more skeptical of? That question could decide the race.
-Kirby Wilson
So far, we’re treading familiar ground — all of this was addressed in each of the first two debates.
-Kirby Wilson
“Nobody should have to choose between keeping warm and buying groceries or other necessities,” Collins said.
The senator then criticized Jackson, whose leadership she said led to higher energy prices when compared to the rest of New England.
-Kirby Wilson
The 58-year-old former logger and state Senate president has been teasing this line of attack on social media today, since it’s the three-month anniversary of immigration agents killing Johan Sebastián Guerrero in Biddeford.
Collins, 73, parried similar attacks at last week’s debates, calling the shooting horrific and calling for an impartial investigation. She has also defended the need to preserve U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a federal agency Jackson wants to abolish.
Beyond that, it will be interesting to see if Jackson can recapture the energy and sharpness he displayed during their first meeting last Tuesday. He was able to put Collins on the defensive and deliver memorable lines that have had long tails in social media. Can he do it again?
Collins, meanwhile, was much sharper during their second debate last Thursday. She fully displayed her knowledge and experience, while putting Jackson on the defensive on issues like abortion and his leadership at the State House. Does she have any surprises in store?
Polling shows a tight race and it’s not clear that either candidate has said or done anything to change that — at least so far.
-Randy Billings

title: ‘Sleepy Hollow’ in Auburn, jack-o’-lanterns galore in Paris, Poe and the ‘Declaration’ in Lewiston and much more
text:
Come to the cabaret, old chum, in Auburn
AUBURN — L/A Community Little Theatre will open its 87th season with the Tony Award-winning musical “Cabaret.”
Set in a seedy cabaret called the Kit Kat Klub in 1929-30, the show tells the story of two doomed romances set against the emergence of antisemitism and fascism in Germany.
CLT’s production of “Cabaret” is based on the 1998 Broadway revival, according to organizers, considered the most revolutionary reenvisioning of the musical, emphasizing “the creeping threat of fascism (and) underscoring the parallels between the rising threat of Nazism in 1929 Berlin and contemporary anxieties about authoritarian resurgence.”
The show will offer seven performances, Friday and Saturday, Oct. 16-17; Thursday to Saturday, Oct. 22-24, at 7:30 p.m.; and Sundays, Oct. 18 and 25, at 2 p.m. All shows at Community Little Theatre, 30 Academy St.
For tickets and more information, go to www.laclt.com. Due to the mature themes in this production, parental discretion is advised.
Learn about history, view the Declaration of Independence in Lewiston
LEWISTON — As part of Maine Historical Society’s statewide commemoration of America’s 250th anniversary, the Maine Museum of Innovation Learning and Labor will welcome a rare original Dunlap Broadside printing of the Declaration of Independence over three days that will also offer readings, discussions, singing, storytelling and more.
Admission to the entire museum and viewing of the document is free. Advance reservations are encouraged. Free timed tickets to see the Declaration of Independence during regular museum hours are available at www.mainehistory.org.
Among the events:
Thursday, Oct. 15, 5-6:30 p.m.: Reading the Republic: A special book club event. A private viewing of the Declaration will be followed by a discussion of “The Hamilton Affair ” by Elizabeth Cobbs. Space is limited. Email [email protected] to sign up.
Friday, Oct. 16, 11-11:30 a.m.: Student presentation of the national anthem and Declaration of Independence. The Lewiston High School Chamber Singers will perform “The Star-Spangled Banner,” followed by a reading of the Declaration by sixth grade students from Montello Elementary School. Timed tickets encouraged by going to www.mainehistory.org.
Friday, Oct. 16, 5-6:30 p.m.: The Declaration of Independence: An Inspiring Riddle. A panel discussion with scholars from Bates College, Bowdoin College and the University of Maine on the Declaration’s uniqueness and why it continues to inspire more than 250 years later. Space is limited. Reserve a free ticket by going to www.mainehistory.org.
Saturday, Oct. 17, 1-2 p.m.: A Revolutionary Storytime! Read aloud and design challenge. Young historians can enjoy a special story time with the Lewiston Public Library and then try their hand at writing like they did in 1776, using feather quills and ink.
For more information, go to www.mainehistory.org. The Maine MILL is at 1 Beech St.
Channel Poe and bust a move in Lewiston
LEWISTON — The Lewiston Public Library will present its second annual literary ball — the Edgar Allan Poe Masquerade Ball — on Saturday, Oct. 17, in Callahan Hall.
Doors will open at 6:30 p.m., and the dance will run from 7-9 p.m. The ball will feature waltzing and other Victorian dancing as well as themed refreshments, games, and photo opportunities.
The free, after-hours event is open to participants ages 13 and up. No registration is required. Costumes and fancy dress are encouraged. Dancers of all ability levels, with or without partners, are welcome to attend.
For more information call 207-513-3134 or email [email protected]. The library is at 200 Lisbon St.
Hear from a Ukraine cultural expert in Lewiston
LEWISTON – Oleh Kotsyuba, director of Print and Digital Publications at the Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute, will join Bates College professor Cheryl Stephenson for a discussion about how sharing Ukrainian culture can serve as both a form of resistance and a source of political power as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues into its fifth year.
The talk, titled “Culture as Shield, Culture as Weapon: Why Ukraine Matters More Than Ever Today,” will take place at the Bates College Muskie Archives, room 201, 70 Campus Ave., on Monday, Oct. 19, at 6 p.m.
Kotsyuba, who is also chief online editor at the Ukraine journal Krytyka, will explore why sharing reliable knowledge about Ukraine is especially urgent today, organizers say.
The event is free and open to the public, and no registration is required.
Enjoy a Jack-o’-Lantern Spectacular in Paris
PARIS — The McLaughlin Garden and Homestead’s annual Jack-O’-Lantern Spectacular returns Thursday-Saturday, Oct. 15-17, with a magical new theme: “Enchanted Forest.”
Visitors are invited to step into a world of beautifully illuminated paths, hand-carved pumpkins, light displays and Halloween spirit, as well as more than 500 pumpkins intricately carved and displayed throughout the garden, say organizers.
Guests are invited to warm up inside the historic barn with complimentary warm spiced apple juice.
Fully gutted pumpkins will be available for carving Tuesday-Wednesday, Oct. 13-14, from 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. No registration is necessary, and all are welcome to stop by, carve a pumpkin, and help support the event.
Admission to the Spectacular is $8 per person or two for $15. Children 2 and younger are free. Proceeds benefit the nonprofit McLaughin Garden and Homestead.
For more information, go to mclaughlingarden.org or call 207-743-8820. The garden is at 97 Main St., South Paris.
Catch ‘Sleepy Hollow’ ballet in Auburn
AUBURN — The Dance Center’s Ballet LA will present an original production of “Sleepy Hollow” at the Donald M. Gay Performing Arts Center on Saturday, Oct. 17, at 1 and 5 p.m.
In it, Ichabod Crane will compete for the affection of Katrina Van Tassel, striving to outshine the dashing Brom Bones. “Who will ultimately triumph, and will we encounter the legendary Headless Horseman?” organizers ask.
Tickets are $18 with a $2.50 per ticket software fee. Children 2 and younger, sitting on a lap, do not need a ticket.
For tickets and more information go to thedancecenterla.com or email [email protected].
The Donald M. Gay Performing Arts Center is at Edward Little High School, 77 Harris St.
Listen to dulcimer at Oasis of Music in Lewiston
LEWISTON — On Wednesday, Oct. 14, “Keith Prairie will bring his voice and hammer dulcimer to share his special approach to folk music at the Oasis of Music,” say organizers. The program will begin at 12:30 p.m.
The Oasis of Music is at Trinity Commons, 247 Bates St. Admission is free, with donations accepted. Free parking is available in the Agora parking lot. For more information call 207-344-3106.
Have an event you’d like to get in? Email details to [email protected] to be considered for inclusion in the weekly listing. And add your event to the Sun Journal calendar here: www.sunjournal.com/events-calendar/.

Here’s what’s on the ballot in Standish
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Standish residents will see three referendum questions and notable races for Maine House, Senate, governor and U.S. Senate on their November ballots.
Election Day voting will be held at the Standish Municipal Center from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Absentee voting has already started, and voters can request a ballot online, in the town clerk’s office, by phone or mail before Oct. 29. There will be extended hours for in-person absentee voting on Wednesday, Oct. 21, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and Wednesday, Oct. 28, from 7:30 a.m. to 7 p.m.
MOBILE HOME PARK RENT CONTROL
Voters will decide whether to enact a mobile home park rent stabilization ordinance. If passed, the ordinance would limit how much mobile home park owners can raise rents each year. Several Maine towns have passed similar measures.
Residents of Pine Tree Estates this summer collected enough signatures on a citizen’s petition for the measure to appear on the ballot. The Standish Town Council also passed an emergency moratorium to temporarily enforce it before the election.
Pine Tree Estates is owned by RHP Properties, the largest private operator of manufactured home communities in the U.S., and has raised lot rents to rates residents say are unaffordable and threatening to their livelihoods. Opponents say the ordinance would negatively impact local mobile home park owners and that the town should avoid regulating private businesses.
CHARTER AMENDMENTS
Two of the three referendums on the ballot will ask voters to weigh in on changes to the town’s charter.
The first change would reduce the number of meetings necessary for the Standish Town Council to adopt an ordinance from three to two. The charter requires a new ordinance to be introduced at one meeting, read at a second meeting, and undergo a public hearing and potential adoption at a third meeting. If voters approve the change, the proposed ordinance would instead be introduced at a first meeting, followed by a public hearing and potential adoption at the second.
Town Manager Tashia Pinkham said the change would increase efficiency. She said the town and local business have faced challenges completing tasks because of how long the current process takes.
Opponents at the public hearing for the measure said they think the three meetings are necessary to ensure residents have enough time to hear about and weigh in on possible ordinance changes.
Another charter amendment on the ballot would increase the total cost of the town’s capital expenditures requiring approval by referendum vote from $75,000 to $150,000. Public Works Director John Cross said it has been 18 years since that threshold was last increased.
MAINE SENATE & HOUSE
Standish voters will decide between Democratic candidate Nathan Burnett and Republican candidate and current Maine House District 85 Rep. Kimberly Pomerleau for Maine Senate District 22.
Democratic candidate Cassandra Anne Dove is facing Republican Mark Walker in Maine House District 84, and Democratic candidate Paul Welch is up against Republican Adrienne Paul in Maine House District 85.
CUMBERLAND COUNTY RACES
Democrat Paul Aranson, of Scarborough, is running uncontested for Cumberland County judge of probate, as is incumbent Democrat Kevin Joyce for Cumberland County sheriff.
Incumbent Jacqueline Sartoris, of Brunswick, and challenger Stephanie Anderson, of Cape Elizabeth, are facing off for the District 2 Attorney seat.
Read more about candidates’ campaign goals on the Press Herald Voter Guide.

Breeze Airways will offer direct flights between Portland and Myrtle Beach
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Breeze Airlines will add nonstop, year-round flights next year between the Portland International Jetport and Myrtle Beach International Airport in South Carolina.
The airline started offering that route this year with one stop, where passengers do not need to change planes. Now, the flights will be direct on Thursdays and Sundays starting May 2027.
“Every route we add to our network starts with the same question: Where can Breeze’s direct service bring travelers a convenience they don’t already enjoy today?” said David Neeleman, founder and CEO of Breeze Airways, said in a news release. “These new routes and destinations now bring Breeze’s high-value, low-cost service to these cities, making affordable travel to great destinations more convenient than ever.”
Breeze Airways currently offers 15 destinations with 11 nonstop options from Portland.
Last year was the busiest year ever for the jetport, with nearly 2.6 million passengers. Nine airlines provided service to 27 nonstop destinations in 2025. American Airlines carried more than 726,000 people, nearly one-third of all travelers in and out of Portland.
Breeze, which had added several new destinations in recent years, accounted for 180,000 travelers, or more than 7%, according to jetport officials.
In the first six months of 2026, the total number of passengers was lagging slightly behind the same period last year, according to the jetport’s website.

title: ‘Unimaginable grief’: 5 dead, 3 injured after crash involving police car, officials say
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) - Five people were killed in a crash involving a Memphis police car, according to authorities
A total of five people were killed early Sunday when their vehicle collided with a Memphis police car at Hickory Hill and East Raines roads.
The vehicle carried six people; however, the sixth person remains in the hospital in critical condition.
Officials identified four of the five victims as 20-year-old Rodney McNeal, 21-year-old Syria Fifer, 20-year-old Messiah Lee and 19-year-old Carlesha Fifer.
A makeshift memorial was created Monday at the crash site.
Memphis Mayor Paul Young released a statement Monday morning: “Five young people lost their lives last night, and their families, along with the families of others involved, are facing unimaginable grief today. My deepest prayers go out to everyone affected by this tragedy. I ask Memphis to keep these families in our thoughts as they face the difficult days ahead.”
The family of Syria Fifer has set up a GoFundMe to help with expenses.
Two Memphis police officers were also injured and have since been released from the hospital.

title: CVS to pay $315M over opioid prescriptions in major DOJ settlement
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday.
The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of providing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.”
It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis.
“Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement.
CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.”
The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing.
The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids.
The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden’s administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills,” or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose.
It alleged that poor staffing levels coupled with performance metrics and incentive compensation policies implemented by the company led to pharmacists racing to fill prescriptions without confirming they were legitimate. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says.
Under the settlement, CVS must also “implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement.
Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently.
Most of the settlements -- and dollars -- have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart.
___
Associated Press reporter Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report from Philadelphia.

title: Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off in third debate
text:
Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off in third Maine debate
Tuesday's debate hosted by WMTW media partners WABI and WAGM
Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson square off in third Maine debate
Tuesday's debate hosted by WMTW media partners WABI and WAGM
Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson faced off in their third debate Tuesday night. The debate was hosted by WMTW media partners WABI and WAGM at WABI's studio in Bangor. You can watch the a recap in the video player above or the full debate in the YouTube video embedded below.
Last week, Collins and Jackson participated in a Senate debate hosted by Maine's Total Coverage. The candidates sparred on issues that included tariffs on Canadian goods, oil prices and abortion access.
During our debate, Jackson claimed that Collins and her husband, Thomas Daffron, are making money off the war with Iran. Collins said the claim is "absolutely outrageous" and demanded an apology from Jackson, who did not offer any specific evidence about how the senator and her husband are profiting off the war.
Later in the debate, Collins claimed that electric rates in Maine became the fourth in the nation under Jackson's leadership as president of the State Senate. PolitiFact found that the senator's claim was an exaggeration.
The Maine's Total Coverage debate on Thursday, Oct. 8, was the second between Collins and Jackson, who had their first debate on Oct. 6.
You can watch the entire Maine's Total Coverage U.S. Senate debate in the video player embedded below, or on the WMTW-TV YouTube channel.
Collins is seeking to win her sixth term in the U.S. Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before. She was uncontested in the June 9 primary, as she was the only candidate to qualify for the Republican primary ballot.
Jackson has only been in the Senate race for just over two months. The former Maine Senate president finished third in the gubernatorial primary, but was chosen as the Democratic Senate nominee on July 25 at a special nominating convention. The Maine Democratic Party had to find a replacement candidate for the Senate primary winner, Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race on July 8 following allegations of sexual assault.
Jackson's political experience
Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from Fort Kent, led a weeklong blockade along the border with Quebec in 1998, when Maine loggers were protesting the hiring of Canadian loggers who were coming into Maine and driving down pay rates. The standoff ended with Jackson being escorted away by police, and he went on to fight for better logger and wood hauler protections as a state lawmaker.
In 2000, Jackson ran for the Maine House of Representatives as a Republican but lost out on the House District 151 seat. He ran for the same seat as an independent two years later and was victorious, and became a Democrat in 2004 before the end of his first term. Jackson was elected later that year to serve the new House District 1, and was reelected in 2006.
In 2008, Jackson ran for the State Senate and was elected to represent District 35. He won reelection in 2010 and 2012 before running to represent Maine's 2nd Congressional District in the U.S. House in 2014. Jackson lost the 2014 Democratic primary to Emily Cain, who wound up losing the CD2 general election to Republican Bruce Poliquin.
Jackson led U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential campaign in Maine in 2016 and helped the independent from Vermont win the state's caucus. Sanders campaigned with Jackson in Maine over the weekend.
In 2016, Jackson was reelected to the Maine Senate to represent the 1st District and then chosen by fellow Democrats to be the Senate's minority leader. He was reelected in 2018 and became Senate president after Democrats won a majority in the chamber, and he held that role while being reelected two more times in 2020 and 2022. Jackson left office in December 2024 due to term limits.
More on Collins' experience
Collins grew up in Caribou, where her family runs a sixth-generation lumber business. Both of her parents served as mayor of Caribou, and her father served in both chambers of the Maine Legislature.
After graduating from St. Lawrence University in 1975, Collins began working as a legislative assistant for U.S. Rep. Bill Cohen, a Republican from Maine. Cohen was eventually elected to the U.S. Senate in 1978 and, in 1981, Collins was promoted to staff director of the Oversight of Government Management Subcommittee of the Committee on Governmental Affairs.
Collins remained on Cohen's staff until 1987, when Maine Gov. John McKernan appointed her as commissioner of the Maine Department of Professional and Financial Regulation. In 1992, President George H.W. Bush appointed Collins as director of the Small Business Administration's New England regional office. After President Bill Clinton took office in January 1993, Collins served as deputy state treasurer of Massachusetts.
In 1994, Collins won the Republican primary for Maine governor, becoming the first woman to be nominated for the office. She wound up finishing third in the election behind Democrat Joseph E. Brennan and the winner, independent Angus King, who is now Collins' fellow U.S. senator from Maine. Collins was named the founding executive director of the Center for Family Business at Husson University after the 1994 gubernatorial election.
Two years later, Collins ran for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Cohen, her former boss, and went on to defeat Brennan in the 1996 general election. Collins was reelected in 2002, 2008, 2014 and most recently in 2020, when she became the first Republican woman to win a fifth term in the Senate.
Collins, the most senior Republican woman in the Senate and the seventh-most senior senator, currently serves as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. She previously chaired the Committee on Governmental Affairs (2003-05), Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (2005-07) and Special Committee on Aging (2015-21).

title: Voter registration deadline arrives as new citizens register
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The deadline to register to vote in the midterms ends Tuesday for Kansas, Maine, West Virginia, Oregon and the District of Columbia.
Ninety-eight people born in 50 different countries became American citizens Tuesday morning at the federal courthouse in downtown Washington. The newest citizens navigated interviews, green cards, tests and paperwork to finish the citizenship process - swearing an oath to the U.S. Constitution and flag.
Once out of the courtroom, many completed their first civic duty as Americans and registered to vote. Groups including the League of Women Voters were set up to make the process easy.
Tuesday marks the last day to register in D.C.
According to census data, there are about 174 million registered voters in the U.S. In the last election, 154 million Americans cast ballots.
Some states also allow voters to register at the polls when they go to vote. More information about state registration status is available at vote.org.

title: A promise to mom, a century-old farm: How these families kept developers at bay
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Home ownership has been the bedrock of the American dream, mainly driven by single homeowners.
But corporate buyers are changing that landscape, according to The Lincoln Institute of Land Policy and the Center for Geospatial Solutions. In a 2025 report, the group wrote that “this trend is reducing the housing stock available to individual homebuyers.”
In order to buck that trend as well as preserve the environment, there’s a non-profit in South Carolina working with homeowners who wish to protect their properties from development long after they’re gone.
Two Upstate South Carolina families have placed more than 250 acres under conservation easements through Upstate Forever, permanently restricting development on land that has been in their families for generations.
The announcement is part of a broader milestone for the organization, which now protects more than 40,000 acres across a 10-county area.
A conservation easement
Under a conservation easement, landowners retain ownership of their property. The easement places legal restrictions on what can ever be built there, shielding the land from future development regardless of who owns it.
Scott Park of Upstate Forever said the arrangement functions as a charitable donation.
“Conservation easements, they’re in essence a charitable donation, so that’s why Upstate Forever can be a grantee of these conservation easements,” Park said. “So the landowner is the grantor; they grant those restrictions to Upstate Forever. We are the forever steward, so we’re almost a partner in the pocket of that landowner now for as long as that landowner owns that piece of property.”
The properties
Ed Lomas’s Moore Farm, located near Horsepen Creek in Greenville County, spans 110 acres and has been in his family for more than 100 years. The property, once used for cotton farming, has been used for raising cattle since around the 1950s. It is now surrounded by new neighborhoods.
“Twenty years ago, you would wait for cars to come by maybe every few minutes,” Lomas said. “Now it’s a constant stream, especially first thing in the morning.”
Lomas said the easement process took about a year and a half. He said he pursued it after watching other families lose their land.
“I actually had a phone call from a family friend about a year ago saying they had exactly that scenario,” Lomas said. “They were older, they couldn’t take care of it, it was going to be left to the children, it was going to be a big mess. They felt that was their only option, just to sell the land.”
Lomas said the property will be safe and family members “will not be able to be pressured into selling it as a development.”
Alice Smith’s property, Duck Haven, is a 146-acre tract in Pickens County with rolling fields that connect to the Saluda River. Her grandparents purchased the land in the 1940s, and Smith said she made a promise to her mother to keep it intact.
“I made a promise to my mother that I would find a way to keep the land together,” Smith said.
Smith said she chose conservation over development offers.
“My grandparents bought it in the 40’s, and it was actually most, from what I’ve discovered, it was mostly farmland when they bought it,” she said.
‘Salt of the earth’
Park said the organization is seeing growing demand from landowners facing development pressure.
“You meet landowners like Ed and Alice that are just salt of the earth,” Park said. “They just want to protect their property. They see the development pressure that’s coming around them and they are pretty much, they are laser focused on getting these properties protected, and we’re happy to be a partner in that.”
Both Lomas and Smith said they want other families to know the option exists.
“There are opportunities and ways to protect and conserve the property you may have,” Lomas said.
“I’m not well-to-do, I’m not really well connected, but if for some reason I can plant a seed in anyone, that if I’m able to do this, they can too,” Smith said.
Smith said the easement ensures the land will remain as it is beyond her lifetime.
“What your family sacrificed and worked so hard for did not go to waste and a developer is not going to be able to ever touch it, and even when I’m gone, it’s still going to stay like this,” she said.

title: Former officer identified as suspect in cold case murder
text:
CHICAGO (CNN) - Chicago police say they have solved the murder of an 8-year-old girl that happened more than 65 years ago, identifying a former Chicago police officer as the killer.
Authorities say Thomas F. McInerney Jr. murdered Gloria Kowalewicz shortly after joining the Chicago Police Department in 1959.
Kowalewicz was found shot to death in 1960 after she was abducted while walking to church.
Chicago police collected evidence at the time, including a fingerprint from the girl’s purse.
The murder remained unsolved until recently, when police say they used advanced DNA technology to identify the killer as McInerney.
McInerney retired from the department in 1987 as a violent crimes detective. He then moved to Las Vegas, Nevada, where he died in 2006 at the age of 70.

title: Deadly Casco Bay algae bloom dissipating, impacts still being assessed
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An algae bloom that wiped out shellfish in parts of Casco Bay is dissipating as town officials and scientists assess the extent of the mortality and its impacts on the harvesting industry.
Officials have been monitoring a bloom of the phytoplankton Karenia mikimotoi — which is not harmful to humans but puts significant stress on shellfish — since it was reported in Casco Bay in early September.
Phytoplankton cell counts are declining in inner Casco Bay, the nonprofit Friends of Casco Bay said in an Oct. 9 update. But some areas are continuing to see fallout from the bloom, as low dissolved oxygen levels suffocate shellfish.
The bloom spurred the Department of Marine Resources last month to shut down shellfish harvesting in Maquoit Bay in Brunswick and the eastern side of Middle Bay in Harpswell, where clamdiggers noticed dramatic die-offs of softshell clams and worms. The department reopened harvesting in Maquoit Bay on Oct. 8 as the brown-colored tide began clearing up.
In an update the next day, the department said that “satellite imagery has shown an overall declining trend in both nearshore and offshore bloom activity over the past week,” but that elevated cell counts were still present in some areas of Muscongus and Penobscot bays.
Softshell clam harvesters said last month that the lasting financial impact of the bloom will be substantial.
Brunswick Coastal Resource Manager Dan Devereaux said in an email Tuesday that it would take many months “to understand the immediate and longer-term impacts … to the wild and farmed shellfish crops.”
Deveraux said oxygen levels are returning to normal in the mudflats, and his team is starting to find surviving softshell clams and worms, but in much lower densities than before the bloom.
“I think we are through the worst of it and are headed toward being on the mend. The mending portion will take time,” he said.
The Department of Marine Resources is asking those in the fishing industry to report signs of low oxygen, water discoloration and odors. Karenia mikimotoi appears as brown or almost black water depending on its density. The department will share updates on the situation on its website.
