title: AI doomsday fears overshadow current threats, expert says
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Some of the loudest voices in artificial intelligence have warned the technology could someday threaten humanity. A global AI security leader told us those catastrophic headlines are drowning out threats that are already here.
Adam Ely, general manager of AI security at Check Point, a cybersecurity company, said researchers raising alarms about AI are right to call for attention but said the technology does not signal the end of humanity.
“The researchers today are really saying, ‘Hey, let’s be deliberate and pay attention.’ But no, I don’t think this is the end of humanity by any means,” Ely said.
Ely compared the reaction to AI to early fears about automobiles.
“It’s like the people that when cars were first invented said, ‘Wow, this is scary. All humans are going to die.’ And we found safety along the way. Brakes, airbags, crash testing. Technology is very similar,” Ely said.
He said the comparison to cars does not mean AI should go unchecked.
As the technology continues to evolve and becomes a part of daily life, whether directly or indirectly, Ely said we have to think “about what is appropriate and not appropriate.”
His concern is not a far-off doomsday scenario but how AI is already being used.
“We’re seeing more sophisticated groups, and some of this will be military around the world. Some of this will be the most sophisticated cyber crime actors using AI to breach companies and to steal data, to steal money, or even to potentially take down critical infrastructure. Those are real today,” Ely said.
Asked whether an industry pause on AI development is realistic or whether bad actors will keep moving ahead regardless, Ely said we need to find a way to “match pace with safety.”
“Put the right safe guards in place so that they don’t go rogue,” Ely said.
He encouraged people to learn how AI tools work and use them wisely.

Protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates, and partners is a top priority. We apologize for any inconvenience this issue may have caused customers and partners.

title: Broadway Bridge Replacement Enters Final Stretch On I-95 Near Bangor Through End Of Year
text:
Traffic in the area of the Broadway Bridge in Bangor will get a little trickier this week, as crews get ready for the final phases of the bridge replacement project.
What And When Will This All Happen?
According ot the Maine Department of Transportation, crews will be working on shoulder reconstruction along with milling and pavement in the southbound area of I-95 near Broadway beginning on Friday, October 16th and running through the weekend.
This means the traffic pattern will be changing to accommodate the work, so motorists are asked to use caution and be aware.
How Will The Work Impact Travel?
Officials with the Maine DOT say the work will be done in phases, in order to prepare for the transition from the temporary bridge to the new permanent one.
Phase 1:
"The southbound high-speed lane will be closed to traffic while crews complete milling and paving at both ends of that lane."
We're told the southbound travel lanes will stay open, along with the on and off ramps in the area, so motorists will still have access to those avenues.
Phase 2:
"The southbound high-speed lane will be opened to traffic across the new bridge. The southbound travel lane and the Exit 185 southbound off-ramp will be closed while crews complete excavation, milling, and paving at the north end of the travel lane and ramp."
Read More: Maine Fall Fun: Take Amtrak to Celtics & Bruins Games
During that time, drivers should follow the signs for the detour, which will take them to the Stillwater Exit (186) and down Stillwater Ave to Broadway, so they can bypass all of the work.
Phase 3
Once crews have completed the milling, paving, and excavation, they will start Phase 3 by reopening the Exit 185 southbound off-ramp.
"The southbound high-speed lane will remain open to traffic across the new bridge, and the southbound travel lane will remain closed."
Read More: Llewellyn Estes Bridge Removal Work Begins In Old Town
They may have to close the on-ramp temporarily to finish up work on the ends of the ramp and travel lane.
If that happens, motorists will be detoured down Broadway to Stillwater Ave and will have access to the interstate via the on-ramp at Exit 186.
Phase 4:
All of the new southbound lanes and ramps will open across the new bridge.
The Maine DOT says they will have plenty of message boards, signs, and cones around the area, letting folks know of the upcoming transitions and helping to guide them through the changes.
If we all just slow down, stay alert, exercise a little patience and understanding, and cooperate with the changes, knowing they're important and necessary, we'll all hopefully get through this weekend without incident.
The Broadway Bridge Project broke ground in 2023 and is scheduled to officially wrap up by the end of this year.

title: Analysis: UMaine men’s hockey puts on encouraging performance against national power Quinnipiac
text:
The University of Maine men’s hockey team didn’t play like a Hockey East seventh-place team over the weekend in its 2-1 loss and 5-3 victory over Quinnipiac University, which came into the weekend ranked sixth in the country and is now seventh in one poll and eighth in the other.
UMaine was chosen seventh in the Hockey East preseason coaches poll.
The Black Bears probably deserved a better fate.
They shouldn’t have lost Friday night. They found themselves trailing 2-1 after the first period despite outshooting Quinnipiac 18-5.
But that’s hockey.
Energized by the enthusiastic crowd, as they were all weekend, they wound up with a 34-22 edge in shots over the course of the game.
Quinnipiac protected its lead effectively, showing why the Bobcats have played in the last seven NCAA Tournaments, including an NCAA championship run in 2023, and why they have been the ECAC regular season titlists the last six years.
They have averaged 29 wins the past five seasons and are the preseason favorite to win the regular season title again.
Rand Pecknold’s Bobcats have a lot of offensive skill, but they also know how to play team defense.
Quinnipiac had scored 16 goals in its previous two games against New Hampshire (10-2) and defending Hockey East tournament champ Merrimack (6-3) and UMaine limited the Bobcats to few high-percentage scoring chances throughout the evening.
The Black Bears, now 2-2, didn’t generate the number of high-percentage chances they could have with their superior offensive zone time and puck possession, but scoring is going to be a work in progress throughout the season.
This team isn’t blessed with a number of natural goal-scorers as only three forwards have scored more than seven goals in a college season: left wingers Owen Fowler and Tanner Klimpke and center Max Scott.
But the Black Bears can compensate by getting to the net front, winning puck battles in the offensive zone and putting shots on net — and that’s what they did Saturday night. They do have depth up front and work tirelessly.
It is a fun team to watch with its aggression and physicality.
The Black Bears do a good job swarming the puck and limiting the opponents’ time and space with it. They do occasionally get exposed, as they did on Ethan Wyttenbach’s game-winning breakaway goal Friday night. But that’s bound to happen.
On Saturday, UMaine rallied from a 3-2 deficit after Quinnipiac had overcome a pair of one-goal deficits to take a lead.
After allowing two goals on eight shots in the first period, senior Albin Boija saved 14 of 15 the rest of the way, including a couple of gems to backstop the victory.
He looked like the Boija of two years ago when he was a second team All-American. And he had to be, because the team wasn’t as sharp defensively as it was on Friday night.
Boija squared himself to the shooters, was on his angles and tracked the puck efficiently.
He could minimize his movement because he was in a good position and controlled his rebounds better.
If UMaine is going to contend for an NCAA Tournament berth, that is the type of goaltending they will need from Boija or Canisius transfer Petter Wickstrom Stumer.
Boija had his struggles last year, but his Saturday performance should give him confidence.
He had 20 stops in the Friday night loss and couldn’t be faulted on either goal.
The defense corps was impressive both nights, and UMaine sixth-year head coach Ben Barr said it is the most mobile defense corps he has had at UMaine.
That is so important when it comes to breaking the puck out of the zone. They have the ability to skate the puck out on their own, and they are also able to recover quickly if they get caught out of position.
In addition, the forwards are committed to helping out on the defensive side.
The Black Bears blocked 34 shots over the two nights.
Sophomore Lukas Peterson and junior transfer Isa Parekh have a real offensive flair to their games and the other blueliners can also chip in.
Barr has said from day one he really enjoys coaching this team and the work ethic and culture have been exceptional.
“We’ve learned a lot about ourselves in the first four games. We’re a .500 team right now. There is a lot of season in front of us and nobody in that locker room wants to be just average,” Barr said.
For Bemidji State transfer Parekh, who scored the tying goal Saturday, and UMass Lowell transfer right wing Lee Parks, who notched the game-winner, their first games playing for the Black Bears at a packed and rowdy Alfond Arena were special.
Parks did play a Hockey East playoff game for UMass Lowell at Alfond Arena two years ago. UMaine won 7-1.
“Standing on the line for player introductions, I was going ‘Oh my God.’ I had never played in a building like this. It was ridiculous,” said Parekh, who was chosen the Hockey East Defender of the Week. “It was amazing to see how loud the crowd gets when we get a [scoring] chance or score a goal. To see how into they are is great.”
Veteran forwards Owen Fowler, Charlie Russell, Max Scott and Sully Scholle all played well and Barr said he needs them to continue to be productive on a regular basis.
Only two players on the 28-man roster have yet to play: forward Ross Campbell, who has had mononucleosis, and third-string goalie Colin Ronan.
Campbell is expected to be ready for the two-game home series against Colgate in two weekends.
Twelve players have registered at least a point, and Parks has a three-game goal-scoring streak.
“You can’t name a better power forward than him right now,” Parekh said.
Junior defenseman Chris Romaine, who had to be helped off the ice after suffering a head injury following a hit by Alex Kostov in the first period of Saturday’s game, is listed as day-to-day by Barr.

title: Maine’s September housing market broke the usual mold
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Each month, when Maine Listings and the Maine Association of Realtors release their reports on the state of the housing market, there are a few facts that can almost always be relied on: Cumberland County will be the most expensive county in Maine, and York County will be the second. A critical shortage of inventory will continue to squeeze buyers. Competition will be fierce, and houses will be snapped up quickly.
Last month, none of that was true.
Here are three takeaways from Maine’s September market.
1. High prices in unexpected places
Statewide, the median sale price was $415,000 last month, a 2.6% increase from September 2025, but a roughly 2% decrease from August’s median of $424,050, according to data from Maine Listings.
The modest year-over-year change belies massive price increases in several coastal counties.
In Lincoln and Knox counties, the median sale price skyrocketed more than $100,000 in just a year. In Hancock County, it might as well have, jumping $99,000.
Sagadahoc County also increased substantially, jumping from $490,000 to $577,500.
Those increases also shook up the longstanding rankings of Maine’s priciest counties.
Lincoln County was the most expensive in the state, with a median sale price of $606,500. It was followed by Cumberland County, with a median of $599,900.
Sagadahoc, Hancock and York counties rounded out the top five.
Six of the 16 counties had a median price of over half a million dollars.
Maine’s housing market is small, and in counties with fewer homes changing hands, it only takes a few high-ticket sales to skew the numbers.
For example, in Cumberland County, where year-over-year prices increased a little over 3%, there were 307 sales. In Knox County, where prices shot up 31%, there were 50.
In Islesboro, the lone September home sale clocked in at $3 million, making it the state’s most expensive municipality.
2. Late summer slowdown
Sales fell for the third consecutive month, despite buyers having more options than they’ve had since late 2019.
Real estate agents bought and sold 1,532 homes last month, a 1.4% decrease from the month before, according to Maine Listings.
Meanwhile, there were 6,505 homes on the market in September, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
Sales were also down year-over-year, with 4.5% fewer homes changing hands than in September 2025. And that’s with more than 1,000 more homes to choose from.
“Aside from the traditional slowdown from the summer months, increasing inflationary pressure and higher mortgage rates without a comparable downward adjustment in pricing have sidelined some buyers, especially first-time buyers with no equity from previous home purchases,” Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors, said in a news release.
Houses are also taking longer to sell, sitting on the market for an average of 21 days last month, compared to just 10 days in June, according to Maine Listings.
According to Lawrence Yun, chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, on a seasonally adjusted basis, August and September marked the two slowest months of the year for home sales nationwide.
Nationally, sales fell just shy of 2% year over year, while prices rose just over 1% to a median of $422,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Regionally, sales in the Northeast dropped 4% while the median sale price increased nearly 5% to $523,600.
3. Hard-to-swallow interest rates
In theory, more inventory and a slower pace of sales should mean more time and less competition for buyers, leaving more room for negotiations, said Oberg, who is also an associate broker at Oberg Insurance and Real Estate Agency in Bridgton.
But there’s one snag: Interest rates are the highest they’ve been in three years.
Interest rates were already elevated (6.71%) at the start of September. Then, two weeks later, the Federal Reserve increased its rate by a quarter of a point to curb inflation, and mortgage rates responded.
Last week, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage was 7.40%, according to mortgage buyer Freddie Mac. Rates haven’t been that high since November 2023.
A year ago, the average mortgage rate was 6.3%.
If someone bought a $415,000 home, put 20% down and secured that 6.3% rate, they could expect a monthly payment of about $2,833, not including any HOA fees, according to Fannie Mae, another mortgage buyer.
With the current interest rate of 7.4%, that monthly payment would increase to $3,076. That’s another $244 a month, or almost $3,000 a year.
“Increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home,” said Yun, at the national association.
The Federal Reserve is anticipating another rate hike at the end of the year.

title: Cautious optimism for job market outlook ahead of election
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. labor market appears to have stalled. Several recent months have seen negative job growth, and just 29,000 jobs were created last month.
The Bank of America Institute looked into their job data, and believes, despite poor top line numbers, there is reason for optimism.
“Our overall impression is things are not too bad. Now obviously we had a weak payrolls just last week, print from last week, but actually in our data, it’s consistent really with fairly decent employment growth overall,” said David Tinsley, Bank of America Institute senior economist.
The Bank of America Institute notes lower income household wages are starting to catch up to higher income household wages. Also, more people are switching jobs, with July showing the highest rate of job changes in more than three years.
“One of the things we also see in our data is that the raises people get when they switch has moved higher over the last year or so,” Tinsley said.
Economists believe there are many components leading to lower job creation, but the idea that AI is leading to mass layoffs is currently overblown.
“We just don’t see that yet. I mean the data is not playing out to back that up,” said Sean Murphy, with the Bipartisan Policy Center.
Murphy said one issue is that Americans don’t have the skillset for the kinds of skilled trade jobs that are in demand.
“And many of those are really good paying family wage type of jobs, but we just don’t necessarily have the workforce to fill them,” Murphy said.
Murphy believes Congress could improve the situation by supporting legislation that funds job training to set Americans up for success for the jobs of tomorrow.
“Really thinking about how do we get more strategic about how do we connect the talent to opportunity moving forward,” Murphy said.
The economy and employment have consistently topped polls of voters’ concerns.

title: Saco father detained by ICE at jetport on way to visit deaf son
text:
You have a registered email address and password on pressherald.com, but we are unable to locate a paid subscription attached to these credentials. Please verify your current subsription or subscribe.
Nguinamau Celestino’s wife dropped him off at the Portland jetport at 3 a.m. to catch an early flight to Washington, D.C. He was on his way to visit Abel, his youngest son, who had just begun his first semester at a high school for the deaf.
Nguinamau never arrived.
Celestino’s daughter, Margarida, 24, said her brother checked their father’s location on his phone after his flight was scheduled to land. He was at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Scarborough.
Margarida, a medical technician based in Auburn, woke at 6 a.m. to two missed calls from her dad, which she returned, but he didn’t pick up. She was on her way to work when her mom called; Margarida told her employer there was a family emergency and headed to Saco, where her parents live, to put the pieces together.
“Usually we see videos of people being taken, but unfortunately, everything with my dad was so silent,” she said. “Nobody said anything.”
The Celestino family — which includes Nguinamau, his wife Sukombo, their eldest Margarida and three sons, Lionel, 21, Nludi, 18, and Abel, 15 — are originally from Angola, later lived in Namibia and came to the U.S. in 2017 as asylum seekers. Their application is still ongoing. Only Margarida has a green card.
Advertisement
Early on Friday, Oct. 9, Margarida said her father walked into the airport and went straight to security. He saw ICE agents around, but didn’t have any reason to think they were there for him. But when he showed his ID to a TSA agent, she said, ICE agents looked at his picture, said they were there for Celestino, and detained him.
Immigration enforcement has been ramping up at airports nationwide, and local advocates said there were several detentions at the jetport in August, including of asylum seeker and registered nurse Debora Kapisha, who has since been released.
Margarida said her father has no criminal history, but agents told him he had overstayed his visa.
An ICE spokesperson confirmed Tuesday that Nguinamau was arrested during “targeted operations” last week, and said that he entered the country legally but violated the terms of his lawful admission and “remained in the U.S. illegally for nearly eight years.”
He was processed at the Scarborough facility, but by the time Margarida’s husband arrived at 9 a.m., Nguinamau had already been transferred out of the state. Margarida’s husband, a U.S. citizen, had come to bring Nguinamau a jacket, because she heard from another detained family member that the facility is chilly, and Nguinamau gets cold easily.
The agency’s online detainee locator showed Tuesday that Celestino is now being held at the Strafford County Corrections facility in Dover, New Hampshire.
Advertisement
Margarida said her father has been in touch every day via phone, and seems to be doing alright. The family organized a GoFundMe, which has raised nearly $30,000, and they’ve transferred some funds to him. He was able to keep his medications, but she said his work authorization card, Social Security card and Angolan ID were all missing from his wallet when they picked up his belongings.
Nguinamau works in plumbing and HVAC for Pine State Services, and got his associate’s degree at Southern Maine Community College. All of the Celestino children attended Portland Public Schools, including King Middle and Casco Bay High.
Their youngest sibling, Abel, received special services at East End Community School and played for the Baxter Seagulls, an ASL basketball team for students with the Maine Educational Center for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing.
“Our Deaf and Hard of Hearing community has always been strengthened by the connections we build, the families we support, and our willingness to stand together when someone is in need. This is a time to put those values into action,” center co-directors Steve Connolly and Catherine Lushman wrote in the post.
Connolly and Lushman said they were drafting letters to Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, asking them to intervene on behalf of the Celestino family.
For now, Margarida is worried about the impact Nguinamau’s detention will have on the rest of her family. Her mom has lupus and high blood pressure, and travels to Boston every three weeks for treatment, which she worries could be impacted by her husband’s detention.
Abel, who was awaiting his father’s visit in D.C., had to leave his school for the long weekend, and the family scrambled to find a friend in the city to look after him. The friend stepped up to the challenge, Margarida said, but it wasn’t the same as Abel spending the weekend with his father.
Riley covers education for the Press Herald. Before moving to Portland, she spent two years in Kenai, Alaska, reporting on local government, schools and natural resources for the public radio station KDLL...

title: Why There Have Been Less Humpty Chips on Store Shelves in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Why There Have Been Less Humpty Chips on Store Shelves in Maine
For just about 80 years, Humpty Dumpty potato chips have been part of Maine snack culture.
Most people who grow up in the state end up falling in love with at least one Humpty Dumpty flavor, from their version of BBQ or salt n' vinegar to more unique flavors like ketchup or all dressed.
But over the past few months, that snack staple has been more difficult to find on store shelves across the state of Maine.
And there's one specific reason why.
A Packaging Shortage is The Problem For Humpty Dumpty Chips in Maine
According to a social media post, one of the biggest reasons you may be seeing less Humpty Dumpty potato chips on store shelves revolves around their distinct bags.
There has been a packaging shortage from the supplier to Humpty Dumpty, leaving the chip company unable to deliver as much product to stores as they typically would.
That packaging shortage has primarily caused problems with the largest-sized Humpty Dumpty chip flavors as well as the smallest-sized snack bags.
Humpty Dumpty Expects to Return in Full to Maine Store Shelves Soon
There have been a lot of rumors swirling as to what the cause of the Humpty Dumpty shortage has been in Maine and whether or not the chip brand was being phased out.
The Humpty Dumpty chip brand is owned by Minnesota-based Old Dutch Foods which manufactures their potato chips in Canada. Some believed that the shortage on store shelves was caused by issues related to tariffs involving the United States and Canada.
That isn't the case. In fact, Humpty Dumpty chips should be returning to store shelves across Maine in near full stock before the end of the year.

title: Political candidates must value an effective and ethical justice system
text:
Jason Cherry, a Maine attorney with a practice focused on data privacy and criminal law, is a former special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. While at the FBI, he served as an assistant section chief for more than 430 employees and a budget of $150 million as well as a legal instructor.
I am interested in voting for a U.S. Senate candidate who understands the importance of an objective, professional and efficient U.S. Justice Department. Presidents from both political parties have shown overt favoritism to donors and other individuals in exchange for favors or to appease allies.
The Clinton administration was notorious for the 11th-hour pardon of 140 people, to include Marc Rich, a serial fraudster. On the other side, the Trump administration has granted over 1,900 pardons (and counting) across his terms in office.
The extensive list of pardons includes several fraudsters who have stolen hundreds of millions of dollars. These acts of “clemency” raise costs in healthcare, defense and other industries if the perpetrators of the fraud can expect to be freed by their political connections and influence. They fear no repercussions, so their behavior will continue onward.
In addition, these political indulgences send an extremely demoralizing message to everyone working diligently to establish an objective, professional and efficient justice system in their town, county, state and nation. Furthermore, the legitimacy of the entire justice system is at stake as these political indulgences send an alarming message to the public. Why should anyone obey the laws if they can get use their political influence to avoid any repercussions?
It is unclear why the U.S. Congress has not acted to restore legitimacy to the federal system of justice by restricting these apparent pay-to-pardon schemes. Perhaps, like many states, it is time to consider forming bipartisan clemency boards to prevent the executive branch from engaging in political indulgences.
As an FBI special agent, I took an oath to uphold the U.S. Constitution and to protect and serve the public. The acronym and motto of the FBI (Fidelity, Bravery and Integrity) used to mean only one thing — service and protection of my neighbors, my community, state and nation. Given the rampant rise in political indulgences, particularly the enabling of lawlessness in D.C., fidelity to whom? Bravery for whom? Integrity to whom and for what?
In his farewell address of Sept. 19, 1796, President George Washington described the importance of our justice system: “The due administration of justice is the firmest pillar of good government, I have considered the first arrangement of the judicial department as essential to the happiness of the country, and to the stability of its political system.”
The need for federal and state legislators to function as a true check and balance to restore legitimacy to our national justice system is long overdue. Instead, what is happening is a number of blank checks are being written in exchange for pardons galore.
I find it difficult to vote for a political party or politician who does not understand the importance of an objective, professional, efficient and ethical justice system, but merely stands aside or even enables the practice of unethical behaviors like these modern-day political indulgences.

title: Man accused of shooting at teens in homecoming prank says they drove toward him
text:
ADDIS, La. (WAFB/Gray News) — A man accused of firing a shot at high school students during a homecoming prank says he feared for his safety and did not know the people outside his home were teenagers.
Josiah Arrington was arrested and charged with aggravated assault with a firearm following the incident Tuesday night, Oct. 6, at the Riverboat Trailer Park in Addis.
According to the police chief, the teenagers were participating in homecoming festivities when they mistakenly went to Arrington’s home, believing it belonged to a friend.
The chief said Arrington came outside and yelled at the teenagers, who then tried to leave. As they were driving away, the chief said Arrington fired a shot that struck their vehicle.
No one was injured.
However, Arrington said there is more to what happened before he pulled the trigger.
Arrington says teens drove toward him
Arrington said he was preparing to step outside to smoke a cigarette and drink coffee when he encountered two or three people dressed in all black and wearing masks near his porch.
He said he had no idea who they were or why they were on his property.
“I just kept screaming, ‘What are you doing in my yard? What are you doing in my yard? What are you doing in my yard?’” Arrington said.
Arrington claims that as he approached the road, the individuals got into their vehicle and accelerated toward him, forcing him to jump out of the way.
“So as I met the road, they jumped into drive and sped towards me. I jumped to the side, and I fired one shot, expecting it to be a warning shot, not to injure anybody, not to hit the vehicle,” Arrington said.
Arrington acknowledged firing the shot but insisted he was not trying to strike the vehicle or hurt anyone. He said he did not realize the bullet had struck the car.
The police chief described the teenagers as trying to flee when Arrington fired. The chief did not mention a vehicle driving toward Arrington.
‘I didn’t know they were high school students’
Arrington repeatedly emphasized that he did not know the people outside his home were teenagers.
He said the darkness, their clothing, and the masks prevented him from identifying them.
“I didn’t know they was high school students, man. Please put it out there. I didn’t know that they were high school students, man. I wouldn’t hurt no kids,” Arrington said.
Arrington said his daughter recently graduated from high school and that he has young children in his life. He insisted he would never intentionally hurt children.
He also expressed regret over the incident and apologized to the teenagers and their families, acknowledging that the experience could have been traumatic for them.
“I’m sorry that happened to them because I know that could be traumatic to their life too. So I also want to apologize to them,” Arrington said.
Despite his explanation, Arrington was charged with aggravated assault with a firearm.
Police chief warns homecoming pranks are going too far
The shooting comes after police received several reports of homecoming pranks going too far in the area.
The police chief said what started as a tradition of students toilet-papering their friends’ homes has escalated in some cases to property damage.
He said students have worn masks and all black to disguise themselves, which he advises against. He said police have received reports of students throwing ketchup, mustard, and barbecue sauce on cars, garage doors, and concrete. Police have also received reports of paintball guns being used, leaving damage to homes.
The chief said he issued a warning Monday night, one day before the shooting, urging students to stop damaging property and encouraging parents to keep track of what their children are doing.
While he stressed that not all students participating in homecoming traditions are causing problems, he said some have taken things too far.
He also warned homeowners to understand the laws surrounding the use of firearms, emphasizing that people fleeing a property does not, by itself, justify shooting at them.
The chief said Tuesday’s incident could have ended much differently, adding that he is thankful no one was injured.
“And I beg that anybody that has kids or whatever, please don’t, you know, don’t fire a shot at kids or towards kids or anything like that, especially if they’re trying to just get away and run off,” the chief said.
The chief encouraged parents to know where their children are, what they are doing and to make sure homecoming traditions do not turn traumatic.

What was that light? SpaceX launch lights up skies across several states
text:
(Gray News) - A SpaceX rocket launch from Florida early Tuesday morning lit up the sky in several states including Georgia, Virginia and North Carolina.
A Falcon 9 rocket launched a robotic Dragon capsule at 6:33 a.m. from Florida’s Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.
Shortly after, the rocket could be seen in the sky in several states.
In McDonough, Georgia, Brent Tovar took a video of the SpaceX rocket, not knowing what it was at first.
“That’s pretty cool,” he said.
Sam Clay shared a photo taken in Richmond, Virginia.
In Florida, North Carolina and Georgia, several people reported seeing a “space jellyfish” as a result of the rocket leaving behind a trail of exhaust that expanded and spread out in the thin upper air. The phenomenon typically happens when a launch happens during early morning or evening twilight.
The rocket is delivering 6,300 pounds of supplies to the International Space Station.
After an approximate 52-hour flight, Dragon will autonomously dock with the orbiting laboratory on Thursday around 11:00 a.m.

title: Former officer identified as suspect in cold case murder
text:
CHICAGO (CNN) - Chicago police say they have solved the murder of an 8-year-old girl that happened more than 65 years ago, identifying a former Chicago police officer as the killer.
Authorities say Thomas F. McInerney Jr. murdered Gloria Kowalewicz shortly after joining the Chicago Police Department in 1959.
Kowalewicz was found shot to death in 1960 after she was abducted while walking to church.
Chicago police collected evidence at the time, including a fingerprint from the girl’s purse.
The murder remained unsolved until recently, when police say they used advanced DNA technology to identify the killer as McInerney.
McInerney retired from the department in 1987 as a violent crimes detective. He then moved to Las Vegas, Nevada, where he died in 2006 at the age of 70.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Mixed Precipitation Arrives Friday, Gusty Winds Follow Saturday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Tuesday. We’re dealing with a cold and unsettled stretch of weather across northern Maine, with rain and snow continuing tonight before showers gradually taper off during the day Wednesday. A brief break arrives Thursday, but it does not last long. Our next storm system arrives Friday, bringing widespread precipitation back to the region. Depending on the exact track of the system, some locations could see snow mix in with the rain before gusty northwest winds develop behind it Saturday.
Temperatures tonight will hover near the freezing mark across much of Aroostook County, with Presque Isle and Caribou both falling to around 32 degrees and Houlton closer to 31. Colder locations across western and northern Aroostook County could fall into the upper 20s.
Rain will continue through the overnight hours, but with temperatures this close to freezing, some snow will continue to mix in, especially across northern and western portions of the region. Around an inch of snow accumulation is possible across parts of northwestern Aroostook County, while amounts farther east should remain lighter.
Rain continues into Wednesday morning before gradually becoming more scattered during the afternoon. Temperatures remain chilly, with highs only reaching the upper 40s across much of northern Aroostook County, including around 48 degrees in Caribou and 50 degrees in Presque Isle. Houlton looks to reach the lower 50s.
As the system exits, winds turn northwesterly and begin to increase Wednesday night, setting us up for a breezy but drier Thursday.
Thursday will provide a brief break between storm systems, with sunshine returning across the region. The tradeoff will be gusty northwest winds, especially during the morning and midday hours. The latest computer model guidance shows gusts generally reaching around 25 to 35 mph across Aroostook County, with localized gusts closer to 40 mph possible in spots.
Temperatures will remain chilly as well, with highs generally only reaching the mid to upper 40s. Winds gradually ease later Thursday, with quieter conditions expected Thursday night before our next system arrives Friday.
That next storm system will bring widespread precipitation back into northern Maine Friday. The exact track remains important, as a farther-south track would allow more cold air to remain in place and increase the potential for snow, while a farther-north track would favor more rain.
Current forecasts support a rain and snow mix across northern Aroostook County Friday, with rain becoming more dominant farther south. Precipitation continues Friday night, with snow becoming increasingly possible again as colder air wraps into the system.
Friday remains a First Alert Weather Day because of the potential for mixed precipitation and travel impacts, with gustier northwest winds then becoming a concern behind the system Saturday.
The wind becomes another concern behind the system. Northwest winds are expected to strengthen as the storm pulls away, with gusts potentially reaching around 30 to 40 mph across parts of northern Maine. That could result in a few isolated power outages and additional tree or limb damage, especially if any wet snow accumulation occurs before the stronger winds arrive.
Saturday looks much colder as well, with highs only reaching the mid to upper 30s across much of northern Aroostook County. Any lingering snow or rain showers should gradually taper off through the morning before drier conditions return later in the weekend.
For more details on tonight’s rain and snow, the brief break Thursday and our next First Alert Weather Day on Friday, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

Caregivers for older Mainers are facing mounting challenges
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Marvella Heard has faced more challenges than most in caring for her aging father.
She spent over a year back in her hometown in New York, after she discovered her father was living in squalor, his health was deteriorating, his meager finances were in jeopardy and his house was in foreclosure, she said.
A Navy veteran and retired federal prison employee, she stepped in and wrangled repeatedly with family members, government officials and social service agencies — even after she became her father’s legal guardian, she said.
“He was living in filth when I got there,” said Heard, 56, of Biddeford. “He had no food, no clean clothes. He didn’t recognize me at first.”
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
Now 79, Samuel Heard has since been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and heart disease, and the retired hospital worker has mobility issues that require him to use a walker, his daughter said.
Despite many setbacks, Heard said she managed to navigate unfamiliar caregiver territory by being resourceful, searching the internet for solutions and being tenacious when she ran into roadblocks. She still struggles to reconcile how hard it was to help her father.
“I was treated awfully — the system didn’t support me at all,” Heard said. “We had confrontations again and again, and I just wanted to take care of my dad.”
Finally, last December, Heard was able to move her father to her home in Biddeford, where they’ve settled into a routine of medical appointments, grocery shopping, barber shop visits and adult daycare programs.
THE ROLE TAKES A TOLL
While Heard’s experience was severe, a growing number of Mainers are facing challenges as caregivers for aging and disabled loved ones. They’re providing assistance with all aspects of daily living, including meals, medications, bathing, dressing, toileting, transportation and advocacy at medical appointments and in long-term care.
Most of that help goes unpaid and can take a significant toll on other areas of their lives, consuming free time and affecting job performance. The role reversal of caring for once-vital adults can be emotionally devastating, and managing their complicated medical needs and finances can be overwhelming. Some caregivers also support their loved ones financially — Heard figures she has spent about $3,000 on her father’s behalf.
She and others in the thick of it have learned the benefits of planning ahead, becoming expert problem solvers and seeking support from other caregivers. They don’t have to look far.
In 2025, an estimated 310,000 Mainers provided the full-time equivalent of 220 million hours of unpaid care for aging or disabled adult family members valued at $5.5 billion, according to AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. That value of that care more than doubled in the past decade, up from $2.2 billion provided by 178,000 Mainers in 2015.
The same is true nationwide, where the value of adult family caregiving also has more than doubled, from $470 billion to $1 trillion in the same period, and the number of caregivers increased 22.5%, from 40 million to 59 million, according to Caregiving in the US 2025, the latest report from AARP and NAC.
The exponential increase has solidified family caregivers as an invaluable contingent in the wider landscape of long-term care, AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said. It doesn’t matter if the help is provided to loved ones at home, in assisted living or at a skilled nursing facility.
“The long-term care system would crumble without those family caregivers,” Bonam said. “Whether what they do is big or small, without caregivers spending hours and personal resources while juggling other responsibilities, the system would collapse.”
CAREGIVING IN THE OLDEST STATE
As the oldest state, Maine is on the leading edge of this trend — nearly one-quarter of 1.4 million residents are age 65 and up. At the same time, it has a shortage of 2,300 workers to care for older Mainers as they age, according to the progressive Maine Center for Economic Policy.
Yet the important role that family caregivers play in filling the gap is critically undervalued, advocates say, especially when at least 60% of caregivers are juggling jobs outside the home and nearly 30% are part of the so-called sandwich generation, caring for both an adult and children.
“The federal and state funding and services available right now don’t cover the tip of the iceberg,” Bonam said.
Some MaineCare recipients may receive funding to pay a family member to provide care, but it comes with significant restrictions. The State Respite Care Program provides funding so family caregivers of dementia patients can hire occasional help, but there’s often a waiting list.
The new Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave program may be providing some relief — 11.6% of 4,720 claims approved in the first three months, April through June, were to care for family members with serious health conditions, according to the Maine Department of Labor.
Some advocates are pushing for a non-refundable federal tax credit up to $5,000 for eligible working family caregivers to cover 30% of qualified expenses. However, this proposal also comes with restrictions and would cover only a small portion of care provided. In Maine, that care is valued at $25 per hour or about $52,000 annually based on a 40-hour work week, according to AARP.
Although family caregiver funding is widely recognized as lacking, advocates say it’s not showing up as a legislative priority despite dire predictions that the need will only intensify.
“There’s been a tremendous increase over the past 10 years and that’s just going to continue,” said Amanda Rector, state economist. “We have more people not only over 65, but also over 75. That’s a larger older population that will need more care from a smaller younger population that’s still working.”
The issue may draw more attention as more families and employers experience the impact of caregiving on daily living, especially in a labor market with a worker shortage, Rector said.
“If (a caregiver is) a really valuable worker, they may not be working at their best,” she said. “You may want to provide support to relieve their mental and financial stress so they don’t leave.”
REACHING OUT FOR HELP
Jim Vollmar started showing signs of vascular dementia nearly a decade ago, when the former build contractor and his wife, Clare Herrmann, were living in Georgia.
“He started not remembering things he should have remembered, like my birthday or what we did last week,” said Herrmann, who, like her husband, is now 78.
Initially, Herrmann cared for him on her own, reluctant to even ask friends for help. But the difficulty mounted as his disease progressed, so she decided to accept her daughter’s invitation to come live with her family in Portland.
As Herrmann prepared to move north, the retired office manager reached out to the Southern Maine Agency on Aging for guidance on what services and programs would be available to them, including peer support groups she still attends.
After the couple moved to Portland in 2024 — into an accessory dwelling unit they had built at her daughter’s house — Herrmann was relieved to have backup assistance from her daughter, son-in-law and grandchild. Still, she was overwhelmed by round-the-clock responsibilities.
Again, she reached out to SMAA, who helped her secure respite care for her husband so she could have a few hours off each week. One of the first things she did was take a meditation course.
“I wanted to learn how to chill,” Herrmann said. “I was so hyperaware of everything, I never really slept because I didn’t want him to fall and I didn’t want him to leave the house. He never did, but I worried about it.”
Herrmann reached out to SMAA again last spring, after her husband broke his left femur in a fall and it became clear he needed to be in a memory care facility. The agency helped her find Fallbrook Woods in Portland, where he lives now.
“They have been so supportive,” Herrmann said of SMAA. “Whenever I call, they always know who to refer me to. I can’t even enumerate all they ways they have helped me.”
REBRANDING WITH CAREGIVERS IN MIND
SMAA this month changed its name to AgeMaine and launched a new website, support network and membership program to better serve family caregivers.
“We want to create one place where family caregivers can find trusted information and training, connect with other caregivers, and get help figuring out what resources and services are available,” CEO Megan Walton said.
AgeMaine.org/Caregiver, a caregiver-focused page that goes live Oct. 16, will start as an online resource hub for information and support, then expand to provide individualized guidance for family caregivers and help employers support workers who are caring for an aging adult. The agency will eventually offer a paid membership option, but the cost and structure have yet to be established, Walton said.
“We want more caregivers sharing their experiences and letting legislators know what they’re going through,” Walton said. “Peer support especially is so important. It can be so valuable to hear that other people are going through the same thing.”
The goal is to help caregivers like Marvella Heard find the support they need. While her father, Samuel, regularly attends adult daycare programs at the Samuel L. Cohen Center in Biddeford, which is an AgeMaine facility, she said she has yet to participate in caregiver support groups and other programs.
She admits that she should.
“I’m burned out because nobody is taking care of me,” Heard said. “Everybody needs a break sometimes, and I need a break, like, yesterday.”

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in York
text:
York voters will decide on a handful of local issues on Election Day, including a $500,000 ambulance funding question, a ban on Flock cameras and on single-use plastics.
In-person voting will take place on Nov. 3 at York High School from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Absentee voters should request their ballots by Oct. 29, and early voters can hand their ballots in at the town clerk’s office anytime before that date.
Here’s what residents will be considering.
SINGLE-USE PLASTIC BAN
In May 2025, York became the first Maine town to ban single-use plastics when a group of high schoolers proposed an ordinance in an effort to reduce waste.
Over a year in, voters now have the opportunity to make the ban — which applies to stir sticks, straws and utensils — permanent by getting rid of a sunset clause. If that clause stays in place, it would effectively end the entire ordinance on Dec. 31.
Town officials told the Press Herald in September that they were initially hesitant to make the ban permanent because earth-friendly materials usually cost more and they weren’t sure if local businesses could afford the change.
But several restaurant owners and workers have said they’d support a permanent ban, and that they’ve managed to find affordable alternatives.
The York Select Board unanimously recommends that voters lift the sunset clause.
EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT AMENDMENT
Voters will decide whether state and federal disaster relief funds should become a part of the town’s emergency management ordinance.
Right now, emergency assistance funds, including federal reimbursements for public infrastructure repairs like the Cliff Walk restoration, are treated independently.
Voting “yes” on the article wouldn’t change how assistance funds are used — it would just organize them under the emergency management ordinance umbrella.
A new line would be added to the financial authority section of the ordinance, mandating that town officials can vote and use assistance funds so long as the amount doesn’t exceed available state or federal dollars awarded to the town.
The Select Board unanimously recommends passing the article.
REVENUE BOND QUESTION
Voters will weigh in on an ordinance, submitted by citizen petition, titled “Revenue-Bond Preference for Self-Sustaining Capital Projects.”
In short, the ordinance aims to avoid using property tax-backed general obligation bonds for capital projects deemed to be wants, not needs. It defines “needs” as projects that are essential in maintaining safety, legal compliance and other core municipal functions, whereas “wants” are projects that would enhance quality of life but are not essential.
Any project under consideration would have to undergo a feasibility assessment to determine revenue, operating expenses and other criteria outlined in the ordinance.
If passed, the ordinance would allow the Select Board to continue to use general obligation bonds to fund “needs” projects.
For projects that are “wants,” though, the type of bond would be determined by the feasibility assessment. If the assessment determines that the project would generate a certain level of revenue, then it could only be funded by revenue bonds. If not, the project would require majority approval by the town Budget Committee, which would have to explain its decision.
The Select Board unanimously opposes this proposal.
‘STOP ALPRs’ ORDINANCE
Amid a nationwide debate over Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers, York voters will have the opportunity to immediately implement a new ordinance banning the technology in town.
The ordinance, which was proposed through an August citizen petition called “Stop ALPRs,” gained the support of 115 residents. Some said at a public hearing that the cameras violated their Fourth Amendment rights.
On Sept. 14, York police Chief Owen Davis told the Select Board that all such cameras in town — including four on public property — were being immediately removed, and that the department’s contract with Flock would be terminated. Two cameras located on private property but operated by law enforcement were also removed.
Four Select Board members recommended passage, while Vice Chair Marla Johnson voted against it, saying the ordinance as written could ban technology other than surveillance cameras that law enforcement has found beneficial.
YORK AMBULANCE FUNDING
In July, York Ambulance Association told the Select Board it needed an additional $180,000 to sustain it through the end of its contract with the town next summer. By August, the independent EMS service’s shortfall grew to $350,000, triggering a special budget referendum.
If approved, the town will allocate a total of $500,000 to the service. That includes $150,000 the town already committed to the service in a May vote as its annual contribution. The town would then pay the service $300,000 from its unassigned fund balance, with the rest to be paid in installments so long as York Ambulance can meet a set of conditions each month.
The Select Board has repeatedly expressed frustration with the ambulance nonprofit over a lack of transparency and communication, saying the funding issue could’ve been mitigated had it been raised earlier. Members have also questioned the service’s long-term financial stability.
Voting “no” would create a gap in essential emergency services, as York Ambulance would likely run through its available cash by the end of November.
Regardless of the outcome of the vote, the Select Board intends to consider alternatives to extending its contract with the company, like building an in-house EMS service. The select board voted 5-0 to recommend passage, while the Budget Committee voted 5-2.
WIRELESS COMMNUICATIONS FACILITIES ORDINANCE
Voters will consider an amendment to the town’s existing wireless communications facilities ordinance that would clarify the requirements for mounting antennae and define certain structures.
If approved, the ordinance would no longer include “water towers, utility poles and towers, light poles or light stanchions” in the location requirements for WCFs. Instead, those locations would be simplified to “utility structures.”
The amendment would add definitions under the “support structure” section of the ordinance for residential structures and utility structures while removing a definition for “existing nonresidential structure.”
Any structure containing a legal dwelling unit, per the town’s zoning ordinance, would constitute a residential structure. A utility structure is one that supports electric transmission, like telephone poles, or other essential utilities like water towers.
The Select Board recommends passage 4-1.
COUNTY ELECTIONS
Voters will also weigh in on the York County sheriff race, choosing between Democratic incumbent William King and Republican challenger David Corbett.
A third candidate, independent Brian Pellerin, dropped out of the race in September and took on a position as Wells’ police chief. His name will still appear on the ballot because of the timing of his departure from the race.
Another ballot item will ask voters countywide whether they support eliminating an elected treasurer position, which some officials say is purely a ceremonial role.
The sole candidate for the position, Bobby Mills, is seeking a nonconsecutive term and thinks keeping the position could save voters some money, because then a similar but more expensive role on the Budget Committee could be eliminated instead.
If county residents decide to eliminate the elected treasurer position, the role would become one that is appointed internally by county officials.
STATE RACES
York voters will also choose a District 35 state senator. Democratic incumbent Rep. Michele Meyer is facing Republican Julie Rakic.
Voters in House District 146 — covering western York, as well as part of Wells and all of Ogunquit — will choose a state representative. Democratic incumbent Gerry Runte Jr., currently serving his second term, is facing former District 149 Rep. Bradley Moulton, a Republican.
In House District 147, covering coastal areas of York, Democratic incumbent Holly Sargent is seeking reelection unopposed.

title: Man arrested after Newry hit-and-run crash
text:
NEWRY, Maine (WABI) - A man was arrested after a hit-and-run crash involving a motorcycle in Newry.
Henry Clark, 23, of Kittery Point, was taken into custody, according to the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office.
The crash happened at the intersection of Mayville and Bear River Roads just before 4 p.m. Saturday.
Clark was passing a truck parked on the side of the road when he hit a motorcycle driven by Donald Dyer, 67, of Standish. Dyer was turning onto the road as Clark was passing, authorities said.
Dyer was thrown from the motorcycle. Officials said was taken to the hospital with significant injuries.
Clark was arrested shortly after the crash as authorities found his vehicle parked at a gas station.
He is facing charges of reckless conduct, driving to endanger, OUI, and assault with a dangerous weapon.

title: ‘Unimaginable grief’: 5 dead, 3 injured after crash involving police car, officials say
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) - Five people were killed in a crash involving a Memphis police car, according to authorities
A total of five people were killed early Sunday when their vehicle collided with a Memphis police car at Hickory Hill and East Raines roads.
The vehicle carried six people; however, the sixth person remains in the hospital in critical condition.
Officials identified four of the five victims as 20-year-old Rodney McNeal, 21-year-old Syria Fifer, 20-year-old Messiah Lee and 19-year-old Carlesha Fifer.
A makeshift memorial was created Monday at the crash site.
Memphis Mayor Paul Young released a statement Monday morning: “Five young people lost their lives last night, and their families, along with the families of others involved, are facing unimaginable grief today. My deepest prayers go out to everyone affected by this tragedy. I ask Memphis to keep these families in our thoughts as they face the difficult days ahead.”
The family of Syria Fifer has set up a GoFundMe to help with expenses.
Two Memphis police officers were also injured and have since been released from the hospital.

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Announces Home Video Release
text:
‘The Odyssey’ Announces Home Video Release — Including a $300 Steelbook
The details are officially out for the home video release of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey. The 4K and Blu-ray will be available on November 17 (“months before [the film is] available on subscription streaming services” the press release declares) and will include more than 90 minutes of bonus features about the making of the film, including featurettes about the film’s Trojan horse, shooting on location, the score, the special effects, and more.
But that’s not really news; pretty much every blockbuster gets a 4K and Blu-ray release. The news is the fact that the film is not only getting a steelbook release — it’s getting a “Limited Edition 4K Ultra HD Premium Giftset” steelbook that will set you back $300.
$300 bones for one movie? $300 bones for one movie.
Of course, it comes with a bunch of extras besides the movie. It includes the book Filming the Odyssey, which normally retails for $75 all by itself, with a different cover the standard release, plus a 70mm film cell, and a certificate of authenticity. The steelbook itself inside this premium set also features different box art than the standard steelbook, which retails for $39.99.
READ MORE: DVDs That Are Still Worth a Ton of Money
Limited-edition steelbooks have become sought after collectibles among some physical media die-hards, with exclusive and hard-to-find discs selling for big bucks on the secondary market.
Christopher Nolan’s version of The Odyssey is the second-biggest film of 2026 to date, with over $1.78 billion in worldwide grosses. The movie stars Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, and many more. It looks to be a major player during the pending awards season as well.
Amazon currently has the Limited Edition 4K Ultra HD Premium Giftset of The Odyssey up for pre-order for $299.99. Do you think it’s going to sell out? Would you spend $300 for a 4K steelbook? If not, what’s the most you would spend for a steelbook? Actually: If you would spend $300 on a steelbook, what’s the most you would spend for a steelbook? I want to know where we’re going to find the ceiling of this nascent steelbook market.

title: Formula 1 announces return of African Grand Prix in Rwanda in early 2030s
text:
Formula 1 announces return to Africa with grand prix in Rwanda in early 2030s
Formula 1 announced on Tuesday that Rwanda will host a race from "the early 2030s" when the series returns to Africa after about 40 years.
Related video above: IndyCar Freedom 250 races through DC in historic first
The African Grand Prix will have a 10-year contract and take place at a track in Bugesera, southeast of the capital Kigali. F1 said the purpose-built track will be ready "early in the next decade."
Rwandan President Paul Kagame said at a launch event in Kigali that it was "a success and a milestone for the entire continent, especially for the African fans," adding he hoped it could lead to more F1 events in Africa.
Racing in Africa will fulfill a long-held ambition for seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, the only Black driver in F1. The 41-year-old British driver has said he has been "fighting in the background" for years to have a race in Africa.
"I've always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa," Hamilton recently said. "It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, and the most beautiful continent. We're on all the other continents but that one, and there should be no reason for it."
The last time F1 raced in Africa was the South African Grand Prix in 1993.
"Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1," F1 President and chief executive Stefano Domenicali said. "With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.
"Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."

title: Kroger to lay off 3,000 employees as it leans into artificial intelligence
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) - Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.
“Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.”
Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.”
Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer.
Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO.
Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities.
Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells.
Kroger has also felt pressure from fast-growing discount chains like Aldi and Lidl and online behemoths like Amazon.
Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed.
A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value.
Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee.
Albertsons is facing the same competitive headwinds as Kroger and other grocery chains as customers turn to cheaper alternatives and faster delivery from bigger retailers.
On Tuesday during its second-quarter earnings conference call with investors, CEO Susan Morris alluded to further cost-cutting and streamlining of the company’s structure, including layoffs.
“We did some work last year and saw a substantial reduction in headcount, but quite frankly, there’s more to be had,” Morris said. ”And you’ll see us taking aggressive action there in the next 12 to 18 months as well.”
Kroger shares fell 2.2% in afternoon trading Tuesday, to $61.21. Albertsons rose 2.8% but its shares are down more than 25% this year.

title: Proposed livestreamed execution raises concerns
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The first livestreamed execution in American history has forced the country to ask itself an uncomfortable question: is this who we are?
Nidal Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad December 3 at Fort Hood. Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in a 2009 mass shooting at the Texas Army base. It would be the first military execution since 1945, and the first public execution since 1937.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the unprecedented decision October 7 during an interview with the conservative broadcast outlet Real America’s Voice. President Donald Trump doubled down and backed Hegseth’s decision late last week.
“Exposure to graphic images of that kind of violence is not good for you,” said Alison Holman, a psychology professor at UC Irvine who specializes in collective trauma.
Her research has shown that witnessing graphic violence can cause post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms.
“Our team has had young people reaching out from across the country saying they’ve seen these acts of horrific violence,” Holman said about her research into the long-term impacts of witnessing trauma. “I’m not saying that it will cause PTSD, but… it is definitely associated with PTSD symptoms that are distressing and can increase a person’s sense of worry about the future and can disrupt their ability to function.”
Many Republicans quickly shared concern about what a state-sanctioned live execution would do to America’s collective humanity.
“Seneca warned that Rome’s bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) wrote on X. “The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”
Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.), who is a veteran running for re-election in a swing district, shared similar concerns.
“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X last week. “The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”
Across the world, Pope Leo reiterated his opposition to the death penalty as a whole. Pietro Parolin, the Vatican Secretary of State, said in part, “It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle.”
Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, stopped short of opposing the livestream, but said he wouldn’t watch. Holman urges people not to watch, but knows that is difficult in this technological age.
“You could open up a social media account and a video would start on its own, by itself, auto-start, and you could see something before you really had a chance to turn it off,” Holman explained.
Holman said a public execution goes against current American culture, but is painfully reminiscent of a darker time, when lynchings of mostly Black people took place, particularly in the South.
“[A lynching] was considered something that they should all go and watch,” said Holman. “So I guess in some ways, the live streaming of this really isn’t totally counter to our culture, but it’s bringing back a part of our culture that we had put behind us.”
The Federal Bureau of Prisons bans the recording and broadcasting of executions, but Hasan’s case is through military courts, which have a whole other set of governing rules.
A public or video-distributed execution, by any method, is exceptionally rare in the 21st century. Recent examples include Iran, Somalia and videos of beheadings from the Taliban and ISIS.
Shortly after Hegseth posted on X confirming his decision, Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.) quoted it to add his concern.
“I absolutely support the sentence of death,” Scott started. “But live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Some, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, have shared concerns a video of executions — particularly an ideological extremist like Hasan — would serve as a recruitment tool for America’s adversaries.
Legal proceedings could delay the execution, which is common in death penalty cases. If Hasan faces the firing squad in December, it is unclear what a livestream would logistically look like and if any media outlet or digital platform would be willing to share any part of it.
When asked about the possible livestream as he departed for Alaska, President Trump would only confirm “they’re looking at it.”
